Interview Guide — Introduction · Project Discussion · Scenario Questions

how to introduce yourself · architecture walkthrough · request flow · scenario-based answers · what interviewers actually test
🌟 Section 1 — Tell Me About Yourself
Your introduction decides the direction of the interview. Mention only skills and projects you are confident discussing in depth. A 90-second structured introduction: (1) Current role + years of experience. (2) The ONE project you want to discuss. (3) The specific technology decision you are proud of. (4) What you are looking for next. Then stop — do not list every technology you have ever touched.
  • Formula: Role + Project + Tech Decision + Goal"I am a backend engineer with 4 years of experience at XYZ, where I built the order management service handling 500K daily transactions using Spring Boot and Kafka. I introduced the Outbox pattern to solve a data consistency issue between our payment and inventory services — that is the project I am most proud of. I am looking for a role where I can work on distributed systems at larger scale."
  • What NOT to say: Listing 15 technologies (you will be asked about each). Vague statements ("I worked on various backend services"). Your life story. More than 2 minutes.
  • Control the direction: Interviewers follow up on what you mention. If you say "Kafka", expect Kafka questions. If you are not confident about Kubernetes, do not mention it. Your introduction is a menu — serve only what you can cook.
    • 🏭 Section 2 — Project Discussion (the longest part) — covering architecture, request flow (QPS and back-of-envelope estimation are expected), security, and deployment
    Be ready to explain your project from 6 angles. Interviewers hop between these angles based on their interest. Prepare a 2-minute architecture overview, then short answers for each angle.
  • Architecture: Draw/describe the components. "We have a React frontend, Spring Boot API layer, PostgreSQL for transactional data, Redis for caching, and Kafka for async event processing between services." Know the reason for each choice.Q: "Why Kafka and not a direct REST call?" A: "The inventory update is async and can tolerate a few seconds of delay. Kafka decouples the services — if inventory service is down, the event is queued and retried automatically."
  • Request Flow: Trace one request end-to-end. "User places order → POST /orders hits API Gateway → JWT validated → OrderService creates order in DB → publishes OrderPlaced event to Kafka → InventoryService consumes event → deducts stock → publishes InventoryUpdated → OrderService marks order CONFIRMED."
  • Security: How is authentication/authorization handled? "JWTs issued on login, verified by a filter in each service. Role-based access: ADMIN can see all orders, USER can only see their own."
  • Database Design: Key tables, relationships, indexes. "Three core tables: orders (id, customer_id, status, created_at), order_items (order_id, product_id, qty, price), customers. Index on orders(customer_id, status) for the most frequent query."
  • Deployment: "Dockerized services, GitHub Actions CI/CD pipeline builds and pushes images to ECR, Kubernetes deployments with readiness probes and horizontal pod autoscaling."
  • Challenges Solved: Prepare ONE specific technical challenge. The format: Problem → Why it was hard → What you tried first → What actually worked → What you learned. Avoid vague answers like "we had performance issues" — say exactly what the bottleneck was and how you measured it.
    • 📌 Section 3 — Scenario-Based Questions
    Interviewers test understanding, not definitions. They want to see how you think through a real problem, not hear you recite a textbook answer. Use this structure for every scenario: (1) Understand and clarify the constraint. (2) Identify the root cause or bottleneck. (3) Propose layered solutions (quick win → proper fix). (4) State the trade-offs.
    Scenario answers — production thinking framework
    // Q1: "How would you optimize a slow API?" (never say 'add caching' immediately) // Step 1 — Measure first: "What is the p99 latency? Is it slow for all users or specific ones?" // Step 2 — Identify layer: "Is it slow in the DB, in the service, or in the network?" // - DB slow? -> EXPLAIN ANALYZE, add index, fix N+1, paginate large results // - Service slow? -> Profile with async-profiler, check thread contention, look for blocking I/O // - Network? -> Check payload size, add compression (gzip), move computation closer to user (CDN) // Step 3 — Fix: "If N+1 is the issue: add JOIN FETCH. If repetitive DB calls: add Redis cache." // Step 4 — Validate: "After fix, compare p99 before/after. Set up a performance test." // Q2: "How do you handle concurrent requests updating the same data?" // "First clarify: how often does this happen and what is the consequence of a race condition?" // Low conflict (most reads, rare writes) -> Optimistic locking (@Version) — no lock overhead // High conflict (many concurrent writes to same row) -> Pessimistic locking (SELECT FOR UPDATE) // Cross-service conflict -> Distributed lock (Redis SETNX) or DB-level atomic UPDATE WHERE version=? // Payment/financial -> Always DB atomic: UPDATE accounts SET bal=bal-? WHERE id=? AND bal>=? // Q3: "How would you debug a production issue?" // 1. Don't panic. Check metrics first: CPU, memory, error rate, latency (Grafana/Datadog) // 2. Check logs: structured logs with trace_id, filter by error level (ELK / CloudWatch) // 3. Check recent deployments: "Did we deploy in the last 2 hours?" -> rollback if yes // 4. Thread dump if threads are stuck: jstack or /actuator/threaddump // 5. Heap dump if OOM: jmap -dump:format=b,file=heap.hprof -> Eclipse MAT // 6. Isolate: reproduce in staging with same traffic pattern // 7. Fix, deploy, monitor. Write incident report. // Q4: "What happens if one microservice goes down?" // Depends on the dependency type: // Synchronous dependency -> Circuit Breaker (Resilience4j): open after failures, return fallback // Async dependency -> Kafka: producer continues publishing, consumer retries when service recovers // Critical dependency -> Bulkhead: isolate thread pool so other services are unaffected // Shared DB dependency -> Read replicas: reads continue even if primary is slow // User-facing -> Graceful degradation: return cached/partial response instead of 500
    🏭 Practice Scenario — Put It All Together
    An interviewer says: "Tell me about a challenging technical problem you solved in your last project." You have 3 minutes. How do you structure this answer to demonstrate SDE-2 level thinking?
    The interviewer wants to see: problem identification, debugging approach, multiple solutions considered, trade-off reasoning, and measurable outcome. Not just "we had a bug and fixed it".
    STAR + Trade-offs format: Situation: "Our order service was causing duplicate payments — roughly 0.1% of orders were charged twice. This is a critical bug in a financial system." Task: "I needed to identify why duplicates were occurring, fix it without downtime, and ensure it could never happen again." Action: "First I added structured logging with a correlation ID to trace each payment request. I found the issue: our mobile clients retry on network timeout, and our payment endpoint was not idempotent. The same request could succeed twice if the first response was lost in transit. I implemented idempotency keys: the client generates a UUID per payment intent, the server stores the result keyed by this UUID with a UNIQUE DB constraint. A retry with the same key returns the stored result without reprocessing." Result: "Zero duplicate payments in the 3 months since deployment. The solution also improved our incident response — each payment now has a traceable idempotency key in logs." Trade-off you considered: "I considered using a distributed lock (Redis SETNX) instead, but the DB unique constraint is simpler, more durable, and does not require additional infrastructure."
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: Interviewer asks "Why do you want to leave your current company?" How do you answer without damaging your candidacy?
    💡 Think First
    Never speak negatively about your current employer. Frame everything as what you are moving TOWARD, not what you are running FROM. What genuinely motivates you about the new role?
    ➔ Complete Answer
    Good answers are forward-looking and specific: "I have learned a lot about [specific domain] but I want to work on [larger scale / different domain / a specific technology]. This role seems like a great fit because [specific reason about this company]." Avoid: "My manager is terrible", "the company is sinking", "I am underpaid" — even if true. Interviewers remember negative candidates. If you were laid off: be direct and brief. "The company did a round of layoffs that affected my team. I took some time to reflect on what I want next and I am excited about this opportunity because..."
    Q: "Do you have any questions for us?" — what should an SDE-2 candidate ask?
    💡 Think First
    This is an opportunity, not a formality. Asking about ping-pong tables is bad. Asking about engineering practices, on-call, technical debt, or team structure signals seriousness.
    ➔ Complete Answer
    Strong questions: "What does the on-call rotation look like and how is incident response handled?" (reveals operational maturity). "What is the biggest technical challenge the team is currently facing?" (reveals real work, not the interview-polished version). "How does the team approach technical debt — is there dedicated time for refactoring?" (reveals engineering culture). "What does the first 90 days look like for someone joining this team?" (shows you are thinking about impact). "How are architectural decisions made — is it top-down or does the team have autonomy?" (reveals decision-making culture). Avoid: "What is the salary?" (save for HR), "How soon can I get promoted?" (too early), "What does the company do?" (you should know this already).
    🎯 Practice Task
    Write your own 90-second "Tell me about yourself" using the formula: Role + ONE project + specific tech decision + what you want next. Then prepare a 3-minute project walkthrough covering: (1) architecture in one sentence, (2) request flow for the most important endpoint, (3) one security decision, (4) one database decision, (5) one challenge you solved. Practice saying it out loud — not just writing it.
    💡 HintThe most common mistake: mentioning 10 technologies in 90 seconds. Pick ONE project, go deep. Interviewers respect depth over breadth. Every technology you mention is an invitation to be asked about it. Only invite topics you are confident with.
    ➡ Template — fill in your details
    Interview — 90-second introduction template
    // 90-second introduction template "I am a [role] with [N] years of experience, currently at [Company]. My most significant project has been [ONE project name] — [one sentence: what it does and scale]. I was responsible for [your specific contribution]. One decision I am particularly proud of: [specific tech decision + WHY]. For example: 'We switched from polling to WebSocket push for order status updates, which reduced latency from 30 seconds to under 2 seconds and cut our server load by 40%.' I am looking for a role where [specific: larger scale / specific domain / specific tech]. I am excited about this position because [specific reason about THIS company/role]." // Project walkthrough template (3 minutes) "The system handles [N] [requests/orders/users] per [day/second]. Architecture: [frontend] talks to [API layer] backed by [DB], with [cache] for performance and [Kafka/queue] for async processing between [service A] and [service B]. Request flow for placing an order: 1. POST /orders → JWT validated at API Gateway 2. OrderService: validate request → write to DB (optimistic lock) → publish to Kafka 3. InventoryService: consume event → check stock → update → emit result 4. OrderService: mark CONFIRMED or CANCELLED based on inventory result Security: [JWT/OAuth2] with [role-based access / resource-level auth]. DB design: [key tables + one important index decision]. Key challenge: [problem → what I tried → what worked → measured result]."

    OOP — 4 Pillars

    encap · abstract · inherit · poly
    🧠 Intuition
    Think of it as modelling the real world in codeEvery "thing" in your system — Car, User, Order — becomes a class (a blueprint). Every action it does — drive, login, pay — becomes a method. Every property it has — color, name, amount — becomes a field. OOP is vocabulary your brain already uses. You just need to translate it into class syntax.
    🏪 Real-World Analogy — The Bank
    Map all 4 pillars to bankingEncapsulation: Your account balance is private. You interact only via deposit() and withdraw() — you can never set balance = -99999 directly.
    Abstraction: ATM shows you "Withdraw ₹500". You never see the core banking protocol underneath.
    Inheritance: SavingsAccount IS-A BankAccount — inherits all base behaviour, adds interestRate.
    Polymorphism: account.calculateInterest() runs differently on SavingsAccount vs FixedDeposit — same call, different result.
    📐 Diagram — 4 Pillars Side by Side
    💻 Code Walkthrough
    Encapsulation
    Abstraction
    Inheritance
    Polymorphism

    Hide the balance. Only controlled methods can change it. This single rule prevents most bugs.

    Java
    public class BankAccount { // private = nobody outside can touch this directly private double balance; private String accountNumber; public BankAccount(String acNo, double initial) { this.accountNumber = acNo; this.balance = initial; } public void deposit(double amount) { if (amount <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Must be positive"); balance += amount; } public void withdraw(double amount) { if (amount > balance) throw new IllegalStateException("Insufficient funds"); balance -= amount; } public double getBalance() { return balance; } // read-only getter } // account.balance = -99999; <-- COMPILE ERROR. Encapsulation wins.

    Define WHAT must happen (interface). Hide HOW it happens (concrete class). Callers only see the contract.

    Java
    public interface PaymentProcessor { // contract — WHAT boolean processPayment(double amount); boolean refund(double amount, String txnId); } class UpiProcessor implements PaymentProcessor { // HOW — hidden public boolean processPayment(double amount) { return upiGateway.charge(amount); } public boolean refund(double a, String id) { ... } } class OrderService { private PaymentProcessor processor; // interface type, not concrete void placeOrder(Order o) { processor.processPayment(o.getTotal()); // works for ANY processor } }
    Java
    class SavingsAccount extends BankAccount { private double interestRate; private int monthlyWithdrawLimit = 3; public SavingsAccount(String acNo, double bal, double rate) { super(acNo, bal); // reuse parent constructor this.interestRate = rate; } public void applyMonthlyInterest() { double interest = getBalance() * interestRate / 12; deposit(interest); // reuse parent method — no code duplication } @Override public void withdraw(double amount) { if (monthlyWithdrawLimit == 0) throw new IllegalStateException("Limit reached"); super.withdraw(amount); // parent validates balance monthlyWithdrawLimit--; } }

    Same loop, same method call. Different behaviour at runtime. Adding Triangle = new class only. Zero loop changes.

    Java
    abstract class Shape { abstract double area(); abstract void draw(); } class Circle extends Shape { double r; double area() { return Math.PI * r * r; } void draw() { System.out.println("Drawing circle"); } } class Rectangle extends Shape { double w, h; double area() { return w * h; } void draw() { System.out.println("Drawing rect"); } } // POLYMORPHISM — same code works for all shapes, present and future List<Shape> shapes = List.of(new Circle(), new Rectangle(), new Triangle()); for (Shape s : shapes) { s.draw(); // JVM picks the right method at runtime System.out.println(s.area()); }
    ⚠ Classic Mistakes
    • Making everything publicStart private, expose only what consumers need. Every public field is a broken encapsulation.
    • Inheritance when you mean compositionLogger should not extend File. Logger USES a File. Ask: "Is a Logger truly a type of File?" If no → composition.
    • God classesA class that handles auth, email, payments, and reporting has 4 reasons to change. Split it.
    📚 Reference
    🌐
    Refactoring.Guru — OOP Concepts
    refactoring.guru/refactoring/what-is-refactoring
    ↗
    🎯
    Days 1–2 GoalModel 3 real systems on paper: Library, Hospital, Online Shop. For each: list all classes, fields, methods. Draw IS-A and HAS-A arrows. No code until you can articulate every relationship verbally.
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Your senior engineer asks: 'Our OrderService has 2000 lines. Refactor it using OOP principles without breaking existing tests.'
    This tests all 4 pillars together. You need to extract responsibilities (encapsulation), identify hierarchies (inheritance), use interfaces (abstraction), and handle polymorphic dispatch for order types.
    Encapsulation first: Extract fields + behavior into cohesive classes (Order, OrderItem, PricingEngine, ShippingCalculator). Private fields, public behaviour-revealing methods. Abstraction: Define interfaces — PaymentProcessor, DiscountStrategy, ShippingStrategy — callers depend on interfaces not implementations. Inheritance: DigitalOrder and PhysicalOrder extend Order, overriding only what differs (shipping logic). Polymorphism: OrderProcessor.process(Order order) calls order.calculateShipping() — the right implementation runs at runtime without if-else chains. Result: each class <200 lines, independently testable.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: What is the difference between abstraction and encapsulation? Give a concrete example from your project.
    💡 Think First
    Candidates swap these constantly. Abstraction = hiding HOW it works — you see the interface, not the engine. Encapsulation = hiding WHAT is inside — fields are private, internal state is protected. Memory aid: Abstraction is the outside view (caller sees only the contract). Encapsulation is the inside guard (internal data is locked away).
    ➔ Complete Answer
    Abstraction: interface PaymentProcessor { void charge(BigDecimal amount); } — the caller programs to this interface and has no idea HOW it charges (Stripe? RazorPay? UPI?). You can swap StripeProcessor for UpiProcessor without changing a single caller. The complexity of HTTP calls, retries, and API keys is completely hidden. Encapsulation: class StripeProcessor implements PaymentProcessor { private final String apiKey; private final HttpClient client; ... } — the fields apiKey and client are private. External code cannot read or corrupt them. All access is controlled through the class's own methods. In one sentence: Abstraction hides the implementation behind an interface (callers don't know HOW). Encapsulation hides the internal state inside a class (callers don't know WHAT is stored). Real project example: PaymentProcessor interface = abstraction. StripeProcessor's private retry logic and API credentials = encapsulation. When you added UPI support, you wrote a new UpiProcessor — zero changes to the checkout flow because abstraction isolated the callers from the implementation detail.
    Q: 'When does inheritance become a design mistake? What do you use instead?'
    💭 Think First
    Inheritance creates tight coupling — subclass depends on superclass internals. Changes to the parent break children. LSP violations cause runtime surprises.
    → Complete Answer
    Inheritance works for true IS-A relationships that don't change (Animal → Dog). It fails when: (1) you inherit to reuse code but the child isn't really a subtype (Stack extending Vector — Java's mistake), (2) deep hierarchies make tracing behavior impossible, (3) you need multiple inheritance. Prefer composition: class OrderProcessor { private final PaymentService payment; private final InventoryService inventory; } — OrderProcessor HAS-A PaymentService instead of IS-A. Behaviour is composed from focused collaborators. Rule of thumb: if you'd write 'is-a' naturally in English, inherit. If 'has-a', compose.
    🎯 Practice Task
    A Stack (push/pop/peek) is often implemented by extending ArrayList or Vector. Explain why this violates LSP, then redesign using composition.
    Hint — think before readingA Stack should only expose push/pop/peek. If you extend ArrayList, it also exposes get(index), add(index, element), remove(index) — callers can bypass the LIFO contract. Liskov: a Stack cannot fully substitute for a List without violating List's expected behavior.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — Stack via composition (correct)
    class Stack<T> { // does NOT extend ArrayList private final Deque<T> data = new ArrayDeque<>(); // HAS-A, not IS-A public void push(T item) { data.push(item); } public T pop() { return data.pop(); } public T peek() { return data.peek(); } public boolean isEmpty() { return data.isEmpty(); } // No get(index), no add(index) — caller can ONLY use Stack as a Stack }

    SOLID Principles

    5 rules that make code extensible — fully expanded, each with its own example
    🧠 Intuition
    The "add feature X" testImagine your Parking Lot runs fine. Now: "Add motorbike slots." If you touch 8 files and break 3 tests, your design failed SOLID. SOLID exists so that every "add feature X" question has a clean answer: one new class, zero edits to existing ones. Every interview question about extension is secretly a SOLID question.
    📐 All 5 Principles — Overview
    1️⃣ Single Responsibility — "One reason to change"
    Real-world testIf you can describe a class's job with "and," it's doing too much. A UserService that handles login AND sends emails AND writes audit logs has 3 reasons to change. Each responsibility should live in its own class — when requirements for one change, only that class is touched.
    Java — SRP violation and fix
    // ✗ BAD — 3 responsibilities in one class class UserService { void registerUser(User u) { // 1. validate + save to DB db.save(u); // 2. send welcome email emailClient.send(u.getEmail(), "Welcome!"); // 3. write audit log auditLog.write("User registered: " + u.getId()); } } // Change email provider? Touch this class. // Change audit format? Touch this class. Too many reasons to change. // ✓ GOOD — each responsibility isolated class UserService { private final UserRepository repo; private final NotificationService notifier; private final AuditLogger audit; void registerUser(User u) { repo.save(u); notifier.sendWelcome(u); audit.logRegistration(u); } } // Each class has ONE reason to change. Email logic lives only in NotificationService.
    💬 Interview Follow-up
    Q: "Isn't this over-engineering for a small app?"

    A: For a throwaway script, no. For production code that will be maintained by a team, SRP pays off the moment two people need to change "user" logic for unrelated reasons and step on each other.

    2️⃣ Open/Closed — "Open for extension, closed for modification"
    The if/else smellOnce a class works, you shouldn't have to edit it to add a feature — you should be able to extend it. The telltale sign you're violating OCP: a chain of if/else or switch statements that grows every time a new type is added.
    💬 Interview Follow-up
    Q: "When is if/else actually fine?"

    A: When the set of cases is genuinely fixed and will never grow — e.g., a 3-way traffic light state. OCP matters when new variants are a realistic future requirement, which is true for almost anything business-facing.

    3️⃣ Liskov Substitution — "Subtypes must honor the parent's contract"
    The classic Square-Rectangle trapIf you can substitute a subclass anywhere the parent is expected, without breaking correctness, you've satisfied LSP. The famous violation: Square extends Rectangle and overrides setWidth() to also change height (to stay square). Code that calls setWidth() expecting only width to change now silently breaks.
    Java — LSP violation and fix
    // ✗ BAD — Penguin violates the Bird contract class Bird { void fly() { System.out.println("Flying"); } } class Penguin extends Bird { void fly() { throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Penguins can't fly!"); } } // Any code that does: for (Bird b : birds) b.fly(); // CRASHES the moment a Penguin is in the list. LSP violated. // ✓ GOOD — restructure the hierarchy around actual capability abstract class Bird { abstract void move(); // every bird CAN move, somehow } interface Flyable { void fly(); } class Sparrow extends Bird implements Flyable { void move() { fly(); } public void fly() { System.out.println("Sparrow flying"); } } class Penguin extends Bird { // no Flyable — and that's correct void move() { System.out.println("Penguin swimming"); } } // Now any Bird can be substituted safely — no surprises.
    💬 Interview Follow-up
    Q: "How do you catch LSP violations in code review?"

    A: Look for overridden methods that throw, do nothing, or weaken a precondition / strengthen a postcondition compared to the parent. Any of those break substitutability.

    4️⃣ Interface Segregation — "Don't force classes to implement what they don't use"
    Fat interfaces create fake implementationsA Printer interface with print(), scan(), fax() forces a BasicPrinter (which can only print) to implement scan() and fax() with empty bodies or exceptions. That's a code smell signaling the interface should be split.
    Java — ISP violation and fix
    // ✗ BAD — fat interface forces unused methods interface Printer { void print(Document d); void scan(Document d); void fax(Document d); } class BasicPrinter implements Printer { public void print(Document d) { /* works */ } public void scan(Document d) { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); } // forced! public void fax(Document d) { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); } // forced! } // ✓ GOOD — split into focused interfaces interface Printable { void print(Document d); } interface Scannable { void scan(Document d); } interface Faxable { void fax(Document d); } class BasicPrinter implements Printable { // only what it actually does public void print(Document d) { /* works */ } } class AllInOnePrinter implements Printable, Scannable, Faxable { // implements all three — genuinely supports them }
    💬 Interview Follow-up
    Q: "Isn't this the same as SRP?"

    A: Related but distinct. SRP is about a class having one reason to change. ISP is about an interface not forcing implementers to depend on methods they don't use. SRP is about classes; ISP is about interface contracts.

    5️⃣ Dependency Inversion — "Depend on abstractions, not concretions"
    The most interview-critical principleHigh-level modules (business logic) shouldn't depend directly on low-level modules (implementation details). Both should depend on interfaces. This is the foundation of dependency injection — what Spring's @Autowired does under the hood.
    Java — Dependency Inversion
    // ✗ BAD: hardcoded dependency — can't test, can't swap class NotificationService { private EmailSender sender = new EmailSender(); // hardwired! void notify(String msg) { sender.send(msg); } } // ✓ GOOD: depends on abstraction, injected from outside interface MessageSender { void send(String msg); } class EmailSender implements MessageSender { ... } class SmsSender implements MessageSender { ... } class PushSender implements MessageSender { ... } class NotificationService { private final MessageSender sender; // interface — not concrete class public NotificationService(MessageSender s) { this.sender = s; } void notify(String msg) { sender.send(msg); } } // Swap SMS ↔ Email ↔ Push with zero changes to NotificationService. // Unit-test with MockSender — no real email server needed.
    💬 Interview Follow-up
    Q: "How does this relate to Spring?"

    A: Spring's @Autowired is dependency injection — the framework wires the concrete MessageSender implementation into NotificationService at runtime, based on the interface type. DIP is the principle; DI is the technique; Spring's IoC container is the tool.

    Q: "Does DIP mean every class needs an interface?"

    A: No — only where you expect multiple implementations, need to mock for testing, or want to decouple layers (e.g., service layer from data layer). Interface-per-class everywhere is over-engineering.

    💡 Spot SOLID Violations in an Interview — Quick Reference
    SRP signal

    Class name contains "And" or the class both fetches data AND does business logic. Split it.

    OCP signal

    Long if/else or switch that checks type to decide behaviour. Ask: "Can polymorphism replace this?"

    LSP signal

    Subclass method throws UnsupportedOperationException or has an empty override. Hierarchy is wrong.

    ISP signal

    An implementing class has multiple methods that just throw or return null/no-op. Interface is too fat.

    DIP signal

    Class uses new ConcreteClass() deep inside a method body instead of accepting it via constructor.

    🎯
    Days 3–4 GoalPick a class from your own past project. Identify which SOLID principles it violates. Refactor it. Write a comment above each changed line: "Changed because: [principle]." This is more effective than reading theory.
    🏭 Production Scenario
    You have a UserService that handles registration, sending welcome emails, and writing audit logs. An interviewer asks you to identify the SOLID violations and fix them.
    A class with 3 responsibilities (user creation, email, audit) violates SRP. It also likely violates OCP — adding a new notification channel (SMS) requires changing UserService. Fixing both gives you a clean design.
    SRP violation: Extract EmailService (send welcome) and AuditService (log action) as separate beans. UserService.register() only creates the user and delegates. OCP violation: Instead of if-SMS/if-EMAIL inside UserService, define interface NotificationChannel { void notifyUserRegistered(User u); }. EmailChannel, SMSChannel implement it. UserService gets List<NotificationChannel> injected — adding WhatsApp channel requires zero changes to UserService. DIP: UserService depends on NotificationChannel (abstract), not EmailService (concrete). Spring injects all implementations automatically.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'Give me a real example of ISP — Interface Segregation — that you would apply in a Spring Boot service.'
    💭 Think First
    ISP: don't force a class to implement methods it doesn't need. A fat interface with 10 methods forces every implementer to provide all 10, even if it only needs 3.
    → Complete Answer
    interface OrderService { Order place(OrderRequest r); Order cancel(String id); Order getById(String id); List<Order> getByCustomer(String cId); } — A reporting service only needs read operations. A fulfilment service only needs place and cancel. Fat interface violates ISP. Fix: split into OrderReader { Order getById; List getByCustomer; } and OrderWriter { Order place; Order cancel; }. Implementations implement one or both. Callers only depend on the interface they actually use.
    Q: 'How does the Open/Closed Principle apply to adding new payment methods without touching existing code?'
    💭 Think First
    OCP: open for extension, closed for modification. New behaviour should add new classes, not change existing ones.
    → Complete Answer
    Java — OCP via Strategy
    interface PaymentProcessor { PaymentResult process(Payment p); } class StripeProcessor implements PaymentProcessor { ... } class RazorpayProcessor implements PaymentProcessor { ... } // Adding UPI: create UpiProcessor. Zero changes to PaymentService. @Service class PaymentService { private final Map<PaymentMethod, PaymentProcessor> processors; public PaymentResult pay(Payment p) { return processors.get(p.method()).process(p); } }
    🎯 Practice Task
    A Logger interface has: log(String msg), logError(Exception e), logToFile(String msg), logToDb(String msg), logToSplunk(String msg). Identify the ISP violation and redesign.
    Hint — think before readingCallers that only want console logging are forced to depend on logToFile, logToDb, logToSplunk methods they'll never call. Each log destination should be a separate interface.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — ISP fix
    interface Logger { void log(String msg); void logError(Exception e); } interface FileLogger extends Logger { void logToFile(String msg); } interface RemoteLogger extends Logger { void logToRemote(String msg); } // SplunkLogger implements RemoteLogger — only logToRemote + base methods // ConsoleLogger implements Logger — no file/remote methods
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Your senior engineer reviews your code and sees: if(user != null && user.getProfile() != null && user.getProfile().getAddress() != null) return city. They say: refactor with SOLID. Which principles are violated?
    A long null-check chain violates both SRP (UserService is doing null-safety work) and OCP (adding a new nullable step requires modifying this chain). The fix uses small focused classes with clear responsibilities.
    SRP violation: UserService mixes user retrieval logic with null-safety navigation. Extract a UserProfileQuery class that encapsulates the navigation chain. OCP violation: every new nullable field means editing this if-chain. Use Optional chain instead: Optional.ofNullable(user).map(User::getProfile).map(Profile::getAddress).map(Address::getCity).orElse("Unknown") — adding a new nullable step is one more .map() with zero modification to existing code. DIP: depend on an abstraction interface ProfileResolver { String getCity(String userId); } — callers depend on the interface, not the null-check implementation.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: Give me a concrete example of the Liskov Substitution Principle being violated in Java.
    💭 Think First
    LSP: if S is a subtype of T, any program using T should work correctly with S without knowing it. A violation means the subclass breaks the contract of the parent.
    → Complete Answer
    Classic violation: java.util.Stack extends Vector. Stack should only expose push/pop/peek. But because it extends Vector, it inherits add(index, element), get(index), remove(index) — operations that bypass the LIFO contract. Code that expects a Stack and calls stack.add(0, element) inserts at the bottom — that is not how a stack works. The subclass (Stack) cannot fully substitute for the parent (Vector) without violating Vector's expected semantics, and also cannot enforce Stack's own semantics. Fix: implement Stack with composition (HAS-A Deque) rather than inheritance (IS-A Vector).
    Q: How does the Dependency Inversion Principle differ from Dependency Injection?
    💭 Think First
    These are often confused. DIP is a design principle about what to depend on. DI is a technique for supplying those dependencies.
    → Complete Answer
    DIP: high-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions. Example: OrderService (high-level) should not import MySQLOrderRepository (low-level). Both should depend on OrderRepository (interface). DI: the mechanism by which the concrete implementation is supplied to the class that depends on the abstraction. Spring does DI: it creates a MySQLOrderRepository instance and injects it into OrderService via the constructor. DIP is the WHY (design rule). DI is the HOW (implementation technique). You can have DI without DIP (inject a concrete class directly — bad), and you can have DIP without DI (use a factory to look up the implementation — valid but more verbose).
    🎯 Practice Task
    Identify all SOLID violations in this class: class UserService { public void processUser(String userId) { User user = db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=" + userId); if(user.isAdmin()) { emailService.sendAdminReport(user.email); db.execute("UPDATE users SET lastLogin=NOW() WHERE id=" + userId); } } }
    Hint — think before readingViolations: SRP (query + email + update = 3 responsibilities), OCP (if-else for admin will grow), SQL injection (string concat), direct DB call (violates DIP — depends on db concrete). Fix: UserRepository interface, EmailService interface, constructor injection, separate AdminReportService.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — SOLID refactor
    // BEFORE: 5 violations in one method // String concat SQL injection, SRP, OCP, DIP (direct db), no abstraction // AFTER: SOLID design @Service class UserLoginService { // SRP: only handles login private final UserRepository repo; // DIP: interface, not concrete private final LoginAuditService audit; // SRP: audit is separate private final NotificationService notify; // SRP: notification separate public void recordLogin(String userId) { // single responsibility User user = repo.findById(userId) // parameterised — no SQL injection .orElseThrow(() -> new UserNotFoundException(userId)); audit.recordLogin(user); // delegated notify.notifyIfRequired(user); // OCP: new notification types = new class } }

    5-Step Interview Framework

    your script for every LLD round
    🧠 Why this is the most important thing you will learn
    Interviewers grade process, not just outputTwo candidates both produce working Parking Lot code. Candidate A jumped in, coded silently for 25 minutes, done. Candidate B spent 5 min clarifying, narrated thinking, justified each pattern, explained trade-offs. Candidate B gets the offer. Every single time. The 5-step framework is what makes you Candidate B.
    📐 Flow Diagram
    💻 Live Walkthrough — Parking Lot
    1 Clarify
    2 Entities
    3 Patterns
    4 Code
    5 Trade-offs
    INTERVIEWER: "Design a Parking Lot." YOU: "Before I start designing, let me clarify a few things.
    — Single-floor or multi-floor?
    — Vehicle types: cars only, or bikes and trucks too?
    — Is payment processing in scope, or just spot allocation?
    — First-come-first-served, or can spots be reserved in advance?
    — Should we track entry and exit times for billing?"

    Wait for answers. Write them down. Then say: "Okay — multi-floor, cars/bikes/trucks, payment in scope, no reservations. Let me proceed."
    "The main entities I see are:
    — ParkingLot — top-level singleton. Contains floors.
    — ParkingFloor — has a list of spots and a ReentrantLock for concurrency.
    — ParkingSpot (abstract) — CompactSpot, LargeSpot, HandicappedSpot extend it.
    — Vehicle (abstract) — Car, Bike, Truck extend it.
    — Ticket — issued on entry. Holds: vehicle, spot, entry time.
    — Payment — calculated on exit from ticket. Uses a PaymentStrategy.

    ParkingLot HAS-MANY ParkingFloors. ParkingFloor HAS-MANY ParkingSpots. Ticket REFERENCES one Vehicle and one Spot."
    "Patterns I'd apply:

    Singleton — ParkingLot. One physical lot = one instance.
    Strategy — PaymentStrategy interface. HourlyPayment, FlatPayment implement it. Adding WeekendRate = new class, zero edits to Ticket.
    Factory — SpotFactory creates the right ParkingSpot type based on floor configuration.
    Observer — DisplayBoard observes spot availability changes and auto-updates. ParkingFloor doesn't import DisplayBoard — fully decoupled."
    Java — start with abstractions, always
    enum VehicleType { CAR, BIKE, TRUCK } abstract class Vehicle { protected String plate; public abstract VehicleType getType(); } class Car extends Vehicle { public Car(String p) { plate = p; } public VehicleType getType() { return VehicleType.CAR; } } abstract class ParkingSpot { protected int spotNo; protected boolean occupied; protected Vehicle vehicle; public abstract boolean canFit(Vehicle v); public synchronized boolean assign(Vehicle v) { if (!occupied && canFit(v)) { vehicle = v; occupied = true; return true; } return false; } } class CompactSpot extends ParkingSpot { public boolean canFit(Vehicle v) { return v.getType() == VehicleType.CAR || v.getType() == VehicleType.BIKE; } }
    "Three things I'd improve:

    1. Concurrency: findAvailableSpot + assign aren't atomic across the floor. I'd wrap both in a single ReentrantLock.lock()...unlock() block per floor to prevent two threads grabbing the same spot.

    2. Scale: The DisplayBoard tracks availability in memory. At scale across multiple buildings, I'd publish spot-change events to a Kafka topic and let the board subscribe.

    3. Search optimisation: Linear scan of spots is O(n). At high occupancy, I'd use a PriorityQueue of free spots per type for O(log n) allocation."
    🎯
    Days 5–7 GoalApply all 5 steps to 3 problems (Library, ATM, Chess) on paper only. Practise saying Steps 1 and 5 out loud until they feel natural. Most people skip this. Don't.
    🏭 Production Scenario
    An interviewer says: "Design a Library Management System." You have 45 minutes. Walk through the 5-step framework live, showing exactly what you say and draw at each step.
    Panic comes from having no structure. The 5-step framework gives you a repeatable skeleton for any LLD problem. Practice it until the first 12 minutes run on autopilot.
    Step 1 — Clarify (0-5 min): "Can I ask a few questions first?" What actors use the system? (Members borrow, Librarians manage, Admin configures.) What core features? (Search books, borrow/return, reservations, fines.) Multi-branch? Digital books? Scale? Confirm 3-4 features. Step 2 — Entities (5-12 min): Book, BookCopy (one-to-many: one book has 5 physical copies), Member, Loan, Reservation. Draw boxes and arrows. Justify each entity. Step 3 — Key operations (12-20 min): borrowBook(memberId, copyId), returnBook(copyId), searchBooks(query), reserveBook(memberId, bookId). For each: happy path, failure modes. Step 4 — Class design (20-35 min): Interfaces and design patterns. FineStrategy (Strategy pattern). NotificationService with Observer. LoanStatus state machine. Write pseudocode for the most interesting method. Step 5 — Edge cases (35-42 min): Concurrent borrow of last copy (CAS/SELECT FOR UPDATE). Reservation queue (FIFO). Overdue detection (scheduled job).
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: The interviewer asks "what if we have 1000 branches and need to find the nearest available copy of a book?" How does your design extend?
    💭 Think First
    This adds a geospatial and distributed inventory dimension. The core OOP design stays the same — you add a search layer on top.
    → Complete Answer
    Add Branch entity with coordinates (lat, lng). BookCopy has a branchId. Search extension: given a member's location, find all copies of Book B across all branches, sort by distance. Implementation: geospatial index in PostgreSQL (PostGIS ST_Distance) or Elasticsearch geo_distance query. The availability check still uses the existing BookCopy.available flag — the search layer filters to available copies first, then sorts by distance. The core borrow/return logic is unchanged — it works on a specific copyId regardless of branch.
    Q: At what point in the interview should you start writing code vs drawing diagrams?
    💭 Think First
    Many candidates skip to code immediately and produce working code for a poorly-understood problem. The interviewer would rather see less code and more reasoning.
    → Complete Answer
    Rule of thumb: spend 60% of the time on design (steps 1-3 and partial 4), 40% on code (step 4 code + step 5). Never write code before you have agreed on the core entities and their relationships. The best 30-minute interview has: 5 min clarification, 10 min entity and operation discussion, 10 min pseudocode for the most complex operation with explicit pattern application, 5 min edge cases. The interviewer is testing your ability to decompose a problem and reason about trade-offs — code is just evidence of that reasoning.
    🎯 Practice Task
    Practice run: apply the 5-step framework to "Design a Parking Lot" in written form. For each step, write exactly what you would say to the interviewer and what you would draw.
    Hint — think before readingStep 1 questions: how many floors, vehicle types, pricing model? Step 2 entities: ParkingLot, ParkingFloor, ParkingSpot, Vehicle, Ticket. Step 3 operations: parkVehicle, exitVehicle, findSpot. Step 4 patterns: Strategy for pricing, Observer for display board. Step 5 edge cases: concurrent arrival, spot unavailability.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — Parking Lot framework application
    // Step 2 — Core entities enum VehicleType { BIKE, CAR, TRUCK } record Vehicle(String plate, VehicleType type) {} class ParkingSpot { private final String id; private final VehicleType type; private final AtomicBoolean occupied = new AtomicBoolean(false); public boolean tryPark() { return occupied.compareAndSet(false, true); } // CAS — one thread wins public void free() { occupied.set(false); } } // Step 4 — Strategy pattern for pricing interface PricingStrategy { BigDecimal calculate(Duration parked, VehicleType type); } class HourlyPricing implements PricingStrategy { public BigDecimal calculate(Duration d, VehicleType t) { long hours = (long) Math.ceil(d.toMinutes() / 60.0); return rateFor(t).multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(hours)); } }
    02
    Creational Patterns
    // Singleton · Factory · Builder · Prototype — control how objects are born
    1️⃣
    Singleton Pattern
    one instance · global access · thread-safe
    🏭
    Factory & Abstract Factory
    decouple creation from usage
    🔨
    Builder Pattern
    readable object construction + validation

    Singleton Pattern

    one instance · global access · thread-safe
    🧠 Intuition
    One president, one config, one loggerSome things must exist exactly once. A DB connection pool — if every class makes its own pool, you get thousands of connections and crash the DB. A Logger — all logs must funnel to one place. A Config manager — one source of truth. Singleton = lazily created, globally accessible, guaranteed single instance, thread-safe.
    📐 How it Works — Diagram
    💻 Three Implementations — Basic to Best
    Naive (broken)
    Double-Checked Lock
    Enum (best)

    ⚠ Race condition: two threads both see instance==null simultaneously and create two separate instances.

    Java — BROKEN in multithreaded env
    public class Logger { private static Logger instance; // no volatile! private Logger() {} public static Logger getInstance() { if (instance == null) { // Thread A checks: null instance = new Logger(); // Thread B also checks: null → BUG! } return instance; } }

    volatile ensures the write is visible to all threads. Double-check avoids locking on every call after the instance is created.

    Java — Thread-Safe
    public class Logger { private static volatile Logger instance; // volatile = all-thread visibility private PrintWriter writer; private Logger() { try { writer = new PrintWriter(new FileWriter("app.log", true)); } catch (IOException e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); } } public static Logger getInstance() { if (instance == null) { // 1st check — no lock cost synchronized (Logger.class) { if (instance == null) { // 2nd check — inside lock instance = new Logger(); } } } return instance; } public synchronized void log(String level, String msg) { writer.println("[" + level + "] " + msg); writer.flush(); } }

    Effective Java Item 3: Enum Singleton is serialisation-safe, thread-safe by JVM guarantee, and the simplest to write.

    Java — Enum Singleton (recommended)
    public enum Logger { INSTANCE; // JVM creates exactly one, thread-safely, on class load private PrintWriter writer; Logger() { // enum constructor — called once try { writer = new PrintWriter(new FileWriter("app.log", true)); } catch (IOException e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); } } public synchronized void log(String level, String msg) { writer.println("[" + level + "] " + msg); writer.flush(); } } // Usage anywhere — zero boilerplate: Logger.INSTANCE.log("INFO", "Order #1234 placed");
    ⚠ When NOT to Use Singleton
    • It hides dependenciesAny class can call Logger.INSTANCE without declaring a dependency. Makes code hard to understand and test.
    • Unit testing nightmareYou can't inject a mock Logger — the singleton is baked in. Prefer constructor injection with an interface.
    • Safe uses onlyLogger, ConfigManager, DB connection pool, thread pool — stateless or carefully managed state only.
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Your application has a DatabaseConnectionPool implemented as a Singleton. A load test shows two connection pools exist, each with half the expected connections. What went wrong?
    Classic double-instantiation race condition. Two threads checked instance==null simultaneously before either created the object. Both create a new pool. This is the broken DCL without volatile.
    Root cause: if(instance==null){ instance=new Pool(); } — Thread A checks (null), Thread B checks (null), A creates, B creates. Two pools exist. Fix 1 — volatile + DCL: private static volatile Pool instance; — volatile prevents instruction reordering, the second null-check inside synchronized ensures only one creation. Fix 2 — static holder (preferred): private static class Holder { static final Pool INSTANCE = new Pool(); } — JVM guarantees class loading is thread-safe; Holder only loads when getInstance() is first called. Zero explicit synchronization.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'When would you NOT use Singleton? What are the downsides?'
    💭 Think First
    Singleton is one of the most abused patterns. Think about testability, hidden dependencies, and global mutable state.
    → Complete Answer
    Problems: (1) Testability: you can't inject a mock — every test gets the same global instance. (2) Hidden coupling: any class can call getInstance() — dependencies are invisible in the constructor. (3) Global mutable state: if the Singleton holds state, any code anywhere can corrupt it. (4) Classloader issues: different classloaders can create multiple instances. Spring's @Bean with singleton scope solves all this: the container manages the lifecycle, you inject the dependency via constructor (visible, testable, replaceable in tests with @MockBean).
    Q: 'What happens to a Singleton in a multi-JVM deployment (Kubernetes with 3 pods)?'
    💭 Think First
    Singleton is JVM-scoped, not cluster-scoped. Think about what shared state means across pods.
    → Complete Answer
    Each JVM (pod) has its own Singleton instance — 3 pods = 3 instances of the Singleton. If the Singleton holds in-memory state (counters, caches, rate limit buckets), each pod has an independent copy. Writes on Pod A are invisible to Pods B and C. Fix: move shared state to a distributed store — Redis for counters/caches, a database for persistent state. The Singleton can still exist per-JVM but its state is stored externally and accessed via Redis/DB calls.
    🎯 Practice
    Implement ConfigManager as Singleton. Then write a unit test for a class that uses it. Notice how hard it is to mock. This teaches the trade-off more than any explanation.
    💡 Hint — think before readingUse the static holder idiom for thread-safety. For testability, add a package-private setInstanceForTesting(). Write a test that replaces the singleton before calling the code under test.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — solution
    class ConfigManager { private static class Holder { static final ConfigManager I = new ConfigManager(); } private static volatile ConfigManager override; public static ConfigManager getInstance() { return override != null ? override : Holder.I; } static void setInstanceForTesting(ConfigManager m) { override = m; } public String get(String k) { return props.getProperty(k); } } // Unit test: @Test void testWithMock() { ConfigManager mock = Mockito.mock(ConfigManager.class); when(mock.get("key")).thenReturn("testval"); ConfigManager.setInstanceForTesting(mock); assertEquals("testval", new MyService().process()); ConfigManager.setInstanceForTesting(null); // cleanup }
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement a thread-safe Singleton ConfigManager that: lazily loads config from a file on first access, returns a cached Map on subsequent calls, and is testable (allows replacing the instance in tests).
    Hint — think before readingUse static holder for thread-safe lazy init. For testability, add a package-private setter that allows tests to inject a mock instance. The holder loads the class (and reads the file) exactly once, on first call to getInstance().
    → Worked Solution
    Java — testable Singleton
    class ConfigManager { private final Map<String,String> config; private ConfigManager() { config = loadFromFile(); } private static class Holder { static final ConfigManager INST = new ConfigManager(); // thread-safe, lazy } private static volatile ConfigManager override = null; // for testing public static ConfigManager getInstance() { return override != null ? override : Holder.INST; } // package-private: only tests call this static void setInstanceForTesting(ConfigManager m) { override = m; } public String get(String key) { return config.get(key); } }

    Factory & Abstract Factory

    decouple creation from usage
    🧠 Intuition
    McDonald's kitchen analogyYou say "Veggie Burger." You don't know which cook, which oven, where the ingredients came from. The kitchen (Factory) handles creation. You just receive a Burger. Factory Pattern: the client says WHAT. The factory decides HOW. The client never imports or knows about concrete classes. Adding a new product = new class + one line in factory. Client unchanged.
    📐 Factory Method vs Abstract Factory
    💻 Full Example — Notification Factory
    Java
    interface Notification { void send(String recipient, String message); } class EmailNotification implements Notification { public void send(String to, String msg) { System.out.println("[EMAIL] to:" + to + " msg:" + msg); } } class SmsNotification implements Notification { public void send(String to, String msg) { System.out.println("[SMS] to:" + to + " msg:" + msg); } } class NotificationFactory { public static Notification create(String type) { return switch (type.toUpperCase()) { case "EMAIL" -> new EmailNotification(); case "SMS" -> new SmsNotification(); case "PUSH" -> new PushNotification(); default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown: " + type); }; } } class AlertService { void alert(String channel, String to, String msg) { NotificationFactory.create(channel).send(to, msg); } } // Adding WhatsApp? One new class + one case. ZERO AlertService changes.
    📚 Reference
    🌐
    Refactoring.Guru — Factory Method
    refactoring.guru/design-patterns/factory-method
    ↗
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Your OrderService currently has: if(type==ONLINE) new OnlineOrderProcessor() elif(type==INSTORE)... Adding a new B2B order type requires modifying OrderService. How do you fix this?
    This is the Open/Closed violation that Factory Pattern solves. The creation logic is scattered in the consumer. Centralise it in a factory, then add new types without touching the consumer.
    Simple Factory: OrderProcessorFactory.create(OrderType) with a switch — still needs modification per new type, but modification is in ONE place. Factory Method (OOP): Abstract OrderService.createProcessor() — each subclass overrides. Good when processors need subclass-specific configuration. Registry (best for Spring): Map<OrderType, OrderProcessor> processors autowired by Spring — all @Component processors register themselves. Zero code changes to add a new type — just create a new @Component class.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'What is the difference between Factory Method pattern and Abstract Factory pattern?'
    💭 Think First
    Factory Method: one product, subclasses decide the concrete type. Abstract Factory: families of related products, one factory creates all members of the family.
    → Complete Answer
    Factory Method: abstract class OrderFactory { abstract OrderProcessor createProcessor(); } — each subclass returns a concrete processor. One product type per factory hierarchy. Abstract Factory: interface UIFactory { Button createButton(); TextField createField(); Dialog createDialog(); } — WindowsUIFactory creates the whole family of Windows widgets; MacUIFactory creates Mac widgets. You swap the entire family by changing the factory. Use Abstract Factory when products must be compatible with each other (all Windows or all Mac — never mixed).
    Q: 'How does Spring's @Component + @Qualifier implement the Factory pattern automatically?'
    💭 Think First
    Spring can auto-discover all implementations and build the registry for you — no switch statement needed.
    → Complete Answer
    Spring — self-registering factory
    interface OrderProcessor { OrderType supports(); void process(Order o); } @Component class OnlineOrderProcessor implements OrderProcessor { public OrderType supports() { return OrderType.ONLINE; } } // Spring injects ALL implementations into OrderService @Service class OrderService { private final Map<OrderType, OrderProcessor> registry; OrderService(List<OrderProcessor> processors) { registry = processors.stream().collect(toMap(OrderProcessor::supports, p->p)); } public void handle(Order o) { registry.get(o.type()).process(o); } // Adding B2B: create B2BOrderProcessor @Component. Zero changes here. }
    🎯 Practice
    Build PaymentProcessorFactory: UpiProcessor, CardProcessor, NetBankingProcessor. Then add WalletProcessor. Count the existing lines you had to modify. Answer should be exactly 1 (the switch case).
    💡 Hint — think before readingStart with the interface. Implement three concrete processors. Use Map> — adding WalletProcessor = adding one map entry, zero other changes.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — solution
    interface PaymentProcessor { void process(Payment p); PaymentType supports(); } @Component class UpiProcessor implements PaymentProcessor { ... } @Component class CardProcessor implements PaymentProcessor { ... } @Service class PaymentFactory { private final Map<PaymentType,PaymentProcessor> reg; PaymentFactory(List<PaymentProcessor> all) { reg = all.stream().collect(toMap(PaymentProcessor::supports, p->p)); } public PaymentProcessor get(PaymentType t) { return reg.get(t); } }
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement a VehicleFactory that creates Car, Bike, or Truck based on a VehicleType enum. Use the Registry pattern (Map-based) so adding a new vehicle type (e.g. Scooter) requires ZERO changes to the factory class.
    Hint — think before readingMap> where each supplier is registered at construction time. Adding Scooter = add one entry to the map at initialization, or use a self-registering pattern where each vehicle class adds itself.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — Registry-based Factory
    class VehicleFactory { private static final Map<VehicleType, Supplier<Vehicle>> REGISTRY = Map.of( VehicleType.CAR, Car::new, VehicleType.BIKE, Bike::new, VehicleType.TRUCK, Truck::new // Add SCOOTER: VehicleType.SCOOTER, Scooter::new — one line, no other change ); public static Vehicle create(VehicleType type) { return Optional.ofNullable(REGISTRY.get(type)) .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown: " + type)) .get(); } }

    Builder Pattern

    readable object construction + validation
    🧠 Intuition — The Telescoping Constructor Problem
    Custom PC builder analogyYou choose CPU, RAM, GPU, storage step by step. Optional components exist. You don't set everything at once. Builder solves this for code. When an object has 4+ parameters — especially optional ones — constructors become unreadable: new User("John", null, null, "j@x.com", 25, true, null, "ADMIN") — what does the 3rd null mean? Nobody knows without reading the constructor signature.
    💻 Before → After + Validation
    Before (bad)
    Builder Pattern
    With Validation
    Java — telescoping constructors, unreadable
    // What does null mean here? Which field is 25? NOBODY KNOWS. new User("John", null, null, "john@email.com", 25, true, null, "ADMIN"); // 6 overloaded constructors just for optional params — TERRIBLE new User("John"); new User("John", "john@email.com"); new User("John", "john@email.com", 25); // ... 5 more overloads
    Java — Builder Pattern
    public class User { private final String name, email; // required private final int age; // optional private final String phone, role; // optional private final boolean isVerified; // optional private User(Builder b) { name=b.name; email=b.email; age=b.age; phone=b.phone; role=b.role; isVerified=b.isVerified; } public static class Builder { private final String name, email; // required — set in constructor private int age = 0; private String phone = null; private String role = "USER"; private boolean isVerified = false; public Builder(String name, String email) { this.name=name; this.email=email; } public Builder age(int a) { this.age=a; return this; } public Builder phone(String p) { this.phone=p; return this; } public Builder role(String r) { this.role=r; return this; } public Builder verified() { isVerified=true; return this; } public User build() { return new User(this); } } } // Beautiful, readable, self-documenting User u = new User.Builder("John", "john@email.com") .age(28).role("ADMIN").verified().build();
    Java — Validation in build()
    public User build() { // Validate before creating — fail fast with clear messages if (name == null || name.isBlank()) throw new IllegalStateException("Name is required"); if (email == null || !email.contains("@")) throw new IllegalStateException("Valid email required"); if (age < 0 || age > 150) throw new IllegalStateException("Invalid age: " + age); // Only after validation — create the (now guaranteed-valid) immutable object return new User(this); } // All fields are final — object is immutable once built. // Safe to share across threads without synchronisation.
    🏭 Production Scenario
    An interviewer shows you this: new Pizza('large','thin','mozzarella',true,false,true,false,'pepperoni'). Explain why this is a problem and refactor it.
    8-argument constructor = telescoping constructor anti-pattern. You can't tell from the call site what each boolean means. In 6 months nobody (including you) will know what position 6 means. Null arguments are common.
    Builder Pattern: The builder accumulates parameters through named methods, validates them in build(), and creates an immutable object. The call site becomes self-documenting: new Pizza.Builder().size(LARGE).crust(THIN).cheese(MOZZARELLA).topping(PEPPERONI).extraCheese().build(). Mandatory fields go in the Builder constructor (size is required). Optional fields have defaults. build() validates: if size==null throw IllegalStateException. Result: immutable Pizza — no setters, all fields final.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'What is the difference between Builder pattern and the Lombok @Builder annotation? When does Lombok fall short?'
    💭 Think First
    Lombok @Builder generates a builder at compile time. But it can't express mandatory fields or cross-field validation.
    → Complete Answer
    Lombok @Builder generates the boilerplate automatically. Limitation: all fields are optional by default — you can call build() without setting 'size' and get a null silently. Workarounds: @NonNull on fields (throws NPE at build time), @Builder.Default for defaults. Falls short for: (1) complex cross-field validation ('if crust==STUFFED then size must be LARGE'), (2) step builders (wizard-style API where you must set field A before field B becomes available), (3) building immutable objects with truly mandatory fields validated at compile time. For complex domain objects, write the Builder by hand. For simple DTOs, Lombok is fine.
    Q: 'What is a Step Builder? When is it more appropriate than a regular Builder?'
    💭 Think First
    Step Builder = wizard-style API where each step returns a different interface exposing only the next valid step. Enforces a sequence at compile time.
    → Complete Answer
    Java — Step Builder (compile-time sequence enforcement)
    // Cant call .cheese() before .size(). Compiler enforces the sequence. interface SizeStep { CrustStep size(Size s); } interface CrustStep { CheeseStep crust(Crust c); } interface CheeseStep { BuildStep cheese(Cheese c); } interface BuildStep { BuildStep topping(String t); Pizza build(); } // Usage: mandatory sequence, compiler enforces each step Pizza p = Pizza.builder() .size(Size.LARGE) // must set size first (SizeStep) .crust(Crust.THIN) // then crust (CrustStep) .cheese(Cheese.MOZZ) // then cheese (CheeseStep) .topping("pepperoni") // optional (BuildStep) .build();
    🎯 Practice
    Build a fluent QueryBuilder: QueryBuilder.select("name","age").from("users").where("age > 18").orderBy("name").limit(10).build() → returns an SQL string. Validate that select() and from() are called before build().
    💡 Hint — think before readingQueryBuilder collects state via fluent methods. build() assembles the SQL. Handle WHERE with a List conditions joined by AND. The mandatory field (table) goes in from(), optional fields use defaults.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — solution
    class QueryBuilder { private String table; private String[] cols; private final List<String> conditions = new ArrayList<>(); private Integer limitVal; public static QueryBuilder select(String... cols) { QueryBuilder q=new QueryBuilder(); q.cols=cols; return q; } public QueryBuilder from(String t) { table=t; return this; } public QueryBuilder where(String c) { conditions.add(c); return this; } public QueryBuilder limit(int n) { limitVal=n; return this; } public String build() { String sql = "SELECT "+String.join(",",cols)+" FROM "+table; if(!conditions.isEmpty()) sql+=" WHERE "+String.join(" AND ",conditions); if(limitVal!=null) sql+=" LIMIT "+limitVal; return sql; } }
    🎯 Practice Task
    Design a Builder for an HttpRequest: mandatory fields are url and method. Optional: headers (multiple), body, timeoutMs (default 5000), followRedirects (default true). Enforce that body can only be set if method is POST or PUT.
    Hint — think before readingPut url+method in the Builder constructor (mandatory). For body restriction: either validate in build() throwing if method is GET but body is set, or use a Step Builder where the POST/PUT step exposes setBody() but the GET step doesn't.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — HttpRequest Builder with validation
    class HttpRequest { final String url, method, body; final Map<String,String> headers; final int timeoutMs; final boolean followRedirects; static class Builder { private final String url, method; // mandatory — in constructor private String body; private int timeoutMs = 5000; private boolean followRedirects = true; private final Map<String,String> headers = new LinkedHashMap<>(); Builder(String url, String method) { this.url=url; this.method=method; } public Builder header(String k, String v) { headers.put(k,v); return this; } public Builder body(String b) { this.body=b; return this; } public Builder timeoutMs(int t) { this.timeoutMs=t; return this; } public HttpRequest build() { if(body!=null && !method.matches("POST|PUT|PATCH")) throw new IllegalStateException("Body not allowed for "+method); return new HttpRequest(this); } } }
    03
    Structural & Behavioral Patterns
    // Observer · Strategy · Decorator · State · Facade · Adapter · Proxy
    👁️
    Observer Pattern
    event-driven · pub-sub · decoupled reactions

    Strategy + State Patterns

    Decorator + Facade + Adapter
