    Observer Pattern

    event-driven · pub-sub · decoupled reactions
    🧠 Intuition
    YouTube subscriptionsChannel (Subject) uploads a video. All subscribers (Observers) are notified automatically. The channel doesn't import or know subscriber types — it just calls notifyAll(). Each subscriber independently decides what to do. Observer = pub-sub. Adding a new subscriber type = new class only, zero change to Subject. This is how event systems, message queues, and reactive frameworks work under the hood.
    📐 Structure Diagram
    💻 Complete Stock Market Example
    Java
    interface StockObserver { void onPriceChange(String stock, double price); } class StockMarket { private final Map<String, List<StockObserver>> subs = new HashMap<>(); public void subscribe(String stock, StockObserver obs) { subs.computeIfAbsent(stock, k -> new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>()).add(obs); } public void unsubscribe(String stock, StockObserver obs) { subs.getOrDefault(stock, List.of()).remove(obs); } public void updatePrice(String stock, double price) { // Notify ALL subscribers — they decide what to do subs.getOrDefault(stock, List.of()) .forEach(o -> o.onPriceChange(stock, price)); } } class PriceAlertObserver implements StockObserver { private final double threshold; public PriceAlertObserver(double t) { threshold = t; } public void onPriceChange(String s, double p) { if (p > threshold) System.out.println("ALERT: " + s + " = ₹" + p); } } // Usage StockMarket m = new StockMarket(); m.subscribe("RELIANCE", new PriceAlertObserver(2500)); m.subscribe("RELIANCE", new GraphUpdaterObserver()); m.subscribe("RELIANCE", new AuditLogObserver()); m.updatePrice("RELIANCE", 2620); // all 3 observers notified!
    🏭 Production Scenario
    You have an OrderService that sends emails, triggers inventory updates, generates invoices, and updates analytics — all in the same method. How do you decouple these without breaking the order placement logic?
    Everything is hardwired. Adding a new reaction (SMS, loyalty points) means modifying OrderService. The Observer Pattern decouples the subject from its observers so you can add/remove reactions without touching OrderService.
    Observer Pattern: OrderService publishes an OrderPlacedEvent. Each downstream concern (EmailNotifier, InventoryUpdater, InvoiceGenerator, AnalyticsRecorder) is an independent observer. In Spring: use ApplicationEventPublisher + @EventListener. @Async makes observers non-blocking. @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT) ensures the event only fires when the order is durably saved — prevents sending emails for rolled-back orders. OrderService has zero knowledge of its observers.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'What is the difference between Observer pattern and the Pub/Sub messaging pattern (Kafka)?'
    💭 Think First
    Both decouple publisher from subscriber. The key difference is synchrony, persistence, and whether publisher and subscriber share the same process.
    → Complete Answer
    Observer (in-process): publisher and observer share the JVM. Event delivery is synchronous (or async via thread pool). No durability — if the app crashes, in-flight events are lost. Good for: intra-service decoupling (Spring Events). Pub/Sub via Kafka (out-of-process): publisher sends to Kafka topic. Subscribers run in different services, different JVMs. Events are durable on disk — consumer can re-read from any offset. Good for: inter-service communication, event sourcing, guaranteed delivery. Rule: Observer for in-service decoupling. Kafka for inter-service communication and durability.
    Q: 'What is the risk of @Async EventListener in Spring and how do you handle failures?'
    💭 Think First
    Async means the event listener runs in a separate thread. What happens if it throws an exception?
    → Complete Answer
    Risk: the exception is swallowed — the caller that published the event doesn't see it. The main transaction has already committed. If the InventoryUpdater @Async listener fails, you have a confirmed order but no inventory reservation. Fix: (1) Add @Async error handler: implement AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler — log the failure, alert the team, put the event into a retry queue. (2) For critical side effects, use Kafka + consumer retry instead of in-process async — failed messages are retried with backoff and go to a dead-letter queue. (3) Design for idempotency: retrying the listener produces the same result as running it once.
    🎯 Practice
    Order management: when order status changes, notify InventoryObserver (reserve stock), EmailObserver (send confirmation), AnalyticsObserver (log event). Adding a new observer must require zero changes to Order class.
    💡 Hint — think before readingDefine OrderObserver interface first. Three concrete observers. OrderService holds a list and calls notifyAll() after each status change. Use @TransactionalEventListener so observers fire only after the DB commit.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — solution
    interface OrderObserver { void onStatusChange(Order o, Status prev, Status next); } @Component class InventoryObserver implements OrderObserver { public void onStatusChange(Order o, Status p, Status n) { if(n==CONFIRMED) inventoryService.reserve(o.items()); } } @Service class OrderService { private final List<OrderObserver> observers; public void updateStatus(Order o, Status next) { Status prev = o.status(); o.setStatus(next); orderRepo.save(o); observers.forEach(obs -> obs.onStatusChange(o, prev, next)); } }
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement an in-memory EventBus (no Spring) that supports: subscribe(eventType, handler), unsubscribe(eventType, handler), and publish(event). Handlers should receive events asynchronously.
    Hint — think before readingMap, List>> for subscriptions. publish() should deliver to all registered handlers asynchronously using an ExecutorService. Use wildcard generics carefully — each handler is a Consumer for a specific event type E.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — in-memory async EventBus
    class EventBus { private final Map<Class<?>, List<Consumer<?>>> handlers = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); private final ExecutorService exec = Executors.newCachedThreadPool(); public <E> void subscribe(Class<E> type, Consumer<E> h) { handlers.computeIfAbsent(type, k -> new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>()).add(h); } public <E> void unsubscribe(Class<E> type, Consumer<E> h) { handlers.getOrDefault(type, List.of()).remove(h); } @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") public <E> void publish(E event) { handlers.getOrDefault(event.getClass(), List.of()).forEach(h -> exec.submit(() -> ((Consumer<E>)h).accept(event))); } }

    Strategy + State Patterns

    swap algorithms · model state machines
    🧠 Strategy Intuition
    GPS navigation analogyYou choose: fastest / avoid tolls / shortest. Same navigator, swappable algorithm. When you see if/else choosing "different ways to do X" in code — that is a Strategy waiting to emerge. The goal: the context (navigator, shopping cart, payment service) doesn't know or care which algorithm runs. It just calls strategy.execute().
    💻 Strategy — if/else to Pattern
    Java — before and after
    // ✗ BEFORE: adding Crypto payment means editing PaymentService class PaymentService { void pay(String method, double amt) { if (method.equals("UPI") ) { /* upi logic */ } else if (method.equals("CARD") ) { /* card logic */ } else if (method.equals("WALLET") ) { /* wallet logic */ } // adding CRYPTO: edit this class → OCP violation } } // ✓ AFTER: Strategy Pattern interface PaymentStrategy { void pay(double amount); } class UpiStrategy implements PaymentStrategy { public void pay(double a) { /*...*/ } } class CardStrategy implements PaymentStrategy { public void pay(double a) { /*...*/ } } class CryptoStrategy implements PaymentStrategy { public void pay(double a) { /*...*/ } } class ShoppingCart { private PaymentStrategy strategy; public void setPayment(PaymentStrategy s) { strategy = s; } public void checkout(double total) { strategy.pay(total); } } // Adding Crypto? New CryptoStrategy class only. ShoppingCart = 0 changes.
    💡 State Pattern — Vending Machine
    When to use State vs if/elseIf an object's behaviour changes based on its internal state AND the state transitions are non-trivial, use State Pattern. Signal words: "when the order is PENDING it can be cancelled, but when SHIPPED it cannot." Each state encapsulates its own behaviour. No giant switch on state allowed.
    💻 Vending Machine State Machine
    📚 References
    🌐
    Refactoring.Guru — Strategy
    refactoring.guru/design-patterns/strategy
    ↗
    🌐
    Refactoring.Guru — State
    refactoring.guru/design-patterns/state
    ↗
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Your PaymentService uses if-else to handle CARD, UPI, WALLET, NETBANKING. Each branch has 50+ lines. Adding BNPL requires touching this method. An interviewer asks you to refactor using a design pattern.
    This is the classic Strategy pattern problem. The algorithm (payment processing logic) varies independently from the context (PaymentService). Encapsulate each algorithm in its own class.
    Strategy Pattern: Interface PaymentStrategy with process(Payment). Each payment method is a concrete strategy. PaymentService holds the selected strategy and delegates. Selection happens at runtime (factory/map lookup). Adding BNPL = new class BNPLStrategy. Zero changes to PaymentService. For State Pattern comparison: Strategy = interchangeable algorithms for the SAME operation (how to pay). State = object changes behaviour as its internal STATE changes (Order: PLACED→CONFIRMED→SHIPPED — each state responds differently to the same event).
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'How is Strategy Pattern different from the State Pattern? Give a concrete example of each from a payment system.'
    💭 Think First
    Both use polymorphism via an interface. The difference is WHO decides which implementation runs and whether it changes during an object's lifetime.
    → Complete Answer
    Strategy: the CLIENT chooses and injects the algorithm. PaymentService.process(payment) where strategy was chosen upfront. The strategy doesn't change during a transaction. State: the OBJECT transitions itself between states. PaymentTransaction with states PENDING→PROCESSING→COMPLETED/FAILED. The transition happens inside the object in response to events. Same method (process()) behaves completely differently depending on current state. Key distinction: Strategy = policy choice. State = lifecycle progression.
    Q: 'Can you combine Strategy and State patterns? Give an example.'
    💭 Think First
    Yes — a State can hold a Strategy. The State decides the behaviour, the Strategy decides HOW to implement that behaviour within the state.
    → Complete Answer
    OrderState pattern where each state holds pricing/shipping strategies: ProcessingState holds a PricingStrategy (the order's pricing is locked when it enters Processing). PricingStrategy might vary (Member discount strategy vs Standard strategy) — that's chosen at order creation. The State manages lifecycle; the Strategy manages the algorithm within that lifecycle. Both patterns work at different axes of variability: State = WHEN (lifecycle position), Strategy = HOW (algorithm choice).
    🎯 Practice (State)
    Build an Elevator state machine: IDLE → MOVING_UP → MOVING_DOWN → DOOR_OPEN. Each state handles floorRequested(), doorButton(), arrived() differently. No if/else on state variable allowed — only State pattern classes.
    💡 Hint — think before readingDefine ElevatorState interface with handleRequest() and display(). Implement IDLE, MOVING_UP, MOVING_DOWN states. Each state's handleRequest() transitions to the next state by calling elevator.setState(newState).
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — solution
    interface ElevatorState { void handleRequest(Elevator e, int floor); String display(); } class IdleState implements ElevatorState { public void handleRequest(Elevator e, int floor) { if(floor > e.currentFloor()) e.setState(new MovingUpState()); else if(floor < e.currentFloor()) e.setState(new MovingDownState()); else e.setState(new DoorOpenState()); } public String display() { return "IDLE"; } }
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement a SortContext that can switch sorting strategies at runtime: BubbleSort, QuickSort, MergeSort. The context exposes setStrategy(SortStrategy) and sort(int[] arr). Show that you can sort the same array with different strategies without changing the context.
    Hint — think before readingSortStrategy interface with sort(int[]). Each algorithm implements it. SortContext has a field SortStrategy currentStrategy. setStrategy() swaps it at runtime. sort() delegates to currentStrategy.sort(). Test: same array sorted first with BubbleSort, then QuickSort — results must be identical but internal algorithm differs.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — Strategy with runtime switching
    @FunctionalInterface interface SortStrategy { void sort(int[] arr); } class SortContext { private SortStrategy strategy; public void setStrategy(SortStrategy s) { this.strategy = s; } public void sort(int[] arr) { strategy.sort(arr); } } // Usage: switch at runtime based on array size SortContext ctx = new SortContext(); ctx.setStrategy(arr.length < 100 ? (SortStrategy) Arrays::sort // built-in for small arrays : arr2 -> mergeSort(arr2, 0, arr2.length-1)); // custom for large ctx.sort(data);

    Decorator + Facade + Adapter

    wrap · simplify · translate
    🧠 Decorator Intuition
    Coffee order analogyStart with BasicCoffee. Add milk → MilkDecorator wraps it. Add sugar → SugarDecorator wraps that. Each layer adds behaviour without modifying the original. Decorator = Russian nesting dolls. It solves class explosion: instead of MilkCoffee, SugarCoffee, MilkSugarCoffee... you have 3 decorators that combine freely.
    💻 Coffee Decorator Example
    Java
    interface Coffee { String getDescription(); double getCost(); } class BasicCoffee implements Coffee { public String getDescription() { return "Basic coffee"; } public double getCost() { return 40; } } // Abstract decorator — implements AND wraps the same interface abstract class CoffeeDecorator implements Coffee { protected Coffee wrapped; public CoffeeDecorator(Coffee c) { wrapped = c; } } class MilkDecorator extends CoffeeDecorator { public MilkDecorator(Coffee c) { super(c); } public String getDescription() { return wrapped.getDescription() + ", milk"; } public double getCost() { return wrapped.getCost() + 15; } } class SugarDecorator extends CoffeeDecorator { public SugarDecorator(Coffee c) { super(c); } public String getDescription() { return wrapped.getDescription() + ", sugar"; } public double getCost() { return wrapped.getCost() + 5; } } // Combine freely at runtime — no new classes needed Coffee order = new SugarDecorator(new MilkDecorator(new BasicCoffee())); System.out.println(order.getDescription()); // Basic coffee, milk, sugar System.out.println(order.getCost()); // 60.0
    💡 Facade vs Proxy vs Adapter — One-Line Distinction
    Facade

    Simplify a complex subsystem. Hotel concierge — you say "I need airport transport," concierge handles taxi, bill, luggage. One simple interface over many subsystems.

    Proxy

    Same interface as real object, but adds: caching, access control, logging. Credit card = proxy for bank account. Same "pay" action, extra controls added.

    Adapter

    Make incompatible interfaces work together. Power adapter for US plug in EU socket. Neither plug nor socket changes — adapter translates.

    Decorator vs Proxy

    Decorator adds new behaviour. Proxy controls access to existing behaviour. Subtle but important: decorator changes what happens; proxy controls whether and how it happens.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    You have a legacy PaymentGateway with method initiatePayment(Map params). Your new code uses Payment objects. You can't modify the legacy class. How do you integrate it?
    Adapter pattern: you have two incompatible interfaces. You can't change the legacy code. The Adapter wraps the legacy object and translates between your interface and theirs.
    Adapter: Create class LegacyGatewayAdapter implements PaymentProcessor. It holds a reference to LegacyPaymentGateway. Its process(Payment) method converts Payment to the Map format the legacy API expects and calls initiatePayment(). Callers use PaymentProcessor — they never see the legacy API. Facade: If you had a complex subsystem (5 classes: AuthService, TokenService, PaymentAPI, AuditService, NotificationService) and wanted one simple method processPayment(), Facade provides that unified interface. Facade simplifies — doesn't convert types. Decorator: Adds behaviour to an object without changing its interface. LoggingPaymentProcessor implements PaymentProcessor, holds a PaymentProcessor delegate, calls delegate.process() and wraps it with logging. Same interface, new behaviour stacked.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'Decorator vs Inheritance for adding behaviour — when does each fail?'
    💭 Think First
    Decorator adds behaviour at runtime without subclassing. Inheritance adds behaviour at compile time via subclassing. When does each break down?
    → Complete Answer
    Inheritance fails when: (1) you need multiple combinations of behaviours (LoggingEncryptedCachingProcessor — you'd need 8 subclasses for 3 features). (2) The superclass changes break all subclasses. (3) You can't modify the base class. Decorator fails when: (1) the component interface has many methods — each decorator must implement all of them even if it only cares about one. (2) Order of decoration matters and is hard to reason about. (3) Identity checks fail: encryptedProcessor instanceof Processor is true but encryptedProcessor == originalProcessor is false. Java I/O streams are the classic Decorator example: BufferedInputStream wraps FileInputStream adds buffering; GZIPInputStream wraps that adds decompression.
    Q: 'Show me how you would add rate limiting, logging, and retry to a PaymentProcessor without modifying it.'
    💭 Think First
    Three cross-cutting concerns, same interface, stacked — this is exactly what Decorator is built for.
    → Complete Answer
    Java — stacked Decorators
    interface PaymentProcessor { Result process(Payment p); } class LoggingDecorator implements PaymentProcessor { private final PaymentProcessor delegate; public Result process(Payment p) { log.info("Processing: {}", p.id()); Result r = delegate.process(p); log.info("Result: {}", r.status()); return r; } } class RetryDecorator implements PaymentProcessor { private final PaymentProcessor delegate; private final int maxAttempts; public Result process(Payment p) { for(int i=0; i<maxAttempts; i++) { try { return delegate.process(p); } catch(TransientException e) { if(i==maxAttempts-1) throw e; } } return null; } } // Compose: rate-limit wraps retry wraps logging wraps real processor PaymentProcessor processor = new RateLimitDecorator(new RetryDecorator( new LoggingDecorator(new StripeProcessor()), 3), 100);
    🎯 Practice
    Build a text formatter using Decorator: PlainText → BoldDecorator → ItalicDecorator → UnderlineDecorator. Each wraps the previous. Output: "<u><i><b>Hello</b></i></u>".
    💡 Hint — think before readingDecorator wraps another object of the same interface. TextComponent has getText(). PlainText returns raw text. BoldDecorator wraps any TextComponent and adds HTML tags. Chain decorators: new Bold(new Italic(new Plain('hello'))).
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — solution
    interface TextComponent { String getText(); } class PlainText implements TextComponent { private final String text; PlainText(String t) { text=t; } public String getText() { return text; } } class BoldDecorator implements TextComponent { private final TextComponent wrapped; BoldDecorator(TextComponent c) { wrapped=c; } public String getText() { return "<b>" + wrapped.getText() + "</b>"; } } class ItalicDecorator implements TextComponent { private final TextComponent wrapped; ItalicDecorator(TextComponent c) { wrapped=c; } public String getText() { return "<i>" + wrapped.getText() + "</i>"; } } // Usage: new BoldDecorator(new ItalicDecorator(new PlainText("hello"))).getText() // Result: <b><i>hello</i></b>
    🎯 Practice Task
    You have a TemperatureSensor interface with getTemperature() returning Celsius. A 3rd-party chart library expects Fahrenheit via getReading(). Write the Adapter.
    Hint — think before readingAdapter implements the 3rd party interface (the target), holds a reference to TemperatureSensor (the adaptee), and converts in getReading(). C to F = (C × 9/5) + 32.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — Temperature Adapter
    interface FahrenheitSensor { double getReading(); } // target (library expects) interface TemperatureSensor { double getTemperature(); } // adaptee (what we have) class CelsiusToFahrenheitAdapter implements FahrenheitSensor { private final TemperatureSensor sensor; // wraps the adaptee CelsiusToFahrenheitAdapter(TemperatureSensor s) { sensor = s; } public double getReading() { return sensor.getTemperature() * 9.0/5.0 + 32; // Celsius → Fahrenheit } } // chart.display(new CelsiusToFahrenheitAdapter(mySensor)) — library never knows about Celsius
    04
    Concurrency Control
    // Threads · Locks · ReadWriteLock · Producer-Consumer — the SDE-2 differentiator
    🔒
    Threads, Locks & Race Conditions
    why concurrent code breaks — and how to fix it

    Threads, Locks & Race Conditions

    why concurrent code breaks — and how to fix it
    🧠 Intuition — The Race Condition
    Two threads, one parking spotThread A reads availableSpots=1. Thread B reads availableSpots=1. Both decide to book. Both write availableSpots=0 and assign the spot. You now have two cars in one spot and availableSpots=0 but two assignments made. This is a race condition — concurrent reads followed by concurrent writes to shared state. The fix: make read+write atomic with a lock.
    📐 Race Condition vs Lock Diagram
    💻 Thread-Safe Parking Floor
    Java — ReentrantLock
    class ParkingFloor { private final List<ParkingSpot> spots; private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); // one per floor public Optional<ParkingSpot> allocateSpot(Vehicle v) { lock.lock(); // ONE thread enters here at a time try { return spots.stream() .filter(s -> !s.isOccupied() && s.canFit(v)) .findFirst() .map(s -> { s.assign(v); return s; }); // read+assign = atomic } finally { lock.unlock(); // ALWAYS in finally — even if exception thrown } } // tryLock — don't block forever (for time-critical paths) public Optional<ParkingSpot> allocateWithTimeout(Vehicle v) throws InterruptedException { if (lock.tryLock(500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { try { return allocateSpot(v); } finally { lock.unlock(); } } return Optional.empty(); // couldn't get lock in 500ms } }
    💡 ReadWriteLock — For Read-Heavy Systems
    When reads dominateConfig read 10000x/sec, updated once/minute. A plain lock blocks all readers even when they could safely run concurrently. ReadWriteLock rule: multiple readers run together. A writer gets exclusive access — no readers or other writers. Perfect for: LRU Cache, Rate Limiter config, in-memory stores.
    💻 Producer-Consumer with BlockingQueue
    Java — async logging system
    class AsyncLogger { // BlockingQueue handles all wait/notify logic for you private final BlockingQueue<String> queue = new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(1000); private final Thread writer; public AsyncLogger() { writer = new Thread(() -> { while (true) { try { String msg = queue.take(); // blocks if queue empty — no busy-wait if (msg.equals("POISON")) break; // graceful shutdown writeToFile(msg); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }, "log-writer"); writer.start(); } // Producers call this from any thread — non-blocking public void log(String msg) { if (!queue.offer(msg)) { // offer = non-blocking, returns false if full System.err.println("Log queue full — dropping: " + msg); } } public void shutdown() throws InterruptedException { queue.put("POISON"); // signals writer thread to stop writer.join(); } }

    ↗
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Two threads both call withdraw() on the same BankAccount simultaneously. Both read balance=1000, both check 1000>=500 passes, both subtract 500, both write 500. Final balance: 500 instead of 0. Fix it.
    This is a classic check-then-act race condition. The read-check-write sequence is not atomic. Multiple threads interleave between the check and the write.
    Option 1 — synchronized method: Makes the entire method a critical section. Only one thread at a time. Simple, correct. Downside: coarse-grained, blocks all threads even for reads. Option 2 — AtomicReference with CAS: Read current balance, compute new balance, compare-and-set — retry if another thread changed it. Lock-free, high throughput for low contention. Option 3 — Database pessimistic lock: SELECT FOR UPDATE — only one transaction can hold the lock on the row. Correct across multiple app instances (pods). This is the production answer for financial systems.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'What is a deadlock? How would you detect and prevent one in Java?'
    💭 Think First
    Deadlock: Thread A holds lock L1, waits for L2. Thread B holds L2, waits for L1. Both blocked forever. How do you prevent this from happening?
    → Complete Answer
    Detection: Thread dump (jstack) shows BLOCKED threads in a cycle. JConsole/VisualVM shows deadlock graphically. Prevention strategies: (1) Lock ordering: always acquire locks in the same order. If every thread acquires L1 before L2, no cycle is possible. (2) tryLock with timeout: lock.tryLock(500, MILLISECONDS) — if can't acquire in time, release held locks and retry later. (3) Avoid nested locks: don't call external code while holding a lock. (4) Use concurrent collections: ConcurrentHashMap eliminates most explicit locking needs.
    Q: 'Explain the Java Memory Model. What does happens-before mean and why does it matter?'
    💭 Think First
    Without happens-before guarantees, Thread A's writes may not be visible to Thread B even after Thread A finishes writing. The JMM defines when visibility is guaranteed.
    → Complete Answer
    The JMM defines happens-before (HB) relationships: if action A HB action B, then A's effects are visible to B. Key HB rules: (1) unlock HB subsequent lock of the same monitor. (2) volatile write HB subsequent volatile read of the same variable. (3) Thread.start() HB any action in the started thread. (4) All actions in thread T HB Thread.join(T). Why it matters: without these, the CPU and compiler can reorder instructions for performance. A double-checked locking without volatile works by accident on x86 but breaks on ARM because the write to instance can be reordered. volatile forces a memory barrier — the write is flushed to main memory before the store completes.
    🎯 Practice
    Simulate 100 threads trying to book the last 5 parking spots. Without lock: observe double-bookings. With ReentrantLock: exactly 5 spots allocated, rest rejected. Print which thread got which spot.
    💡 Hint — think before readingUse Semaphore(5) to model the 5 spots. Each thread calls acquire() before parking and release() when leaving. Run 20 threads. At any point, available permits should never go below 0.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — solution
    class ParkingLot { private final Semaphore spots = new Semaphore(5, true); // fair=true public void park(String car) throws InterruptedException { spots.acquire(); System.out.println(car + " parked. Available: " + spots.availablePermits()); Thread.sleep(100); spots.release(); System.out.println(car + " left. Available: " + spots.availablePermits()); } } // Test: assert availablePermits() never < 0 under concurrent access
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement a thread-safe counter that supports increment(), decrement(), and get() used by 100 concurrent threads. Show three implementations: synchronized, AtomicInteger, and LongAdder. Explain the trade-offs.
    Hint — think before readingsynchronized gives mutual exclusion but contention is high under 100 threads. AtomicInteger uses CAS — better throughput but CAS retries under high contention. LongAdder maintains per-thread cells and combines on get() — best throughput for write-heavy workloads, slightly stale reads.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — three counter implementations
    // Option 1: synchronized — correct but high contention at scale class SyncCounter { private int n; public synchronized void inc() {n++;} public synchronized int get() {return n;} } // Option 2: AtomicInteger — lock-free CAS, good for moderate contention class AtomicCounter { private final AtomicInteger n = new AtomicInteger(); public void inc() {n.incrementAndGet();} public int get() {return n.get();} } // Option 3: LongAdder — best throughput for high-write, eventual-consistent read class AdderCounter { private final LongAdder n = new LongAdder(); public void inc() {n.increment();} public long get() {return n.sum();} } // LongAdder: maintains per-CPU-cache-line cells → zero contention on increment // sum() adds all cells — may read slightly stale values // Ideal for metrics, event counters, rate tracking

    Parking Lot — Full Design

    entities, patterns, concurrency, end to end
    📐 Complete Class Diagram
    PARKING LOT — COMPLETE CLASS DIAGRAM WITH PATTERNS APPLIED
    💻 End-to-End Walkthrough
    Entities
    Allocate Spot
    Exit + Payment
    Java
    public class ParkingLot { private static ParkingLot instance; private final List<ParkingFloor> floors = new ArrayList<>(); private ParkingLot() {} public static synchronized ParkingLot getInstance() { if (instance == null) instance = new ParkingLot(); return instance; } public void addFloor(ParkingFloor f) { floors.add(f); } public Ticket parkVehicle(Vehicle v) { for (ParkingFloor f : floors) { Optional<ParkingSpot> spot = f.allocateSpot(v); if (spot.isPresent()) { return new Ticket(v, spot.get(), LocalDateTime.now()); } } throw new IllegalStateException("Parking full"); } }
    Java — already shown thread-safe ParkingFloor.allocateSpot()
    // See Week 4 for the full ReentrantLock implementation. // Key idea: find + assign must be ONE atomic operation, // otherwise two threads can grab the same spot. floor.allocateSpot(vehicle); // returns Optional<ParkingSpot>
    Java — exit flow with Strategy payment
    interface PaymentStrategy { double calculate(Ticket t); } class HourlyPayment implements PaymentStrategy { public double calculate(Ticket t) { long hours = Duration.between(t.getEntryTime(), LocalDateTime.now()).toHours() + 1; return hours * 20; // ₹20/hour } } class ExitService { private PaymentStrategy strategy; public ExitService(PaymentStrategy s) { strategy = s; } public double processExit(Ticket ticket) { double amount = strategy.calculate(ticket); ticket.getSpot().free(); // mark spot free again return amount; } } // Swap HourlyPayment for FlatRatePayment, WeekendPayment — zero code change here.
    🏭 Production Scenario
    An interviewer says: 'Design a Parking Lot system for 5 floors, 3 vehicle types, hourly billing, and show me how to handle 1000 concurrent vehicle arrivals without double-booking.'
    This has two parts: (1) OOP class design — the hierarchy, relationships, responsibilities. (2) Concurrency — how do you prevent two threads allocating the same spot? Work through OOP first, then address concurrency.
    Class Hierarchy: Vehicle (abstract) → Car/Bike/Truck. ParkingSpot(id, type, AtomicBoolean occupied). ParkingFloor(List<ParkingSpot>). ParkingLot(singleton, List<ParkingFloor>, Map<ticketId,Ticket>). Ticket(spotId, vehicleId, entryTime). FeeStrategy interface → HourlyFee. Concurrency: ParkingSpot.tryPark() uses CAS: occupied.compareAndSet(false, true) — exactly one thread wins per spot. The lot scans all spots calling tryPark() until one succeeds. Per-type Semaphores give fast 'lot full' rejection without scanning. At scale: pre-allocate spot ranges to each app instance to eliminate cross-instance coordination.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'How would you add a reservation system — book a spot in advance for a time window?'
    💭 Think First
    Reservations introduce temporal complexity: a spot can be AVAILABLE now but RESERVED from 3pm-5pm. Need to check both current state and future bookings.
    → Complete Answer
    Add SpotReservation(spotId, startTime, endTime, userId). Spot state becomes: AVAILABLE / RESERVED / OCCUPIED. When a vehicle arrives with a reservation: validate reservationId, check reservation hasn't expired, transition to OCCUPIED. When scanning for available spots for walk-ins: exclude spots with active reservations covering the requested time window. For walk-in duration estimation: assume average 2-hour stay for overlap checking. Scheduled job releases expired reservations every minute.
    Q: 'How do you calculate the fee if the vehicle parks overnight spanning midnight?'
    💭 Think First
    Simple hours * rate breaks if you span time boundaries with different rates. Think about how to handle daily caps and rate changes.
    → Complete Answer
    Store entryTime as Instant (UTC). On exit: compute Duration.between(entry, exit). For simple hourly: Math.ceil(minutes/60.0) * hourlyRate. For overnight with daily cap: iterate hour-by-hour or use LocalDateTime with rate schedule lookup. Daily cap: min(totalCalculated, dailyCap). Store all fee components in the Ticket for audit. Never recalculate — store the calculated fee at exit time.
    🎯 Practice
    Implement this end-to-end in 40 minutes. Time yourself. Focus first on class hierarchy + patterns, then add concurrency as a second pass.
    💡 Hint — think before readingClass hierarchy first: Vehicle, ParkingSpot (AtomicBoolean occupied), ParkingFloor (List), ParkingLot. tryPark() uses compareAndSet(false, true) — exactly one thread wins per spot. Build in this order: entities, then parkVehicle(), then addDisplayBoard().
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — solution
    class ParkingLot { private final List<ParkingFloor> floors; public Optional<Ticket> park(Vehicle v) { for(ParkingFloor f : floors) { for(ParkingSpot s : f.spotsFor(v.type())) { if(s.tryPark()) // CAS - atomic return Optional.of(new Ticket(s, v, Instant.now())); } } return Optional.empty(); // lot full } public void exit(Ticket t) { t.spot().free(); BigDecimal fee = feeStrategy.calculate(Duration.between(t.entryTime(), Instant.now()), t.vehicleType()); paymentService.charge(t.vehicle(), fee); } }
    🎯 Practice Task
    Extend the Parking Lot design to show real-time availability on a digital display board per floor. The board should update in <100ms when a spot is taken or freed without polling. Design the data flow.
    Hint — think before readingObserver Pattern: ParkingSpot fires SpotEvent(floor, type, isOccupied) on state change. DisplayBoard observes all spots. ConcurrentHashMap stores counts atomically. No polling — event-driven push.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — event-driven display board
    record SpotEvent(int floor, VehicleType type, boolean occupied) {} class DisplayBoard { private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, AtomicInteger> available = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); public void onSpotChanged(SpotEvent e) { String key = e.floor() + ":" + e.type(); available.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new AtomicInteger(0)) .addAndGet(e.occupied() ? -1 : 1); // occupied=-1, freed=+1 refreshDisplay(); } public void refreshDisplay() { available.forEach((k,v) -> System.out.printf("%s: %d spots%n", k, v.get())); } }

    Chess & Elevator — Pattern Recognition

    polymorphic movement · state machine scheduling
    🧠 Chess — Key Insight
    Polymorphic movement is the heart of this problemBoard holds Cells. Each Cell may have a Piece. Piece is abstract with method getValidMoves(board) — King, Queen, Rook, Bishop, Knight, Pawn each override it differently. The Game class doesn't know HOW each piece moves — it just calls piece.getValidMoves() and trusts polymorphism. This is the cleanest real-world demo of polymorphism in any LLD problem.
    💻 Chess Entity Skeleton
    Java
    abstract class Piece { protected Color color; protected Position position; public abstract List<Position> getValidMoves(Board board); } class Knight extends Piece { public List<Position> getValidMoves(Board board) { // L-shaped movement — 8 possible offsets int[][] offsets = {{1,2},{2,1},{-1,2},{-2,1},{1,-2},{2,-1},{-1,-2},{-2,-1}}; List<Position> moves = new ArrayList<>(); for (int[] off : offsets) { Position p = new Position(position.row+off[0], position.col+off[1]); if (board.isValidAndNotSameColor(p, color)) moves.add(p); } return moves; } } class Game { private Board board; private Deque<Move> history = new ArrayDeque<>(); // for undo public boolean movePiece(Position from, Position to) { Piece piece = board.getPiece(from); if (!piece.getValidMoves(board).contains(to)) return false; // polymorphism! history.push(new Move(from, to, piece, board.getPiece(to))); board.movePiece(from, to); return true; } public void undo() { if (!history.isEmpty()) board.revert(history.pop()); } }
    🧠 Elevator — Key Insight: State Pattern + Scheduling
    Two layers: per-car state machine + multi-car schedulingEach ElevatorCar has a state (Idle, MovingUp, MovingDown, DoorOpen) — classic State pattern. The ElevatorController decides WHICH car serves a request — a scheduling algorithm. Recognize this split immediately: state pattern for behaviour, strategy pattern for car selection.
    ⚠ Scheduling — The SDE-2 Follow-up Question
    AlgorithmHow it worksStarvation risk
    Nearest CarPick the closest idle/same-direction carHigh — far floors starve under load
    SCAN (elevator algo)Sweep up serving all up-requests, then sweep downNone — like a disk scheduler sweep
    Round Robin per carDistribute requests evenly across carsLow — but not always optimal travel time
    Interview answer: "I'd start with nearest-car for simplicity. If starvation becomes a concern, I'd switch to SCAN — the scheduling strategy is injected via an interface, so swapping algorithms requires zero changes to ElevatorCar."
    📚 Reference
    🎓
    Grokking the OOD Interview — Elevator & Chess chapters
    educative.io/courses/grokking-the-object-oriented-design-interview
    ↗
    🏭 Production Scenario
    An interviewer asks: 'Design a Chess game. Focus on the move validation and piece hierarchy. How many classes would you have and why?'
    Chess is about piece behaviour polymorphism. Each piece knows its own legal moves. The Board delegates to pieces. The Game orchestrates state. Don't enumerate all pieces — explain the hierarchy and delegation principle.
    Hierarchy: Piece (abstract, has color, position, abstract isValidMove(from,to,board)). Subclasses: King, Queen, Rook, Bishop, Knight, Pawn — each overrides isValidMove with its own logic. Board: 8×8 grid of Optional<Piece>. Provides getPiece(Position), isEmpty(Position), isEnemyAt(Position, Color). Game: maintains currentTurn, checks isInCheck(), isCheckmate(), handles en passant and castling state. MoveValidator: calls piece.isValidMove() then verifies the move doesn't leave own King in check (simulate move, check for check, undo). Interview tip: Bishop moves diagonally = abs(dx)==abs(dy) && no piece in path. Knight: (abs(dx)==1&&abs(dy)==2)||(abs(dx)==2&&abs(dy)==1) — no path check. Pawn: most complex (direction, double-first-move, capture diagonally, en passant, promotion).
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'How do you check if a King is in check? Walk through the algorithm.'
    💭 Think First
    In check = at least one enemy piece can legally move to the King's position in the NEXT move. How do you check this efficiently?
    → Complete Answer
    Iterate all enemy pieces. For each enemy piece, call piece.isValidMove(enemyPos, kingPos, board). If any returns true, the King is in check. Optimization: instead of checking all pieces, compute 'attack rays' from the King's position — scan diagonals (bishop/queen attacks), ranks/files (rook/queen attacks), knight-jump positions, pawn-capture positions. First piece found in each ray determines if that attack type exists. This reduces from O(pieces × board) to O(1) per attack type.
    Q: 'How would you implement the undo feature (take back a move) in Chess?'
    💭 Think First
    Command Pattern! Each move is a command. Undo reverses it. But Chess has special state: captured pieces, castling rights, en passant target — all need to be restored.
    → Complete Answer
    MoveCommand stores: fromPos, toPos, movingPiece, capturedPiece (nullable), previous castling rights, previous en passant target. execute(): update board, clear en passant, update castling rights. undo(): restore board to exact previous state — put movingPiece back at fromPos, restore capturedPiece at toPos, restore castling rights and en passant target. Game holds a Deque<MoveCommand> as undo stack. Ctrl+Z = stack.pop().undo(). This is exactly how chess engines implement takebacks.
    🎯 Practice
    Build core chess (no castling/en-passant) in 35 minutes, then add undo. Build a 1-car elevator, then extend to 3 cars — the extension should require zero ElevatorCar changes, only Controller changes.
    💡 Hint — think before readingChess Pawn: direction is +1 row for WHITE, -1 for BLACK. First move can be 2 squares (only if hasMoved==false). Capture is diagonal (dc==1, dr==dir, enemy at destination). Elevator SCAN: use two TreeSets (upQueue, downQueue). Moving up: process smallest in upQueue first.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — solution
    // Pawn move validation class Pawn extends Piece { public boolean isValidMove(Position from, Position to, Board b) { int dir = color==WHITE ? 1 : -1; int dr = to.row()-from.row(), dc = Math.abs(to.col()-from.col()); if(dc==0 && dr==dir && b.isEmpty(to)) return true; // one step forward if(dc==0 && dr==2*dir && !hasMoved && b.isEmpty(to)) return true; // first move 2 squares if(dc==1 && dr==dir && b.hasEnemy(to,color)) return true; // diagonal capture return false; } } // Elevator SCAN class Elevator { TreeSet<Integer> upQueue = new TreeSet<>(); TreeSet<Integer> downQueue = new TreeSet<>(Comparator.reverseOrder()); Direction dir = UP; public void processNext() { if(dir==UP && !upQueue.isEmpty()) moveTo(upQueue.pollFirst()); else if(!downQueue.isEmpty()) { dir=DOWN; moveTo(downQueue.pollFirst()); } else if(!upQueue.isEmpty()) { dir=UP; moveTo(upQueue.pollFirst()); } } }
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement isValidMove() for a Rook. The Rook moves horizontally or vertically any number of squares but cannot jump over pieces.
    Hint — think before readingRook move is valid if: (1) same row OR same column (not both — that would be no movement). (2) No piece lies between start and end positions in the path. Check path by iterating from start to end (exclusive) in the direction of movement.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — Rook move validation
    class Rook extends Piece { public boolean isValidMove(Position from, Position to, Board board) { if(from.equals(to)) return false; boolean sameRow = from.row() == to.row(); boolean sameCol = from.col() == to.col(); if(!sameRow && !sameCol) return false; // not horizontal or vertical // Check if destination is occupied by own piece if(board.hasFriendlyPiece(to, color)) return false; // Check path: iterate from start (exclusive) to end (exclusive) int dr = Integer.signum(to.row() - from.row()); // direction: -1, 0, or 1 int dc = Integer.signum(to.col() - from.col()); int r = from.row()+dr, c = from.col()+dc; while(r != to.row() || c != to.col()) { if(!board.isEmpty(new Position(r,c))) return false; // piece in the way r += dr; c += dc; } return true; } }

    Splitwise — Debt Simplification

    the real challenge isn't CRUD, it's the algorithm
    🧠 Intuition — What's Actually Hard Here
    It's not tracking who paid — it's minimizing transactionsIf A owes B ₹100 and B owes C ₹100, naive settlement needs 2 transactions. But A could just pay C directly — 1 transaction. The core algorithm: compute net balance per person (positive = owed money, negative = owes money), then greedily match the biggest creditor with the biggest debtor repeatedly. Everything else (Users, Groups, Expenses) is CRUD around this core.
    📐 Debt Simplification Visual
    💻 Greedy Settlement Algorithm
    Java — minimize transaction count
    class SettlementService { // Step 1: compute net balance per user across all expenses public List<Transaction> simplifyDebts(Map<String,Double> netBalances) { PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<String,Double>> creditors = new PriorityQueue<>((a,b) -> Double.compare(b.getValue(), a.getValue())); // max-heap PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<String,Double>> debtors = new PriorityQueue<>((a,b) -> Double.compare(a.getValue(), b.getValue())); // min-heap (most negative first) for (var e : netBalances.entrySet()) { if (e.getValue() > 0) creditors.add(e); else if (e.getValue() < 0) debtors.add(e); } List<Transaction> result = new ArrayList<>(); while (!creditors.isEmpty() && !debtors.isEmpty()) { var credit = creditors.poll(); var debit = debtors.poll(); double amount = Math.min(credit.getValue(), -debit.getValue()); result.add(new Transaction(debit.getKey(), credit.getKey(), amount)); double remCredit = credit.getValue() - amount; double remDebit = debit.getValue() + amount; if (remCredit > 0.01) creditors.add(Map.entry(credit.getKey(), remCredit)); if (remDebit < -0.01) debtors.add(Map.entry(debit.getKey(), remDebit)); } return result; // minimum-transaction settlement plan } }
    💡 The Split Types — Strategy Pattern
    EqualSplit

    totalAmount / numPeople. Simplest — each person pays the same share.

    ExactSplit

    Each person's amount specified explicitly. Validate: sum of shares must equal total expense.

    PercentSplit

    Each person's percentage specified. Validate: percentages must sum to exactly 100%.

    Why Strategy

    Expense holds a List<Split>. Adding a new split type (e.g. ShareBasedSplit) = new class only, zero changes to Expense or Group.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    4 friends go on a trip. Alice pays ₹1200 for dinner (all 4), Bob pays ₹800 for taxi (Bob, Carol, Dave), Carol pays ₹600 for hotel (all 4). Show the minimum transactions to settle all debts.
    Calculate net balance per person = total paid - total owed. Then apply the two-pointer greedy: pair the biggest debtor with the biggest creditor, settle as much as possible, repeat.
    Net balances: Alice: paid 1200, owes 300+150=450 → net +750. Bob: paid 800, owes 0+267+150=417 → net +383. Carol: paid 600, owes 300+267+150=717 → net -117. Dave: paid 0, owes 300+267+150=717 → net -717. Settle: Sort: Dave(-717), Carol(-117), Bob(+383), Alice(+750). Dave→Alice ₹717 (Dave done, Alice: +33). Carol→Alice ₹33 (Alice done, Carol: -84). Carol→Bob ₹84. Total: 3 transactions (minimum possible for 4 people).
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'Why is 3 transactions the minimum for 4 people? Prove it.'
    💭 Think First
    Think graph theory: in a debt graph, how many edges do you need at minimum to connect N nodes?
    → Complete Answer
    For N people, minimum transactions = N-1. Proof: any valid settlement must zero out every person's net balance. Each transaction zeros out at least one person's balance (the person who reaches 0 after paying/receiving). With N people, you need at least N-1 transactions to zero out N-1 people (the last one is automatically zero — the sum of all net balances is always 0 because every debt has two sides). The two-pointer greedy achieves N-1 transactions because each iteration eliminates at least one person (whoever reaches 0 first).
    Q: 'How does Splitwise handle a group trip with 20 people where some people paid in USD and some in INR?'
    💭 Think First
    Multi-currency means you need a common reference currency. But exchange rates fluctuate — what rate do you use?
    → Complete Answer
    Snapshot exchange rate at expense creation time. Alice paid $100 when 1 USD = 83 INR → store both the original ($100 USD) and the base-currency equivalent (₹8300). All net balances are calculated in the base currency (INR). Display shows the user's preferred currency, converted from base using current rates for display only. Never recalculate historical expenses with new rates — the snapshot is the canonical record. This mirrors how accounting works: transactions are recorded at the rate on the transaction date.
    🎯 Practice
    Implement Splitwise with Equal and Exact splits, then the settlement algorithm above. Add Percent split as an extension — it should require zero changes to Expense or Group classes.
    💡 Hint — think before readingaddExpense: for each participant (except payer), add their share to balance[participant][payer] and subtract from balance[payer][participant]. settle: compute net balance per person, use max-heap for creditors and min-heap for debtors, greedily match largest creditor with largest debtor.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — solution
    class ExpenseBook { private final Map<String,Map<String,Double>> bal = new HashMap<>(); public void addExpense(String paidBy, double total, Map<String,Double> shares) { shares.forEach((user, share) -> { if(user.equals(paidBy)) return; bal.computeIfAbsent(user, k->new HashMap<>()).merge(paidBy, share, Double::sum); bal.computeIfAbsent(paidBy, k->new HashMap<>()).merge(user, -share, Double::sum); }); } public List<String> settle() { Map<String,Double> net = computeNetBalances(); PriorityQueue<double[]> creditors = new PriorityQueue<>((a,b)->b[1]>a[1]?1:-1); PriorityQueue<double[]> debtors = new PriorityQueue<>((a,b)->a[1]<b[1]?1:-1); // ... two-pointer greedy ... } }
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement the addExpense() and getBalance(userId) methods. addExpense takes: paidBy, amount, list of participants, SplitType (EQUAL or EXACT with amounts). getBalance returns how much the user owes (+) or is owed (-).
    Hint — think before readingStore a Map> where balance[A][B] = how much A owes B. On addExpense: for each participant, calculate their share, update balance[participant][paidBy] += share and balance[paidBy][participant] -= share. getBalance: sum all values in balance[userId] (positive = owes others, negative = owed by others).
    → Worked Solution
    Java — Splitwise core methods
    class ExpenseBook { private final Map<String, Map<String, Double>> bal = new HashMap<>(); public void addExpense(String paidBy, double total, Map<String, Double> shares) { // shares: {userId → amount} shares.forEach((user, share) -> { if(user.equals(paidBy)) return; // user owes paidBy += share bal.computeIfAbsent(user, k->new HashMap<>()).merge(paidBy, share, Double::sum); // paidBy is owed by user -= share bal.computeIfAbsent(paidBy, k->new HashMap<>()).merge(user, -share, Double::sum); }); } public double getBalance(String userId) { // positive = userId owes this much total; negative = owed this much return bal.getOrDefault(userId, Map.of()).values().stream() .mapToDouble(Double::doubleValue).sum(); } }

    Ride Sharing — Matching + State Machine

    two systems working together
    🧠 Intuition — Two Independent Challenges
    1. Matching, 2. State MachineMatching: given a rider request, which available driver gets assigned? (Strategy pattern — NearestDriver, HighestRated, LowestFare). State Machine: a ride moves through REQUESTED → ASSIGNED → ARRIVED → IN_PROGRESS → COMPLETED (or CANCELLED at certain points). Each state allows different valid actions.
    📐 Ride State Machine
    💻 Entity Skeleton
    Java
    enum RideState { REQUESTED, ASSIGNED, ARRIVED, IN_PROGRESS, COMPLETED, CANCELLED } interface MatchingStrategy { Optional<Driver> findDriver(Location pickup, List<Driver> available); } class NearestDriverStrategy implements MatchingStrategy { public Optional<Driver> findDriver(Location pickup, List<Driver> drivers) { return drivers.stream() .filter(Driver::isAvailable) .min(Comparator.comparingDouble(d -> d.getLocation().distanceTo(pickup))); } } class Ride { private RideState state = RideState.REQUESTED; private Driver driver; public void assignDriver(Driver d) { if (state != RideState.REQUESTED) throw new IllegalStateException("Cannot assign — wrong state"); this.driver = d; d.setAvailable(false); // atomic flip needed in real system state = RideState.ASSIGNED; } public void cancel() { if (state == RideState.IN_PROGRESS || state == RideState.COMPLETED) throw new IllegalStateException("Too late to cancel"); state = RideState.CANCELLED; if (driver != null) driver.setAvailable(true); } }
    ⚠ Interview Follow-ups to Prepare
    • Scale"How do you handle driver location updates at scale?" → In-memory geospatial index (QuadTree or Geohash). Mention it, don't implement.
    • Race condition"What prevents 2 riders matching to the same driver?" → Atomic compareAndSet on driver.isAvailable, or a per-driver lock.
    • Mid-ride cancellation"Driver cancels after ASSIGNED?" → Transition back to REQUESTED, trigger re-matching, notify rider via Observer.
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Design the matching algorithm for a ride-sharing app. When a rider requests a trip, how do you assign the best driver? What happens if no driver accepts?
    Matching is an optimization problem with constraints: proximity, driver rating, vehicle type, driver direction of travel. The naive nearest-driver approach misses the direction constraint.
    Matching algorithm: (1) Geospatial query: find all drivers within radius R (use geohash or PostGIS ST_DWithin). (2) Filter: only AVAILABLE drivers, matching vehicle type. (3) Score = w1×(1/distance) + w2×rating + w3×directionMatch (heading towards rider). (4) Offer to top-scored driver with 15s timeout. If rejected/timeout: expand radius, offer to next driver. State machine: Ride states: REQUESTED→DRIVER_ASSIGNED→DRIVER_EN_ROUTE→TRIP_IN_PROGRESS→COMPLETED. Each state transition is an event. The state machine prevents invalid transitions (can't cancel a COMPLETED ride).
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'How do you handle the surge pricing calculation?'
    💭 Think First
    Surge is a supply/demand ratio. How do you calculate it in real-time for a geographic area?
    → Complete Answer
    Divide the city into H3 hexagons (Uber's approach) or geohash cells. Every 30 seconds: count active ride requests and available drivers in each cell. SurgeMultiplier = max(1.0, requestCount/driverCount × baseMultiplier). Cap at some maximum (e.g., 3×). Store in Redis with 60s TTL. When pricing a ride: lookup the surge for the pickup cell. Display to rider before confirmation. Update surge asynchronously — don't make riders wait for surge recalculation.
    Q: 'A driver cancels after being assigned. How do you handle the rider's experience?'
    💭 Think First
    Driver cancellation should be transparent to the rider — they shouldn't have to start over. But how do you prevent the app from showing 'searching' indefinitely?
    → Complete Answer
    On driver cancellation: ride transitions back to REQUESTED state automatically. Matching service immediately re-runs the matching algorithm — rider sees 'Finding a new driver' with progress indicator. If too many cancellations on the same ride (> 3): flag the ride, potentially increase offered price to drivers or escalate to support. Driver cancellation rate is tracked — penalise drivers with high cancellation rates by reducing their matching priority. Rider compensation: if cancellation is the driver's fault, waive the next booking fee or provide credits.
    🎯 Practice
    Build the Ride state machine first (transitions only). Then add matching. Then fare calculation with surge pricing as a Strategy. Layer it — don't build everything at once.
    💡 Hint — think before readingRideState enum: each state holds a Set of allowed transitions. validateTransition() throws if not allowed. FareCalculator: base + per_km * distance + time_factor * duration. Test: trace a full ride from REQUESTED to COMPLETED.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — solution
    enum RideState { REQUESTED(Set.of(DRIVER_ASSIGNED,CANCELLED)), DRIVER_ASSIGNED(Set.of(DRIVER_EN_ROUTE,CANCELLED)), DRIVER_EN_ROUTE(Set.of(IN_PROGRESS,CANCELLED)), IN_PROGRESS(Set.of(COMPLETED)), COMPLETED(Set.of()), CANCELLED(Set.of()); private final Set<RideState> allowed; public void validateTransition(RideState next) { if(!allowed.contains(next)) throw new IllegalStateException(this+"->"+next); } }
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement the Ride state machine as a Java enum with allowed transitions. The transitions are: REQUESTED→DRIVER_ASSIGNED, DRIVER_ASSIGNED→DRIVER_EN_ROUTE or CANCELLED, DRIVER_EN_ROUTE→TRIP_IN_PROGRESS or CANCELLED, TRIP_IN_PROGRESS→COMPLETED.
    Hint — think before readingEnum with a Set of allowed next states per state. validateTransition() throws if the transition isn't in the allowed set. This ensures no invalid state changes can happen regardless of what other code does.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — Ride state machine enum
    enum RideState { REQUESTED (Set.of(DRIVER_ASSIGNED, CANCELLED)), DRIVER_ASSIGNED(Set.of(DRIVER_EN_ROUTE, CANCELLED)), DRIVER_EN_ROUTE(Set.of(TRIP_IN_PROGRESS, CANCELLED)), TRIP_IN_PROGRESS(Set.of(COMPLETED)), COMPLETED (Set.of()), CANCELLED (Set.of()); private final Set<RideState> allowed; RideState(Set<RideState> a) { allowed = a; } public void validateTransition(RideState next) { if(!allowed.contains(next)) throw new IllegalStateException(this + " → " + next + " not allowed"); } }

    LRU Cache — O(1) Get and Put

    HashMap + Doubly Linked List
    🧠 The Two-Part Insight
    Why HashMap + Doubly Linked List, specifically?You need get() in O(1) → HashMap. You need to track "least recently used" order and update it in O(1) → Doubly Linked List, because removing a node from the middle is O(1) IF you already have a pointer to it (which the HashMap gives you). HashMap maps key → node pointer. The DLL is ordered by recency: head = most recent, tail = least recent. On get: move node to front. On overflow: evict from tail.
    📐 Data Structure Diagram
    💻 Complete Implementation
    Java — LRU Cache from scratch
    class LRUCache { private class Node { int key, val; Node prev, next; Node(int k, int v) { key=k; val=v; } } private final int capacity; private final Map<Integer,Node> map = new HashMap<>(); private final Node head = new Node(-1,-1); // dummy sentinel — no null checks needed private final Node tail = new Node(-1,-1); // dummy sentinel public LRUCache(int capacity) { this.capacity = capacity; head.next = tail; tail.prev = head; } public synchronized int get(int key) { if (!map.containsKey(key)) return -1; Node n = map.get(key); remove(n); addToFront(n); // move to MRU position return n.val; } public synchronized void put(int key, int val) { if (map.containsKey(key)) remove(map.get(key)); Node n = new Node(key, val); map.put(key, n); addToFront(n); if (map.size() > capacity) { Node lru = tail.prev; // the actual LRU node remove(lru); map.remove(lru.key); // THIS is why Node stores key — to evict from map too } } private void addToFront(Node n) { n.next = head.next; n.prev = head; head.next.prev = n; head.next = n; } private void remove(Node n) { n.prev.next = n.next; n.next.prev = n.prev; } }
    ⚠ Concurrency Follow-up — SDE-2 Question
    • Race on list orderTwo threads calling get() simultaneously can both try to move their node to front, corrupting the list. The "synchronized" above is a simple fix but serializes all access.
    • Better: ReadWriteLockSince get() also mutates list order (moves to front), it technically needs a write lock too — meaning LRU cache doesn't benefit as much from ReadWriteLock as a pure-read cache would.
    • Production-gradeLibraries like Caffeine use a different approach — asynchronous, lock-free ring buffers to avoid contention even on "writes" caused by reads.
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Implement an LRU cache with O(1) get() and O(1) put(). A distributed system has millions of cache misses per second — what data structure makes both operations O(1)?
    HashMap gives O(1) get/put by key. But it can't track access order for LRU eviction. You need a data structure that also knows the order. Think about combining two data structures.
    HashMap + Doubly Linked List: HashMap key→Node gives O(1) lookup. Doubly linked list maintains access order (most-recent at head, LRU at tail). get(): find node in map, move it to head (O(1) with prev/next pointers). put(): if key exists update and move to head. If new key: add at head, if over capacity remove tail node AND its map entry. Both O(1). The doubly linked list is critical — singly linked can't do O(1) node removal. In Java: LinkedHashMap with accessOrder=true + removeEldestEntry override does this in one line.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'Why does Java LinkedHashMap support LRU? What is accessOrder mode?'
    💭 Think First
    LinkedHashMap is a HashMap with a doubly linked list maintained in parallel. accessOrder=true changes its iteration order from insertion order to access order.
    → Complete Answer
    By default LinkedHashMap maintains insertion order. With accessOrder=true: every get() and put() moves the accessed entry to the tail of the internal doubly linked list — exactly like the LRU invariant. Override removeEldestEntry() to return true when size > capacity → the eldest entry (LRU) is automatically evicted. This is a production-ready LRU cache in Java: new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) { protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry e) { return size() > MAX; } }. Limitation: NOT thread-safe. For concurrent LRU use ConcurrentLinkedHashMap from Caffeine library.
    Q: 'How do you make your LRU cache thread-safe for a production multi-threaded environment?'
    💭 Think First
    Your HashMap+LinkedList implementation uses synchronized which serializes all reads AND writes. Is there a better approach?
    → Complete Answer
    Option 1: synchronized on all methods — correct, simple, but every thread blocks on every operation even reads. Option 2: ReadWriteLock — concurrent reads, exclusive writes. Put/evict acquires write lock. Get (with access order update) needs write lock too (reordering the list). Doesn't help much. Option 3: Caffeine — Google's production LRU cache: uses per-segment locking + ring buffer for deferred access order updates. Reads are nearly lock-free. Eviction runs in a background thread from the ring buffer. This is what Spring Cache uses under the hood. For interviews: describe the synchronized version as the simple correct answer, then mention Caffeine for production.
    🎯 Practice
    Implement without using Java's LinkedHashMap. Test: put(1,1), put(2,2), get(1)→1, put(3,3) [evicts key 2], get(2)→-1. Then explain why LinkedHashMap with accessOrder=true would also work as a shortcut.
    💡 Hint — think before readingUse dummy head/tail sentinels to eliminate null checks. addToHead() and removeNode() are the two primitives everything else builds on. The HashMap stores key->Node for O(1) lookup. On put: if key exists, update and move to head. If new, add to head; if over capacity, remove tail AND map.remove(tail.key).
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — solution
    class LRUCache<K,V> { private final int cap; private final Map<K,Node<K,V>> map = new HashMap<>(); private final Node<K,V> head = new Node<>(), tail = new Node<>(); { head.next=tail; tail.prev=head; } public V get(K k) { Node<K,V> n=map.get(k); if(n==null)return null; rm(n); addH(n); return n.v; } public void put(K k, V v) { Node<K,V> n = map.getOrDefault(k, new Node<>(k,v)); n.v=v; rm(n); addH(n); map.put(k,n); if(map.size()>cap) { Node<K,V> t=tail.prev; rm(t); map.remove(t.k); } } private void rm(Node<K,V> n) { n.prev.next=n.next; n.next.prev=n.prev; } private void addH(Node<K,V> n) { n.next=head.next; n.prev=head; head.next.prev=n; head.next=n; } static class Node<K,V> { K k; V v; Node<K,V> prev,next; Node(){} Node(K k,V v){this.k=k;this.v=v;} } }
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement LRUCache from scratch using only Node (with key, value, prev, next) and HashMap. No LinkedHashMap. Capacity 3: put A, put B, put C, get A, put D (should evict B — LRU after A was accessed).
    Hint — think before readingDoubly linked list with dummy head and tail sentinels simplifies edge cases. addToHead() and removeNode() are helpers. get() calls removeNode + addToHead. put() calls addToHead, then if over capacity calls removeTail + map.remove(tail.key).
    → Worked Solution
    Java — LRU from scratch
    class LRUCache<K,V> { private final int cap; private final Map<K, Node<K,V>> map = new HashMap<>(); private final Node<K,V> head = new Node<>(), tail = new Node<>(); // sentinels { head.next = tail; tail.prev = head; } LRUCache(int cap) { this.cap = cap; } public V get(K key) { Node<K,V> n = map.get(key); if(n==null) return null; remove(n); addHead(n); return n.val; } public void put(K key, V val) { Node<K,V> n = map.get(key); if(n==null) { n = new Node<>(key, val); map.put(key, n); } else { n.val = val; remove(n); } addHead(n); if(map.size() > cap) { Node<K,V> lru=tail.prev; remove(lru); map.remove(lru.key); } } private void remove(Node<K,V> n) { n.prev.next=n.next; n.next.prev=n.prev; } private void addHead(Node<K,V> n) { n.next=head.next; n.prev=head; head.next.prev=n; head.next=n; } static class Node<K,V> { K key; V val; Node<K,V> prev,next; Node(){} Node(K k,V v){key=k;val=v;} } }

    Rate Limiter — 3 Algorithms

    Token Bucket · Leaky Bucket · Sliding Window
    🧠 Why Rate Limiting
    Protect APIs, ensure fairnessDecide whether to allow or reject a request based on how many that user already made recently. Three algorithms exist with different trade-offs. Know all three — interviewers love asking "which would you pick and why?"
    📐 Token Bucket Visual
    💻 Token Bucket Implementation
    Java — thread-safe token bucket
    class TokenBucket { private final int capacity; private final double refillRatePerMs; private double tokens; private long lastRefillTime; private final Object lock = new Object(); public TokenBucket(int capacity, double refillPerSecond) { this.capacity = capacity; this.tokens = capacity; this.refillRatePerMs = refillPerSecond / 1000.0; this.lastRefillTime = System.currentTimeMillis(); } public boolean allowRequest() { synchronized (lock) { refill(); if (tokens >= 1) { tokens -= 1; return true; // allowed } return false; // rejected — no tokens left } } private void refill() { long now = System.currentTimeMillis(); double elapsed = now - lastRefillTime; tokens = Math.min(capacity, tokens + elapsed * refillRatePerMs); lastRefillTime = now; } } // Per-user rate limiting: Map<String, TokenBucket> userBuckets = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); userBuckets.computeIfAbsent(userId, k -> new TokenBucket(5, 1.0)).allowRequest();
    💡 Algorithm Comparison Table
    AlgorithmAllows BurstsMemoryBest For
    Token BucketYes, up to capacityO(1) per userGeneral APIs — most common choice
    Leaky BucketNo, smooths outputO(queue size)Payment processing, fixed-rate consumers
    Sliding Window LogPrecise, no burst slackO(requests in window)Strict compliance / billing accuracy
    📚 References
    📙
    Figma Engineering — Rate Limiting Deep Dive
    figma.com/blog/an-alternative-approach-to-rate-limiting
    ↗
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Your public API is getting hammered — 10,000 requests/second to a single endpoint from 50 different clients. Some clients are legitimate (100 req/s), one is a scraper (9,500 req/s). Design a rate limiter.
    You need per-client rate limiting, not global. Client identified by API key or IP. Must work across multiple app servers (distributed). Must be fast (adds <5ms to request).
    Algorithm choice: Token Bucket — handles burst naturally. Clients can burst up to bucket capacity, then throttled to refill rate. Implementation: Redis is the distributed counter store. Lua script makes the check+decrement atomic (no race conditions across servers). Key = 'rl:{clientId}:{window}'. Hash with 'tokens' and 'last_refill'. Lua: compute elapsed time, add tokens = elapsed * refillRate (capped at capacity), if tokens >= 1 decrement and allow, else deny with 429. All atomic. Returns 0 or 1. Response headers: X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset, Retry-After on 429.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'Explain the edge case with Fixed Window counter — the boundary burst problem.'
    💭 Think First
    Fixed window resets at exact time boundaries. What happens if a client sends all their quota in the last second of one window and the first second of the next?
    → Complete Answer
    With 100 req/min fixed window: Client sends 100 at 0:59 (last second of minute 1) and 100 at 1:00 (first second of minute 2). Both pass. In the 2-second span around the boundary, client sent 200 requests — 2× the limit. Sliding Window Counter fixes this: approximate sliding window by blending current and previous window counts proportionally. Formula: count = prevWindowCount × (1 - elapsed/windowSize) + currentWindowCount. This eliminates the boundary spike with minimal overhead (just 2 counters per client).
    Q: 'How do you implement rate limiting at the API Gateway level versus in the application?'
    💭 Think First
    Both are valid. Think about where each approach wins and where it fails.
    → Complete Answer
    API Gateway (Nginx, Kong, AWS API Gateway): rate limiting before traffic reaches your app. Protects against DDoS cheaply. Zero application code. Limitation: coarse-grained (IP or API key only), hard to apply business rules (premium vs free tier). Application level: fine-grained (per user, per endpoint, per plan tier), can apply business logic (admin exempt, paid users get higher limits). Limitation: every pod needs access to shared state (Redis). Best practice: two layers. Gateway does coarse IP-based flood protection. Application does business-aware per-user rate limiting.
    🎯 Practice
    Implement Token Bucket and Sliding Window Counter. Compare memory usage and accuracy trade-offs in a short write-up — this exact comparison is a common follow-up question.
    💡 Hint — think before readingToken Bucket: tokens refill at rate/second up to capacity. On each request: compute elapsed time since last refill, add tokens, cap at capacity, check if >=1. Sliding Window: LinkedList of timestamps; removeFirst() while oldest is outside window; size() is the count.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — solution
    class TokenBucket { private final double rate, cap; private double tokens; private long lastRefill = System.currentTimeMillis(); TokenBucket(double rate, double cap) { this.rate=rate; this.cap=cap; tokens=cap; } public synchronized boolean allow() { long now = System.currentTimeMillis(); tokens = Math.min(cap, tokens + rate*(now-lastRefill)/1000.0); lastRefill = now; if(tokens>=1) { tokens--; return true; } return false; } } class SlidingWindow { private final int limit; private final long windowMs; private final Deque<Long> timestamps = new ArrayDeque<>(); synchronized boolean allow() { long now = System.currentTimeMillis(); while(!timestamps.isEmpty() && now-timestamps.peekFirst() > windowMs) timestamps.pollFirst(); if(timestamps.size()<limit) { timestamps.addLast(now); return true; } return false; } }
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement a sliding window rate limiter using Redis ZADD (sorted set). Store timestamps of requests as members. To check: remove all members older than 1 minute, count remaining, allow if count < limit.
    Hint — think before readingZADD key currentTimestamp memberUUID. ZREMRANGEBYSCORE key 0 (currentTime-60000). ZCARD key. If ZCARD < limit: allow and return 1. Else deny and return 0. All in a Lua script for atomicity.
    → Worked Solution
    Java + Redis — sliding window log
    private static final String LUA = """ local now = tonumber(ARGV[1]) local limit = tonumber(ARGV[2]) local window = tonumber(ARGV[3]) -- ms redis.call('ZREMRANGEBYSCORE', KEYS[1], 0, now - window) local count = redis.call('ZCARD', KEYS[1]) if count < limit then redis.call('ZADD', KEYS[1], now, now .. ':' .. math.random()) redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], 120) return 1 end return 0 """; public boolean isAllowed(String clientId, int limit, long windowMs) { Long result = redis.execute(new DefaultRedisScript<>(LUA, Long.class), List.of("rl:" + clientId), System.currentTimeMillis(), limit, windowMs); return Long.valueOf(1L).equals(result); }

    Task Scheduler & Notification System

    priority queues + retry logic + multi-channel delivery
    🧠 Task Scheduler — What's Being Tested
    Combines 3 conceptsA min-heap (PriorityQueue ordered by scheduledTime — next task always at the top), a background worker thread that waits until the next task is due, and retry logic with exponential backoff on failure. This problem tests whether you can combine data structures + concurrency + error handling in one design.
    💻 Scheduler Core
    Java — priority-based scheduler
    class ScheduledTask implements Comparable<ScheduledTask> { Runnable task; long scheduledTimeMs; int retryCount = 0; static final int MAX_RETRIES = 3; public int compareTo(ScheduledTask o) { return Long.compare(scheduledTimeMs, o.scheduledTimeMs); // min-heap by time } } class TaskScheduler { private final PriorityBlockingQueue<ScheduledTask> queue = new PriorityBlockingQueue<>(); private final ScheduledExecutorService executor = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(4); public void schedule(Runnable task, long delayMs) { ScheduledTask st = new ScheduledTask(); st.task = task; st.scheduledTimeMs = System.currentTimeMillis() + delayMs; executor.schedule(() -> runWithRetry(st), delayMs, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); } private void runWithRetry(ScheduledTask st) { try { st.task.run(); } catch (Exception e) { if (st.retryCount < ScheduledTask.MAX_RETRIES) { st.retryCount++; long backoffMs = (long) Math.pow(2, st.retryCount) * 1000; // exponential backoff executor.schedule(() -> runWithRetry(st), backoffMs, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); } else { System.err.println("Task failed permanently after " + st.retryCount + " retries"); } } } }
    💡 Notification System — Chain + Observer
    Combine 2 patterns based on requirementsObserver: multiple channels react to one event (send email AND push). Chain of Responsibility: try Email, if it fails try SMS, if that fails try Push. Clarify upfront: "Should all channels fire in parallel, or fall back sequentially?" The answer determines which pattern you actually need.
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Design a Task Scheduler + Notification System. Users create tasks with due dates. When a task is due, send a push notification. 10M users, 100M tasks. Notifications must arrive within 30 seconds of the due time.
    This combines two problems: efficient due-date detection (scanning 100M rows every 30s is too slow) and reliable async notification delivery (push can fail — need retry). Solve each separately.
    Due-date detection: Do not scan all tasks every 30 seconds. Instead, maintain a Redis sorted set: ZADD due_tasks {dueEpochMs} {taskId}. When a task is created or its due date is changed, update the sorted set. A scheduler thread runs every 30s: ZRANGEBYSCORE due_tasks 0 now — fetches only tasks due NOW. Remove them from the sorted set, publish each to Kafka. O(due_tasks_in_window) not O(all_tasks). Notification delivery: Kafka consumer reads the task, looks up the user's push token from UserDevice table, calls FCM/APNs. On failure: retry with exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, max 3 tries). Dead-letter queue for permanently failed deliveries — stored for in-app notification fallback. Retry idempotency: each notification has a UUID. FCM accepts an idempotency key — duplicate sends are deduplicated at the provider level.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: A user has 5 devices (phone, tablet, work phone, laptop). How do you send to all of them?
    💭 Think First
    One user, many devices, each with its own push token. Fan-out within the notification system.
    → Complete Answer
    UserDevice table: (userId, deviceId, platform, pushToken, lastSeenAt). On notification trigger: SELECT pushToken FROM user_devices WHERE userId=? AND lastSeenAt > now()-30days (active devices only). For each token: publish a PushTask{token, payload} to Kafka. Each is delivered independently. If one device token is expired (app uninstalled): FCM returns InvalidToken — remove that row from user_devices. This clean-up happens asynchronously after the notification attempt.
    Q: How do you batch notifications? Instead of one push per task, send "You have 5 tasks due today" as a digest.
    💭 Think First
    Per-task notifications at 100M tasks scale = 100M push notifications/day. Batching reduces noise and cost.
    → Complete Answer
    Digest aggregation: instead of triggering a notification per task immediately, collect all due tasks per user in a time window (e.g., 5-minute window). At the end of the window: aggregate all due tasks for each user into one notification. Implementation: when a task becomes due, publish to a Kafka topic. A Flink or Kafka Streams job groups by userId with a 5-minute tumbling window, collecting all task IDs. At window close: emit one AggregatedNotification{userId, taskIds, count}. The notification consumer reads this and sends one push: "5 tasks due: Buy groceries, Call dentist, ..." with a deep link to the task list. Per-user rate limiting: max 3 digest notifications per day to avoid overwhelming users.
    🎯 Practice
    Build a TaskScheduler supporting one-time delayed tasks and repeating tasks. Then build a NotificationService that fires across all user-preferred channels in parallel via ExecutorService, with one retry per channel on failure.
    💡 Hint — think before readingScheduler: PriorityQueue ordered by scheduledTime. Background thread: peek at head of queue; if scheduledTime <= now, poll and execute; else sleep until scheduledTime. For repeating tasks: after execution, re-add with next trigger time.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — solution
    class TaskScheduler { private final PriorityQueue<ScheduledTask> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparing(ScheduledTask::runAt)); private final Object lock = new Object(); public void schedule(Runnable r, Instant at) { synchronized(lock) { pq.offer(new ScheduledTask(r,at)); lock.notifyAll(); } } public void start() { Thread t = new Thread(() -> { while(!Thread.interrupted()) { synchronized(lock) { while(pq.isEmpty() || pq.peek().runAt().isAfter(Instant.now())) lock.wait(pq.isEmpty() ? 1000 : Duration.between(Instant.now(),pq.peek().runAt()).toMillis()); pq.poll().run(); } } }); t.setDaemon(true); t.start(); } }
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement the due-task detector. It reads from a Redis sorted set every 30 seconds, fetches all tasks due now, publishes each to Kafka, and removes them from the sorted set atomically.
    Hint — think before readingZRANGEBYSCORE to find due tasks. For atomicity (no task processed twice): use a Lua script that does ZRANGEBYSCORE + ZREMRANGEBYSCORE atomically, or use ZRANGEBYSCORE then ZREM within a pipeline. Publish each taskId to Kafka.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — due-task detection with Redis sorted set
    @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 30_000) public void detectDueTasks() { long now = System.currentTimeMillis(); // Atomic Lua: range + remove in one operation (no double-processing) String lua = """ local ids = redis.call('ZRANGEBYSCORE', KEYS[1], 0, ARGV[1]) if #ids > 0 then redis.call('ZREMRANGEBYSCORE', KEYS[1], 0, ARGV[1]) end return ids """; List<String> taskIds = redis.execute( new DefaultRedisScript<>(lua, List.class), List.of("due_tasks"), String.valueOf(now) ); if (taskIds != null) { taskIds.forEach(id -> kafka.send("task-due-events", id)); log.info("Published {} due tasks", taskIds.size()); } }
