    Multithreading & Race Conditions

    the concepts AND the scenario answers interviewers actually want
    🧠 Mental Model
    Threads share the same whiteboard (heap). Each has their own notepad (stack).Objects on the heap — instance variables, static variables, collection elements — are visible to all threads simultaneously. Local variables and method parameters live on the thread's private stack, unreachable by others. A race condition happens when two threads read-modify-write the same heap variable without coordination, and the outcome depends on which thread wins the CPU scheduling lottery.
    ⚠️ Race Condition — Exactly Why counter++ Breaks
    💻 Three Correct Solutions — Know Trade-offs
    synchronized
    AtomicInteger
    LongAdder
    Java — synchronized (mutex)
    class Counter { private int count = 0; public synchronized void increment() { count++; // only one thread at a time — others block waiting } public synchronized int get() { return count; } } // synchronized acquires the intrinsic lock (monitor) on "this". // OS-level blocking — context switch on contention. // Good when: guarding complex multi-line critical sections. // Bad when: high contention on a simple increment → lots of blocking overhead.
    Java — AtomicInteger (CAS, lock-free)
    class Counter { private final AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger(0); public void increment() { count.incrementAndGet(); } public int get() { return count.get(); } } // CAS = Compare-And-Swap: CPU instruction that atomically does: // if (memory == expected) { memory = newValue; return true; } // else { return false; } // No OS involvement, no thread suspension — just a spin retry on conflict. // Faster than synchronized under LOW-to-MODERATE contention. // Under EXTREME contention (thousands of threads): spin-loops waste CPU.
    Java — LongAdder (best for counters under high contention)
    class Counter { private final LongAdder count = new LongAdder(); public void increment() { count.increment(); } public long get() { return count.sum(); } } // LongAdder maintains multiple "Cell" objects — each thread has a // preferred Cell to update (stripe the updates). Under contention, // threads spread across different Cells → near-zero contention. // sum() aggregates all Cells — slightly expensive read. // Use when: write-heavy, many threads, reads are infrequent. // Example: metrics/monitoring counters, request count per endpoint.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q1: "What is the Java Memory Model and why does it matter?"
    💭 Think
    CPUs and JVMs cache values. What guarantees do you have about when a write by Thread A becomes visible to Thread B?
    → Answer
    The JMM defines "happens-before" relationships — formal guarantees about visibility. Key rules: (1) Within a thread, statements happen-before later statements. (2) A monitor unlock happens-before any subsequent lock of the same monitor. (3) A volatile write happens-before any subsequent volatile read of the same variable. Without a happens-before edge, a write by Thread A is NOT guaranteed to be visible to Thread B — the CPU or JIT can cache the value, reorder writes, or optimize away reads entirely. This is why unsynchronized shared state can cause "impossible" bugs like a loop that never exits.
    Q2: "Difference between thread safety and atomicity?"
    💭 Think
    Can something be atomic but not thread-safe? Thread-safe but not atomic?
    → Answer
    Atomicity means an operation completes as a single, indivisible unit — no thread can observe a partial state. Thread safety means a class behaves correctly when multiple threads use it concurrently. A class can be thread-safe without all operations being atomic (e.g., ConcurrentHashMap is thread-safe but its size() is not exact). Atomicity is one mechanism for achieving thread safety, not the only one. Example: Collections.synchronizedList() is thread-safe (synchronized on each method) but "check then act" patterns on it are still not atomic — you need external synchronization.
    🏭 Classic Interview Scenario
    "Design a thread-safe singleton that initializes lazily (not at class load) with minimum locking overhead."
    Options: synchronized method (slow), double-checked locking (tricky), static holder (elegant). Which is correct?
    Option 1 — synchronized (simple but slow)Every getInstance() call acquires a lock even after initialization. Unnecessary overhead. Option 2 — Double-Checked Locking (requires volatile)
    Java
    class Singleton { private static volatile Singleton instance; // volatile IS required public static Singleton getInstance() { if (instance == null) { // fast path — no lock synchronized (Singleton.class) { if (instance == null) { // recheck under lock instance = new Singleton(); // volatile prevents partial construction } } } return instance; } }
    Option 3 — Static Holder (best — no synchronization needed)
    Java
    class Singleton { private static class Holder { static final Singleton INSTANCE = new Singleton(); } public static Singleton getInstance() { return Holder.INSTANCE; } } // Holder class loaded only on first call to getInstance() — lazy. // JVM guarantees class loading is thread-safe — no synchronized needed. // Zero overhead on subsequent calls. This is the preferred pattern.
    🎯 Practice
    Write a BankAccount class supporting concurrent deposits and withdrawals, where a transfer between two accounts must be atomic (both debit and credit happen or neither does).
    Hint — deadlock riskLocking account A then B in one thread, and B then A in another thread → deadlock. How do you enforce a consistent lock order?
    → Worked Solution
    Java — deadlock-safe transfer
    class BankAccount { private final int id; // unique, used for lock ordering private double balance; static void transfer(BankAccount from, BankAccount to, double amount) { // Always lock the lower-id account first — GLOBALLY consistent ordering BankAccount first = from.id < to.id ? from : to; BankAccount second = from.id < to.id ? to : from; synchronized (first) { synchronized (second) { if (from.balance < amount) throw new IllegalStateException("Insufficient"); from.balance -= amount; to.balance += amount; } } } } // Consistent ordering breaks circular wait — one of the 4 Coffman conditions // for deadlock. Thread A and B both try to lock (lower_id first), // so one always gets both locks while the other waits cleanly.

    Executor Framework & Thread Pools

    why you never call new Thread(), CompletableFuture, and production sizing
    🧠 Mental Model
    A thread pool is a restaurant kitchen with a fixed number of chefs and an order queue.When an order arrives (task submitted), a free chef (idle thread) picks it up. If all chefs are busy, the order waits in a queue. You never hire and fire a chef per order — the overhead of "hiring" (thread creation: OS-level resource allocation, stack allocation) is too expensive for short tasks. A pool amortizes that cost across many tasks.
    💻 ThreadPoolExecutor — The Full API You Must Know
    Java — understanding every parameter
    ThreadPoolExecutor executor = new ThreadPoolExecutor( 4, // corePoolSize: always-alive threads (even when idle) 8, // maximumPoolSize: max threads when queue is full 60, TimeUnit.SECONDS, // keepAliveTime: extra threads die after this idle new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100), // bounded queue: prevents OOM under load spikes new ThreadFactoryBuilder() // named threads: "worker-1" in stack traces .setNameFormat("worker-%d").build(), new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy() // backpressure: submitter thread executes task ); // Flow when a task is submitted: // 1. If active threads < corePoolSize → spawn new thread to handle it // 2. If at core limit → put in queue // 3. If queue is full AND active < max → spawn extra thread (above core) // 4. If queue full AND at max → RejectedExecutionHandler fires // // CallerRunsPolicy: submitting thread runs the task itself → naturally slows // the producer, preventing runaway queue growth. Other policies: // AbortPolicy (throws exception), DiscardPolicy (silently drop), DiscardOldestPolicy
    📐 CompletableFuture — Async Composition
    Java — non-blocking async chains
    // Scenario: fetch user, then fetch their orders concurrently, combine results CompletableFuture<User> userFuture = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> userService.findById(userId), executor); CompletableFuture<List<Order>> orderFuture = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> orderService.findByUser(userId), executor); // Combine both results when BOTH complete (non-blocking) CompletableFuture<UserDashboard> dashboard = userFuture.thenCombine(orderFuture, (user, orders) -> new UserDashboard(user, orders)); // Handle errors in the chain dashboard .thenApply(d -> ResponseEntity.ok(d)) .exceptionally(ex -> { log.error("Dashboard build failed", ex); return ResponseEntity.status(500).build(); }) .get(); // only block here if you must — or use join() in completionStage chain // allOf() — wait for N futures, none return value // anyOf() — complete when FIRST of N completes (e.g., race between replicas)
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q1: "Why is newCachedThreadPool() dangerous in production?"
    💭 Think
    What happens if tasks arrive faster than they complete?
    → Answer
    newCachedThreadPool() has core=0, max=Integer.MAX_VALUE, queue=SynchronousQueue (zero capacity). Every submitted task either grabs an idle thread or spawns a new one. Under sustained load, it spawns thousands of threads — each consuming ~512KB of stack by default — until JVM crashes with OutOfMemoryError. Always use a bounded ThreadPoolExecutor in production. newCachedThreadPool() is only appropriate for truly bursty-then-quiet workloads where you're confident tasks are short-lived.
    Q2: "How do you size a thread pool for a web application?"
    💭 Think
    CPU-bound vs I/O-bound work have fundamentally different optimal thread counts.
    → Formulaic answer
    CPU-bound tasks: threads = CPU_cores + 1 (the +1 covers a thread waiting on memory). Adding more threads causes context-switching overhead with no throughput gain.

    I/O-bound tasks: threads = CPU_cores × (1 + wait_time/compute_time). If a DB call takes 50ms and processing takes 5ms, ratio=10 — so 4 cores → up to 44 threads can be useful (most are blocked waiting for I/O while others compute).

    In practice: start with a reasonable default (e.g., 2× core count for mixed workloads), monitor CPU utilization and queue depth under load, tune from there. Never guess without measuring.
    Q3: "What is the difference between execute() and submit()?"
    💭 Think
    What do you lose with execute() that submit() gives you?
    → Answer
    execute() takes a Runnable, returns void — fire and forget, no way to get a result or catch exceptions thrown inside the task (they go to the thread's UncaughtExceptionHandler). submit() takes Runnable or Callable, returns a Future — calling future.get() blocks until completion AND re-throws any exception the task threw, wrapped in ExecutionException. Always use submit() when you need results or proper exception propagation.
    🏭 Scenario: API calls 3 downstream services, returns combined result
    "Your API must call UserService, InventoryService, and PricingService, then combine results. Sequential calls take 150ms each = 450ms total. How do you get this under 200ms?"
    Independent calls don't need to be sequential. What pattern runs them in parallel and waits for all to complete?
    Solution: CompletableFuture.allOf()
    Java
    public ProductPage buildPage(String productId) { CompletableFuture<User> uf = supplyAsync(() -> userService.current(), pool); CompletableFuture<Inventory> iv = supplyAsync(() -> inventoryService.get(productId), pool); CompletableFuture<Price> pf = supplyAsync(() -> pricingService.get(productId), pool); CompletableFuture.allOf(uf, iv, pf).join(); // waits for ALL, throws on any failure return new ProductPage(uf.join(), iv.join(), pf.join()); // Wall time ≈ max(150, 150, 150) = 150ms instead of 450ms // Add timeouts: uf.orTimeout(200, MILLISECONDS) — crucial in production }
    Follow-up the interviewer will ask: "What happens if one service fails?" — allOf() completes exceptionally if any future fails. Wrap in thenApply/exceptionally to return partial results or a graceful fallback.
    🎯 Practice
    Implement a rate-limited task executor: max 10 concurrent tasks, rejects with a custom exception (not silently drops) when overloaded, and logs warnings when queue is 80% full.
    HintAbortPolicy throws RejectedExecutionException — wrap it in your own exception. For queue monitoring, subclass ThreadPoolExecutor and override execute().
    → Worked Solution
    Java
    class MonitoredExecutor extends ThreadPoolExecutor { private static final int QUEUE_CAPACITY = 100; MonitoredExecutor() { super(10, 10, 0L, MILLISECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(QUEUE_CAPACITY), r -> { throw new ServiceOverloadedException("System at capacity"); }); } @Override public void execute(Runnable command) { int queueSize = getQueue().size(); if (queueSize > QUEUE_CAPACITY * 0.8) { log.warn("Task queue at {}% capacity", (queueSize * 100 / QUEUE_CAPACITY)); } super.execute(command); } }

    Deadlock, Starvation & Livelock

    three distinct failure modes — and how to diagnose each in production
    🧠 Three Different Problems, Often Confused
    Deadlock: everyone waits, nothing moves. Starvation: one waits forever while others proceed. Livelock: everyone moves, nothing progresses.Classic analogy: two people in a corridor — deadlock is both stop and wait for the other; starvation is one always stepping aside while the other always walks through; livelock is both simultaneously step left, then right, then left forever — active but going nowhere.
    ⚠️ Deadlock — The 4 Conditions (Coffman)
    1. Mutual Exclusion

    A resource can only be held by one thread at a time. (Required for correctness — can't usually eliminate.)

    2. Hold and Wait

    A thread holds resource A while waiting for resource B. Fix: acquire all needed locks atomically, or release and retry.

    3. No Preemption

    Locks can't be forcibly taken. Fix: use tryLock(timeout) — if you can't get the second lock, release the first and retry.

    4. Circular Wait

    Thread A waits for B's lock, Thread B waits for A's lock. Fix: enforce a global lock acquisition ORDER — breaks the cycle at its root.

    💻 Deadlock + Fix
    Java — deadlock and the consistent-ordering fix
    // ✗ DEADLOCK — thread A: lock1 then lock2; thread B: lock2 then lock1 Object lock1 = new Object(), lock2 = new Object(); new Thread(() -> { synchronized(lock1) { synchronized(lock2) {/**/} } }).start(); new Thread(() -> { synchronized(lock2) { synchronized(lock1) {/**/} } }).start(); // Both grab their first lock, wait for the other's → deadlock // ✓ FIX 1 — consistent ordering (always lock1 then lock2) new Thread(() -> { synchronized(lock1) { synchronized(lock2) {/**/} } }).start(); new Thread(() -> { synchronized(lock1) { synchronized(lock2) {/**/} } }).start(); // Both try to grab lock1 first → one gets it, proceeds; other waits cleanly // ✓ FIX 2 — tryLock with timeout (backs off on failure) boolean transfer(ReentrantLock fromLock, ReentrantLock toLock) throws InterruptedException { while (true) { if (fromLock.tryLock(50, MILLISECONDS)) { try { if (toLock.tryLock(50, MILLISECONDS)) { try { /* do transfer */ return true; } finally { toLock.unlock(); } } } finally { fromLock.unlock(); } } Thread.sleep(1); // backoff before retry } }
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Two threads in your payment service are stuck. Thread-A holds a lock on AccountA and is waiting for AccountB. Thread-B holds a lock on AccountB and is waiting for AccountA. Neither can proceed. Production is blocked. How do you detect, diagnose, and fix this?
    This is the classic deadlock. You need to detect it at runtime and prevent it in code. Detection: thread dump. Prevention: consistent lock ordering. What order should you always acquire locks in?
    Detection: jstack <pid> or kill -3 <pid> generates a thread dump. Look for 'Found 1 deadlock' section. It shows exactly which thread holds which lock and what it is waiting for. In Spring Boot: GET /actuator/threaddump also shows this. Root cause: Thread-A acquires locks in order A→B. Thread-B acquires locks in order B→A. Circular wait = deadlock. Fix — lock ordering: Always acquire locks in a consistent global order (e.g., by account ID: lower ID first). Both threads will always try to lock the lower-ID account first — no circular wait possible. Alternative — tryLock with timeout: lock.tryLock(500, MILLISECONDS) — if cannot acquire in 500ms, release what you hold and retry. Avoids deadlock at the cost of retry complexity. Prevention checklist: (1) Never hold a lock while calling external code. (2) Acquire multiple locks in a consistent order. (3) Prefer database-level locking (SELECT FOR UPDATE) over application locks for cross-service resources.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q1: "How do you detect a deadlock in a running JVM?"
    💭 Think
    The JVM knows about its own threads and locks. How do you ask it?
    → Production answer
    jstack <pid> — outputs all thread states. Look for "Found one Java-level deadlock:" — the JVM literally prints this, the thread names, and which lock each is holding/waiting for. In Spring Boot apps, GET /actuator/threaddump gives the same information via HTTP without needing SSH access to the server. For automated detection, use ThreadMXBean:
    Java
    ThreadMXBean bean = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean(); long[] deadlocked = bean.findDeadlockedThreads(); if (deadlocked != null) { // alert! get thread info for each id ThreadInfo[] info = bean.getThreadInfo(deadlocked); // log or alert with thread names and lock info }
    Q2: "Explain livelock with a Java code example."
    💭 Think
    Threads are running (not blocked) but making no real progress.
    → Answer
    Java — livelock pattern
    // Both threads try to be "polite" — keep yielding to each other volatile boolean aActing = false, bActing = false; // Thread A while (true) { aActing = true; while (bActing) { aActing = false; Thread.yield(); aActing = true; } // yield to B // do work aActing = false; } // Thread B does the symmetric thing — both keep yielding, neither works // Fix: add randomized backoff — randomly sleep 0-100ms before retrying // so they don't repeatedly synchronize on yielding at the same instant
    Q3: "What is starvation and how does a fair lock fix it?"
    💭 Think
    Non-fair locks favor threads that are already scheduled — who loses?
    → Answer
    Default synchronized and ReentrantLock(false) use "barge-in" — a thread releasing a lock doesn't queue the next waiter, any thread can grab it immediately. Under high contention, a low-priority or recently-woken thread may lose every time → starvation. ReentrantLock(true) (fair lock) uses a strict FIFO queue of waiting threads — longest-waiter gets it next. Cost: 30-40% throughput reduction under high contention. Use fair locks when starvation would cause correctness issues (e.g., request processing must complete in bounded time per SLA), not by default.
    🎯 Practice
    You have a library book-lending system: books are locked for checkout. Implement checkout(User, Book) and return(Book) such that two users can check out different books simultaneously but the same book cannot be checked out twice.
    HintLock per book, not per user. Use ConcurrentHashMap + computeIfAbsent to create locks lazily per book ID. This gives per-book granularity.
    → Worked Solution
    Java
    class Library { private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, ReentrantLock> bookLocks = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); private final Map<String, String> checkedOut = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); // bookId→userId public boolean checkout(String userId, String bookId) { ReentrantLock lock = bookLocks.computeIfAbsent(bookId, k -> new ReentrantLock()); lock.lock(); try { if (checkedOut.containsKey(bookId)) return false; // already out checkedOut.put(bookId, userId); return true; } finally { lock.unlock(); } } public void returnBook(String bookId) { ReentrantLock lock = bookLocks.get(bookId); if (lock == null) return; lock.lock(); try { checkedOut.remove(bookId); } finally { lock.unlock(); } } } // Two users checking out different books → different locks → truly parallel. // Two users trying to check out the SAME book → same lock → one wins, one gets false.

    volatile vs synchronized

    visibility vs atomicity — the most misunderstood concurrency distinction
    🧠 Mental Model
    volatile = a shared whiteboard everyone can read instantly. synchronized = a locked private room where you work alone.Without volatile, each thread might read a locally cached copy of a variable (in CPU register or L1 cache) and never see updates from other threads. volatile forces every read/write to go to main memory — eliminating the caching problem. But volatile does NOTHING for race conditions on compound operations (read-modify-write). synchronized provides BOTH: visibility (on unlock) AND exclusivity (mutual exclusion).
    💻 When Each Is Correct
    Java — volatile correct use vs wrong use
    // ✓ volatile CORRECT — single-writer flag, no compound operation class Worker implements Runnable { private volatile boolean running = true; // writer: external thread; reader: this thread public void run() { while (running) { /* process */ } // without volatile, JIT may hoist this read out of } // the loop and never re-check → infinite loop public void stop() { running = false; } // called from another thread } // ✗ volatile WRONG — still races on compound operations class Counter { private volatile int count = 0; public void increment() { count++; // READ count (atomic, visible), ADD 1, WRITE (atomic, visible) // The 3 steps are individually visible but NOT executed as one unit. // Thread A reads 5, Thread B reads 5, both write 6 → lost update. // volatile fixes visibility — it doesn't fix non-atomicity. } } // ✓ Double-checked locking requires volatile to prevent partial construction private static volatile Config instance; // volatile ensures constructor completion // visible before reference is published — without volatile, another thread could // see a non-null reference to a partially-constructed object
    ⚠️ Comparison Matrix
    PropertyvolatilesynchronizedAtomicInteger
    Visibility guaranteeYesYes (on unlock)Yes
    Atomicity for compound opsNoYes (one thread at a time)Yes (CAS)
    Thread blockingNeverYes (waiting threads block)No (spin on contention)
    Performance costLowMedium (lock overhead)Low-Medium
    Best forFlags, status, reference publicationMulti-field invariants, complex logicSingle numeric counter/flag
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q1: "Explain happens-before as it relates to volatile."
    💭 Think
    It's not just about the volatile variable itself — what about non-volatile writes before it?
    → Key insight
    A volatile write "flushes" ALL preceding writes from the writing thread's cache. A volatile read "refreshes" ALL subsequent reads in the reading thread. So if Thread A writes non-volatile field x=1, then writes volatile flag=true, and Thread B reads volatile flag and sees true, Thread B is ALSO guaranteed to see x==1. This is the "piggybacking" pattern — use one volatile flag to publish a bundle of state changes safely.
    Q2: "When should you use AtomicReference instead of volatile for an object reference?"
    💭 Think
    volatile on a reference gives visibility. What does AtomicReference add?
    → Answer
    volatile Object ref gives you a visible reference — any thread reading it sees the latest published value. AtomicReference adds compareAndSet() (CAS) — you can conditionally update the reference only if it's still a specific value, enabling lock-free algorithms like "if current config == oldConfig, replace with newConfig" without a synchronized block. If you only need to publish a new immutable object reference (e.g., a new config snapshot), volatile alone is sufficient and simpler.
    🏭 Scenario: Hot-Reload Configuration
    "Your app loads config from a file on startup. Ops team wants to reload config at runtime without restarting. 100 worker threads read config on every request. How do you make this thread-safe?"
    Worker threads only READ. One config-reload thread writes. Is synchronized overkill?
    Solution: volatile reference to immutable config object
    Java
    class ConfigHolder { private volatile AppConfig current; // reference swap is atomic; volatile ensures visibility public AppConfig get() { return current; } // lock-free read — 100 threads, zero contention public void reload() { AppConfig newConfig = loadFromFile(); // build new immutable config current = newConfig; // single volatile write — atomic reference swap // All readers: either see old complete config or new complete config. // No reader sees a half-built config because AppConfig is immutable — // built fully before the reference is published. } }
    Why this works: AppConfig is immutable — all its fields set in constructor, no setters. Worker threads reading current see either the old or new complete, valid config. The volatile write of the reference flushes all of AppConfig's initialization writes, so no thread sees a partially-initialized object.
    🎯 Practice
    Without using synchronized or Atomic classes, implement a thread-safe "once" flag — a boolean that can only transition from false to true, never back — using only volatile. Prove it's correct.
    HintSingle writer, multiple readers. The transition is one-way. Does volatile alone work here?
    → Worked Solution + Proof
    Java
    class OnceFlag { private volatile boolean done = false; public void markDone() { done = true; } // only call from ONE thread public boolean isDone() { return done; } // safe from any thread } // PROOF OF CORRECTNESS: // Write: single writer calling markDone() — no race between writers. // Read: volatile guarantees any thread calling isDone() after markDone() returns // sees done=true. JMM happens-before: volatile write HB volatile read. // One-way transition: false→true only, never reset → no invariant violation possible. // // This would NOT work if multiple threads could call markDone() simultaneously — // then you'd need AtomicBoolean.compareAndSet(false, true) to win the race atomically.

    volatile vs synchronized

    visibility guarantee vs atomicity + visibility guarantee
    🧠 Intuition
    volatile solves visibility. synchronized solves visibility AND atomicity.Without volatile, a thread might cache a variable's value in a CPU register or core-local cache, never seeing updates another thread makes. volatile forces every read/write to go through main memory, guaranteeing visibility. But volatile does NOT make compound operations (like count++) atomic — for that, you need synchronized or Atomic classes, which provide both visibility AND mutual exclusion.
    📐 The Classic volatile Use Case — Flag Variables
    💻 Correct Usage Pattern
    Java
    // ✓ CORRECT use of volatile — simple flag, single writer, multiple readers class Worker implements Runnable { private volatile boolean running = true; // guarantees visibility across threads public void run() { while (running) { // without volatile, this loop might NEVER see running=false // do work } } public void stop() { running = false; } // called from another thread } // ✗ WRONG use of volatile — compound operation, NOT atomic class Counter { private volatile int count = 0; public void increment() { count++; // STILL a race condition! volatile only fixes visibility, not atomicity } // count++ is read-modify-write — 3 separate steps, still interleaveable } // Fix: use synchronized, or AtomicInteger, for compound operations.
    💡 Comparison Table
    Aspectvolatilesynchronized
    Guarantees visibilityYesYes
    Guarantees atomicityNo (single read/write only)Yes (entire block)
    Can block threadsNoYes — other threads wait
    Performance costLowHigher (lock acquisition overhead)
    Best forSimple flags, single-writer stateCompound operations, multi-field invariants
    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "Is volatile ever enough for a counter?"

    A: Only if exactly one thread ever writes to it and others only read (single-writer, multi-reader). The moment multiple threads write, you need atomicity too — volatile alone isn't sufficient.

    Q: "What's a 'happens-before' relationship?"

    A: The JMM (Java Memory Model) guarantee that a write to a volatile variable happens-before any subsequent read of that same variable by another thread — meaning all writes that occurred before the volatile write are also guaranteed visible after the read. This is the formal basis for the double-checked locking pattern requiring volatile.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    A flag boolean running = true is used to stop a background thread: while(running) { doWork(); }. Another thread sets running = false. But the background thread never stops. Why?
    Without volatile, each thread has its own CPU-cache copy of running. The write to false on Thread B stays in B's cache and is never flushed to main memory where Thread A reads from.
    volatile: guarantees visibility — writes are immediately flushed to main memory, reads always fetch from main memory. Prevents CPU-cache staling. Does NOT guarantee atomicity of compound operations. synchronized: guarantees both visibility AND mutual exclusion (atomicity). More expensive than volatile — involves a monitor lock. Fix for flag: volatile boolean running = true — the write is visible to all threads immediately. When volatile is enough: single writer, multiple readers, simple assignment (not compound). When you need synchronized: check-then-act, read-modify-write (count++), compound state updates across multiple variables.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: Why is count++ not atomic even if count is volatile?
    💭 Think First
    volatile guarantees visibility but not atomicity. count++ is actually three operations. What are they?
    → Complete Answer
    count++ decompiles to: (1) READ count from memory into register, (2) INCREMENT the register value, (3) WRITE register back to memory. Two threads can both read the same value (e.g. 5), both increment to 6, both write 6 — the net result is 6 instead of 7. volatile only ensures reads/writes individually are visible to all threads — it does not make the three-step sequence atomic. Fix: AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() uses a single CAS instruction that is hardware-atomic. Or use synchronized to wrap the three steps.
    Q: What is the Java Memory Model happens-before relationship and why does it matter?
    💭 Think First
    The JMM defines when one thread's writes are guaranteed to be visible to another thread's reads. Without happens-before, the compiler and CPU can reorder operations.
    → Complete Answer
    Happens-before (HB): if A HB B, then all writes by A before the HB relationship are visible to B. Key HB rules: (1) monitor unlock HB subsequent lock of the same monitor, (2) volatile write HB subsequent volatile read of the same variable, (3) Thread.start() HB all actions in the started thread, (4) all actions in thread T HB Thread.join(T) returning. Why it matters: without HB, the JIT compiler can reorder instructions, the CPU can execute out-of-order, and caches can defer writes. Volatile and synchronized establish HB, creating memory barriers that prevent unsafe reordering.
    🎯 Practice
    Write a worker thread loop controlled by a non-volatile boolean flag set by the main thread. Run it — observe it may never stop (JIT optimization caches the read). Add volatile and confirm it stops reliably.
    💡 Hint — think before readingThink through the data structures first. What classes do you need? What are their relationships? Write class signatures before any method bodies.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — approach
    // Step 1: Define interface / abstract class // Step 2: Choose the right collection (List/Map/Set/Queue) // Step 3: Implement operations one by one // Step 4: Add concurrency if needed (AtomicX / synchronized) // Step 5: Test each operation independently
    🎯 Practice Task
    Fix this broken lazy singleton: class Config { static Config instance; static Config get() { if(instance==null) instance = new Config(); return instance; } }. First make it thread-safe with synchronized, then with volatile + DCL, then with the static holder idiom. Explain which is best.
    Hint — think before readingSynchronized: simple but every call to get() acquires a lock even after initialization. DCL + volatile: double-checked locking eliminates the lock after first creation — volatile prevents instruction reordering during construction. Static holder: cleanest — class loading is inherently thread-safe, no explicit synchronization needed.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — three singleton fixes
    // Option 1: synchronized — correct but slow (lock on every call) static synchronized Config get() { if(instance==null) instance = new Config(); return instance; } // Option 2: DCL + volatile — fast after first creation private static volatile Config instance; static Config get() { if(instance==null) { synchronized(Config.class) { if(instance==null) instance = new Config(); }} return instance; } // Option 3: static holder — BEST: lazy, thread-safe, zero synchronization private static class Holder { static final Config I = new Config(); } static Config get() { return Holder.I; } // Holder loaded on first call only
