    Java 8 Streams

    declarative pipelines · lazy evaluation · parallel streams · every follow-up
    🧠 Mental Model
    A stream is a recipe, not a list. Nothing is cooked until you say "serve."When you call .filter().map().sorted(), you're building a pipeline of transformations — no element is touched yet. The moment you call a terminal operation (.collect(), .count(), .findFirst()), Java executes the entire pipeline lazily: each element flows through all stages before the next element starts. This enables short-circuit optimizations: if you want findFirst(), Java stops after finding one match — it doesn't process the remaining 999,999 elements.
    📐 Pipeline Execution Model
    💻 Patterns Interviewers Actually Test
    Java — stream patterns from real interviews
    // 1. Group by department, find max-salary employee per department Map<String, Optional<Employee>> topPerDept = employees.stream() .collect(Collectors.groupingBy( Employee::getDept, Collectors.maxBy(Comparator.comparing(Employee::getSalary)) )); // 2. Flat-map — explode nested collections into one stream List<String> allSkills = employees.stream() .flatMap(e -> e.getSkills().stream()) // each employee has List<String> skills .distinct() .collect(Collectors.toList()); // 3. Partition into two groups (true/false) Map<Boolean, List<Employee>> seniorJunior = employees.stream() .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(e -> e.getYears() > 5)); // 4. Reduce — custom aggregation double totalSalary = employees.stream() .mapToDouble(Employee::getSalary) .sum(); // or .reduce(0.0, Double::sum) // 5. Collectors.toMap with merge function (handle duplicate keys) Map<String, Long> wordCount = words.stream() .collect(Collectors.toMap( w -> w, w -> 1L, Long::sum // merge fn: if key exists, sum the values ));
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q1: "Can you reuse a stream? What happens if you try?"
    💭 Think
    A stream is a single-use pipeline. What does "consumed" mean?
    → Answer
    No — a stream can only be consumed once. After a terminal operation executes, the stream is in a "closed" state. Calling any operation on it again throws IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed. To iterate the data again, create a fresh stream from the source collection. This is a deliberate design: streams don't hold data themselves, they process data from an underlying source, and re-traversal may not be possible (e.g., for I/O streams).
    Q2: "When should you NOT use parallelStream()?"
    💭 Think
    What assumptions does parallel execution break?
    → Answer (be specific)
    Avoid parallelStream() when:
    (1) Small collections — thread-pool overhead + fork/join coordination exceeds the work saved.
    (2) I/O-bound operations — parallelStream uses ForkJoinPool.commonPool() which has core-count threads. Blocking I/O in workers exhausts this shared pool, hurting ALL parallel streams JVM-wide (including framework internals).
    (3) Stateful operations with side effects — e.g., adding to an ArrayList inside a parallel forEach. ArrayList is not thread-safe; results will be corrupted.
    (4) Encounter-order-sensitive operations — findFirst() on an unordered parallel stream may return any match, not the first in list order.
    Rule of thumb: measure before parallelizing. A sequential stream over 1M CPU-bound elements is a good candidate. A parallel stream over 100 elements with 5ms DB calls per element is almost certainly slower.
    Q3: "What's the difference between map() and flatMap()?"
    💭 Think
    map produces one output per input. What does flatMap do when the output is itself a collection?
    → Answer with example
    map(f) applies f and wraps each result — if f returns a List, you get a Stream<List<T>>. flatMap(f) applies f AND flattens one level — if f returns a Stream or Collection, you get a Stream<T> with all elements merged. Classic analogy: map is like calling a function on each gift box and getting a box of boxes back. flatMap opens all the boxes and hands you a single pile of contents.
    🏭 Live Coding Scenario
    "Given a list of orders, find the top 3 customers by total spend, and return their names in descending order."
    Steps: group by customer → sum amounts → sort → limit → extract names. Can you write this as one stream chain?
    Java
    List<String> top3 = orders.stream() .collect(Collectors.groupingBy( Order::getCustomerName, Collectors.summingDouble(Order::getAmount) )) // Map<String, Double> .entrySet().stream() .sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Double>comparingByValue().reversed()) .limit(3) .map(Map.Entry::getKey) .collect(Collectors.toList()); // Interview tip: talk through each step as you write it. // "First I group by customer and sum their order amounts, // giving me a Map. Then I stream the entries, sort by value descending, // take the top 3, and extract just the names."
    🎯 Practice
    Given a list of strings, find the first string that starts with "A", has length > 5, and return its uppercase version. Return "NONE" if not found. Write it two ways: imperative and stream.
    HintStream way: filter twice, findFirst() (short-circuits!), map to uppercase, orElse. The short-circuit is the key advantage to mention.
    → Worked Solution
    Java
    // Imperative String result = "NONE"; for (String s : strings) { if (s.startsWith("A") && s.length() > 5) { result = s.toUpperCase(); break; } } // Stream — same logic, more declarative String result2 = strings.stream() .filter(s -> s.startsWith("A") && s.length() > 5) .findFirst() // SHORT-CIRCUITS — stops at first match .map(String::toUpperCase) .orElse("NONE"); // Key point: findFirst() + filter() does NOT process the whole list. // If the match is at index 3, elements 4-N are never touched.

    Optional in Java

    making the absence of a value explicit in the type system
    🧠 Intuition
    Optional forces you to confront "this might not exist" at compile timeReturning null from a method is a silent contract — callers might forget to check, leading to NullPointerException at runtime, often far from the actual bug. Optional<T> wraps a value that may or may not be present, and its API (isPresent, orElse, map) forces callers to explicitly handle the empty case, catching bugs at compile time instead of in production.
    💻 Before → After
    Java
    // ✗ BEFORE — silent null contract, easy to forget the check public User findUserById(String id) { return userMap.get(id); // returns null if not found — caller might not check! } User u = findUserById("123"); System.out.println(u.getName()); // NullPointerException if not found — crashes far from root cause // ✓ AFTER — Optional forces explicit handling public Optional<User> findUserById(String id) { return Optional.ofNullable(userMap.get(id)); } Optional<User> userOpt = findUserById("123"); // Option 1: provide a default User u1 = userOpt.orElse(User.GUEST); // Option 2: provide a default computed lazily (only if needed) User u2 = userOpt.orElseGet(() -> createGuestUser()); // Option 3: throw a meaningful exception if missing User u3 = userOpt.orElseThrow(() -> new UserNotFoundException(id)); // Option 4: chain transformations safely — skipped entirely if empty String name = userOpt.map(User::getName).orElse("Unknown"); // Option 5: act only if present, no return value needed userOpt.ifPresent(user -> System.out.println("Found: " + user.getName()));
    ⚠ Common Optional Mistakes
    • Calling .get() without checking isPresent()This defeats the entire purpose — it throws NoSuchElementException, just trading one runtime exception for another. Always use orElse/orElseThrow/map instead.
    • Using Optional as a field or method parameter typeOptional was designed as a RETURN type to signal "this might be absent." Using it for fields adds serialization complexity and is generally discouraged by the Java team itself.
    • Wrapping collections in OptionalReturn an empty List/Map instead of Optional<List> — empty collections are already a safe, iterable "nothing here" signal.
    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "Does Optional eliminate NullPointerException entirely?"

    A: No — it shifts the responsibility to the type system for return values specifically. You can still misuse it (calling .get() blindly) or have null creep in elsewhere. It's a design discipline, not a silver bullet.

    Q: "Why shouldn't Optional be used for method parameters?"

    A: It adds an extra wrapping/unwrapping step for callers and doesn't compose well with method overloading. The cleaner pattern is overloaded methods or a Builder for optional parameters — Optional is meant specifically as a return-type signal.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    Your senior engineer reviews your code and sees: if(user != null && user.getProfile() != null && user.getProfile().getAddress() != null) { ... }. They say 'use Optional'. Rewrite this correctly.
    Each null check is guarding against a missing value. Optional chains these checks declaratively — null checks vanish because map() and flatMap() skip on empty.
    The rewrite: Optional.ofNullable(user).map(User::getProfile).map(Profile::getAddress).map(Address::getCity).orElse("Unknown"). Each map() short-circuits on empty — no NPE possible, no explicit null checks. Use flatMap() when the method itself returns Optional (e.g., userRepo.findById() returns Optional<User>). Pitfall: Optional.get() without isPresent() throws NoSuchElementException — worse than NPE because it's unexpected. Always use orElse/orElseGet/orElseThrow.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'Should Optional be used as a method parameter? As a field type?'
    💭 Think First
    Optional was designed for return types only. Using it as parameter or field has specific downsides.
    → Complete Answer
    As parameter: callers can pass null for the Optional itself — you haven't solved anything. It also forces callers to wrap values in Optional.of() unnecessarily. Use overloaded methods or @Nullable annotation instead. As field: Optional is not Serializable — putting it in an entity or DTO breaks serialization. As return type: exactly the right use — signals to callers that the value might be absent and forces them to handle it. Rule: Optional is a return type tool, not a general null replacement.
    Q: 'What is the difference between orElse() and orElseGet()? When does it matter?'
    💭 Think First
    Both provide a default value. But one is always evaluated, the other is lazy. When does this matter?
    → Complete Answer
    orElse(value): the expression is evaluated eagerly — even if the Optional contains a value. orElseGet(supplier): the supplier is only called if Optional is empty. Critical when the default is expensive: optional.orElse(expensiveDbCall()) — expensiveDbCall() runs every time even when Optional has a value! Fix: optional.orElseGet(() -> expensiveDbCall()) — lambda only runs when empty. Rule: orElse for cheap literals/constants. orElseGet for anything computed or fetched.
    🎯 Practice
    Refactor a repository method that currently returns null on missing records to return Optional<T> instead. Update all call sites to use orElseThrow with a custom exception rather than null checks.
    💡 Hint — think before readingThink through the data structures first. What classes do you need? What are their relationships? Write class signatures before any method bodies.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — approach
    // Step 1: Define interface / abstract class // Step 2: Choose the right collection (List/Map/Set/Queue) // Step 3: Implement operations one by one // Step 4: Add concurrency if needed (AtomicX / synchronized) // Step 5: Test each operation independently
    🎯 Practice Task
    Write a method getUserCity(String userId) that: fetches the user from a repository (returns Optional), gets their profile (User.getProfile() returns Optional), gets their address (Profile.getAddress() returns Optional
    ), and returns the city string or "Unknown".
    Hint — think before readingChain flatMap for Optional-returning methods (getProfile, getAddress since they return Optional), and map for plain-value methods (getCity). orElse at the end provides the default.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — Optional chain
    public String getUserCity(String userId) { return userRepo.findById(userId) // Optional<User> .flatMap(User::getProfile) // Optional<Profile> — flatMap because returns Optional .flatMap(Profile::getAddress) // Optional<Address> .map(Address::getCity) // Optional<String> — map because returns String .orElse("Unknown"); // String — default if any step was empty } // Zero null checks. Zero NPE risk. Each step short-circuits if empty.

    LRU Cache Design in Java

    production-style — the shortcut AND the from-scratch version
    🧠 Intuition
    Two ways to build it: the quick way and the "I understand it" wayJava's LinkedHashMap has a built-in accessOrder mode that reorders entries on access — perfect for LRU with minimal code. But interviewers often want the from-scratch HashMap + Doubly Linked List version (covered in the LLD section) to test whether you understand WHY it works, not just that the library exists.
    💻 The Production Shortcut — LinkedHashMap
    Java — LinkedHashMap-based LRU (production-ready)
    class LRUCache<K, V> extends LinkedHashMap<K, V> { private final int capacity; public LRUCache(int capacity) { // accessOrder=true: reorders entries by access time, not insertion time super(capacity, 0.75f, true); this.capacity = capacity; } @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) { return size() > capacity; // LinkedHashMap calls this after every put() — } // returning true auto-evicts the LRU entry } // Usage — looks like a normal Map, LRU eviction happens automatically LRUCache<Integer, String> cache = new LRUCache<>(3); cache.put(1, "A"); cache.put(2, "B"); cache.put(3, "C"); cache.get(1); // access 1 — moves it to most-recently-used cache.put(4, "D"); // evicts 2 (the actual LRU), not 1 // NOT thread-safe by default — wrap with Collections.synchronizedMap() for concurrent use, // or implement custom locking as shown in the LLD section for finer control.
    💡 Shortcut vs From-Scratch — Interview Strategy
    ApproachWhen to Use
    LinkedHashMap shortcutIf asked to "design a cache in Java" with no constraint on libraries — mention it exists, then offer to also show the underlying mechanism
    HashMap + DLL from scratchIf asked an LLD-style question testing data structure understanding (most common) — always default to this unless told otherwise
    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "Why mention the LinkedHashMap version at all if they want from-scratch?"

    A: It signals you know the standard library deeply AND can build the underlying mechanism — saying "Java actually has this built in via LinkedHashMap's accessOrder mode, but let me show you how it works underneath" is a strong opening that demonstrates both breadth and depth.

    Q: "How would you make this cache thread-safe with good read concurrency?"

    A: Wrap critical sections with ReentrantReadWriteLock — but note that get() in an LRU cache also mutates (reorders), so it technically needs a write lock too, limiting how much ReadWriteLock actually helps versus a plain cache.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    An interviewer asks: 'Design and implement an LRU cache for a user-profile service. It must be thread-safe, support TTL (entries expire after 30 minutes), and handle 50K reads/second.'
    Three constraints: LRU eviction (data structure choice), thread-safety (synchronization strategy), TTL (expiry mechanism). Each constraint adds complexity. Address them one at a time.
    Data structure: LinkedHashMap(accessOrder=true) gives O(1) LRU. Thread-safety: Collections.synchronizedMap wraps it — but coarse lock serializes reads. For 50K/s: use Caffeine library (lock-striped, near-lock-free reads). TTL: Caffeine supports expireAfterWrite(30, MINUTES) natively. Each entry has a creation timestamp; background cleanup runs periodically. With plain LinkedHashMap: store Entry{value, expiresAt} as the value, check expiry on get() and remove if expired. Problem: expired entries accumulate. Fix: add a cleanup thread that scans every minute, or use a separate DelayQueue of expiring keys.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'Why is Caffeine preferred over Guava Cache in production Spring Boot applications?'
    💭 Think First
    Both are in-process caches. Think about performance benchmarks and Spring's default choice.
    → Complete Answer
    Spring Boot 2.x and later defaults to Caffeine over Guava Cache because: (1) Performance: Caffeine uses W-TinyLFU eviction policy (better hit rate than LRU in real workloads) + ring-buffer-based access order recording (reads are near-lock-free). Benchmarks show 3-10× higher throughput than Guava. (2) Statistics: built-in cache hit rate, load time, eviction count metrics. (3) Java 8+ API: Guava Cache predates Java 8 — its API is verbose. Caffeine's API is cleaner. (4) Spring integration: add spring-boot-starter-cache + caffeine dependency → @Cacheable annotations automatically use Caffeine.
    Q: 'How do you handle cache stampede (thundering herd) when many threads simultaneously miss the same key?'
    💭 Think First
    Cache miss → all threads go to DB simultaneously → DB overload. How do you serialize the first load while others wait?
    → Complete Answer
    Caffeine handles this automatically with its loading cache: cache.get(key, k -> dbService.load(k)) — for a given key, only ONE thread runs the loader; others block waiting for the result, then get it from cache. Without Caffeine: use a ConcurrentHashMap of CompletableFutures as a request-coalescing layer. inFlight.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> db.load(k))) — first thread creates the future, others get the same future and join() it. When done, put in cache and remove from inFlight.
    🎯 Practice
    Implement both versions side by side. Write a single test suite that runs against both implementations to confirm they produce identical eviction behavior for the same sequence of operations.
    💡 Hint — think before readingThink through the data structures first. What classes do you need? What are their relationships? Write class signatures before any method bodies.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — approach
    // Step 1: Define interface / abstract class // Step 2: Choose the right collection (List/Map/Set/Queue) // Step 3: Implement operations one by one // Step 4: Add concurrency if needed (AtomicX / synchronized) // Step 5: Test each operation independently
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement a simple TTL-aware LRU cache using LinkedHashMap. Entries expire 10 seconds after insertion. get() must return empty for expired entries even if they're in the map.
    Hint — think before readingWrap values in a record CachedEntry{value, expiresAt}. In get(): check if CachedEntry.expiresAt is before Instant.now() — if expired, remove and return empty. Override removeEldestEntry for capacity-based LRU eviction.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — TTL LRU cache
    class TtlLRUCache<K,V> { record Entry<V>(V value, Instant expiresAt) { boolean expired() { return Instant.now().isAfter(expiresAt); } } private final long ttlSeconds; private final Map<K, Entry<V>> cache; TtlLRUCache(int capacity, long ttlSeconds) { this.ttlSeconds = ttlSeconds; cache = new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) { protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K,Entry<V>> e) { return size() > capacity; } }; } public synchronized Optional<V> get(K key) { Entry<V> e = cache.get(key); if(e == null) return Optional.empty(); if(e.expired()) { cache.remove(key); return Optional.empty(); } return Optional.of(e.value()); } public synchronized void put(K key, V value) { cache.put(key, new Entry<>(value, Instant.now().plusSeconds(ttlSeconds))); } }

    Microservices Architecture — Deep Dive

    Spring Boot service communication · API Gateway · Eureka · Config Server · Circuit Breaker · the complete picture
    🧠 Why This Section Exists
    This was the #1 gap: "I assumed Spring Boot was enough. Instead I was asked about service communication, API Gateway, Eureka, Config Server, Circuit Breaker."Knowing how to build ONE Spring Boot service is not the same as knowing how to build a system of 20 services that discover each other, share config, handle failures gracefully, and remain observable. This section covers the full microservices ecosystem — every component an SDE-2 interviewer expects you to know. Key principles: Each service owns a bounded context (clear domain boundary, its own DB schema). Services are loosely coupled — they communicate via APIs or events, not shared databases. Independent deployment: a change to the Order service deploys without touching the Payment service. This is the fundamental promise of microservices — and the source of its complexity.
    📐 The Complete Spring Microservices Stack
    💻 Component 1: Service Discovery with Eureka
    Spring Boot — Eureka server + client setup
    // ─── Eureka SERVER (one dedicated service) ─────────────────────────────── @SpringBootApplication @EnableEurekaServer public class DiscoveryServer { public static void main(String[] a) { SpringApplication.run(DiscoveryServer.class, a); } } // application.yml (Eureka server) // eureka.client.register-with-eureka: false ← don't self-register // eureka.client.fetch-registry: false // ─── Every MICROSERVICE registers as a Eureka CLIENT ───────────────────── @SpringBootApplication @EnableEurekaClient // auto-registers on startup, sends heartbeats every 30s public class OrderService { ... } // application.yml (each microservice) // spring.application.name: order-service ← this is its registry name // eureka.client.service-url.defaultZone: http://eureka-host:8761/eureka/ // ─── Calling another service BY NAME (Eureka resolves IP) ──────────────── @LoadBalanced // tells RestTemplate to resolve via Eureka + load balance @Bean public RestTemplate restTemplate() { return new RestTemplate(); } // Usage: // restTemplate.getForObject("http://user-service/users/{id}", User.class, userId); // "user-service" is resolved to an actual IP by Eureka — no hardcoded host!
    💻 Component 2: Feign Client (Declarative HTTP)
    Spring Boot — Feign replaces manual RestTemplate calls
    // Instead of manually building RestTemplate calls, Feign generates HTTP client from interface @FeignClient(name = "user-service") // name matches spring.application.name in Eureka public interface UserServiceClient { @GetMapping("/users/{id}") User getUserById(@PathVariable("id") String id); @PostMapping("/users") User createUser(@RequestBody CreateUserRequest req); } // In OrderService — inject and use like a local service call @Service public class OrderService { @Autowired private UserServiceClient userClient; // Feign generates the implementation public Order placeOrder(String userId, List<Item> items) { User user = userClient.getUserById(userId); // HTTP call to user-service under the hood // Feign: load-balances, integrates with Eureka, retries, and works with Circuit Breaker } }
    💻 Component 3: Circuit Breaker with Resilience4j
    Spring Boot — fail fast, not cascade
    // Problem: Payment Service is down. Every order request waits 30s for timeout. // 100 requests/s × 30s timeout = 3000 threads blocked → OOM → Order Service dies too. // This is a CASCADING FAILURE — one service taking down others. // Solution: Circuit Breaker opens after N failures → fails immediately instead of waiting @Service public class PaymentService { @CircuitBreaker(name = "payment", fallbackMethod = "paymentFallback") @TimeLimiter(name = "payment") // timeout if call takes too long public CompletableFuture<PaymentResult> processPayment(Order order) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> paymentClient.charge(order)); } // Called when circuit is OPEN or timeout fires public CompletableFuture<PaymentResult> paymentFallback(Order order, Exception ex) { log.warn("Payment circuit open, queuing for retry", ex); pendingPaymentQueue.add(order); // store for async retry return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(PaymentResult.PENDING); } } // application.yml: // resilience4j.circuitbreaker.instances.payment: // slidingWindowSize: 10 ← track last 10 calls // failureRateThreshold: 50 ← open at 50% failure rate // waitDurationInOpenState: 30s ← wait before trying again (half-open) // permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState: 3
    💻 Component 4: Spring Cloud Config Server
    Spring Boot — centralized config, no env-var sprawl
    // Config Server: reads config from Git repo, serves to all microservices @SpringBootApplication @EnableConfigServer public class ConfigServer { ... } // application.yml (Config Server): // spring.cloud.config.server.git.uri: https://github.com/org/config-repo // Folder structure in config-repo: // order-service.yml ← order-service default config // order-service-prod.yml ← order-service PROD overrides // user-service.yml // application.yml ← shared config for ALL services // Each microservice's bootstrap.yml (loaded before application.yml): // spring.cloud.config.uri: http://config-server:8888 // spring.profiles.active: prod ← selects order-service-prod.yml // Benefits: // - One place to change DB URLs, feature flags, timeouts for all services // - Git history of all config changes // - /actuator/refresh endpoint to reload config without restart // - Encrypt sensitive values: {cipher}AQA...
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q1: "How do microservices communicate — REST vs messaging? When do you choose each?"
    💭 Think
    Does the caller need an immediate response? Can the action be async?
    → Decision framework
    REST/gRPC (synchronous): Use when the response is needed immediately to proceed — e.g., "validate this payment before confirming the order." Caller blocks until response. Tighter coupling, shared availability (if downstream is down, caller fails).

    Kafka/RabbitMQ (async messaging): Use for "fire and notify" — e.g., "order placed → notify inventory service, notification service, analytics service." Caller doesn't wait. Services decouple: inventory being slow doesn't slow order placement. Enables the Saga pattern for distributed transactions. Downside: eventual consistency, harder to debug.

    Rule of thumb: User-facing critical path → REST. Internal side effects and cross-service workflows → messaging.
    Q2: "Explain the Saga pattern for distributed transactions."
    💭 Think
    You can't do a 2-phase commit across microservices. How do you handle "transfer money: debit A AND credit B" when they're separate services?
    → Saga Choreography
    Saga — event-driven approach
    // Each service does its local transaction, then publishes an event // Next service listens and does its part // On failure: publish a COMPENSATING event to undo prior steps // Happy path: // OrderService: save order (status=PENDING) → publish OrderCreated // PaymentService: charge card → publish PaymentSucceeded // InventoryService: reserve items → publish ItemsReserved // OrderService: listens → update order (status=CONFIRMED) // Failure path (payment fails): // PaymentService → publish PaymentFailed // OrderService: listens → cancel order (status=CANCELLED) // No items were reserved yet — no compensating action needed there // Key: each step is a LOCAL transaction. The saga is the sequence. // Eventual consistency: order is CONFIRMED only after all steps succeed.
    Q3: "How do you handle API versioning in microservices?"
    💭 Think
    Service A at v1, Service B that calls it upgrades to expect v2 response — how does this not break?
    → Answer
    Strategy 1 (URI versioning): /api/v1/orders and /api/v2/orders coexist — old callers use v1, new callers use v2. API Gateway routes by prefix. Old version deprecated after migration window.
    Strategy 2 (Header versioning): Accept: application/vnd.company.v2+json — cleaner URLs but harder to test.
    Consumer-driven contract testing (Pact): Each consumer publishes what it expects from a producer. Producer runs contract tests on every build — catches breaking changes before deployment. This is the production-grade approach for CI/CD microservice environments.
    🚨 Production Scenario — The Cascade Failure
    "Monday morning. Order service starts returning 500s. CPU spikes. Logs show timeout errors from payment-service. Payment service itself is healthy but slow."
    Root cause: No circuit breaker. Payment service was slow (DB issue) → every order request opened a connection and waited 30s. 100 req/s × 30s = 3000 waiting threads. Thread pool exhausted → order service OOM.

    Immediate fix: Restart order service. Temporarily route requests without payment (queue for retry).

    Long-term fix: Add @CircuitBreaker + @TimeLimiter. Set timeout to 3s on payment calls. Circuit opens at 50% failure rate → fallback queues orders, payment retried async. One service being slow can no longer take down another.

    Also add: Bulkhead — separate thread pools for different downstream calls. Payment calls use their own pool of 20 threads. Even if exhausted, user-service calls use a different pool and remain unaffected.
    💼 "Explain Your Project" Angle
    Interviewer: "Your project uses Spring Boot — how did you handle service-to-service communication?"
    If monolith: "It was a monolith — services communicated via direct method calls. If I were to migrate to microservices, I'd introduce Kafka for event-driven async flows (like notifications and analytics) and Feign clients with circuit breakers for synchronous service calls where immediate response is needed."

    If microservices: "We used Feign clients registered via Eureka for synchronous calls between services. For async workflows — like triggering email after order confirmation — we used Kafka. We had a Config Server pulling from Git for centralized configuration. Circuit breakers (Resilience4j) on all external service calls prevented cascade failures, which we learned the hard way after a payment-service slowdown took down order service in staging."
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Your Stream pipeline processes 10M order records. It runs for 20 minutes then throws OutOfMemoryError. What went wrong?
    Streams are lazy — they process one element at a time, not loading everything into memory. But some operations break this. Think about which terminal or intermediate operations collect results.
    Root cause: Calling .collect(toList()) at the end keeps all 10M results in memory simultaneously. Or: using .sorted() on an unsorted source — sorted() is a stateful intermediate operation that must see ALL elements before emitting any, so it buffers the entire stream in memory. Fix: If you need to sort: sort in the database query (ORDER BY), not in the stream. If you need to collect results: batch-process with pagination — process 1000 records at a time, write results incrementally. Stream memory model: filter(), map(), flatMap() are lazy (process one element, emit one element). sorted(), distinct(), limit() are stateful (may buffer). collect() is a terminal that buffers. Rule: Never call .sorted() on a stream of more than ~100K elements in production. Never .collect() more than available heap / element size.
    🎯 Practice
    Design the complete flow for: "User places an order → payment is charged → inventory reserved → confirmation email sent." Specify: which calls are synchronous REST vs async Kafka events, where the circuit breaker lives, and how you handle a payment failure.
    Architecture hintCritical user-facing path (place order + charge payment) → synchronous REST. Post-confirmation side effects (email, analytics, inventory) → Kafka events. Circuit breaker around payment call. Payment failure → compensating transaction (cancel order).
    → Worked Architecture
    Flow design
    // SYNCHRONOUS PATH (user waits for this): // POST /orders → OrderService // 1. Validate cart (local) // 2. @CircuitBreaker → PaymentService.charge() [REST, timeout 5s] // └─ Success → save order(CONFIRMED), publish OrderConfirmed event // └─ Failure → return 402 Payment Required (no order saved) // ASYNC PATH (user doesn't wait, happens in background): // OrderConfirmed event on Kafka → // InventoryService: reserve items → publish InventoryReserved // NotificationService: send confirmation email (fire and forget) // AnalyticsService: log conversion event // SAGA COMPENSATION (inventory reservation fails after payment succeeded): // InventoryService publishes ReservationFailed // OrderService listens → call PaymentService.refund() → update order(CANCELLED) // NotificationService sends cancellation email // KEY DECISIONS TO MENTION: // - Payment is sync (user needs immediate result) // - Everything after payment confirmation is async (decoupled, no user wait) // - Circuit breaker prevents payment slowness from killing order service // - Kafka guarantees inventory/notification get the event even if temporarily down
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Your Stream pipeline processes 10M order records. It runs 20 minutes then throws OutOfMemoryError. The operations are: stream().filter().sorted().map().collect(toList()). What is the root cause?
    Streams are lazy but some operations break laziness. Which operation in this chain must buffer the entire stream before emitting a single element?
    Root cause: sorted() is a stateful intermediate operation — it must see ALL 10M elements before emitting any (you cannot sort a partially-seen list). It buffers everything in heap. Plus collect(toList()) at the end holds all results. Two full-stream buffers for 10M records = OOM. Fix: Sort in the SQL query (ORDER BY) — let the database use its index. Remove sorted() from the stream. Process results in batches (pagination) so you never load all 10M into the JVM. Rule: Never call sorted(), distinct() on streams of more than ~100K elements. Never collect() more records than available heap permits.

    Idempotent APIs

    making retries safe — critical for distributed systems
    🧠 Intuition
    Calling it once or calling it five times produces the same resultNetworks fail. A client sends a "charge ₹500" request, the response is lost due to a timeout, and the client retries — did the charge happen once or twice? An idempotent API guarantees that repeating the same request (with the same idempotency key) never causes duplicate side effects, making safe retries possible.
    📐 Idempotency Key Flow
    💻 Implementation Pattern
    Java — Spring Boot idempotency filter
    @PostMapping("/payments") public ResponseEntity<PaymentResponse> createPayment( @RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") String idempotencyKey, @RequestBody PaymentRequest request) { // 1. Check if we've already processed this exact key Optional<PaymentResponse> cached = idempotencyStore.get(idempotencyKey); if (cached.isPresent()) { return ResponseEntity.ok(cached.get()); // return the SAME response, don't reprocess } // 2. Process normally — this should happen exactly once per unique key PaymentResponse response = paymentService.process(request); // 3. Store the result keyed by idempotency key (with a TTL, e.g. 24 hours) idempotencyStore.put(idempotencyKey, response, Duration.ofHours(24)); return ResponseEntity.ok(response); } // Critical: step 1 (check) and the eventual store must be atomic to avoid // two concurrent retries both passing the check and double-processing. // Use a DB unique constraint on idempotency_key, or a distributed lock (Redis SETNX).
    💡 Idempotent by HTTP Method (REST Convention)
    MethodNaturally Idempotent?Why
    GETYesRead-only, no side effects regardless of repeat count
    PUTYes"Set this resource to X" — repeating produces the same final state
    DELETEYes"Ensure this resource is gone" — already-deleted is still the same end state
    POSTNo, by default"Create a new resource" — repeating naturally creates duplicates unless an idempotency key is added explicitly
    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "Why is POST not naturally idempotent, and how do you fix that?"

    A: POST means "create," and calling create twice naturally makes two resources. The fix is an explicit client-generated idempotency key sent in the request, which the server uses to detect and dedupe retries — exactly the pattern shown above. Stripe's payment API is the textbook real-world example.

    Q: "What happens if two retries arrive at the exact same moment (race)?"

    A: The check-then-store sequence must be atomic, otherwise both requests pass the "not found" check and both process. Use a DB unique constraint (insert fails on duplicate key) or a Redis SETNX as a distributed lock before processing.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    A payment API is called with idempotency-key: 'pay-xyz-123'. The client's network drops and they retry the same request 3 times. How do you ensure the user is only charged once?
    Without idempotency: 3 retries = 3 charges. The server must recognise repeated requests and return the same response without re-executing the logic.
    Implementation: Extract the Idempotency-Key header. Check Redis: GET idempotency:{key}. If found: return the cached response (deserialised from JSON). If not found: process the payment, store the result: SET idempotency:{key} {responseJson} EX 86400 (24h TTL), return the response. Critical: the check-and-store must be in the same transaction or use Redis SET NX to handle concurrent duplicate requests (two threads both see 'not found', both process). Redis SET NX: only one succeeds → other waits or returns 'processing'. Store a 'PROCESSING' sentinel first, then update to the final result.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'What is the difference between idempotent and safe HTTP methods?'
    💭 Think First
    Safe = no side effects. Idempotent = same result regardless of how many times called. Are these the same?
    → Complete Answer
    Safe methods produce no side effects: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS. Idempotent methods: same result whether called 1 or N times. GET/HEAD are both safe AND idempotent. PUT (update to same state) and DELETE (deleting an already-deleted resource returns 404 but that's still idempotent — the resource is absent) are idempotent but not safe. POST is neither safe nor idempotent by default — each call creates a new resource. To make POST idempotent: use client-provided idempotency keys as above. PATCH is not idempotent by default (increment operations aren't), but can be if the patch sets an absolute value.
    Q: 'How do you handle idempotency for an operation that spans multiple microservices?'
    💭 Think First
    If service A calls B and C, and A retries, B and C might get called twice. How do you propagate idempotency?
    → Complete Answer
    Propagate the idempotency key downstream: when A calls B, it passes the same idempotency key (or a derived one: key + ':b'). Each service independently checks its own idempotency store. For the distributed case, a Saga pattern with compensating transactions handles partial failures: if B succeeds but C fails, C's failure is retried (with idempotency key) until it succeeds, or a compensating action undoes B's effect. The idempotency key scopes the entire saga — retrying the whole saga is safe because each step checks its own key.
    🎯 Practice
    Build a small Spring Boot endpoint with idempotency key support backed by a database unique constraint. Fire 10 concurrent identical requests and verify only one actually creates a record.
    💡 Hint — think before readingThink through the data structures first. What classes do you need? What are their relationships? Write class signatures before any method bodies.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — approach
    // Step 1: Define interface / abstract class // Step 2: Choose the right collection (List/Map/Set/Queue) // Step 3: Implement operations one by one // Step 4: Add concurrency if needed (AtomicX / synchronized) // Step 5: Test each operation independently
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement an IdempotencyFilter in Spring that: intercepts all POST requests with an Idempotency-Key header, checks Redis, returns the cached response if present, otherwise proceeds and caches the response before returning.
    Hint — think before readingOncePerRequestFilter, extract header, check Redis, if hit wrap and return cached response. If miss, use ContentCachingResponseWrapper to capture the response body after the filter chain runs, then store in Redis.
    → Worked Solution
    Spring — IdempotencyFilter
    @Component class IdempotencyFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter { @Autowired StringRedisTemplate redis; static final String PREFIX = "idempotency:"; protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, FilterChain chain) throws IOException, ServletException { String key = req.getHeader("Idempotency-Key"); if(key == null || !"POST".equals(req.getMethod())) { chain.doFilter(req, res); return; } String cached = redis.opsForValue().get(PREFIX + key); if(cached != null) { // replay cached response res.setStatus(200); res.setContentType("application/json"); res.getWriter().write(cached); return; } ContentCachingResponseWrapper wrapped = new ContentCachingResponseWrapper(res); chain.doFilter(req, wrapped); // process normally String body = new String(wrapped.getContentAsByteArray()); redis.opsForValue().set(PREFIX + key, body, Duration.ofHours(24)); // cache result wrapped.copyBodyToResponse(); } }

    SQL vs NoSQL

    choosing the right data model for the problem
    🧠 Intuition
    Structured + relationships vs flexible + scale-firstSQL databases (Postgres, MySQL) enforce a rigid schema and excel at relationships and ACID transactions — perfect when data integrity and complex joins matter (banking, orders). NoSQL databases (MongoDB, Cassandra, DynamoDB) trade strict schema and joins for horizontal scalability and flexible data shapes — better when you have massive scale, evolving schemas, or simple access patterns.
    💡 Decision Table
    FactorChoose SQLChoose NoSQL
    Data relationshipsComplex joins, foreign keysMostly independent documents/rows
    SchemaFixed, well-understood upfrontEvolving, varies per record
    Consistency needStrong (ACID) — banking, inventoryEventual consistency acceptable
    Scale patternVertical scaling, read replicasHorizontal scaling across many nodes natively
    Example use caseOrder management, financial ledgersUser activity feeds, IoT sensor data, catalogs
    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "Can you use both in the same system?"

    A: Yes — polyglot persistence is common. E.g., Postgres for order/payment data (needs ACID), Redis for session/cache data, Elasticsearch for full-text product search. Pick the right tool per access pattern rather than forcing one database to do everything.

    Q: "What does CAP theorem say about this choice?"

    A: In a network partition, you must choose between Consistency and Availability. Traditional SQL setups typically favor Consistency (CP); many NoSQL systems are tuned for Availability (AP) — e.g., DynamoDB favors AP with eventual consistency by default, though it offers a strongly consistent read option too.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    An interviewer asks: 'You're designing a new feature — user activity feed (like Twitter's timeline). The team is debating SQL vs Cassandra. Walk us through your decision.'
    Activity feeds have specific access patterns: write-heavy (millions of events/second), read by userId (always), no complex joins, can tolerate eventual consistency. These constraints guide the choice.
    SQL fails here: A single 'events' table with 100M rows → index on userId still does sequential scans at scale. JOINs for enrichment (user profile, event metadata) multiply latency. Horizontal sharding SQL is painful — schema migrations across shards, cross-shard queries for feeds that span multiple users. Cassandra wins here: Partition key = userId → all events for a user on one node (O(1) read). Clustering key = eventTimestamp DESC → pre-sorted, latest events first. Wide-column stores 10K events per user as one row. Write throughput: 1M writes/sec across a cluster. Eventual consistency is acceptable for feeds — a 50ms delay before an event appears is fine. SQL wins for: financial transactions (ACID, complex queries, auditability), relational data with complex joins, reporting.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'What is eventual consistency and why does it matter for NoSQL databases?'
    💭 Think First
    Eventual consistency means reads may return stale data for some time after a write. Why would you accept this in a production system?
    → Complete Answer
    Eventual consistency = the system guarantees that, given no new updates, all replicas will eventually converge to the same value. The 'eventually' is usually milliseconds to seconds. You accept this for: (1) Availability: if the primary replica is slow/down, you can still read from a replica (AP in CAP). (2) Latency: reading from the nearest replica avoids cross-datacenter round trips. (3) Throughput: no need to coordinate all replicas before returning. You reject eventual consistency for: financial balances, inventory counts, any place where reading stale data causes incorrect business decisions. In practice: use strong consistency for writes that matter, eventual consistency for reads that can tolerate brief staleness.
    Q: 'What are the ACID properties and which NoSQL databases sacrifice which ones?'
    💭 Think First
    ACID: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. NoSQL databases trade some of these for performance and scalability.
    → Complete Answer
    Atomicity: all-or-nothing writes. Cassandra: single-partition writes are atomic; multi-partition are not (use lightweight transactions or Saga). MongoDB 4.x added multi-document transactions. Consistency: every read reflects the latest committed write. Cassandra: eventual by default, configurable quorum. Isolation: concurrent transactions don't see each other's intermediate state. Most NoSQL: no isolation across operations. Durability: committed data survives crashes. All production NoSQL databases (with AOF/write-ahead log) provide durability. BASE = Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent — the NoSQL alternative to ACID.
    🎯 Practice
    Design the data model for an e-commerce platform using both: Postgres schema for Orders/Payments (with foreign keys), and a MongoDB document shape for Product Catalog (with nested, varying attributes per category).
    💡 Hint — think before readingThink through the data structures first. What classes do you need? What are their relationships? Write class signatures before any method bodies.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — approach
    // Step 1: Define interface / abstract class // Step 2: Choose the right collection (List/Map/Set/Queue) // Step 3: Implement operations one by one // Step 4: Add concurrency if needed (AtomicX / synchronized) // Step 5: Test each operation independently
    🎯 Practice Task
    Your e-commerce app has: Orders table (relational, ACID needed), Product catalog (read-heavy, semi-structured attributes vary by category), and User sessions (key-value, TTL, high volume). Which database for each and why?
    Hint — think before readingMap each use case to its access pattern and consistency requirements. Orders: ACID needed → PostgreSQL. Product catalog: flexible schema, read-heavy → MongoDB or PostgreSQL with JSONB. Sessions: key-value + TTL → Redis.
    → Worked Solution
    Architecture decision
    // Orders: PostgreSQL (ACID, relational, complex queries, auditable) // - payment + inventory updates in one transaction (atomicity) // - complex joins: order + items + customers + payments // Product catalog: MongoDB (flexible schema) // - Electronics: {cpu, ram, storage} vs Clothing: {size, color, material} // - No fixed schema — each category has different attributes // - Read-heavy (1000:1 reads:writes), denormalized for fast page loads // User sessions: Redis (O(1) get/set, TTL built-in, 100K ops/sec) // SET session:{sessionId} {userJson} EX 3600 // GET session:{sessionId} → returns null (expired) or session data // No joins, no transactions, simple key-value, automatic expiry

    Database Indexing

    how a query goes from O(n) table scan to O(log n) lookup
    🧠 Intuition
    An index is the book's table of contents, not the book itselfWithout an index, finding a row matching WHERE email='x@y.com' means scanning every row (O(n)). An index is a separate, sorted data structure (usually a B-Tree) mapping column values to row locations — letting the database binary-search to the answer in O(log n) instead of scanning everything.
    📐 B-Tree Index Diagram
    💻 Practical SQL Example
    SQL
    -- Without an index: full table scan, O(n) SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'jane@example.com'; -- On a 10 million row table, this could take seconds -- Create an index on the column you filter/search by frequently CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email); -- Now the same query: O(log n) — milliseconds, even at 10M rows -- Composite index — order of columns MATTERS CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_date ON orders(user_id, created_at); -- Speeds up: WHERE user_id = ? AND created_at > ? -- Does NOT speed up: WHERE created_at > ? alone (user_id must be the leading column used) -- EXPLAIN shows whether your index is actually being used EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'jane@example.com'; -- Look for "Index Scan" in the output, not "Seq Scan"
    ⚠ The Trade-off Nobody Mentions
    • Indexes slow down writesEvery INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must also update every index on that table. A table with 10 indexes has 10x the index-maintenance cost per write.
    • Indexes consume disk and memoryEach index is a full separate data structure. Indexing every column "just in case" bloats storage and can hurt cache efficiency.
    • Don't index low-cardinality columnsA "status" column with only 3 possible values (ACTIVE/INACTIVE/DELETED) gains little from indexing — the database often still has to scan a large fraction of matching rows.
    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "When would adding an index make a query SLOWER?"

    A: Never makes reads slower, but heavy write workloads suffer — every write now also updates the index structure. If a table is write-heavy and the indexed column is rarely queried, the index is pure overhead.

    Q: "What's the difference between a clustered and non-clustered index?"

    A: A clustered index determines the PHYSICAL order rows are stored on disk (usually the primary key) — a table can have only one. Non-clustered indexes are separate structures pointing back to the row location, and a table can have many.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    EXPLAIN ANALYZE on your query shows a Seq Scan on a 50M-row orders table. The query filters by customer_id AND status. You add an index on customer_id — but performance barely improves. Why?
    Single-column index on customer_id helps when filtering by customer alone. But with an AND status filter, the database might do an index scan then a filter (re-check condition) on millions of rows if most customers have many orders.
    Root cause: Index on (customer_id) finds all orders for that customer (maybe 10,000 rows), then sequentially scans those 10,000 rows to filter by status='ACTIVE' (maybe 100 rows). Fix: Composite index on (customer_id, status) — the database can seek directly to the (customer, ACTIVE) combination. LEFT-PREFIX RULE: the index can be used for: WHERE customer_id=? (prefix), WHERE customer_id=? AND status=? (full), but NOT for WHERE status=? alone (no prefix). Better: Partial index — CREATE INDEX ON orders(customer_id) WHERE status='ACTIVE' — tiny index, only active orders, perfect for the common query pattern.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'What is a covering index and when does it eliminate the heap access entirely?'
    💭 Think First
    A covering index means all the columns the query needs are IN the index — so the database never touches the actual table rows.
    → Complete Answer
    Regular index: find row IDs from index, then fetch each row from heap (random I/O). Covering index: the index itself contains all columns in SELECT + WHERE — the database reads only the index, skips the heap entirely. This is an 'Index Only Scan' in EXPLAIN. Example: SELECT id, status, created_at FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42 with index on (customer_id, status, created_at, id) — all 4 columns in the index → Index Only Scan, no heap access → dramatically faster for read-heavy queries. Trade-off: larger index, slower writes (index must be updated on every row change).
    Q: 'When does adding an index HURT performance?'
    💭 Think First
    Indexes aren't free. Every write (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) must update all indexes on the table.
    → Complete Answer
    Indexes hurt when: (1) Write-heavy tables: each INSERT on orders updates all indexes — if orders has 10 indexes, you're doing 10 B-tree insertions per order. (2) Low cardinality columns: index on status with 5 distinct values — the database might do an index scan returning 20% of the table, then a heap access for each. Full table scan is faster. (3) Tiny tables: <1000 rows — sequential scan is faster than B-tree traversal. (4) Unused indexes: still updated on every write. Audit with pg_stat_user_indexes: idx_scan=0 means the index is never used — drop it.
    🎯 Practice
    Create a table with 1 million rows. Run a WHERE query on an unindexed column and time it with EXPLAIN ANALYZE. Add an index, rerun, and compare both timing and query plan (Seq Scan vs Index Scan).
    💡 Hint — think before readingThink through the data structures first. What classes do you need? What are their relationships? Write class signatures before any method bodies.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — approach
    // Step 1: Define interface / abstract class // Step 2: Choose the right collection (List/Map/Set/Queue) // Step 3: Implement operations one by one // Step 4: Add concurrency if needed (AtomicX / synchronized) // Step 5: Test each operation independently
    🎯 Practice Task
    Write the SQL to create the optimal index for: SELECT id, status, total_amount FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ? AND created_at > ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20. Explain each decision.
    Hint — think before readingThe query filters by customer_id (equality), filters by created_at (range), sorts by created_at DESC, and selects id, status, total_amount. Optimal: composite index with customer_id first (equality), then created_at (range+sort), then covering columns.
    → Worked Solution
    SQL — optimal index with explanation
    -- Covering index: all SELECTed columns + filter columns in the index -- Left-prefix: customer_id first (equality) → created_at next (range+sort) CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_time_covering ON orders(customer_id, created_at DESC) INCLUDE (id, status, total_amount); -- covering columns (non-key) -- Why this exact design: -- 1. customer_id first: equality predicate → index seek to exact partition -- 2. created_at DESC next: matches ORDER BY → no sort step needed -- 3. INCLUDE (id, status, total_amount): covering → Index Only Scan, no heap touch -- 4. LIMIT 20: stops after 20 index entries → reads ~20 rows total -- EXPLAIN will show: Index Only Scan using idx_orders_customer_time_covering -- Cost: O(log n) seek + 20 index row reads ≈ microseconds even on 100M row table

    Redis Caching Strategies

    cache-aside · write-through · write-behind · TTL design
    🧠 Intuition
    Redis sits between your app and your slow database, holding hot data in memoryA database query might take 10-50ms; a Redis lookup takes under 1ms. The strategy question isn't "should I cache" but "how do reads and writes flow through the cache" — different strategies trade off consistency, complexity, and write latency differently.
    📐 Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading) — Most Common Pattern
    💻 Cache-Aside Implementation
    Java — Spring Boot + Redis
    public Product getProduct(String productId) { // 1. Check cache first String cached = redisTemplate.opsForValue().get("product:" + productId); if (cached != null) { return deserialize(cached); // cache HIT — fast path, no DB touched } // 2. Cache MISS — fall back to the database Product product = productRepository.findById(productId) .orElseThrow(() -> new ProductNotFoundException(productId)); // 3. Populate cache for next time, with a TTL to avoid staleness forever redisTemplate.opsForValue().set( "product:" + productId, serialize(product), Duration.ofMinutes(10)); return product; } public void updateProduct(Product product) { productRepository.save(product); // Invalidate (don't update) the cache — next read will repopulate it fresh redisTemplate.delete("product:" + product.getId()); }
    💡 Strategy Comparison
    StrategyWrite PathTrade-off
    Cache-AsideApp writes to DB, then invalidates cacheSimple, resilient to cache failures — most common default
    Write-ThroughApp writes to cache, cache synchronously writes to DBAlways consistent, but write latency = cache + DB
    Write-Behind (Write-Back)App writes to cache, DB updated asynchronously laterFastest writes, but risk of data loss if cache crashes before flush
    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "How do you handle cache stampede (many requests miss simultaneously)?"

    A: Use a distributed lock (Redis SETNX) so only one request repopulates the cache while others wait briefly, or serve slightly stale data while one request refreshes in the background ("stale-while-revalidate").

    Q: "Why use a TTL even on cache-aside?"

    A: Safety net against missed invalidations (e.g., a DB write from another service that didn't go through your invalidation logic) — TTL guarantees eventual consistency even if explicit invalidation is missed.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    Your product page load time is 800ms — most of it is a complex SQL query joining 8 tables. You want to add Redis caching. An interviewer asks: which caching strategy would you use and why?
    There are 4 main caching strategies. The right choice depends on: read:write ratio, consistency requirements, and whether the cache can be the primary data store.
    Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading): Application checks Redis → miss → loads from DB → writes to Redis → returns. Cache only contains what's actually requested. Downside: first request always slow (cache miss). Thundering herd on cache expiry. Fix: pre-warm popular products. Write-Through: Every DB write also writes to cache. Cache is always warm. Downside: write penalty on every update; cache fills with infrequently-read data. Write-Behind (Write-Back): Write to cache immediately, asynchronously flush to DB. Ultra-low write latency. Risk: cache failure = data loss. Use for non-critical high-volume writes (analytics counters). Read-Through: Cache sits in front of DB, manages its own population. Transparent to the application. Use with Caffeine/Redis as a loading cache. For product pages: Cache-Aside with 1-hour TTL. Write-Through on product updates. Pre-warm top-100 products on startup.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'Your cache is evicting entries too aggressively under load. How do you choose the right TTL and eviction policy?'
    💭 Think First
    TTL too short → too many cache misses. Too long → stale data. Eviction policy determines which entries are removed when Redis runs out of memory.
    → Complete Answer
    TTL choice: measure your data's change frequency. Product prices change hourly → 1-hour TTL. User sessions change per login → 24-hour TTL with sliding expiry. Static config data changes rarely → 24-hour TTL. Eviction policies: allkeys-lru (evict least recently used from all keys — good for general cache), volatile-lru (only evict keys with TTL — protects persistent data), allkeys-lfu (evict least frequently used — better hit rate for skewed workloads like product catalogs). For product catalog: allkeys-lfu because top 1% of products get 80% of traffic — LFU keeps them in cache.
    Q: 'How do you handle cache invalidation when the underlying data changes?'
    💭 Think First
    Cache invalidation is one of the hardest problems in CS. When a product price changes, how do you ensure no customer sees a stale price?
    → Complete Answer
    Strategy 1: TTL-based expiry — accept up to 1 hour of staleness, simple, no invalidation code. Works when eventual consistency is acceptable. Strategy 2: Event-driven invalidation — ProductUpdatedEvent (via Kafka or Spring Events) → cache.evict(productId). Next read misses cache → fresh data loaded. Strategy 3: Write-through — product update always updates cache too. Cache always consistent. Strategy 4: Cache versioning — key = 'product:{id}:v{version}'. On update, increment version in DB. Old cache key becomes orphan, expires via TTL. Production hybrid: write-through for critical data (prices, inventory) + TTL fallback (24h) for everything else.
    🎯 Practice
    Implement cache-aside for a product lookup service. Add a deliberate cache stampede scenario (100 concurrent requests on a cold cache) and fix it with a Redis-based lock.
    💡 Hint — think before readingThink through the data structures first. What classes do you need? What are their relationships? Write class signatures before any method bodies.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — approach
    // Step 1: Define interface / abstract class // Step 2: Choose the right collection (List/Map/Set/Queue) // Step 3: Implement operations one by one // Step 4: Add concurrency if needed (AtomicX / synchronized) // Step 5: Test each operation independently
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement a CachedProductService using @Cacheable and @CacheEvict annotations. Products are cached by ID. When a product is updated, the cache must be invalidated. Configure a 30-minute TTL via Caffeine.
    Hint — think before readingAdd spring-boot-starter-cache + caffeine dependency. @EnableCaching on config. Define a CacheManager bean with Caffeine expireAfterWrite(30, MINUTES). @Cacheable('products') on getProduct(). @CacheEvict('products') on updateProduct().
    → Worked Solution
    Spring Boot — Caffeine cache with TTL
    // application.yml // spring.cache.type: caffeine // spring.cache.caffeine.spec: maximumSize=1000,expireAfterWrite=30m @Service class CachedProductService { @Autowired ProductRepository repo; @Cacheable(value = "products", key = "#id") public Product getProduct(String id) { return repo.findById(id).orElseThrow(); // only called on cache miss } @CachePut(value = "products", key = "#product.id") // updates cache with new value @Transactional public Product updateProduct(Product product) { return repo.save(product); // saves + updates cache atomically (not truly atomic but fine) } @CacheEvict(value = "products", key = "#id") public void deleteProduct(String id) { repo.deleteById(id); } }

    Pagination for Large Datasets

    offset-based vs cursor-based — and why offset breaks at scale
    🧠 Intuition
    OFFSET makes the database count and discard rows it doesn't needOFFSET 10000 LIMIT 20 forces the database to scan and discard the first 10,000 matching rows before returning the next 20 — that scan cost grows with the offset. Cursor-based pagination instead says "give me 20 rows after this specific marker," which an index can jump to directly, regardless of how deep into the dataset you are.
    📐 Offset vs Cursor Diagram
    💻 Cursor-Based Implementation
    SQL + Java
    -- ✗ Offset pagination — gets slower as page number grows SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 50000; -- Also has a correctness bug: if rows are inserted/deleted between page -- requests, OFFSET can skip or duplicate rows across pages -- ✓ Cursor pagination — constant time regardless of depth SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id > :lastSeenId -- cursor = last id from previous page ORDER BY id LIMIT 20; // API response includes the cursor for the next page public class PagedResponse<T> { List<T> items; String nextCursor; // e.g., base64-encoded last item's id (or composite key) } // Client calls: GET /orders?cursor=eyJpZCI6MTIzNDV9&limit=20 // Server decodes cursor, queries WHERE id > decodedId, returns next batch + new cursor
    💡 When Offset Is Still Fine
    ScenarioRecommendation
    Admin dashboard, small dataset (<10k rows)OFFSET is fine — simplicity wins, performance difference is negligible
    User needs to jump to "page 50" directlyOFFSET supports this; cursor pagination only supports next/previous, not arbitrary jumps
    Infinite scroll feed, large/growing datasetCursor-based — this is the textbook use case (social feeds, activity logs)
    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "What's the correctness bug with OFFSET you mentioned?"

    A: If a row is deleted from an earlier page while a user is paginating, OFFSET shifts everything after it back by one — causing the next page request to skip a row it should have shown (or show a duplicate, depending on insert/delete direction). Cursor pagination is immune since it's anchored to a stable value, not a position.

    Q: "How do you handle a tie when sorting by a non-unique column?"

    A: Always include a unique tiebreaker in both ORDER BY and the cursor — e.g., ORDER BY created_at, id — otherwise rows with identical created_at values can be skipped or duplicated across pages.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    Your API returns all 1M orders for a customer in a single response. Users complain it takes 30 seconds and the app crashes on mobile. Fix it with pagination. The interviewer then asks: 'OFFSET pagination breaks at scale — what do you use instead?'
    OFFSET pagination (page=5, size=20 → SKIP 100 rows) is simple but has a deep problem: the database must scan and discard all OFFSET rows before returning results. At page 50,000 it scans 1M rows.
    OFFSET pagination: Simple to implement, supports random page access. Problem: OFFSET 1000000 LIMIT 20 reads 1,000,020 rows, discards first million. Degrades linearly with page depth. Good for: small datasets, admin UIs where users rarely go past page 10. Cursor/Keyset pagination: Instead of 'skip N rows', use a WHERE clause on the last seen value. WHERE created_at < :lastSeenTime ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20. The cursor encodes the last seen position. Next page: move forward from that position. O(log n) via index regardless of depth. Limitation: no random page access (can't jump to page 500). Best for: infinite scroll, API pagination, large datasets.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'How do you implement cursor pagination when sorting by a non-unique column?'
    💭 Think First
    If you sort by created_at and two rows have the same timestamp, the cursor is ambiguous — you might miss or duplicate rows.
    → Complete Answer
    Use a composite cursor: (created_at, id) where id is unique. The WHERE clause becomes: WHERE (created_at, id) < (:lastTime, :lastId) — this is unambiguous even when multiple rows share the same timestamp. The cursor you return to the client encodes both values (usually as a base64-encoded JSON or opaque string). The client sends it back as the 'after' parameter. The WHERE clause reconstructs it. This pattern works for any combination of sort columns — just ensure the composite tuple is unique.
    Q: 'How do you handle total count in cursor pagination for showing "Showing results 1-20 of 1,234"?'
    💭 Think First
    COUNT(*) on a large table can be slow. Cursor pagination doesn't naturally know the total.
    → Complete Answer
    Options: (1) Run COUNT(*) once and cache it (acceptable if count changes slowly). (2) Use PostgreSQL's estimate: SELECT reltuples FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'orders' — very fast, approximate (within 1-5%). Good enough for 'about 1,200 results'. (3) Abandon exact counts — show 'Load more' instead of page numbers (Twitter, Instagram approach). (4) Use a dedicated count table updated by triggers. In practice for large tables: exact COUNT is too expensive, use the estimate or abandon the count.
    🎯 Practice
    Implement cursor-based pagination for an orders list API. Test correctness by inserting a new row mid-pagination and confirming no rows are skipped or duplicated, unlike an OFFSET-based version under the same test.
    💡 Hint — think before readingThink through the data structures first. What classes do you need? What are their relationships? Write class signatures before any method bodies.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — approach
    // Step 1: Define interface / abstract class // Step 2: Choose the right collection (List/Map/Set/Queue) // Step 3: Implement operations one by one // Step 4: Add concurrency if needed (AtomicX / synchronized) // Step 5: Test each operation independently
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement a cursor-paginated endpoint: GET /api/orders?cursor={encodedCursor}&limit=20. Returns: {data: [...], nextCursor: '...', hasMore: bool}. Use created_at DESC, id DESC as the sort.
    Hint — think before readingDecode cursor to (lastTime, lastId). Query with WHERE (created_at, id) < (lastTime, lastId) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 21 (fetch 21 to detect hasMore). If 21 rows returned, hasMore=true, encode the 20th row's (time, id) as nextCursor.
    → Worked Solution
    Spring — cursor pagination
    @GetMapping("/api/orders") public PagedResponse<Order> getOrders( @RequestParam(required=false) String cursor, @RequestParam(defaultValue="20") int limit) { Cursor c = cursor == null ? Cursor.start() : Cursor.decode(cursor); List<Order> rows = orderRepo.findPage(c.lastTime(), c.lastId(), limit + 1); boolean hasMore = rows.size() == limit + 1; if(hasMore) rows = rows.subList(0, limit); String nextCursor = hasMore ? Cursor.encode(rows.get(limit-1)) : null; return new PagedResponse<>(rows, nextCursor, hasMore); } // Repository query: @Query("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE (created_at, id) < (:t, :id) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT :n") List<Order> findPage(Instant t, String id, int n);

    REST API Design Best Practices

    resources, status codes, versioning, the conventions interviewers check for
    🧠 Intuition
    URLs are nouns (resources), HTTP methods are verbs (actions)The most common REST design mistake is putting verbs in URLs (/getUser, /createOrder). REST conventions: the URL identifies WHAT resource, the HTTP method identifies WHAT action. /users/123 with GET reads it, with DELETE removes it — same URL, different verb, different action.
    💻 Resource Naming + Status Codes
    REST API design — correct conventions
    // ✗ BAD — verbs in URL, inconsistent casing, no resource hierarchy POST /createNewOrder GET /getOrderById?id=123 POST /deleteOrder/123 // ✓ GOOD — nouns + HTTP verbs + clear hierarchy POST /orders -- create a new order GET /orders/123 -- read order 123 PUT /orders/123 -- replace order 123 entirely PATCH /orders/123 -- partially update order 123 DELETE /orders/123 -- delete order 123 GET /orders/123/items -- nested resource: items within order 123 GET /orders?status=PENDING -- filter via query params, not separate endpoints // Status codes — be precise, don't just return 200 for everything 200 OK -- successful GET/PUT/PATCH 201 Created -- successful POST that created a resource (include Location header) 204 No Content -- successful DELETE, nothing to return 400 Bad Request -- malformed request (validation failure) 401 Unauthorized -- missing/invalid authentication 403 Forbidden -- authenticated but not allowed (authorization failure) 404 Not Found -- resource doesn't exist 409 Conflict -- e.g., duplicate resource, version conflict 422 Unprocessable Entity -- semantically invalid (valid JSON, invalid business rule) 429 Too Many Requests -- rate limit exceeded 500 Internal Server Error -- unhandled server-side failure
    💡 Versioning Strategies
    StrategyExampleTrade-off
    URI versioning/v1/orders, /v2/ordersMost explicit and cache-friendly — most common in practice
    Header versioningAccept: application/vnd.api+json;version=2Clean URLs, but harder to test/discover (can't just paste in browser)
    Query param versioning/orders?version=2Simple but easy to forget/misuse, rarely recommended as primary strategy
    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "PUT vs PATCH — what's the actual difference?"

    A: PUT replaces the ENTIRE resource — fields you omit are treated as removed/reset. PATCH applies a partial update — only the fields you send are changed, everything else stays as-is. Using PUT for partial updates is a common API design mistake.

    Q: "How do you design pagination, filtering, and sorting in a REST API?"

    A: Via query parameters on the collection endpoint: GET /orders?status=PENDING&sort=-createdAt&cursor=xyz&limit=20 — keep the resource URL clean and push all query shaping into params.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    Your API is used by mobile, web, and 3rd-party partners. A partner reports that after an API update, their integration broke. How do you design the API and version it to prevent this?
    API versioning prevents breaking changes from affecting existing clients. But what counts as breaking? And how do you communicate the version?
    Breaking changes: removing a field, renaming a field, changing a field's type, changing HTTP method, removing an endpoint. Non-breaking: adding new fields, adding new endpoints, adding new query parameters. Versioning strategies: (1) URL path: /api/v1/orders — explicit, easy to route, easy to test. (2) Header: Accept: application/vnd.myapi.v1+json — cleaner URLs, harder to test in browser. (3) Query param: ?version=1 — easy but pollutes URL. Best practice: URL path versioning for simplicity. Maintain v1 for at least 12 months after v2 launch. Deprecation headers: Deprecation: true, Sunset: Sat, 01 Jan 2026 00:00:00 GMT.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'What HTTP status codes should your REST API use for these scenarios: validation error, not found, unauthorized, forbidden, rate limited?'
    💭 Think First
    Status codes communicate machine-readable semantics. Wrong codes confuse clients and break retry logic.
    → Complete Answer
    400 Bad Request: client sent invalid data (validation failed, malformed JSON). Include which fields failed and why. 401 Unauthorized: no authentication provided or token expired — client must re-authenticate. 403 Forbidden: authenticated but not allowed — authenticated as user A trying to access user B's data. 404 Not Found: resource doesn't exist. 409 Conflict: resource exists and the action conflicts (duplicate booking, version mismatch in optimistic lock). 422 Unprocessable Entity: syntactically valid but semantically wrong (end date before start date). 429 Too Many Requests: rate limit exceeded. 500 Internal Server Error: server bug — never return stack traces, log them. 503 Service Unavailable: database down, circuit breaker open. Always include a body with error code, message, and request ID.
    Q: 'How do you design a REST API for bulk operations — creating 1000 orders in one request?'
    💭 Think First
    POST /api/orders for one order × 1000 = 1000 HTTP round trips. Bulk operations need a different design.
    → Complete Answer
    POST /api/orders/bulk with body [{order1}, {order2}, ...]. Return 207 Multi-Status with per-item results: [{id: 'o1', status: 201}, {id: 'o2', status: 400, error: 'invalid'}]. This allows partial success — some orders created, some failed. Alternative: async bulk — POST /api/orders/bulk returns 202 Accepted with a job ID. GET /api/jobs/{jobId} polls for status and result. Best for large batches (10K+ items) where synchronous processing would timeout.
    🎯 Practice
    Take a poorly designed API (with verb-based URLs and uniform 200 responses) and redesign it following the conventions above. Write out all endpoints with their correct HTTP methods and expected status codes.
    💡 Hint — think before readingThink through the data structures first. What classes do you need? What are their relationships? Write class signatures before any method bodies.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — approach
    // Step 1: Define interface / abstract class // Step 2: Choose the right collection (List/Map/Set/Queue) // Step 3: Implement operations one by one // Step 4: Add concurrency if needed (AtomicX / synchronized) // Step 5: Test each operation independently
    🎯 Practice Task
    Design the request/response structure for POST /api/v1/orders. Include: request body (with validation), success response (201), validation error response (400), and the idempotency key header.
    Hint — think before readingRequest: OrderRequest record with @NotNull/@Valid annotations. Success: wrap in ResponseEntity with Location header and body. Error: ProblemDetail (RFC 7807) with type, title, status, detail, and per-field violations. Idempotency-Key as a documented header.
    → Worked Solution
    Spring — REST API design
    @PostMapping("/api/v1/orders") public ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> createOrder( @RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") String ikey, @Valid @RequestBody OrderRequest req) { Order order = orderService.create(req, ikey); URI location = URI.create("/api/v1/orders/" + order.getId()); return ResponseEntity.created(location).body(OrderResponse.from(order)); } // Validation error response (auto-handled by @ControllerAdvice): // 400 Bad Request // { "type": "urn:problem:validation-error", // "title": "Validation Failed", "status": 400, // "violations": [{"field": "customerId", "message": "must not be null"}] }

    Authentication vs Authorization

    "who are you" vs "what are you allowed to do"
    🧠 Intuition
    Authentication proves identity. Authorization grants permission.A hotel check-in (showing your ID) is authentication — confirming you are who you claim. The keycard that opens only YOUR room, not every room, is authorization — what you're allowed to access given who you are. Authentication always happens first; authorization decisions depend on the authenticated identity.
    📐 JWT-Based Auth Flow
    💻 Spring Security — AuthZ Example
    Java — Spring Security role-based authorization
    // Authentication: handled by Spring Security filter chain — verifies the JWT, // extracts the user identity, populates SecurityContext. Already done by the time // your controller method runs. // Authorization: decide WHAT this authenticated user can do @RestController public class AdminController { @GetMapping("/orders/{id}") @PreAuthorize("hasRole('USER') or hasRole('ADMIN')") // any authenticated user public Order getOrder(@PathVariable String id) { ... } @DeleteMapping("/orders/{id}") @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") // only admins — authorization failure = 403 public void deleteOrder(@PathVariable String id) { ... } @GetMapping("/orders/{id}/owner-check") public Order getOwnOrder(@PathVariable String id, Authentication auth) { Order order = orderService.findById(id); // fine-grained, resource-level authorization — not just role-based if (!order.getUserId().equals(auth.getName())) { throw new AccessDeniedException("Not your order"); } return order; } }
    💡 Common Confusion — 401 vs 403
    StatusMeansMaps To
    401 Unauthorized"I don't know who you are" — missing or invalid credentialsAuthentication failure
    403 Forbidden"I know who you are, but you can't do this"Authorization failure
    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "Why is JWT verification fast without a DB call?"

    A: A JWT is cryptographically signed by the auth server. The resource server only needs the auth server's public key to verify the signature locally — no network round-trip to check session validity, unlike traditional session-cookie auth which requires a DB/cache lookup per request.

    Q: "How do you revoke a JWT before it expires?"

    A: This is JWT's known weakness — since verification is stateless, you can't simply "delete" a token.
