Solutions: keep token TTLs short (minutes, not days) with refresh tokens, or maintain a server-side blocklist of revoked token IDs (re-introduces a stateful check, trading off some of JWT's statelessness benefit).

    🏭 Production Scenario
    A user logs in (authenticated) and accesses /admin/users. They see a 403. Your senior asks you to explain exactly why they're getting 403 and what system is making that decision.
    This tests the distinction between authentication (who are you?) and authorization (what are you allowed to do?). The 403 means authorization failed — they're identified but not permitted.
    Authentication: Proves identity. Login → JWTService.generateToken(user) → returns signed JWT. Filter extracts and validates JWT → populates SecurityContext with UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken. Authorization: Checks permissions. SecurityFilterChain rule: .requestMatchers('/admin/**').hasRole('ADMIN'). Spring Security checks the SecurityContext — user has roles [USER] but not ADMIN → 403 Forbidden. The components: JwtAuthFilter (authentication) → SecurityContext (stores identity) → Spring Security's AuthorizationFilter (authorization) → 403. In code: @PreAuthorize('hasRole("ADMIN")') on the controller method also works — Method Security vs URL Security.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'What is RBAC vs ABAC? When would you choose each?'
    💭 Think First
    RBAC = Role-Based Access Control. ABAC = Attribute-Based Access Control. Both are authorization models with very different granularity.
    → Complete Answer
    RBAC: permissions are assigned to roles, roles to users. Simple to understand and manage. Example: ADMIN can delete anything, USER can only view. Limitation: can't express 'user can edit their OWN posts only'. ABAC: decisions based on attributes of the subject (user), object (resource), and environment (time, location). Example policy: 'user can access order IF order.customerId == user.id AND request.region == order.region'. More powerful, more complex. Rule of thumb: start with RBAC (covers 90% of apps). Add ABAC rules for resource-ownership checks. Spring Security: @PreAuthorize('#order.customerId == authentication.principal.id') is ABAC-style.
    Q: 'How do you implement row-level security — users can only see their own orders?'
    💭 Think First
    Authorization at the API level (only your routes) is RBAC. Authorization at the data level (only your rows) is row-level security.
    → Complete Answer
    Spring — row-level security
    // Option 1: Repository method scoped to current user @Repository interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order,String> { List<Order> findByCustomerId(String customerId); // always filter by customerId } // Option 2: @PreAuthorize on service method @PreAuthorize("#customerId == authentication.principal.id or hasRole('ADMIN')") public List<Order> getOrders(String customerId) { ... } // Option 3: Hibernate Filter — automatically adds WHERE clause @FilterDef(name="customerFilter", parameters=@ParamDef(name="cId", type=String.class)) @Filter(name="customerFilter", condition="customer_id = :cId") @Entity class Order { ... } // Enable per-request: session.enableFilter("customerFilter").setParameter("cId", userId)
    🎯 Practice
    Build a Spring Boot endpoint with role-based authorization (@PreAuthorize) AND resource-level authorization (checking order ownership). Test both a 401 (no token) and 403 (wrong role) scenario.
    💡 Hint — think before readingThink through the data structures first. What classes do you need? What are their relationships? Write class signatures before any method bodies.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — approach
    // Step 1: Define interface / abstract class // Step 2: Choose the right collection (List/Map/Set/Queue) // Step 3: Implement operations one by one // Step 4: Add concurrency if needed (AtomicX / synchronized) // Step 5: Test each operation independently
    🎯 Practice Task
    Design the authorization model for a multi-tenant SaaS app: users belong to an organization, can have role OWNER/ADMIN/MEMBER within their org, and can only access their org's data. Show the JWT claims and the Spring Security configuration.
    Hint — think before readingJWT claims: sub (userId), orgId, role. Spring Security: extract orgId from JWT into the Authentication object. All repository queries include WHERE org_id = :orgId from the security context. Method security: @PreAuthorize for role checks within the org.
    → Worked Solution
    Spring — multi-tenant security
    // JWT claims: {"sub":"U1","orgId":"ORG-42","role":"ADMIN"} // Custom principal record OrgUserPrincipal(String userId, String orgId, String role) implements UserDetails { public Collection<GrantedAuthority> getAuthorities() { return List.of(() -> "ROLE_" + role); } } // Repository: always scope to org interface ProjectRepo extends JpaRepository<Project, String> { List<Project> findByOrgId(String orgId); // never cross-org leakage } // Service: extract orgId from SecurityContext public List<Project> getProjects() { OrgUserPrincipal p = (OrgUserPrincipal) SecurityContextHolder.getContext() .getAuthentication().getPrincipal(); return projectRepo.findByOrgId(p.orgId()); // always org-scoped }

    Connection Pooling

    why you never open a new DB connection per request
    🧠 Intuition
    Opening a DB connection is expensive — TCP handshake, auth, session setupIf every HTTP request opened a fresh database connection, you'd pay 10-50ms of connection overhead PER REQUEST before even running your query. A connection pool pre-opens a fixed number of connections at startup and hands them out to requests, returning them to the pool when done — eliminating repeated connection setup cost.
    📐 Pool Lifecycle Diagram
    💻 HikariCP Configuration (Spring Boot Default)
    application.yml
    # HikariCP is Spring Boot's default connection pool — fast, lightweight spring: datasource: hikari: maximum-pool-size: 20 # max concurrent connections minimum-idle: 5 # keep at least 5 warm, ready to use connection-timeout: 30000 # ms to wait for a free connection before failing idle-timeout: 600000 # ms before an idle connection is closed (10 min) max-lifetime: 1800000 # ms before a connection is recycled regardless (30 min) # Sizing rule of thumb (from HikariCP's own docs): # pool_size = ((core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count) # For most cloud DBs (SSD-backed): pool_size ≈ core_count * 2 + 1 # MORE connections is NOT always better — too many can overwhelm the DB itself
    ⚠ The Mistake That Causes Pool Exhaustion
    • Forgetting to close/return a connectionIf code acquires a connection but an exception skips the return-to-pool step, that connection is leaked. Repeat enough times and the pool exhausts — new requests hang waiting for a connection that never comes.
    • Always use try-with-resourcesConnection objects implement AutoCloseable specifically so try-with-resources guarantees the connection returns to the pool even on exception.
    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "What happens when the pool is exhausted?"

    A: New requests wait up to connection-timeout milliseconds for a free connection, then throw a timeout exception if none becomes available — this manifests as a sudden spike in request latency/errors, often the first symptom of a connection leak in production.

    Q: "Why not just set pool size very high to avoid exhaustion?"

    A: The database itself has a max_connections limit and each connection consumes DB-side memory. Too many idle connections can actually reduce DB throughput due to context-switching and resource contention — sizing is about matching the DB's actual concurrent processing capacity, not maximizing client-side connections.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    Under load, your Spring Boot app throws 'Unable to acquire connection from pool within 30000ms'. 50 threads are waiting for a DB connection. Connection pool size is 10. What's wrong and how do you fix it?
    The pool is exhausted. 50 threads need connections but only 10 exist. Either: pool is too small, connections are held too long, or there's a connection leak. Diagnose before tuning.
    Diagnose first: Check HikariCP metrics (Spring Boot Actuator): hikaricp.connections.active, hikaricp.connections.pending, hikaricp.connections.timeout. If active=10 and pending=40: pool is too small OR connections held too long. Fix options: (1) Increase pool size: but DB has a max_connections limit (PostgreSQL default 100) — don't exceed it. (2) Reduce connection hold time: use @Transactional only where truly needed. Move non-DB work outside transaction boundaries. (3) Read replicas: route read-only queries to replicas, each with their own pool. (4) Connection leak detection: HikariCP's leakDetectionThreshold=10000 logs when a connection is held >10s. Find the culprit. (5) Async processing: move long-running DB operations to async jobs — don't hold request threads waiting on DB.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'What is the optimal HikariCP pool size formula?'
    💭 Think First
    More connections isn't always better. Too many connections causes context-switching overhead on the DB server.
    → Complete Answer
    HikariCP's recommended formula: pool_size = (number_of_cores × 2) + effective_spindle_count. For a 4-core server with SSD storage: (4 × 2) + 1 = 9 connections. This seems small but it's correct — the DB can only process as many queries in parallel as it has CPU cores. Beyond that, queries queue in the DB, not in the app. 100 threads sending queries to a 9-connection pool: queries queue IN the pool (cheap — thread parks). Vs 100 connections: queries queue IN the DB (expensive — DB holds cursor state, consumes memory, context-switches). The pool is the shock absorber. Set minimum-idle equal to maximum-pool-size to avoid connection ramp-up latency.
    Q: 'How does @Transactional interact with connection pool? When does a connection get acquired and released?'
    💭 Think First
    Connection acquisition timing directly impacts pool utilization. Holding connections too long is the #1 cause of pool exhaustion.
    → Complete Answer
    @Transactional proxies the method. On method entry: Spring calls DataSource.getConnection() — acquires from pool. On method exit (commit or rollback): connection returned to pool. Problem: if your @Transactional method does: 1) DB query, 2) HTTP call to external service (500ms), 3) another DB query — the connection is held throughout the HTTP call. During those 500ms, the connection is idle but not in the pool. Fix: structure code so HTTP calls happen OUTSIDE the transaction. Use @Transactional only for the DB portions. Rule: transactions should be as short as possible — minimize work inside transaction boundaries.
    🎯 Practice
    Configure HikariCP with a deliberately small pool (size=2). Fire 10 concurrent requests each holding a connection for 2 seconds, and observe the queueing/timeout behavior in logs.
    💡 Hint — think before readingThink through the data structures first. What classes do you need? What are their relationships? Write class signatures before any method bodies.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — approach
    // Step 1: Define interface / abstract class // Step 2: Choose the right collection (List/Map/Set/Queue) // Step 3: Implement operations one by one // Step 4: Add concurrency if needed (AtomicX / synchronized) // Step 5: Test each operation independently
    🎯 Practice Task
    Configure HikariCP in a Spring Boot application for a PostgreSQL database with these requirements: maximum 20 connections, fail fast if no connection available after 5 seconds, log connections held longer than 15 seconds, validate connections before use.
    Hint — think before readingapplication.yml with spring.datasource.hikari properties: maximum-pool-size, connection-timeout, leak-detection-threshold, connection-test-query or validation-timeout.
    → Worked Solution
    YAML — HikariCP configuration
    spring: datasource: url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/mydb hikari: maximum-pool-size: 20 # max connections to DB minimum-idle: 20 # keep all 20 connections warm (no ramp-up) connection-timeout: 5000 # fail after 5s if no connection available idle-timeout: 600000 # release idle connections after 10min max-lifetime: 1800000 # replace connections after 30min (prevents stale) leak-detection-threshold: 15000 # log warning if held > 15s validation-timeout: 3000 # timeout for isValid() check pool-name: myapp-pool # for metrics/logging clarity # Monitor via Actuator: # GET /actuator/metrics/hikaricp.connections.active → current active connections # GET /actuator/metrics/hikaricp.connections.pending → queue depth

    Debugging a Slow Spring Boot API

    systematic production diagnosis — the answer interviewers actually want
    🧠 The Key Insight
    Interviewers don't want a lucky guess. They want a systematic elimination process."Check the database" is not an answer. "I'd start by measuring where time is actually being spent, then narrow layer by layer" IS an answer. The process signals senior thinking. The lucky guess signals junior thinking. This section teaches the process.
    📐 The Diagnostic Pyramid
    💻 Step 1: Measure — Spring Boot Actuator + Micrometer
    Spring Boot — endpoint latency distribution
    # application.yml — expose metrics # management.endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,metrics,prometheus # management.metrics.distribution.percentiles-histogram.http.server.requests: true // Now query: GET /actuator/metrics/http.server.requests?tag=uri:/api/orders // Shows: count, mean, max, p50, p95, p99 per endpoint // If p99 is 4000ms but p50 is 100ms → outlier issue (specific inputs trigger slow path) // If p50 is 1500ms → systematic problem (ALL requests are slow) // Spring Boot auto-instruments: HTTP requests, DataSource queries, JVM metrics // Add custom timing for specific operations: @Service public class OrderService { @Autowired MeterRegistry registry; public Order buildDashboard(String userId) { return registry.timer("order.dashboard.build") .record(() -> buildDashboardInternal(userId)); // Now visible at /actuator/metrics/order.dashboard.build } }
    ⚠️ The N+1 Query Bug — Most Common Cause
    Java — detect and fix N+1
    // ✗ N+1: Hibernate lazy-loads items PER ORDER → 1 + N queries // Enable SQL logging to catch: spring.jpa.show-sql=true List<Order> orders = orderRepo.findAll(); // 1 query for (Order o : orders) { o.getItems().size(); // TRIGGERS QUERY PER ORDER! If 500 orders → 501 queries! } // ✓ FIX 1: JOIN FETCH (JPQL) — load everything in 1 query @Query("SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.items") List<Order> findAllWithItems(); // ✓ FIX 2: @EntityGraph — declarative, no JPQL needed @EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"items", "items.product"}) List<Order> findAll(); // ✓ FIX 3: Batch size — reduces N queries to N/batch_size // @BatchSize(size = 50) on the collection — Hibernate loads 50 at once // Better for pagination where JOIN FETCH causes cartesian explosion // DETECTION TOOL: add datasource-proxy to log query count per request // If count > 10 for a single HTTP request → likely N+1
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q1: "The endpoint is slow but SQL logs show only 2 fast queries (< 5ms each). What next?"
    💭 Think
    DB is fast. Where else can time disappear?
    → Systematic next steps
    (1) Check downstream HTTP calls — use @TimedClient or instrument RestTemplate/Feign. A payment-service timeout of 30s would show up here.
    (2) Check serialization — returning deeply nested objects with Jackson can be surprisingly slow. Use ObjectMapper.writeValueAsString timing. Fix: DTOs, @JsonIgnore on cycles, projections.
    (3) Check GC — correlate slow request timestamps with GC log Full GC events. A 250ms Full GC pause appears as a slow request.
    (4) Check thread pool exhaustion — Tomcat has a max thread count (default 200). If all threads are busy, new requests queue. Symptom: request count × avg response time exceeds thread pool capacity.
    (5) Profile with async-profiler — 30-second CPU flame graph shows exactly which method is consuming CPU time. No guessing.
    Q2: "How would you improve an API that handles millions of requests?"
    💭 Think
    This is a system design + optimization layering question. Work through the layers.
    → Layered answer
    Layer 1: Caching — CDN for static responses, Redis for hot computed data. 80% of traffic often hits 20% of data — cache that 20%.
    Layer 2: Async off-critical-path — don't send email/update analytics inline. Queue it. Reduce endpoint response time to just the user-critical operations.
    Layer 3: DB optimization — indexes on query columns, read replicas for read-heavy traffic, connection pooling (HikariCP) sized to DB capacity.
    Layer 4: Horizontal scaling — stateless services + load balancer. Add instances when CPU > 70%.
    Layer 5: Non-blocking I/O — WebFlux + R2DBC for I/O-heavy endpoints where threads spend most time waiting. A single reactive thread can handle thousands of concurrent I/O-bound requests.
    🚨 Production Scenario: "API is slow every day at 9 AM"
    "Monday to Friday, 9:00 AM sharp, P99 latency spikes from 80ms to 4000ms for 10 minutes, then recovers. Users complain every morning."
    Hypothesis 1 — GC pressure from overnight batch: Check GC logs around 9 AM. A nightly report job fills Old Gen; first traffic spike triggers a Full GC.
    Hypothesis 2 — Cold cache: A Redis cache with 8-hour TTL expires overnight. First morning requests all miss cache, hit DB simultaneously (cache stampede).
    Hypothesis 3 — DB connection pool exhaustion: First office traffic spike exhausts HikariCP pool (sized for steady-state, not burst).

    How to distinguish: GC logs (hypothesis 1), Redis hit-rate metrics (hypothesis 2), HikariCP active connection count over time (hypothesis 3). Each has a distinct metric signature — that's why measuring first matters.

    Cache stampede fix: Stagger TTLs with jitter (TTL = 8h + random(0-30min)), or use "refresh ahead" pattern — proactively refresh cache before expiry based on TTL.
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Your high-throughput order service handles 50K requests/second. Under load tests it starts dropping requests at 30K/s. The CPU is at 40%, memory is fine. Where is the bottleneck?
    CPU and memory are not the bottleneck. Think about what else limits throughput: thread count, connection pool, I/O wait, lock contention.
    Diagnosis steps: (1) Thread pool: check Tomcat threadpool — if all threads are WAITING on DB connections, the thread pool is exhausted. (2) Connection pool: HikariCP metrics — hikaricp.connections.pending > 0 means threads queue for connections. (3) Blocking I/O: thread dump shows threads in TIMED_WAITING on SocketRead — slow downstream service. Common fixes: Increase HikariCP pool size (but respect DB max_connections). Move slow I/O to async: CompletableFuture or reactive stack. Use read replicas for read-heavy queries. Add L2 cache (Redis) for repeated reads. Architecture solution: Switch to reactive (WebFlux + R2DBC): non-blocking I/O means one thread handles thousands of in-flight requests. Eliminates the thread-per-request bottleneck. Trade-off: reactive code is harder to write, debug, and maintain.
    🎯 Practice
    "Our /dashboard endpoint takes 3 seconds. It fetches user profile, last 10 orders, unread notification count, and account balance — all sequentially."
    Diagnosis hintSequential independent calls. Wall time = sum of all calls. If each call takes ~750ms, sequential = 3s. What makes 4 independent calls faster?
    → Worked Solution
    Java — parallel calls with CompletableFuture
    // BEFORE: 750ms + 750ms + 750ms + 750ms = 3000ms User user = userService.get(userId); // 750ms Orders orders = orderService.recent(userId); // 750ms long notifs = notifService.unreadCount(userId); // 750ms Balance balance = accountService.balance(userId); // 750ms // AFTER: max(750,750,750,750) = ~800ms (overhead included) CompletableFuture<User> uf = supplyAsync(() -> userService.get(userId), pool); CompletableFuture<Orders> of = supplyAsync(() -> orderService.recent(userId), pool); CompletableFuture<Long> nf = supplyAsync(() -> notifService.unreadCount(userId), pool); CompletableFuture<Balance> bf = supplyAsync(() -> accountService.balance(userId), pool); CompletableFuture.allOf(uf, of, nf, bf) .orTimeout(2, SECONDS) // fail fast — don't wait forever .join(); return new Dashboard(uf.join(), of.join(), nf.join(), bf.join()); // Always add: .orTimeout() to prevent one slow service from holding all threads // Consider: partial results if one call fails (exceptionally() fallback per future)

    Dependency Injection in Spring

    the IoC container, and what @Autowired actually does
    🧠 Intuition
    Spring's IoC container is the concrete realization of the Dependency Inversion Principle (covered in LLD Week 1)Instead of a class creating its own dependencies with `new`, Spring creates and wires objects (beans) together based on their declared dependencies, then hands the fully-assembled object to your code. "Inversion of Control" means: the framework controls object creation/wiring, not your code — control is inverted from your code to the container.
    📐 Container Flow Diagram
    💻 Constructor Injection — The Recommended Pattern
    Java — Spring DI
    @Service public class UserService { private final UserRepository repository; // final = immutable, must be set at construction private final EmailService emailService; // ✓ Constructor injection — Spring auto-detects this single constructor // and supplies the right beans. (@Autowired is optional on constructors // since Spring 4.3 if there's only one constructor.) public UserService(UserRepository repository, EmailService emailService) { this.repository = repository; this.emailService = emailService; } } // ✗ Field injection — works but considered worse practice @Service public class UserService { @Autowired private UserRepository repository; // can't be final, harder to unit test without Spring, } // hides dependencies (not visible in constructor signature) // Unit testing constructor injection — NO Spring context needed @Test void testUserCreation() { UserService service = new UserService(mockRepo, mockEmailService); // plain Java, fast test }
    💡 Bean Scopes
    ScopeBehaviour
    singleton (default)One instance per Spring container, shared across the whole app
    prototypeNew instance every time the bean is requested/injected
    requestOne instance per HTTP request (web apps only)
    sessionOne instance per HTTP session (web apps only)
    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "Why is constructor injection preferred over field injection?"

    A: It makes dependencies explicit and required (can't construct the object in an invalid half-wired state), enables final fields (immutability, thread-safety), and allows plain unit testing without needing a Spring context at all.

    Q: "What's a circular dependency and how does Spring handle it?"

    A: Bean A needs Bean B, and Bean B needs Bean A — Spring throws BeanCurrentlyInCreationException for constructor injection (it genuinely cannot resolve this). Field/setter injection can sometimes work around it via lazy proxies, but a circular dependency is usually a sign of a design problem (likely an SRP violation) that should be refactored, not worked around.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    An interviewer asks: 'What are the three types of dependency injection in Spring? Which do you prefer and why? Then show me a case where field injection breaks your code.'
    Constructor, setter, and field injection. Each has trade-offs around testability, immutability, and mandatory vs optional dependencies.
    Constructor injection (preferred): Dependencies in constructor → object can't be created without them (mandatory). Fields are final (immutable). Testable without Spring — just call the constructor with mocks. Setter injection: Optional dependencies. Can re-inject after construction. Circular dependency workaround. Downside: mutable, object can exist in partially-initialised state. Field injection (@Autowired on field): Concise. But: can't mark fields final. Can't test without Spring context (no constructor to pass mocks). Hides dependencies — class has 10 @Autowired fields, all invisible from outside. Where field injection breaks: Unit test — you'd need to use Reflection or @InjectMocks to inject mocks. If the Spring context isn't running, the field is null → NullPointerException. Constructor injection is always preferable.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'Explain Spring bean scopes. When would you use prototype scope?'
    💭 Think First
    Singleton is the default — one instance per application context. What are the other scopes and when do they matter?
    → Complete Answer
    Singleton (default): one instance, shared everywhere. Prototype: new instance per injection point/getBean() call. Request: one instance per HTTP request (web apps only). Session: one instance per HTTP session. Application: one instance per ServletContext. Use prototype for: stateful beans that shouldn't be shared (user-specific data), heavy objects where each caller needs independent state. Problem with prototype inside singleton: a singleton holds one instance of the prototype (captured at creation time) — it never gets a new one. Fix: inject ApplicationContext and call getBean() per use, or use @Lookup method injection.
    Q: 'What is circular dependency? Spring resolves it for setter/field injection but not constructor injection — why?'
    💭 Think First
    A→B→A. Spring needs to create A to create B, but needs B to create A. How does it break the cycle for setter injection?
    → Complete Answer
    Spring breaks circular deps by creating a partially-constructed bean (after constructor, before property injection) and putting it in an 'early singleton' cache. When A needs B and B needs A: Spring creates A (constructor runs), puts partial A in cache, starts creating B, B needs A → finds partial A in early cache, injects it, B is complete, A's property injection finishes. This works ONLY for setter/field injection because the partial object exists after constructor. Constructor injection: Spring can't create A without B, can't create B without A — there's no partial object to put in cache → BeanCurrentlyInCreationException. The real fix: redesign to eliminate the cycle (SRP violation).
    🎯 Practice
    Refactor a Spring service using @Autowired field injection to constructor injection. Then write a plain JUnit test (no @SpringBootTest, no Spring context) that constructs it directly with mocks.
    💡 Hint — think before readingThink through the data structures first. What classes do you need? What are their relationships? Write class signatures before any method bodies.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — approach
    // Step 1: Define interface / abstract class // Step 2: Choose the right collection (List/Map/Set/Queue) // Step 3: Implement operations one by one // Step 4: Add concurrency if needed (AtomicX / synchronized) // Step 5: Test each operation independently
    🎯 Practice Task
    Write a unit test for OrderService that uses constructor injection. Show that you can test it without any Spring context — just plain JUnit + Mockito.
    Hint — think before readingOrderService has OrderRepository and PaymentService injected via constructor. Test: create mocks with Mockito.mock(), pass to constructor. No @SpringBootTest, no @Autowired — pure Java test that runs in milliseconds.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — unit test with constructor injection
    // Production class — constructor injection @Service class OrderService { private final OrderRepository repo; private final PaymentService payment; OrderService(OrderRepository r, PaymentService p) { repo=r; payment=p; } } // Test — zero Spring context, runs in <100ms @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) class OrderServiceTest { @Mock OrderRepository repo; @Mock PaymentService payment; OrderService sut; // system under test @BeforeEach void setUp() { sut = new OrderService(repo, payment); // plain constructor — no Spring needed } @Test void placeOrder_savesAndCharges() { when(repo.save(any())).thenReturn(new Order("O1")); sut.placeOrder(new OrderRequest()); verify(repo).save(any()); verify(payment).charge(any()); } }

    Handling Millions of Requests — Practical Design

    the layered answer to "how would you scale this?" — with concrete techniques and trade-offs
    🧠 The Scenario They're Really Testing
    "How would you handle millions of requests?" is not a systems design question — it's a practical engineering question about layers.The interviewer wants to hear you systematically apply caching, async processing, pooling, horizontal scaling, and load shedding. Not just "add more servers." Each layer has a specific problem it solves and a trade-off it introduces. Walk through the layers.
    📐 The 7 Layers of Scale
    💻 Concrete Implementation of Each Layer
    Spring Boot — layer by layer
    // L3: Caffeine in-process cache — for data that barely changes (e.g., product catalog) @Bean public Cache productCache() { return Caffeine.newBuilder() .maximumSize(10_000) .expireAfterWrite(5, MINUTES) .recordStats() // exposes hit rate via /actuator/metrics/cache.gets .build(); } // L4: Redis cache-aside — for shared state across multiple app instances @Cacheable(value = "user", key = "#userId") // Spring Cache abstraction → Redis public User getUser(String userId) { return userRepo.findById(userId).orElseThrow(); } @CacheEvict(value = "user", key = "#user.id") // invalidate on update public User updateUser(User user) { return userRepo.save(user); } // L5: Async processing — send email async, don't block the HTTP response @KafkaListener(topics = "order-confirmed") public void onOrderConfirmed(OrderConfirmedEvent event) { emailService.sendConfirmation(event); // runs in separate consumer thread } // Order endpoint returns 200 immediately after publishing event // Email sent asynchronously — user gets it within seconds, not milliseconds // L7: Bulkhead — isolate thread pools per downstream service @Bulkhead(name = "payment", type = Bulkhead.Type.THREADPOOL) public CompletableFuture<PaymentResult> charge(Order o) { ... } // Payment calls use their OWN thread pool — if payment hangs, // only payment threads are blocked. User service threads remain free.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q1: "If you had to pick ONE change to improve throughput most, what would it be?"
    💭 Think
    This is context-dependent — but there's a general rule.
    → Answer
    "It depends on the bottleneck — which is why you measure first. But across most web applications I've seen, the single highest-leverage change is caching at the Redis layer. Most production apps have a small hot dataset (product catalog, user profiles, session data) hit by 80% of traffic. Moving those reads from ~20ms DB queries to <1ms Redis lookups can quadruple throughput with minimal risk. After that: parallelizing independent downstream calls with CompletableFuture is the next highest ROI for latency-heavy endpoints."
    Q2: "What's the trade-off of adding more caching?"
    💭 Think
    Caching is always a trade-off. What do you give up?
    → Honest answer
    Staleness: Cached data can be outdated. A TTL of 5 minutes means users might see 5-minute-old prices. Acceptable for product descriptions; not for stock levels.
    Consistency complexity: Cache invalidation on write is hard. Multi-level caches (L3 + Redis) can have inconsistency between levels.
    Cache stampede: When a popular key expires, thousands of concurrent cache misses all hit the DB simultaneously. Fix: staggered TTL jitter + mutex/lock on repopulation.
    Memory cost: Redis has bounded memory. Large value objects evict others. Need to tune maxmemory and eviction policy (allkeys-lru for most cases).
    The rule: Cache read-heavy, rarely-changing data. Don't cache financial data requiring real-time accuracy. Always define your consistency SLA first, then design the cache policy around it.
    🚨 "How would you handle a flash sale with 1M concurrent users?"
    Classic interview scenario: "Your e-commerce platform has a 60-second flash sale. 1 million users hit the product page simultaneously at T=0."
    Pre-warming: Before T=0, cache the product details in Redis with a TTL extending 30s past sale end. CDN-cache the static page HTML.

    T=0 — product page: CDN serves HTML to millions. Redis serves product details. DB not touched for reads.

    T=0 — add to cart: Queue all cart requests. Use Redis DECR on inventory counter — atomic decrement, only succeeds if > 0. If counter hits 0, reject immediately (no DB hit).

    Checkout flow: Rate limiter at API Gateway (e.g., 10 checkout requests/sec/user). Async: publish checkout event to Kafka, return "Processing" status, confirm via websocket/polling.

    DB protection: Connection pool sized correctly. Read replicas for inventory checks. Write-behind batch: accumulate orders in memory, flush to DB every 100ms in batches.

    Circuit breaker: If payment service can't keep up, queue payments for async retry — don't reject users, show "your order is confirmed, payment processing."
    💼 "Explain Your Project" — Performance Angle
    Interviewer: "How did you optimize performance in your project? What challenges did you face?"
    Template answer: "We had an issue where our [dashboard/search/report] endpoint was taking [Xs]. I profiled it with [Spring Actuator/async-profiler/SQL logs] and found [N+1 queries / sequential external calls / missing index / no caching]. The fix was [JOIN FETCH / CompletableFuture parallel calls / composite index / Redis cache-aside]. After the fix, P99 latency went from [Xs] to [Ys], which [unblocked users / reduced DB load by X% / allowed us to remove N servers]."

    If you didn't do perf optimization in your project, talk about what you WOULD change: "Looking back, I'd add Redis caching for the X endpoint since it reads rarely-changing data on every request, and I'd parallelise the Y and Z service calls that are currently sequential."
    🏭 Production Scenario
    An API endpoint that was returning in 50ms is now returning in 4 seconds. No code was deployed. How do you diagnose it systematically?
    No code change means the problem is environmental: database, external service, network, load, or data growth. Work from the outermost layer inward.
    Systematic diagnosis: (1) Check metrics: Grafana — did request rate spike? Did DB query time spike? Did a dependency become slow? (2) EXPLAIN ANALYZE: run the slow query directly in psql — is it now doing a sequential scan? Did table statistics get stale (ANALYZE needed)? Did data grow past an index threshold? (3) Check locks: pg_locks shows blocking queries — is another query holding a lock on the table? (4) Check external dependencies: is a 3rd-party API returning slowly? Add a timeout if missing. Most common causes of sudden slowdown without deployment: Table bloat → sequential scan. Lock contention from a long-running transaction. Statistics drift → planner chooses a bad plan. Connection pool exhaustion from traffic spike. DNS resolution slowdown for external services.
    🎯 Practice
    Design a leaderboard system: (a) user scores update frequently (10k writes/sec), (b) leaderboard top-100 is queried by every user every 30 seconds, (c) scores must be accurate within 5 seconds. Design the data layer.
    HintRedis Sorted Set (ZADD/ZRANGEBYSCORE) is purpose-built for leaderboards. Writes go to Redis directly; DB is the durable backup. The 5-second accuracy requirement tells you max acceptable TTL for the full leaderboard response.
    → Worked Solution
    Design — Redis Sorted Set leaderboard
    // WRITE PATH (10k/sec updates): // Client → API → Redis ZADD leaderboard {score} {userId} [O(log n), sub-ms] // Async: Kafka consumer batch-writes to Postgres every 30s for durability // READ PATH (top 100, every 30s per user): // Redis ZREVRANGE leaderboard 0 99 WITHSCORES [O(log n + 100)] // Cache this result in Redis key "leaderboard:top100" with TTL=5s // 5s TTL matches your accuracy SLA — at most 5s stale // JAVA: redisTemplate.opsForZSet().add("leaderboard", userId, newScore); // Top 100: Set<ZSetOperations.TypedTuple<String>> top100 = redisTemplate.opsForZSet().reverseRangeWithScores("leaderboard", 0, 99); // TRADE-OFFS TO MENTION: // - Redis is in-memory — if it restarts, scores lost until DB sync // - Solution: Redis persistence (AOF) OR periodic DB-to-Redis sync on startup // - For very large leaderboards (millions of users), consider partitioned sorted sets // or time-windowed leaderboards (today/week/all-time as separate sorted sets)
    SYS
    System Design — Group 1: Collaboration & Productivity Tools
    // Jira-like PM Tool · Real-Time Collaboration · Workflow Automation · Version Control System
    📋
    Project Management Tool (Jira-like)
    issues, boards, workflows
    ✍️
    Real-Time Collaboration Platform
    Google Docs-style concurrent editing
    ⚙️
    Workflow Automation Platform
    Zapier-style trigger-action chains
    🎀
    Version Control System
    Git internals — commits, branches, diffs

    Design a Project Management Tool like Jira

    issues, boards, workflows, permissions — a full product-scale system
    🧠 Intuition — Clarify Before Anything
    This is an intentionally broad prompt — scoping is the actual skill being tested"Design Jira" could mean a dozen different things. Ask: Are we focusing on issue tracking, or also sprints/boards? Do we need real-time updates when multiple people view the same board? What's the scale — a 10-person team or 10,000 organizations? Custom workflows per project, or one fixed workflow?
    📐 High-Level Architecture
    💻 Core Entity Design — LLD Layer Within the System
    Java — issue state machine + workflow
    // Issue state is a State Pattern, but with CONFIGURABLE transitions per project class WorkflowState { String name; // "TODO", "IN_PROGRESS", "DONE" List<String> allowedTransitions; // project-specific — data-driven, not hardcoded enum! } class Workflow { List<WorkflowState> states; boolean canTransition(String from, String to) { return states.stream() .filter(s -> s.name.equals(from)) .anyMatch(s -> s.allowedTransitions.contains(to)); } } class Issue { String id, title, currentState; Workflow workflow; // each project can have a DIFFERENT workflow — key design decision List<IssueObserver> observers; // for real-time board updates + notifications void transitionTo(String newState) { if (!workflow.canTransition(currentState, newState)) throw new InvalidTransitionException(currentState, newState); currentState = newState; observers.forEach(o -> o.onStateChanged(this)); // Observer pattern — board/notification react } } // Why data-driven workflow instead of a hardcoded enum + switch? // Because Jira's killer feature is CUSTOM workflows per project — OCP in action.
    💡 Key Design Decisions to Discuss
    Board real-time updates

    WebSocket connection per active board viewer. Issue Service publishes a state-change event → pushed to all connected clients viewing that board via a pub-sub layer (Redis Pub/Sub or a dedicated WebSocket gateway service).

    Search across millions of issues

    Don't query Postgres directly for full-text search — index issues into Elasticsearch asynchronously via the event stream, keeping the write path fast and the search path scalable independently.

    Permissions model

    Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) at the project level: Admin, Member, Viewer. Combined with resource-level checks (can this user edit THIS specific issue, e.g., only the assignee or admin).

    Multi-tenancy

    Each organization's data is logically isolated — either via a tenant_id column on every table (cheaper, needs discipline) or fully separate schemas/databases per tenant (more isolation, more operational overhead).

    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "How do you handle two people editing the same issue's description simultaneously?"

    A: Optimistic locking with a version number — each issue has a version field, updates check the version hasn't changed since the client last fetched it, rejecting (or merging) conflicting writes. For fully concurrent text editing, you'd need a CRDT/OT approach (see the Real-Time Collaboration topic).

    Q: "How would you scale this to 10,000 organizations with millions of issues each?"

    A: Shard the database by tenant_id (organization), use Elasticsearch for cross-issue search (sharded similarly), cache hot boards in Redis, and use Kafka partitioned by tenant to keep event processing scalable per-tenant.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    Design Jira. 10M users, 500K projects, billions of issues. A PM asks: 'Why does the board load slowly with 10,000 issues per sprint?' How do you diagnose and fix it.
    Board load = query all issues in sprint filtered by status. 10,000 issues means 10,000 rows fetched, sorted, paginated. Without indexes or pre-computation this is catastrophically slow.
    Root cause: SELECT * FROM issues WHERE sprint_id=? fetches 10K rows. Rendering all of them client-side. Fixes at each layer: DB: composite index (sprint_id, status, priority). API: return only the current page (20 items per column), cursor paginated. Read model: maintain a denormalized sprint_board table with pre-aggregated counts per status — only fetch counts for the summary, fetch full items per column lazily. Cache: Redis HSET board:{sprintId} {status} {count} — board summary loaded in <5ms. Schema: Issue(id, projectId, sprintId, status, assigneeId, priority, created, updated). Index: (sprintId, status, priority). Project(id, key, name, ownerId). Sprint(id, projectId, startDate, endDate, goal).
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'How do you implement @mentions in issue comments — notifying users in real time?'
    💭 Think First
    Mention detection is a text parsing problem. Notification delivery is a fan-out problem. Real-time delivery needs WebSocket or SSE.
    → Complete Answer
    Parse comment text on save: regex `@(\w+)` extracts mentioned usernames. Resolve usernames to userIds via user service. Publish MentionEvent{mentioner, mentionees, issueId, commentId} to Kafka topic. NotificationService consumes: for each mentionee, create a Notification record (DB), publish to their WebSocket session if connected (via Redis pub/sub across app instances). If not connected: send push notification (FCM/APNs) or email. Batching: if user is mentioned 10 times in 1 minute, send one digest notification. User preferences: users can opt out of email notifications while keeping in-app.
    Q: 'How does Jira handle permissions — a user can view project A but not project B, and within project A, only certain issue types?'
    💭 Think First
    This is hierarchical, multi-level authorization. Project-level, issue-type-level, field-level. Most of it is ABAC.
    → Complete Answer
    Permission scheme: Project has a PermissionScheme (reusable). Scheme maps Permissions to Roles. User has Roles in each Project they're a member of. Check: hasPermission(userId, projectId, BROWSE_PROJECT) → lookup user's roles in project → check if any role grants BROWSE_PROJECT. Cache: user's permissions per project cached in Redis (invalidated on role change). Issue-type permissions: separate IssueTypeScheme — e.g., only QA role can create Bug issue type. Field-level: FieldConfigurationScheme — certain fields hidden for certain roles. At scale: pre-compute permission sets on role change via async job, cache per user-project pair.
    🎯 Practice
    Sketch the full architecture diagram from scratch in 15 minutes, then implement just the Issue + Workflow state machine classes shown above, with a unit test confirming invalid transitions are rejected.
    💡 Hint — think before readingThink through the data structures first. What classes do you need? What are their relationships? Write class signatures before any method bodies.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — approach
    // Step 1: Define interface / abstract class // Step 2: Choose the right collection (List/Map/Set/Queue) // Step 3: Implement operations one by one // Step 4: Add concurrency if needed (AtomicX / synchronized) // Step 5: Test each operation independently
    🎯 Practice Task
    Design the data model for Jira's sprint board. A sprint has issues. Issues have status (TO DO, IN PROGRESS, DONE). Design the query to efficiently load the board grouped by status with a count per column.
    Hint — think before readingissues table with sprint_id and status columns, composite index. For board summary: GROUP BY status query with index. For board data: cursor-paginated per status column.
    → Worked Solution
    SQL — sprint board query
    -- Schema CREATE TABLE issues ( id UUID PRIMARY KEY, sprint_id UUID NOT NULL, status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL, priority INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 3, title TEXT NOT NULL, assignee_id UUID, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW() ); CREATE INDEX idx_issues_sprint_status ON issues(sprint_id, status, priority); -- Board summary (column counts) — fast with index SELECT status, COUNT(*) as issue_count FROM issues WHERE sprint_id = 'sprint-uuid' GROUP BY status; -- Per-column load (cursor-paginated, 20 items at a time) SELECT id, title, assignee_id, priority FROM issues WHERE sprint_id = 'sprint-uuid' AND status = 'IN_PROGRESS' ORDER BY priority, created_at LIMIT 20 OFFSET 0;

    Design a Real-Time Collaboration Platform

    Google Docs-style — the hardest part is conflict resolution, not the UI
    🧠 Intuition — The Core Problem Is Concurrent Edits
    Two people type in the same paragraph at the same instant — who wins?Naive locking (one editor at a time) kills the collaborative experience. The real solution is one of two algorithm families: Operational Transformation (OT — used by Google Docs) or Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs — used by many newer collaborative editors). Both let edits apply concurrently and converge to the same final state on every client, without locking.
    📐 Operational Transformation Concept
    💡 OT vs CRDT — Which to Mention in an Interview
    ApproachHow it worksTrade-off
    Operational Transformation (OT)Transforms each operation against concurrent ones based on a central server's orderingRequires a central server to sequence operations; well-proven (Google Docs), but transform functions are notoriously tricky to get correct
    CRDTData structure mathematically guarantees convergence regardless of operation orderWorks well in fully peer-to-peer/offline-first scenarios; can have higher memory overhead (tombstones for deleted content)
    Interview-safe answer: "I'd use OT with a central sequencing server for this use case since we have a clear server authority, similar to Google Docs' architecture. I'd consider CRDTs if we needed true offline-first peer-to-peer editing."
    💻 System Architecture
    Architecture flow
    1. Client makes a local edit, applies it OPTIMISTICALLY (instant feedback, no waiting for server) 2. Client sends the operation (insert/delete + position) to the server over WebSocket 3. Server (the single source of truth for ordering) transforms the operation against any concurrent operations it has already accepted, assigns it a sequence number 4. Server broadcasts the transformed operation to ALL other connected clients 5. Each client applies the transformed operation to its local document 6. Periodically, the document state is persisted to durable storage (Postgres/S3) as a checkpoint, with the operation log enabling replay/recovery and "version history" features
    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "How do you handle a client that disconnects and reconnects?"

    A: Client tracks the last sequence number it has applied. On reconnect, it requests all operations since that sequence number from the server and replays them locally to catch up, rather than re-fetching the entire document.

    Q: "How would you implement cursor/presence (seeing where others are typing)?"

    A: Separate, lightweight ephemeral channel (not persisted) — each client broadcasts its cursor position over the same WebSocket as a distinct message type, throttled (e.g., max 10 updates/sec) to avoid flooding.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    Design a real-time collaborative editor like Google Docs. Two users edit the same paragraph simultaneously. How do you handle conflicting edits without last-write-wins?
    Last-write-wins = whoever saves last overwrites the other's changes. Users lose their work. The real problem is concurrent operations on shared state. OT and CRDT are the two main approaches.
    Operational Transformation (OT): Each edit is an operation (Insert('a', position=5), Delete(position=3, len=2)). When two concurrent operations conflict, transform one relative to the other. If User A inserts at position 5 and User B deletes at position 3 (both starting from the same state): A's operation must be adjusted after B's delete shifts positions. Server is the authority — orders all operations, broadcasts transformed versions. Google Docs uses OT. CRDT (Conflict-free Replicated Data Type): Operations are designed so any order of application produces the same result. No server coordination needed. Yjs, Automerge libraries implement CRDTs for text. Figma uses CRDTs. Simpler for interviews: Use OT with a central server. Describe the sequence: client sends op + revision number → server transforms against concurrent ops → broadcasts transformed op to all clients.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'How do you handle a user who goes offline while editing and reconnects?'
    💭 Think First
    Offline editing = local changes accumulate. On reconnect, they must be merged with server state that may have diverged.
    → Complete Answer
    On reconnect: client sends all pending operations with the last known server revision. Server transforms each pending op against all ops that happened since that revision (the 'gap'). Transformed ops are applied to the server document. Result broadcast to all clients. Key: every op includes a client ID and sequence number so duplicates are detected and ignored. Document version stored as a monotonically increasing integer — clients always know if they're behind.
    Q: 'How do you show cursor positions of other users in real time?'
    💭 Think First
    Cursor position is ephemeral presence data — not document state. It changes 50 times per second and doesn't need durability.
    → Complete Answer
    WebSocket connection per user per document. On cursor move: client sends CursorEvent{userId, position, color} via WebSocket. Server broadcasts to all other users in the same document session. No DB persistence — cursor is ephemeral. Server-side: in-memory map of {documentId → {userId → CursorPosition}}. Redis pub/sub for multiple app instances: when user on instance A moves cursor, pub/sub delivers to instances B and C which have other users in the same doc.
    🎯 Practice
    Implement a simplified OT transform function for just two operation types (insert, delete) on a plain text string, and write tests confirming two concurrent operations converge to the same result regardless of application order.
    💡 Hint — think before readingThink through the data structures first. What classes do you need? What are their relationships? Write class signatures before any method bodies.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — approach
    // Step 1: Define interface / abstract class // Step 2: Choose the right collection (List/Map/Set/Queue) // Step 3: Implement operations one by one // Step 4: Add concurrency if needed (AtomicX / synchronized) // Step 5: Test each operation independently
    🎯 Practice Task
    Design the WebSocket message format for a collaborative editor. A user types 'Hello' at position 10 in a document at revision 42. Design the operation message and the acknowledgment message.
    Hint — think before readingOperation message includes: docId, userId, revision (client's last known), and the operation (type, position, content). Server ACK includes the new server revision and the transformed operation if it was modified.
    → Worked Solution
    JSON — WebSocket messages
    // Client → Server: operation { "type": "op", "docId": "doc-123", "userId": "user-456", "revision": 42, "op": { "type": "insert", "position": 10, "content": "Hello", "timestamp": 1720000000000 } } // Server → All clients: transformed operation broadcast { "type": "op", "revision": 43, "userId": "user-456", "op": { "type": "insert", "position": 12, // position adjusted after transforming against concurrent op "content": "Hello" } } // Presence: cursor moved {"type":"cursor","userId":"user-456","position":15,"color":"#FF6B6B"}

    Design a Workflow Automation Platform

    Zapier/n8n-style trigger → action chains
    🧠 Intuition
    It's a directed graph of triggers and actions, executed reliablyA user configures "when a new row is added to this spreadsheet, send a Slack message." The system must: detect the trigger (poll or webhook), execute the configured action chain reliably (even if a downstream service is temporarily down), and let users compose arbitrary multi-step workflows without writing code — this is the Strategy and Chain of Responsibility patterns at system scale.
    📐 Workflow Execution Diagram
    💻 Action Interface — Strategy Pattern at Scale
    Java
    interface WorkflowAction { ActionResult execute(WorkflowContext ctx); boolean isRetryable(Exception e); } class SlackNotifyAction implements WorkflowAction { public ActionResult execute(WorkflowContext ctx) { try { slackClient.send(ctx.get("channel"), ctx.get("message")); return ActionResult.success(); } catch (SlackApiException e) { return ActionResult.failure(e); } } public boolean isRetryable(Exception e) { return e instanceof RateLimitException; // retry rate limits, not auth failures } } class WorkflowEngine { void runWorkflow(Workflow workflow, WorkflowContext ctx) { for (WorkflowAction action : workflow.getActions()) { ActionResult result = executeWithRetry(action, ctx); executionLog.record(workflow.getId(), action, result); // persisted — for debugging + resume-on-crash if (!result.isSuccess() && !action.isRetryable(result.getException())) { notifyWorkflowFailed(workflow, action, result); return; // stop the chain on a non-retryable failure } } } }
    💡 Key Design Decisions
    Reliability — at-least-once execution

    Every step's execution is logged BEFORE attempting it. If the engine crashes mid-workflow, on restart it can resume from the last incomplete step rather than re-running already-succeeded actions (idempotency keys per step help avoid duplicate side effects on resume).

    Trigger detection — webhook vs polling

    Prefer webhooks (push) when the source system supports them — instant, efficient. Fall back to polling (pull, on a schedule) for systems without webhook support, accepting some detection latency.

    User-defined workflows without code

    Store the workflow as a DAG (list of action configs with type + parameters) in the database — the engine interprets this data at runtime rather than requiring custom code per workflow. This is itself the Strategy + Factory pattern combination from the LLD content.

    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "How do you prevent a runaway workflow (infinite loop via misconfiguration)?"

    A: Enforce a max execution step count and a max total runtime per workflow run, and detect cycles in the DAG at creation/save time before allowing a workflow to be activated.

    Q: "How would you scale to millions of active workflows triggering simultaneously?"

    A: Decouple trigger detection from execution via a queue (Kafka/SQS) — triggers publish events, a pool of stateless worker instances consume and execute, scaling horizontally independent of trigger volume.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    Design a workflow automation platform like Zapier. A user creates: 'When a new email arrives in Gmail → extract data with AI → create a Jira ticket'. How do you execute this reliably?
    This is an event-driven pipeline with external API calls. Each step can fail. The pipeline must be: reliable (no lost triggers), resumable (retry from failure point), auditable (what ran when), and observable.
    Architecture: Trigger Source (Gmail webhook) → TriggerService → publishes WorkflowTriggered event to Kafka → WorkflowEngine consumes → executes steps sequentially. Each step result stored in DB (WorkflowRun, StepResult). On step failure: retry with exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, max 3 attempts) → dead-letter queue if all retries exhausted → alert owner. Key entities: Workflow(id, name, trigger, steps[]), WorkflowRun(id, workflowId, startedAt, status, context), StepResult(runId, stepIdx, status, input, output, error). Context propagates data between steps (Gmail email → AI output → Jira ticket ID). Idempotency: each trigger has a unique ID — duplicate webhooks from Gmail are deduplicated.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'How do you handle a step that calls an external API with a rate limit?'
    💭 Think First
    External API rate limits (e.g., Jira allows 100 requests/minute) mean you can't just retry immediately.
    → Complete Answer
    Rate-limited step execution: catch 429 response → read Retry-After header → schedule retry after that delay using a delayed queue (Redis ZADD with score=retryTime). Worker polls the delayed queue (ZRANGEBYSCORE with score ≤ now) every second. Per-API rate limiter using Redis sliding window (ZADD of request timestamps, count before each call). If count ≥ limit: delay this step, don't block the worker thread. Separate worker pools per external API to prevent one rate-limited API from blocking unrelated workflow steps.
    Q: 'How do you implement conditional branching — step 3 runs only if step 2 output contains a keyword?'
    💭 Think First
    Branching requires evaluating conditions against step output at runtime. The condition is user-defined.
    → Complete Answer
    WorkflowStep has a condition: JSONPath or simple expression evaluated against the context. E.g., condition: `{{step2.output.sentiment}} == 'negative'`. Use a safe expression evaluator (SpEL for Java, cel-go). Never eval() user input. WorkflowEngine: after each step, evaluate conditions for all outgoing edges. If condition = true: proceed to that branch's next step. If condition = false: skip branch. If multiple branches: execute all matching branches (parallel fan-out). Store branch decision in StepResult for auditability.
    🎯 Practice
    Implement the WorkflowEngine and 2-3 WorkflowAction implementations above. Add a deliberate failure in the middle action and confirm the engine logs the failure, stops the chain, and doesn't re-run the already-succeeded first action on a manual restart.
    💡 Hint — think before readingThink through the data structures first. What classes do you need? What are their relationships? Write class signatures before any method bodies.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — approach
    // Step 1: Define interface / abstract class // Step 2: Choose the right collection (List/Map/Set/Queue) // Step 3: Implement operations one by one // Step 4: Add concurrency if needed (AtomicX / synchronized) // Step 5: Test each operation independently
    🎯 Practice Task
    Design the data model for a workflow execution. Show: the workflow definition schema, the runtime execution tracking, and how context (data passing between steps) is stored.
    Hint — think before readingWorkflow definition: JSON schema stored in workflows table. Execution: workflow_runs table with status and JSON context. Step results: step_results table with per-step input/output.
    → Worked Solution
    SQL — workflow execution model
    CREATE TABLE workflows ( id UUID PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(200), owner_id UUID, definition JSONB, -- { trigger: {...}, steps: [{type, config, condition}] } enabled BOOLEAN DEFAULT true ); CREATE TABLE workflow_runs ( id UUID PRIMARY KEY, workflow_id UUID REFERENCES workflows(id), status VARCHAR(20), -- RUNNING, COMPLETED, FAILED, PAUSED context JSONB, -- accumulates step outputs: {step0: {...}, step1: {...}} started_at TIMESTAMPTZ, completed_at TIMESTAMPTZ ); CREATE TABLE step_results ( id UUID PRIMARY KEY, run_id UUID REFERENCES workflow_runs(id), step_index INT, status VARCHAR(20), input JSONB, output JSONB, error TEXT, attempts INT DEFAULT 0, next_retry_at TIMESTAMPTZ );

    Design a Version Control System for Documentation

    Git-like internals — commits, branches, diffs, merges
    🧠 Intuition
    A version control system is fundamentally a content-addressable, immutable graph of snapshotsEvery commit is identified by a hash of its content + parent — making each commit immutable and tamper-evident. A branch is just a movable pointer to a commit. This graph structure is what enables Git's core trick: storage is cheap because unchanged content between commits is literally shared, not duplicated.
    📐 Commit Graph Diagram
    💻 Core Data Model
    Java — content-addressable commit graph
    class Commit { String hash; // SHA-256 of (content + parentHash + timestamp + author) String parentHash; // null for the first commit — forms the DAG String contentHash; // points to the actual document snapshot (or diff) String author, message; long timestamp; } class Branch { String name; String headCommitHash; // just a pointer — "creating a branch" is O(1), not a copy! } interface ContentStore { String store(String content); // returns content hash; identical content = identical hash = dedup'd String retrieve(String hash); } class VersionControlService { Commit commit(String branchName, String newContent, String author, String message) { Branch branch = getBranch(branchName); String contentHash = contentStore.store(newContent); // dedup automatically if unchanged Commit commit = new Commit(generateHash(), branch.headCommitHash, contentHash, author, message); commitStore.save(commit); branch.headCommitHash = commit.hash; // move the branch pointer forward return commit; } Branch createBranch(String name, String fromCommitHash) { return new Branch(name, fromCommitHash); // O(1) — just a new pointer to an existing commit } }
    💡 Merge Conflict Detection
    Three-way merge

    Find the common ancestor commit of both branches, then compare each branch's changes against that ancestor. If both branches modified the same line/section differently → conflict, requiring manual resolution. If only one branch changed it → auto-merge that change.

    For document-level (not line-level) versioning

    Since this is "documentation" not code, conflicts might be detected at a paragraph or block level instead of line-by-line — a design choice worth clarifying upfront.

    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "How does Git avoid storing full copies of every file in every commit?"

    A: Content-addressable storage — if a file is unchanged between commits, its content hash is identical, so the underlying blob is referenced (not duplicated). Only genuinely changed content consumes new storage.

    Q: "How would you implement 'blame' (who last changed each line)?"

    A: Walk the commit graph from HEAD backwards, diffing each commit against its parent; track which commit last touched each line. This is inherently O(commits × lines) in the naive case — production Git uses heuristics and caching to speed this up.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    Design a Version Control System (like Git) for documentation. Users can edit pages, see history, diff versions, and branch. 1M users, 10M pages, 100M versions. Walk through the data model.
    Version control for docs = immutable content storage + a graph of commits + branch pointers. The key insight: store content as immutable blobs identified by content hash. Same content stored only once.
    Content-addressable storage: Each version = content hash (SHA-256). If two pages have identical content, they share one blob. Blob table: {hash, content}. PageVersion: {id, pageId, hash, authorId, message, parentId, createdAt}. The parentId links form a DAG (directed acyclic graph) — exactly like Git commits. Branch: {id, pageId, name, headVersionId} — a pointer to the current tip. Diff: on-the-fly using Myers diff algorithm on the two blob contents. For large docs: store diffs instead of full content (delta compression) — each version stores a delta from its parent + periodic full snapshots. Merge: 3-way merge — find common ancestor, merge changes from both branches relative to ancestor.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: 'How do you implement the diff view between two versions efficiently?'
    💭 Think First
    Myers diff algorithm produces a human-readable diff. But running it on every request for large documents is expensive.
    → Complete Answer
    Cache computed diffs: key = SHA256(hash1 + hash2). If cached → return immediately. If not → compute Myers diff → cache in Redis with 1-hour TTL. The cache key is deterministic (based on content hashes, not version IDs) — the same content pair always produces the same diff. For very large documents (100KB+): chunked diff — split into paragraphs, diff paragraph list (structural diff), then diff changed paragraphs (textual diff). This reduces the complexity from O(N²) on the full document to O(P²) on the paragraph list plus O(Np²) for changed paragraphs.
    Q: 'A user merges two branches that both modified the same paragraph. How do you detect and present the conflict?'
    💭 Think First
    Conflict = both branches modified the same region since their common ancestor. The VCS can't auto-resolve this — user must choose.
    → Complete Answer
    3-way merge algorithm: find LCA (lowest common ancestor) of the two branch heads in the commit DAG. Get LCA content, branch A content, branch B content. Run 3-way diff: sections changed in A but not LCA → apply A's change. Sections changed in B but not LCA → apply B's change. Sections changed in BOTH A and B relative to LCA → CONFLICT. Present conflict markers: <<<< A's version ==== B's version >>>> with the LCA version as context. Store the conflict markers in a pending merge state. User resolves each conflict → saves the resolved version as a new commit with both branch heads as parents.
    🎯 Practice
    Implement the Commit/Branch/ContentStore classes above with an in-memory ContentStore using a HashMap keyed by content hash. Write a test that commits the same content twice and confirms it's stored only once (dedup via hash).
    💡 Hint — think before readingThink through the data structures first. What classes do you need? What are their relationships? Write class signatures before any method bodies.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — approach
    // Step 1: Define interface / abstract class // Step 2: Choose the right collection (List/Map/Set/Queue) // Step 3: Implement operations one by one // Step 4: Add concurrency if needed (AtomicX / synchronized) // Step 5: Test each operation independently
    🎯 Practice Task
    Write a SQL query to get the full version history of a page in reverse chronological order, including author name and word count of the content.
    Hint — think before readingJOIN page_versions with users for author name. Word count from content requires string processing — either store it computed or use pg's array_length(string_to_array(content,' ')).
    → Worked Solution
    SQL — version history with author
    SELECT pv.id as version_id, pv.created_at, pv.message as commit_message, u.name as author_name, u.avatar_url, LENGTH(b.content) - LENGTH(REPLACE(b.content,' ','')) + 1 AS word_count, pv.parent_id is null AS is_initial_version FROM page_versions pv JOIN users u ON pv.author_id = u.id JOIN blobs b ON pv.hash = b.hash WHERE pv.page_id = :pageId ORDER BY pv.created_at DESC LIMIT 50;

    Design an API Gateway for Atlassian Services

    single entry point handling routing, auth, rate limiting for many backend services
    🧠 Intuition
    One front door instead of clients knowing about 20 different microservicesWithout a gateway, every client (web, mobile, third-party integrations) needs to know the address of every backend service, handle auth separately for each, and implement rate limiting per-client themselves. An API Gateway centralizes these cross-cutting concerns — routing, authentication, rate limiting, request/response transformation — into one layer, so backend services can stay focused on business logic.
    📐 Gateway Architecture
    💻 Routing + Rate Limiting Layer
    Java — gateway core logic
    class ApiGateway { private final Map<String, ServiceRoute> routeTable; // path prefix -> backend service private final RateLimiter rateLimiter; // Token Bucket, per-client — covered in LLD Week 7 private final AuthValidator authValidator; public Response handleRequest(Request req) { // 1. Authenticate — verify JWT, extract identity (see Java/Backend AuthN section) User user = authValidator.validate(req.getAuthHeader()); if (user == null) return Response.unauthorized(); // 2. Rate limit per user/client if (!rateLimiter.allowRequest(user.getId())) return Response.tooManyRequests(); // 3. Route based on path prefix — Strategy pattern, routes are data-driven ServiceRoute route = findRoute(req.getPath()); if (route == null) return Response.notFound(); // 4. Forward to backend service, with a timeout and circuit breaker try { return route.forward(req, Duration.ofSeconds(5)); } catch (TimeoutException | CircuitOpenException e) { return Response.serviceUnavailable(); } } }
    💡 Key Design Decisions
    Where does the gateway live architecturally?

    Stateless, horizontally scaled behind a load balancer — the gateway itself should never become a single point of failure or a scaling bottleneck for the whole platform.

    Circuit breaker per backend service

    If Bitbucket Service is failing repeatedly, the gateway should "trip" the circuit and fail fast for a cooldown period instead of letting every request hang waiting for a timeout — protects both the gateway's own thread pool and the struggling backend from being hammered further.

    Centralized vs per-service rate limiting

    Centralizing at the gateway is simpler to reason about globally, but a single user hitting one slow endpoint shouldn't necessarily exhaust their entire quota for unrelated endpoints — per-route limits within the per-user budget is the more nuanced design.

    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "Doesn't the gateway become a single point of failure?"

    A: Mitigated by running multiple stateless gateway instances behind a load balancer with health checks — any single instance failing doesn't take down the platform. State (rate limit counters, etc.) lives in Redis, shared across instances.

    Q: "How do you avoid the gateway becoming a latency bottleneck?"

    A: Keep gateway logic lightweight (auth check, rate limit check, routing — all fast, in-memory or cached operations), avoid synchronous calls to slow systems within the gateway itself, and cache routing/auth decisions where safe (e.g., short-TTL JWT validation cache).

    🏭 Production Scenario
    Design an API Gateway for a microservices platform. 500 services, 50K requests/second. A request for /orders/{id} needs to be routed, authenticated, rate-limited, and logged — all in <5ms added latency.
    An API Gateway has 5 cross-cutting concerns: routing, auth, rate limiting, logging, load balancing. Each must add minimal latency. Wrong approach: synchronous call to a separate service per concern.
    Architecture: API Gateway is a reverse proxy. Incoming request → auth filter (validate JWT signature locally, no DB call, <1ms) → rate limit (Redis atomic increment, <2ms) → async logging (fire-and-forget to Kafka) → route to upstream (service registry cache, refreshed every 5s). Service discovery: services register with Consul on startup. Gateway caches URL mapping. Health checks evict unhealthy instances. Circuit breaker: Resilience4j wraps each upstream call — after 5 failures in 10s, open circuit, return 503 fast (no upstream call).
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: How does the API Gateway handle authentication without hitting the auth service on every request?
    💭 Think First
    If every request calls the auth service, auth becomes the bottleneck. JWT solves this — but what about token revocation?
    → Complete Answer
    JWT is self-contained: signature verification uses the public key (in-memory). The gateway never calls the auth service per request. Token revocation: maintain a Redis blocklist of revoked JTI (JWT ID) claims. Gateway checks: EXISTS blocklist:{jti} — O(1), under 2ms. Only revoked tokens need a blocklist check — legitimate tokens pass via pure cryptographic verification. Gateway pre-loads the public key on startup, refreshes via JWKS endpoint hourly on a background thread.
    Q: How do you implement request transformation — renaming a field before forwarding to the upstream service?
    💭 Think First
    Sometimes the external API contract differs from the internal service interface. The gateway can bridge the gap.
    → Complete Answer
    Request transformation pipeline: parse incoming request → apply transformation rules configured per route → forward transformed request. Rules: header rename (X-External-User to X-Internal-User-Id), body field rename, query param aliasing. Implement as a chain of filters: TransformationFilter reads route config, applies each rule in order. For body transformation: parse JSON, apply JSONPath-based rules, re-serialize. Performance: cache compiled JSONPath expressions. Only parse/transform bodies when a transformation config exists for that route.

    🎯 Practice Task
    Design the routing configuration for an API Gateway. Routes: /api/v1/orders/* goes to order-service, /api/v1/users/* to user-service, /api/v1/products/* to product-service. Show the data model and routing algorithm.
    Hint — think before readingRoute stored as {pattern, serviceId, stripPrefix, methods[]}. Routing uses longest-prefix matching. ServiceId is resolved to live instances via the service registry.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — gateway routing
    record Route(String pattern, String serviceId, boolean stripPrefix, Set<String> methods) {} class Router { private final List<Route> routes; // ordered: most-specific first private final ServiceRegistry registry; public URI route(String path, String method) { Route matched = routes.stream() .filter(r -> r.methods().contains(method)) .filter(r -> path.startsWith(r.pattern().replace("*", ""))) .findFirst().orElseThrow(() -> new RouteNotFoundException(path)); String upstreamPath = matched.stripPrefix() ? path.substring(matched.pattern().replace("*","").length()) : path; return URI.create(registry.getInstance(matched.serviceId()) + upstreamPath); } }

    Database Design

    normalization, sharding, and replication — the foundational system design topic
    🧠 Intuition
    Three independent questions: how is data structured, how is it split, how is it duplicatedNormalization is about structure — eliminating redundancy via relationships. Sharding is about splitting one logical dataset across multiple physical machines for scale. Replication is about duplicating data across machines for availability and read scaling. These are orthogonal decisions — a sharded database can also be replicated, and a normalized schema can still be sharded.
    📐 Sharding Strategies
    💡 Decision Framework
    DecisionChoose When
    Normalize (3NF)Write-heavy, data integrity critical, relationships matter — typical OLTP systems
    DenormalizeRead-heavy, joins are the bottleneck, can tolerate some redundancy for speed
    Hash shardingNeed even load distribution, queries are mostly by exact key lookup
    Range shardingRange queries are common (e.g., "all orders in January"), can manage hotspot risk
    Master-replica replicationRead-heavy workload — route reads to replicas, writes to master
    Multi-master replicationNeed writes accepted in multiple regions — accept added conflict-resolution complexity
    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "How do you handle a query that needs to join data across two shards?"

    A: Avoid it at the schema level if possible (choose a shard key that keeps related data together — e.g., shard by user_id so a user's orders and profile are co-located). If unavoidable, the application layer fans out queries to multiple shards and merges results — this is genuinely expensive and a sign the sharding key may need reconsidering.

    Q: "What's replication lag and why does it matter?"

    A: The delay between a write hitting the master and that write becoming visible on read replicas. A user who just wrote data and immediately reads from a replica might see stale data — solved via "read your own writes" patterns (route that specific read to the master, or to a replica known to be caught up).

    🏭 Production Scenario
    Design the database schema for a multi-tenant SaaS platform with 10K tenants, each with millions of rows. An enterprise customer demands their data is isolated from other tenants.
    Multi-tenancy has 3 strategies with different isolation/cost trade-offs. Enterprise isolation demand constrains the choice. Work through each option with trade-offs before recommending.
    Strategy 1 — Shared schema, tenant_id column: All tenants in one table. PostgreSQL row-level security enforces isolation. Cheapest. Risk: RLS bug leaks data. Strategy 2 — Separate schema per tenant: One DB, one schema per tenant. Strong isolation. Migrations run per schema. Strategy 3 — Separate DB per tenant: Maximum isolation. Enterprise customers pay for this. Complex: connection routing, separate backup, migrations per DB. Hybrid (recommended): Small tenants on shared schema; enterprise tenants get their own DB. Tenant registry stores {tenantId, tier, dbConnectionString}.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: A tenant grows to 1TB on the shared DB. How do you move them to a dedicated DB with zero downtime?
    💭 Think First
    Live migration while the tenant actively uses the system. Steps must be ordered so the cutover window is under 1 second.
    → Complete Answer
    (1) Provision new DB. (2) Initial snapshot via pg_dump then restore. (3) Logical replication captures ongoing changes. (4) Wait until lag under 1 second. (5) Brief write-pause for this tenant only (circuit breaker at gateway). (6) Final sync: drain remaining lag. (7) Update tenant registry dbConnectionString. (8) Resume traffic. Total user-visible downtime under 1 second.
    Q: How do you run schema migrations across 10,000 tenant schemas without locking tables?
    💭 Think First
    ALTER TABLE on millions of rows can lock for minutes. Across 10K schemas that could take days if done naively.
    → Complete Answer
    Use non-locking DDL: PostgreSQL ADD COLUMN with a default is instant for nullable columns. For non-nullable: add nullable column, backfill in batches (1000 rows at a time with sleep between), add NOT NULL constraint after backfill completes. Parallelize: N threads each handle a batch of schemas. Track state: migration_history table per schema — idempotent migrations can be safely re-run. Deploy new code before migration completes: handle both old and new schema. Remove backward-compat shim once all schemas migrated.
    🎯 Practice
    Design the schema for a multi-tenant SaaS product (your choice of domain). Decide on a sharding key, justify it, and identify which queries would require cross-shard fan-out under your chosen scheme.
