    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement the tenant isolation middleware in Spring Boot. Every request must be scoped to the correct tenant. Show ThreadLocal context, the filter, and how it protects repository queries.
    Hint — think before readingTenantContext (ThreadLocal) holds tenantId, populated from JWT claim by a filter. Repository queries always include WHERE tenant_id = TenantContext.get(). Finally block clears the ThreadLocal to prevent leakage.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — tenant isolation middleware
    class TenantContext { private static final ThreadLocal<String> CTX = new ThreadLocal<>(); public static void set(String id) { CTX.set(id); } public static String get() { return CTX.get(); } public static void clear() { CTX.remove(); } // MUST be called in finally } @Component class TenantFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter { protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, FilterChain chain) throws IOException, ServletException { try { TenantContext.set(extractTenantFromJwt(req)); chain.doFilter(req, res); } finally { TenantContext.clear(); // prevent leakage to next request on same thread } } } // Repository: always filter by tenantId List<Order> findByTenantId(String tenantId); // never cross-tenant

    Design a Logging & Monitoring System

    observability at scale — collection, storage, querying, alerting
    🧠 Intuition
    Logs are write-heavy, append-only, and queried for needles in haystacksA logging system at scale must ingest millions of log lines per second from thousands of service instances, store them cheaply, and let engineers search/filter them fast during an incident — when speed matters most. This is fundamentally different from a typical CRUD database workload: extremely high write volume, rare but latency-critical reads.
    📐 Pipeline Architecture
    💡 Key Design Decisions
    Why buffer with Kafka instead of writing directly to the search index?

    Elasticsearch indexing is relatively slow and can become a bottleneck under burst traffic (e.g., an incident causing a 100x spike in error logs). Kafka absorbs the burst, and the indexer consumes at a sustainable pace, never losing data even if it falls behind temporarily.

    Log retention and cost

    Hot tier (Elasticsearch, fast search) for recent logs (e.g., 7 days), cold tier (S3/cheap object storage) for older logs, often compressed and only searchable via a slower batch query path — balances query speed against storage cost.

    Structured logging

    Logs should be emitted as structured JSON (not free-text) with consistent fields (timestamp, service, level, trace_id) — enables fast, precise filtering instead of regex-searching raw text.

    Distributed tracing correlation

    Every log line should carry a trace_id that's propagated across service boundaries (via request headers), letting engineers reconstruct the full path of a single request across many microservices during debugging.

    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "How do you alert on metrics derived from logs without scanning everything?"

    A: Pre-aggregate in the streaming layer — the alerting consumer maintains rolling counters (e.g., error rate per service per minute) directly from the Kafka stream, triggering alerts on threshold breaches without ever touching the search index, which is reserved for human investigation.

    Q: "What happens if the indexer falls behind during a traffic spike?"

    A: Kafka retains messages for a configured retention period (e.g., 7 days), so the indexer can catch up once the spike subsides without data loss — this is exactly why the buffering layer exists rather than writing directly to Elasticsearch.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    Design a logging and monitoring system for 100 microservices each producing 10K log lines/second — 1M logs/sec total. Collect, store, query, and alert with no log loss.
    1M logs/sec = 86B logs/day. You cannot write raw logs directly to a DB. The pipeline needs buffering, compression, tiered storage, and near-real-time alerting — all independently scalable.
    Pipeline: Service stdout (structured JSON) → Filebeat sidecar → Kafka (buffer, 7-day retention) → two consumers: (1) ElasticSearch indexer for recent queryable logs, (2) S3 archiver (Parquet, compressed). Structured logging: every line is JSON with timestamp, level, service, traceId, spanId, message. TraceId correlates logs across all services for one request. Alerting: Flink reads Kafka, counts ERROR rate per service per minute, triggers PagerDuty when rate exceeds threshold. Metrics vs Logs: Prometheus scrapes /metrics for aggregated counters/histograms → Grafana dashboards. Logs are for debugging individual events.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: A user says their order is stuck. How do you trace it through 10 microservices?
    💭 Think First
    The request touched 10 services each with separate logs. Without correlation you search 10 systems manually.
    → Complete Answer
    Distributed tracing via OpenTelemetry: API Gateway generates a TraceId (128-bit UUID). It propagates via the traceparent HTTP header to every downstream service. Each service creates a child Span, logs with traceId+spanId in every line. Span data sent to Jaeger. Query: search by orderId to find traceId, then open Jaeger to see the complete waterfall of all 10 service spans — durations, errors, the exact SQL query that was slow. The stuck span is immediately visible.
    Q: Log storage costs are growing. Reduce them 80% without losing diagnostic capability.
    💭 Think First
    Most logs are never queried. Selective retention and tiered storage are the levers.
    → Complete Answer
    Tiered retention: Hot (ElasticSearch, 7 days): only ERROR + WARN + sampled 10% of INFO. Query under 1s. Warm (30 days): compressed indices, query in 5-30s. Cold (S3/GCS, 2 years): Parquet compressed 10:1, queryable via Athena. Sampling: 1% of INFO logs from high-volume services. Head-based: sample 1 in 100 requests, store ALL logs for sampled requests (full trace). Tail-based: always store complete traces that contain errors. Result: 90% of storage saved; critical diagnostic data preserved.
    🎯 Practice

    Implement structured logging with AOP in Spring Boot. Every method annotated @Logged must emit a JSON log line with: traceId from MDC, method name, duration in ms, and SUCCESS or ERROR status.
    Hint — think before readingAOP @Around interceptor catches the ProceedingJoinPoint. Reads MDC for traceId. Records start time. Logs method name and duration in the finally block. Logback JSON layout formats the MDC fields automatically.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — AOP structured logging
    @Aspect @Component class LoggingAspect { private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(LoggingAspect.class); @Around("@annotation(Logged)") public Object logExecution(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp) throws Throwable { String method = pjp.getSignature().toShortString(); long start = System.currentTimeMillis(); try { Object result = pjp.proceed(); log.info("method={} durationMs={} status=OK traceId={}", method, System.currentTimeMillis()-start, MDC.get("traceId")); return result; } catch (Throwable t) { log.error("method={} durationMs={} status=ERROR error={} traceId={}", method, System.currentTimeMillis()-start, t.getMessage(), MDC.get("traceId")); throw t; } } } // Filter sets MDC on every request: // MDC.put("traceId", extractOrGenerateTraceId(request));

    Design a Distributed Messaging System

    Kafka-style — partitions, offsets, consumer groups, delivery guarantees
    🧠 Intuition
    A durable, ordered, replayable log — not just a queueUnlike a traditional message queue (where a message disappears once consumed), a distributed log retains messages for a configurable period, letting multiple independent consumers read the same stream at their own pace, and even "replay" from an earlier point. This single property — durability + replayability — is what makes systems like Kafka foundational to event-driven architectures.
    📐 Partitions & Consumer Groups
    💡 Core Design Decisions
    Why partitions?

    A single ordered log can only be processed by one consumer at a time without breaking order. Splitting a topic into multiple partitions lets multiple consumers process in parallel, while still guaranteeing ORDER WITHIN each partition (not across the whole topic).

    Choosing a partition key

    Messages with the same key (e.g., order_id) always land in the same partition, guaranteeing they're processed in order relative to each other — critical for state machines like order status updates.

    Delivery guarantees

    At-most-once (fire and forget, can lose messages), at-least-once (retry until acknowledged, can duplicate), exactly-once (requires idempotent consumers + transactional writes — the hardest and most expensive guarantee).

    Replication for durability

    Each partition is replicated across multiple broker nodes (e.g., replication factor 3) — if one broker dies, a replica takes over as the new leader, no data loss.

    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "What happens if a consumer crashes mid-processing?"

    A: It depends on when the offset is committed. If committed AFTER successful processing (at-least-once), a crash before commit means the message is reprocessed by another consumer in the group after a rebalance — safe but requires idempotent processing logic downstream.

    Q: "How do you guarantee ordering for a specific entity (e.g., one user's events) across the whole system?"

    A: Use that entity's ID as the partition key — all of that entity's messages land in the same partition, and partitions guarantee order. You sacrifice some parallelism for entities with very high message volume, but most real-world entities don't need cross-entity ordering anyway.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    Design a distributed messaging system like Kafka from first principles. 1M messages/second, durable, ordered within a partition, replayable by consumers. Walk through partitioning, replication, and consumer groups.
    This tests distributed systems fundamentals. The key insight is that a single ordered log cannot scale beyond one machine — you partition for parallelism, replicate for durability, and use consumer groups for load balancing.
    Core concepts: Topic = logical channel. Partition = ordered, append-only log with monotonically increasing offsets. Producer sends to partition by key hash (same key always to same partition — ordering guaranteed per key). Consumer group: each partition assigned to exactly one consumer — max parallelism = partition count. Replication: each partition has 1 leader + N-1 followers. acks=all waits for all ISR (in-sync replicas) to confirm write before acknowledging producer — durable. Replayability: consumers commit offsets explicitly. Consumer can seek to offset 0 and re-read entire history. Retention: configurable (default 7 days).
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: A Kafka consumer is processing slowly and consumer lag is growing. How do you scale?
    💭 Think First
    Consumer lag means messages are produced faster than consumed. Kafka has a specific parallelism constraint that limits your scaling options.
    → Complete Answer
    Each partition is consumed by exactly one consumer per group. Max parallelism = number of partitions. If you have 10 partitions and lag grows: add consumers up to 10 (one per partition). Beyond 10: must increase partition count first — plan this upfront, reducing partitions is not possible without data loss. Also optimize the consumer itself: batch DB writes instead of per-message, add consumer-side caching, or process in parallel within each consumer using a thread pool for CPU-bound work.
    Q: How does Kafka guarantee exactly-once message processing?
    💭 Think First
    At-least-once: consumer may process a message twice if it crashes after processing but before committing the offset. How do you close that gap?
    → Complete Answer
    Producer idempotence (enable.idempotence=true): each producer has a PID + sequence number. Broker deduplicates retries from the same producer. Transactional consumers: read message, process it, write result AND commit offset in a single Kafka transaction. If consumer crashes mid-transaction it rolls back — the message is reprocessed but the output write also rolls back, and idempotent processing means the final result is the same. In Spring Kafka: @KafkaListener + @Transactional + KafkaTransactionManager + database TransactionManager — both commit or both roll back.
    🎯 Practice
    Design the partitioning strategy for an order-events topic in an e-commerce system. Justify your partition key choice and explain what ordering guarantees it provides (and what it doesn't).
    💡 Hint — think before readingThink through the data structures first. What classes do you need? What are their relationships? Write class signatures before any method bodies.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — approach
    // Step 1: Define interface / abstract class // Step 2: Choose the right collection (List/Map/Set/Queue) // Step 3: Implement operations one by one // Step 4: Add concurrency if needed (AtomicX / synchronized) // Step 5: Test each operation independently
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement a simple consumer offset manager. When a consumer processes a message it commits the offset. On restart the consumer reads from the last committed offset, never reprocessing already-handled messages.
    Hint — think before readingMap of {groupId:topic:partition -> nextOffset}. commitOffset stores offset+1 (next to read). getStartOffset returns 0 if never committed (start from beginning).
    → Worked Solution
    Java — offset management
    class OffsetManager { // Production: stored in Kafka __consumer_offsets topic or external DB private final ConcurrentHashMap<String,Long> store = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); public void commitOffset(String group, String topic, int part, long offset) { store.put(group+":"+topic+":"+part, offset + 1); // next to consume } public long getStartOffset(String group, String topic, int part) { return store.getOrDefault(group+":"+topic+":"+part, 0L); } } // Spring Kafka — manual commit after successful processing: @KafkaListener(topics="orders", groupId="order-processor") public void process(ConsumerRecord<String,Order> rec, Acknowledgment ack) { orderService.process(rec.value()); // process first ack.acknowledge(); // commit offset only after success // If process() throws: no ack → message replayed on restart }

    Kafka vs RabbitMQ — When to Use Each

    pull-based log vs push-based queue · consumer groups · replay · routing · the decision framework
    🧠 Mental Model
    Kafka = a durable replayable log. RabbitMQ = a smart message router. Kafka stores messages on disk and lets consumers read at their own pace — replay from offset 0. RabbitMQ pushes messages to consumers and deletes them on acknowledgment. Like a bulletin board vs email inbox.
    DimensionKafkaRabbitMQ
    ModelPull-based log (consumers poll)Push-based queue (broker pushes)
    Message retentionConfigurable (days/GB). Replayable.Deleted after consumer ACK
    OrderingGuaranteed within a partitionGuaranteed within a single queue
    ThroughputMillions/sec — sequential disk I/OTens of thousands/sec
    Consumer groupsEach group gets all messages independentlyCompeting consumers share a queue
    RoutingSimple: topic + partition keyComplex: exchanges, bindings, routing keys
    Use caseEvent streaming, audit log, analytics pipelineTask queues, RPC, complex routing, priority
    Replay old eventsYes — seek to any offsetNo — message gone after ACK
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Your e-commerce system sends order events to inventory, email, and analytics services. The team debates Kafka vs RabbitMQ. Three services need the same OrderPlaced event. Analytics is being deployed 2 weeks later and needs history. Which do you choose?
    Think: (1) Do multiple independent services need the SAME event? (2) Does any service need replay/history? (3) What is the throughput? All three point to one answer.
    Choose Kafka: Three independent services all need the same OrderPlaced event — each gets its own consumer group, each reads all messages independently. Analytics needs to replay 2 weeks of history on deployment — Kafka retains messages for 7 days by default (configurable to longer). High throughput e-commerce typically exceeds 10K orders/sec at peak. When RabbitMQ wins: Task distribution where ONLY ONE worker picks up a job (image resize queue). Priority queues (high-priority orders processed first). Complex routing rules (route based on message headers, exchange types). Low-latency RPC patterns (request-reply). Dead letter queues for failed messages with automatic retry. Rule: Kafka for event streaming (fan-out, replay, high throughput). RabbitMQ for task queues (one consumer picks up the job, complex routing, low latency).
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: Your Kafka consumer restarts mid-batch. Which messages get reprocessed and how do you prevent duplicate processing?
    💡 Think First
    Kafka offsets are committed by the consumer. If it crashes before committing the offset, what happens on restart?
    ➔ Complete Answer
    On restart: consumer reads from last committed offset. All messages after that offset are redelivered — at-least-once delivery by default. Duplicates are possible. Prevention: (1) Idempotent consumer: each message has a unique ID. Before processing, check if ID is in a processed-set (Redis SET or DB unique constraint). If present, skip. (2) Kafka exactly-once: enable.idempotence=true + transactional.id — Kafka deduplicates producer retries. Combined with transactional consumers: read-process-write in one Kafka transaction. (3) Manual offset commit after success: ack.acknowledge() only after the DB write succeeds — prevents loss but not duplicates if crash during processing. Best practice: design consumers to be idempotent regardless of delivery guarantee.
    Q: Explain Kafka consumer group rebalancing. What triggers it and what is the impact on processing?
    💡 Think First
    Rebalancing redistributes partitions among consumers. It is triggered by membership changes. What happens to message processing during a rebalance?
    ➔ Complete Answer
    Triggers: (1) New consumer joins the group. (2) Consumer leaves or crashes (missed heartbeat within session.timeout.ms). (3) Partition count increases. Impact: during rebalancing, ALL consumers in the group pause consumption — the coordinator revokes all partition assignments, then reassigns. This pause can be seconds to minutes for large groups. Mitigations: (1) Sticky assignor: minimize partition movement, keep existing assignments where possible. (2) Incremental cooperative rebalancing (Kafka 2.4+): only revoke/assign the partitions that actually need to move — others keep consuming uninterrupted. (3) Set max.poll.interval.ms higher than your longest processing time to prevent spurious rebalances caused by slow consumers.
    🎯 Practice Task
    Design the Kafka setup for an e-commerce platform. Three consumers: InventoryService, EmailService, AnalyticsService. All need OrderPlaced events. AnalyticsService is deployed 2 weeks after the system goes live. Show: topic design, partition key choice, consumer group names, and how Analytics replays historical events.
    💡 HintOne topic per event type. Partition key = orderId (ordering per order) or customerId (ordering per customer). Each service = separate consumer group. For Analytics replay: reset offset to earliest using the CLI tool.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Kafka — multi-consumer setup with replay
    // Topic: 1 topic per event type, partitioned by customerId // customerId as key = same customer's orders on same partition = ordered per customer kafka-topics.sh --create --topic order-events --partitions 12 --replication-factor 3 // Each service has its OWN consumer group = each gets ALL messages independently // inventory-service-group reads order-events -> updates stock // email-service-group reads order-events -> sends confirmation // analytics-group reads order-events -> updates dashboards // Spring Kafka consumer configuration per service: spring.kafka.consumer.group-id=inventory-service-group spring.kafka.consumer.auto-offset-reset=latest // new groups start from now // 2 weeks later: Analytics deployed, needs ALL historical events // Reset analytics-group offset to earliest (beginning of log): kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \ --group analytics-group --topic order-events \ --reset-offsets --to-earliest --execute // Analytics now replays ALL events since day 1 automatically // Other groups (inventory, email) are unaffected - they keep their own offsets

    Kafka Deep Dive — Consumer Groups · Offsets · Performance Tuning

    group coordinator · __consumer_offsets · batch.size · linger.ms · compression · exactly-once · duplicate prevention
    🧠 Consumer Group Internals (Q33, Q34, Q35)
    Kafka — consumer group mechanics
    // CONSUMER GROUP: set of consumers that cooperate to consume a topic // Each partition assigned to EXACTLY ONE consumer in the group at any time // Multiple groups: each group gets ALL messages (independent consumption) // GROUP COORDINATOR: one broker is elected as the coordinator for each consumer group // Coordinator manages: member joins/leaves, partition assignment, heartbeat tracking // Consumer sends heartbeat every heartbeat.interval.ms (default 3000ms) // If no heartbeat within session.timeout.ms (default 45000ms): coordinator removes consumer // Triggers REBALANCE: all consumers temporarily stop, partitions reassigned // OFFSET MANAGEMENT: __consumer_offsets (internal Kafka topic) // Committed offset = the position the consumer promises it has processed up to // On restart: consumer reads from committed offset (not from the beginning) spring.kafka.consumer.auto-offset-reset=earliest // new group: start from beginning spring.kafka.consumer.auto-offset-reset=latest // new group: start from now spring.kafka.consumer.enable-auto-commit=false // manual commit for exactly-once processing // Manual offset commit after processing (at-least-once) @KafkaListener(topics = "orders") public void consume(ConsumerRecord<String,OrderEvent> record, Acknowledgment ack) { processOrder(record.value()); // process FIRST ack.acknowledge(); // commit offset AFTER — ensures at-least-once // If crash between process() and ack(): message re-delivered on restart // Fix: make processOrder() idempotent (check DB before processing) } // WHAT HAPPENS WHEN CONSUMER CRASHES (Q33) // 1. Consumer stops sending heartbeats // 2. Group coordinator waits session.timeout.ms (45s default) // 3. Coordinator triggers rebalance: revokes all partitions // 4. Remaining consumers join new partition assignment // 5. Each consumer reads from last COMMITTED offset for its new partitions // 6. Messages after last commit are redelivered (at-least-once)
    Kafka Performance Tuning (Q37)
    Kafka — producer and consumer performance config
    // PRODUCER THROUGHPUT TUNING batch.size=65536 // default 16KB. Larger batch = fewer network requests = higher throughput linger.ms=10 // wait 10ms to fill the batch before sending. Trades latency for throughput. compression.type=snappy // snappy: fast compression (lz4 even faster). Reduces network + disk. acks=1 // leader ACK only. acks=all for durability (waits for all replicas). buffer.memory=67108864 // 64MB buffer. If full: block or throw (controlled by max.block.ms) // CONSUMER THROUGHPUT TUNING fetch.min.bytes=1048576 // wait until 1MB available before returning — fewer fetches, more data per fetch fetch.max.wait.ms=500 // max wait even if fetch.min.bytes not met max.poll.records=500 // process 500 records per poll. Increase for batch processing. // PARTITION COUNT: more partitions = more parallelism // Rule: partitions >= consumers. If 10 consumers: need >= 10 partitions // Too many partitions: more open file handles, longer rebalance, more metadata // Sweet spot: 3x the number of brokers per topic // REPLICATION + DURABILITY replication.factor=3 // 3 copies. Survive 2 broker failures. min.insync.replicas=2 // with acks=all: at least 2 replicas must ACK before success // DUPLICATE PREVENTION (Q36) enable.idempotence=true // producer: dedup retries using sequence numbers. No duplicate on retry. // Consumer-side: store processed message IDs in Redis SET or DB unique constraint // Before processing: IF EXISTS redis.sismember("processed", msgId) -> skip // After processing: redis.sadd("processed", msgId) EX 86400 (24h TTL)
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Your Kafka consumer service processes payment events. During a deploy, one consumer instance crashes mid-batch. When the service restarts 2 minutes later, you find 50 payments were processed twice — customers were charged double. How did this happen and how do you prevent it permanently?
    The consumer processed messages but crashed BEFORE committing the offset. On restart, Kafka redelivered from the last committed offset — causing reprocessing. This is the at-least-once delivery guarantee. How do you make the consumer idempotent so double-processing has no effect?
    Root cause: enable.auto.commit=true (default) commits offsets every 5 seconds regardless of processing status. Consumer processed 50 payments in 3s, crashed before the 5s auto-commit — all 50 were redelivered. Fix 1 — Manual commit: Disable auto-commit. Commit offset ONLY after successful DB write. At-least-once delivery, but processing is idempotent. Fix 2 — Idempotent processing: Each payment event has a unique paymentId. Before charging: SELECT 1 FROM processed_payments WHERE payment_id = ? FOR UPDATE. If exists: skip (already processed). If not: process and INSERT payment_id. The INSERT has a UNIQUE constraint — concurrent duplicate processing causes one to fail gracefully. Fix 3 — Kafka transactions (exactly-once): Set transactional.id on producer, isolation.level=read_committed on consumer. Kafka guarantees each message is delivered and processed exactly once within the transaction. Most complex but strongest guarantee. Production choice for payments: Fix 1 + Fix 2 (idempotent processing) — simpler, works across broker restarts, and handles all failure modes.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: How does Kafka guarantee message ordering? When does ordering break and how do you fix it?
    💡 Think First
    Kafka guarantees ordering WITHIN a partition. Messages with the same partition key always go to the same partition. What breaks ordering across partitions?
    ➔ Complete Answer
    Within a single partition: messages are totally ordered — consumers read in the exact order they were produced. Kafka appends to a partition sequentially, never reorders. Across partitions: NO ordering guarantee. Two messages in different partitions can be consumed in any order. Ordering breaks when: (1) Producer sends with null key — messages round-robin across partitions, no ordering. (2) Producer retries — without enable.idempotence=true, a retry after a timeout can arrive after a later message. Fix: set enable.idempotence=true — Kafka uses sequence numbers to detect and deduplicate out-of-order retries. (3) Multiple consumers in a group — partition A is processed by Consumer 1, partition B by Consumer 2. Both partitions may have events for the same order, consumed in any interleave. Fix: use a single partition (throughput penalty) OR use a partition key (order_id, customer_id) to route all related events to the same partition — ordering guaranteed within that key.
    Q: How do you improve Kafka consumer throughput when a single consumer cannot keep up with the producer?
    💡 Think First
    One consumer processes N messages/second. Producer produces 10N messages/second. Consumer lag grows. You cannot make one consumer faster than its processing logic allows. How do you scale horizontally?
    ➔ Complete Answer
    Scale consumers = scale partitions (they must match). Step 1: increase partition count on the topic (kafka-topics.sh --alter --partitions 20). Step 2: add more consumer instances in the same consumer group — each gets some partitions. Max parallelism = partition count (extra consumers beyond partition count sit idle). Additional optimisations: (1) max.poll.records: increase from 500 to 2000 — process more records per poll loop. (2) Parallel processing within one consumer: use a thread pool inside the @KafkaListener — but be careful with offset commit ordering. (3) fetch.min.bytes + fetch.max.wait.ms: tune to fetch larger batches with fewer network round trips. (4) Batch processing: accumulate N records, process as a batch (e.g., bulk DB insert), then commit. (5) Async processing: submit each record to a CompletableFuture pool, await all, then commit offset — maximises throughput but complicates error handling.
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement an idempotent Kafka consumer for payment events. Requirements: (1) Manual offset commit — only after successful DB write. (2) Idempotency check — if paymentId already in processed_payments table, skip (return 200, do not charge). (3) On DB failure — do NOT commit offset (let Kafka retry). (4) Show the Spring @KafkaListener config and the idempotency check logic. (5) Write a test that sends the same event twice and verifies the payment is only charged once.
    💡 Hintspring.kafka.consumer.enable-auto-commit=false. @KafkaListener with Acknowledgment parameter. Try INSERT INTO processed_payments(payment_id) — if DataIntegrityViolationException (UNIQUE violation): already processed, skip. Only call ack.acknowledge() after successful processing. Test: send same message twice, assert paymentRepo.count() == 1.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Spring Kafka — idempotent consumer with manual commit
    # application.yml spring.kafka.consumer: enable-auto-commit: false # manual commit only auto-offset-reset: earliest group-id: payment-processor // Idempotent consumer @KafkaListener(topics = "payment-events") public void process(ConsumerRecord<String, PaymentEvent> record, Acknowledgment ack) { String paymentId = record.value().paymentId(); try { // Idempotency: INSERT with UNIQUE constraint on payment_id processedRepo.insert(paymentId); // throws if duplicate paymentService.charge(record.value()); // actual payment processing ack.acknowledge(); // commit ONLY on success } catch (DataIntegrityViolationException e) { log.info("Duplicate payment {}, skipping", paymentId); ack.acknowledge(); // already processed — safe to commit and move on } catch (Exception e) { log.error("Failed to process {}, will retry", paymentId, e); // Do NOT ack — Kafka will redeliver on next poll } } // Test: send same event twice, assert charged once @Test void duplicateEvent_chargedOnce() { var event = new PaymentEvent("pay-123", BigDecimal.TEN); kafkaTemplate.send("payment-events", event); kafkaTemplate.send("payment-events", event); // duplicate Thread.sleep(2000); assertEquals(1, paymentRepo.countByPaymentId("pay-123")); // only charged once }

    Design a Search Engine for Knowledge Base Articles

    inverted index, relevance ranking, and the trade-offs behind both
    🧠 Intuition — Why You Can't Just LIKE '%query%'
    A SQL LIKE query scans every row; a search engine scans noneAn inverted index flips the problem: instead of "for each document, does it contain this word," it pre-computes "for this word, which documents contain it." Searching becomes a fast lookup into this pre-built index rather than a scan over every document — the same fundamental idea as a database index, applied to free text.
    📐 Inverted Index Diagram
    💻 Simplified Inverted Index Implementation
    Java
    class InvertedIndex { // term -> set of document IDs containing it private final Map<String, Set<String>> index = new HashMap<>(); void indexDocument(String docId, String content) { for (String token : tokenize(content)) { // lowercase, strip punctuation, remove stop words index.computeIfAbsent(token, k -> new HashSet<>()).add(docId); } } Set<String> search(String query) { List<String> terms = tokenize(query); if (terms.isEmpty()) return Set.of(); Set<String> result = new HashSet<>(index.getOrDefault(terms.get(0), Set.of())); for (int i = 1; i < terms.size(); i++) { result.retainAll(index.getOrDefault(terms.get(i), Set.of())); // AND semantics — intersect doc sets } return result; } } // This is the educational core. Production search adds: relevance ranking (TF-IDF/BM25), // fuzzy matching, stemming, and distributed sharding of the index itself — see below.
    💡 Relevance Ranking — Beyond Just Matching
    TF-IDF (Term Frequency × Inverse Document Frequency)

    Scores a document higher if a query term appears often IN that document (TF), but lower if the term is common ACROSS all documents (IDF) — e.g., "the" appears everywhere and shouldn't boost relevance, while a rare technical term appearing 5 times in one doc strongly signals relevance.

    BM25

    A refinement of TF-IDF used by Elasticsearch/Lucene by default — adds saturation (10th occurrence of a word matters much less than the 2nd) and document length normalization (a short doc matching isn't penalized vs. a long doc with the same absolute term count).

    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "How would you scale this index to millions of documents?"

    A: Shard the index itself (e.g., by document ID hash) across multiple nodes — each shard handles a subset of documents, queries fan out to all shards in parallel, and results are merged and re-ranked. This is exactly how Elasticsearch distributes itself, and is why production systems use it rather than reimplementing this from scratch.

    Q: "How do you keep the index up to date as articles are edited?"

    A: Two approaches: synchronous re-indexing on every write (simple, but slows writes) or asynchronous indexing via an event queue (the article service publishes an "article updated" event, a separate indexer consumes and updates the search index) — trading a small indexing delay for decoupled, faster writes.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    Design a search engine for a knowledge base like Confluence. 10M documents, 1M queries/day. Relevance-ranked results in under 200ms. How do you design the indexing and retrieval?
    SQL LIKE queries are O(n) — they scan every row. At 10M documents that is catastrophically slow. You need an inverted index: a mapping from each term to the list of documents containing it.
    Inverted index: index[word] = [{docId, termFrequency, positions}]. TF-IDF ranks documents: TF (frequency in doc) x IDF (log(totalDocs/docsContainingWord)) — rare words score higher. BM25 (Elasticsearch default) improves on TF-IDF with document length normalization. Indexing pipeline: Document saved → Kafka → Indexer: tokenise (lowercase, split), remove stopwords (the, a, is), stem (running → run) → update Elasticsearch. Query execution: parse → tokenise same way → look up posting lists → intersect (AND) or union (OR) → BM25 score → top-K. Elasticsearch handles all of this. Design your own tokenizer pipeline to match domain terminology.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: How do you implement autocomplete for the search box with under 50ms latency?
    💭 Think First
    Full-text search indexes are optimised for word matching, not prefix matching. Autocomplete needs a different structure.
    → Complete Answer
    Separate autocomplete layer: Elasticsearch completion suggester uses an FST (Finite State Transducer) optimised for prefix lookup. Alternatively: pre-compute top-K suggestions per prefix and cache in Redis. Key format: suggest:{prefix} -> JSON array of top-5 suggestions, ranked by historical search frequency. Update from search logs weekly. Redis lookup is O(1), under 1ms. For fresh documents not yet in Redis: fall back to Elasticsearch completion field. Hybrid: Redis for hot prefixes (covers 95% of traffic), Elasticsearch for the long tail.
    Q: A user types a misspelled word. How does the search engine find the intended term?
    💭 Think First
    Edit distance: a misspelled word is N character edits away from the correct word. You need to find the closest indexed terms efficiently.
    → Complete Answer
    Fuzzy search: Elasticsearch fuzziness=AUTO matches terms within N Levenshtein edits (0 for 1-2 char terms, 1 for 3-5 chars, 2 for 6+ chars) using Levenshtein automata — evaluated in O(dictionary size) but with aggressive pruning. Phonetic matching via Soundex/Metaphone index catches spelling variants that sound alike (centre/center). Did-you-mean suggestions: at query time, for each query term with 0 results, find the nearest term in the index using a BK-tree (metric tree) — O(log n) nearest-neighbour search by edit distance.
    🎯 Practice
    Implement the InvertedIndex class above, then add a basic TF-IDF scoring function that ranks matching documents by relevance instead of returning an unordered set.
    💡 Hint — think before readingThink through the data structures first. What classes do you need? What are their relationships? Write class signatures before any method bodies.

    Write the Elasticsearch query for: find documents containing "kubernetes" OR "k8s" in the title (boosted 3x over body), filtered to category=devops, return top 10 with highlighted snippets.
    Hint — think before readingbool query with should clauses (OR logic), field-level boost on title, filter for category, highlight configuration for matched fragments.
    → Worked Solution
    Elasticsearch — boosted multi-field query
    { "query": { "bool": { "should": [ {"match": {"title": {"query": "kubernetes", "boost": 3}}}, {"match": {"title": {"query": "k8s", "boost": 3}}}, {"match": {"body": {"query": "kubernetes"}}}, {"match": {"body": {"query": "k8s"}}} ], "filter": [{"term": {"category": "devops"}}], "minimum_should_match": 1 } }, "size": 10, "highlight": { "fields": { "title": {"number_of_fragments": 1}, "body": {"number_of_fragments": 2, "fragment_size": 150} } } }

    Design a Real-Time Analytics Platform

    stream processing, windowed aggregation, and the latency-accuracy trade-off
    🧠 Intuition
    You can't run a SQL aggregate query over an infinite, never-ending stream"Show me the number of active users in the last 5 minutes, updated every second" requires fundamentally different machinery than a batch report. Stream processing frameworks (Kafka Streams, Flink) compute aggregations over sliding/tumbling time windows incrementally, updating results continuously as new events arrive, rather than re-scanning historical data on every query.
    📐 Windowing Diagram
    💡 Key Design Decisions
    Windowing strategy

    Tumbling (fixed, non-overlapping — "events per minute") for simple periodic metrics. Sliding (overlapping — "rolling 5-min average") for smooth, continuously-updating dashboards. Session windows (gap-based — "user activity sessions") for behavioral analytics.

    Late-arriving events

    Network delays mean an event timestamped 10:00:05 might arrive at 10:00:12, after its window has theoretically closed. Watermarking (a configurable "how late is too late" threshold) decides whether to include late events in already-emitted aggregates or drop them.

    Exactly-once processing

    Critical for accurate counts — if the stream processor crashes and reprocesses some events, naive counting would double-count. Frameworks like Kafka Streams provide exactly-once semantics via transactional offset commits tied to state updates.

    Pre-aggregation vs raw event storage

    Store BOTH: pre-aggregated rollups (fast for dashboards showing "last hour") AND raw events in cold storage (for ad-hoc historical queries that don't fit a pre-computed window) — a common lambda-architecture-style trade-off.

    💻 Conceptual Aggregation Logic
    Pseudocode — windowed count aggregation
    // Conceptual model of what Kafka Streams / Flink do under the hood class TumblingWindowAggregator { Map<Long, AtomicLong> windowCounts = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); // windowStart -> count long windowSizeMs = 60_000; // 1 minute windows void onEvent(Event e) { long windowStart = (e.timestamp / windowSizeMs) * windowSizeMs; // bucket the event windowCounts.computeIfAbsent(windowStart, k -> new AtomicLong()).incrementAndGet(); } void onWindowClose(long windowStart) { long finalCount = windowCounts.get(windowStart).get(); emitMetric("events_per_minute", windowStart, finalCount); // push to dashboard/alerting windowCounts.remove(windowStart); // free memory — don't accumulate forever } }
    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "How do you handle an event arriving after its window has already closed and emitted?"

    A: A configured grace period (watermark) keeps the window "open for late data" for a bounded extra time. Beyond that, late events are either dropped (accepting slight inaccuracy for speed) or trigger a correction/retraction emitted to downstream consumers, depending on accuracy requirements.

    Q: "How would you scale this to handle millions of events per second?"

    A: Partition the stream (by user_id or event type), running independent aggregator instances per partition in parallel — identical principle to Kafka partitioning, ensuring related events land on the same aggregator for correct counting.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    Design a real-time analytics platform. Events flow in at 5M/second (clicks, purchases). Business wants: a live dashboard showing events/second, plus the ability to query total revenue by product by day for the last 90 days in under 2 seconds.
    5M events/sec = 432B events/day. You cannot query raw events for dashboards — too slow. You need a streaming layer for real-time and pre-aggregated storage for historical queries. These are two different problems.
    Speed layer (real-time): Kafka → Flink sliding window → compute events/sec, revenue/min → write to Redis for live dashboard. Dashboard polls Redis every second, response under 1ms. Batch layer (historical): Same Kafka data → Spark hourly batch → write aggregated Parquet to S3 → load into data warehouse (Redshift/BigQuery). Pre-aggregate daily: revenue_daily table with (product_id, date, total_revenue, order_count). The 90-day query becomes SELECT SUM(revenue) GROUP BY product_id, date — 90 rows per product, trivially fast. Kappa simplification: Run only Flink, handle both paths by replaying historical Kafka data from offset 0 for backfill.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: How do you handle late-arriving events? A mobile app buffers events and sends them 2 hours late.
    💭 Think First
    Streaming windows assume events arrive roughly in order. Late events arrive after the window result was already published.
    → Complete Answer
    Watermark-based windowing in Flink: the watermark is the system estimate of the maximum event time seen. Allowed lateness of 2 hours: late events still update the window result for up to 2 hours after the window closes. After that, late events go to a side output stream for separate processing or discarding. For batch aggregations: the nightly Spark job runs at 2am to ensure all events from the previous day (including up to 2-hour-late arrivals) have reached Kafka. If a significant batch of late events arrives later: Spark reruns the aggregation for affected days using the upsert pattern (ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE).
    Q: The live dashboard shows events/second. How do you compute and serve this with under 1 second lag?
    💭 Think First
    Exact events-per-second from 5M events/sec in real time requires a sliding window aggregation. Where does this computation happen and how is the result served?
    → Complete Answer
    Flink or Kafka Streams sliding window: count events in a 60-second tumbling window advancing every 1 second. Output: {timestamp, count}. Write to Redis key metrics:eps with 10s TTL. Dashboard polls Redis every second — under 1ms response. For per-service breakdown: Redis Hash {service:checkout -> 120, service:browse -> 4800000}. Approximate unique user counts with HyperLogLog: exact counting at 5M/s requires too much memory, HLL gives 2% error using only 12KB regardless of cardinality. Use PFADD per event and PFCOUNT for the dashboard.
    🎯 Practice
    Implement the TumblingWindowAggregator above. Simulate a stream of timestamped events (including some out-of-order/late ones) and observe how late events are handled with and without a grace period.
    💡 Hint — think before readingThink through the data structures first. What classes do you need? What are their relationships? Write class signatures before any method bodies.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — approach
    // Step 1: Define interface / abstract class // Step 2: Choose the right collection (List/Map/Set/Queue) // Step 3: Implement operations one by one // Step 4: Add concurrency if needed (AtomicX / synchronized) // Step 5: Test each operation independently
    🎯 Practice Task
    Design the pre-aggregation SQL that runs as a nightly job to populate the revenue_daily table, which backs the 90-day revenue dashboard query. Handle late arrivals and idempotency.
    Hint — think before readingINSERT ... SELECT from the events table for the previous day only. Include a 2-hour buffer for late arrivals. Use ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE for idempotency so re-running the job is safe.
    → Worked Solution
    SQL — nightly incremental aggregation
    -- Run at 02:00 daily — processes previous day with 2h late-arrival buffer INSERT INTO revenue_daily (product_id, date, total_revenue, order_count) SELECT product_id, DATE(event_time) AS date, SUM(revenue) AS total_revenue, COUNT(DISTINCT id) AS order_count FROM events WHERE event_type = 'purchase' AND DATE(event_time) = CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 day' AND event_time >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 day 2 hours' GROUP BY product_id, DATE(event_time) ON CONFLICT (product_id, date) DO UPDATE SET total_revenue = EXCLUDED.total_revenue, order_count = EXCLUDED.order_count; -- Dashboard query — hits revenue_daily, not raw events SELECT product_id, SUM(total_revenue) FROM revenue_daily WHERE date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '90 days' GROUP BY product_id ORDER BY 2 DESC;

    Design a Scalable Authentication & Authorization System

    millions of users, SSO, token lifecycle — at platform scale
    🧠 Intuition — System Design Scale, Not Just the API-Level Concept
    This extends the AuthN/AuthZ concept from the Java/Backend section to platform scaleThe earlier Java topic covered HOW a single request authenticates (JWT verification, Spring Security). This system design question asks: how does the ENTIRE platform issue, refresh, revoke, and validate tokens for millions of users across dozens of services, including SSO across multiple products (think Atlassian's single login working across Jira, Confluence, Bitbucket)?
    📐 SSO Architecture
    💡 Core Design Decisions
    Short-lived access tokens + long-lived refresh tokens

    Access tokens (JWT, 15 min TTL) are verified statelessly by every service — no DB call needed, fast. Refresh tokens (longer TTL, stored server-side, revocable) are exchanged for new access tokens periodically, giving you both speed (stateless access checks) AND the ability to revoke a compromised session (by invalidating the refresh token).

    Centralized AuthZ data, decentralized enforcement

    Roles/permissions live in a central service, but each downstream service caches/embeds the relevant claims in the JWT itself (or a short-TTL local cache) to avoid a network call to the central service on every single request — critical for not making auth the platform's bottleneck.

    Handling permission changes mid-session

    If a user's role changes (e.g., revoked admin access), the change won't take effect until their current access token expires (since tokens are self-contained). For sensitive permission downgrades, you may need a server-side revocation list checked for high-privilege operations specifically, accepting the added complexity.

    Scaling token issuance

    The Central Auth Service itself must be highly available and horizontally scaled — it's a single point of failure for ALL login traffic across the entire platform if not designed carefully (multiple regions, read replicas for user credential lookups, etc.).

    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "How do you revoke ALL of a user's sessions immediately (e.g., account compromised)?"

    A: Maintain a "tokens issued before timestamp X are invalid" marker per user (or a short blocklist of specific token IDs) — checked by a lightweight, heavily-cached lookup at the gateway layer, balancing the speed benefit of stateless JWTs against the need for occasional immediate revocation.

    Q: "How does this scale to handle a traffic spike (e.g., Monday morning login surge)?"

    A: Auth Service is stateless and horizontally scaled behind a load balancer; user credential lookups hit a read-optimized, cached datastore (Redis in front of the user DB); token issuance itself is CPU-bound (signing) and scales linearly with more instances.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    Design a scalable authentication and authorization system for 100M users, 500 microservices, and multiple client types. Every service must verify identity and permissions without the auth service becoming a bottleneck.
    If every service calls the auth service per request, the auth service must handle 50K × 500 = 25M calls/second. That is impossible for a single service. The key is distributing the verification work.
    Authentication: OAuth2 Authorization Server (Keycloak or Spring Authorization Server) issues JWT access tokens (15-min TTL) and refresh tokens (7-day TTL, stored in DB). Every service verifies JWT locally using the cached public key — zero auth service calls per request. Auth service only involved at login and refresh. Authorization: JWT carries coarse-grained roles. For fine-grained: Open Policy Agent (OPA) sidecar per service — policy evaluated locally, no network call. Central policy service pushes policy bundles to all OPA sidecars. Service-to-service: mTLS or Istio service mesh handles service identity via certificates.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: A user account is compromised. How do you immediately revoke their access across all 500 services?
    💭 Think First
    JWTs are stateless — you cannot delete them. How do you force immediate logout across a distributed system?
    → Complete Answer
    Token version approach: user has a tokenVersion integer in the DB. JWT carries the tokenVersion claim at issue time. On compromise: increment tokenVersion in DB and Redis. Every service: after verifying JWT signature, check Redis for this userId tokenVersion. If JWT version is less than the Redis version: reject with 401. Redis lookup is O(1), under 2ms. Alternative: JTI blocklist — add the JTI (JWT ID) of all the user's active tokens to Redis with TTL equal to the remaining token lifetime. Also delete all refresh tokens from DB so the attacker cannot get new access tokens.
    Q: How do you handle authentication for partner APIs with different rate limits and scopes from regular users?
    💭 Think First
    Partners typically use API keys rather than user JWTs. They need separate rate limits, permission scopes, and audit trails.
    → Complete Answer
    API key credential type: key issued per partner, stored as bcrypt hash + metadata (partnerId, scopes, rateLimit) in DB. At API Gateway: detect API key in header. Look up hash in Redis (cached on first use, TTL 5 minutes). Extract partnerId and scopes. Create a synthetic authentication context with partnerId as subject and scopes as authorities. Rate limiting: per API key using the partner-specific limit from DB. Audit: all API key requests logged with partnerId, endpoint, timestamp, response status — for billing, debugging, and compliance.
    🎯 Practice
    Sketch the full token issuance and refresh flow, including what happens when a refresh token is used after the user has been deactivated. Design the revocation-check mechanism and justify its caching strategy for minimal latency impact.
    💡 Hint — think before readingThink through the data structures first. What classes do you need? What are their relationships? Write class signatures before any method bodies.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — approach
    // Step 1: Define interface / abstract class // Step 2: Choose the right collection (List/Map/Set/Queue) // Step 3: Implement operations one by one // Step 4: Add concurrency if needed (AtomicX / synchronized) // Step 5: Test each operation independently
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement the JWT validation utility used by every microservice. It must: verify the signature with the public key, check expiry, check the revocation blocklist via Redis, and return the user principal.
    Hint — think before readingJwtValidator uses JJWT library to parse and verify the token. Checks Redis blocklist by JTI after signature verification. Returns a typed UserPrincipal or throws AuthException with a specific reason.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — JWT validation in every service
    @Component class JwtValidator { private final PublicKey publicKey; // loaded from JWKS on startup private final StringRedisTemplate redis; public UserPrincipal validate(String token) { try { Claims claims = Jwts.parserBuilder() .setSigningKey(publicKey).build() .parseClaimsJws(token).getBody(); // Blocklist check — O(1), under 2ms if (Boolean.TRUE.equals(redis.hasKey("blocklist:" + claims.getId()))) throw new AuthException("Token revoked"); return new UserPrincipal( claims.getSubject(), claims.get("orgId", String.class), claims.get("roles", List.class) ); } catch (JwtException e) { throw new AuthException("Invalid token: " + e.getMessage()); } } }

    Design the Snake Game

    a focused LLD problem testing grid state management and clean collision logic
    🧠 Intuition
    The core insight: the snake's body is a Deque, not an arrayMovement = add a new head in the direction of travel, remove the tail (unless food was just eaten, in which case keep the tail — the snake grows). A Deque (double-ended queue) gives O(1) operations at both ends, which is exactly what's needed — no other data structure fits this access pattern as naturally.
    📐 Movement Diagram
    💻 Full Implementation
    Java
    class SnakeGame { private final Deque<int[]> snake = new ArrayDeque<>(); // front = head, back = tail private final Set<String> occupied = new HashSet<>(); // O(1) self-collision check private final int width, height; private List<int[]> food; private int foodIndex = 0, score = 0; public SnakeGame(int width, int height, int[][] food) { this.width = width; this.height = height; this.food = Arrays.asList(food); snake.addFirst(new int[]{0, 0}); // start at top-left occupied.add("0,0"); } // Returns score, or -1 if game over public int move(String direction) { int[] head = snake.peekFirst(); int newRow = head[0], newCol = head[1]; switch (direction) { case "U" -> newRow--; case "D" -> newRow++; case "L" -> newCol--; case "R" -> newCol++; } // Wall collision if (newRow < 0 || newRow >= height || newCol < 0 || newCol >= width) return -1; boolean ateFood = foodIndex < food.size() && food.get(foodIndex)[0] == newRow && food.get(foodIndex)[1] == newCol; String newHeadKey = newRow + "," + newCol; String tailKey = null; if (!ateFood) { int[] tail = snake.peekLast(); tailKey = tail[0] + "," + tail[1]; // tail will move away — won't count as self-collision target } // Self collision: occupied by body (excluding the tail spot that's about to vacate) if (occupied.contains(newHeadKey) && !newHeadKey.equals(tailKey)) return -1; snake.addFirst(new int[]{newRow, newCol}); occupied.add(newHeadKey); if (ateFood) { foodIndex++; score++; } else { int[] removedTail = snake.removeLast(); occupied.remove(removedTail[0] + "," + removedTail[1]); } return score; } }
    💡 The Self-Collision Edge Case Most People Miss
    Why excluding the tail mattersIf the snake's NEXT move happens to land exactly where its CURRENT tail is, that's actually valid — the tail is about to vacate that cell in the same move (assuming no food eaten). Forgetting this check causes false "game over" results on a legitimate move that just happens to trail closely behind itself.
    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "Why use a HashSet alongside the Deque instead of just scanning the Deque for collision checks?"

    A: Scanning the Deque for self-collision is O(n) per move. The HashSet gives O(1) lookup — critical as the snake grows long, since collision checking happens on every single move.

    Q: "How would you extend this for a multiplayer version?"

    A: Each snake becomes its own Deque+Set pair on a SHARED board state. Collision checks now also include other snakes' occupied cells. The game loop becomes server-authoritative (clients send direction inputs, server computes and broadcasts the resulting state) to prevent cheating — same WebSocket broadcast pattern as the Chat Application topic.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    Design the Snake Game. The snake moves on a grid, eats food, grows in length. If it hits a wall or itself, game over. An interviewer wants to see clean OOP: what classes, what state, what update loop?
    Snake is a state machine with a very tight game loop. The key challenge: how does the snake grow? How do you detect self-collision? Think about what data structure represents the snake body most efficiently.
    Core classes: Snake (body as Deque), Direction (UP/DOWN/LEFT/RIGHT), Food (position), GameBoard (width, height). Snake body as Deque: head at the front. On each tick: addFirst(newHead), if food eaten keep tail (snake grows), else removeLast (snake moves). O(1) for both operations. Self-collision detection: maintain a HashSet in parallel with the Deque. addFirst checks if newHead is in the set — if yes, game over. Add newHead to set; if not growing, remove the tail from set. O(1) collision check. Food placement: generate random position not occupied by the snake — use the set to check. Game loop: fixed-interval timer (100ms per tick). On each tick: compute newHead from current head + direction. Check wall collision. Check self-collision. Check food collision. Update state.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: How do you make the snake game multiplayer — two snakes on the same board competing?
    💭 Think First
    Multiplayer adds a second snake, snake-vs-snake collision, and possibly a real-time networking layer. The OOP model extends cleanly.
    → Complete Answer
    Add a second Snake instance. On each tick: compute both snakes new heads. Cross-collision: check if snake A's new head is in snake B's body set — if yes, snake A dies (or both die if they hit each other head-on simultaneously). Food: when eaten by either snake, place new food. Score: track separately per snake. For networked multiplayer: server is the authority for game state. Each client sends direction inputs. Server runs the game loop, broadcasts the full game state every tick. Clients render the received state. Latency tolerance: server accepts direction inputs with a small buffer window (last-received direction used for the current tick if no new input arrives).
    Q: How would you implement an undo feature — go back one tick?
    💭 Think First
    The Command Pattern makes undo natural. Each tick is a Move command. Undo = reverse the last move. But can you actually reverse a snake move?
    → Complete Answer
    Store the previous state before each tick: previousHead and removedTail (the position that was removed on the last non-growing tick). Undo: removeLast (remove the new head), addLast (restore the tail position if it was removed), remove newHead from position set, add tail back to position set. The food state also needs to be restored if the last move ate food. A MoveRecord{addedHead, removedTail, foodEaten} captures everything needed. Stack of MoveRecords enables unlimited undo. This is exactly the Command Pattern: each move is a command with execute() and undo(). The game holds an undo stack.
    🎯 Practice
    Implement the SnakeGame class above and write tests covering: normal movement, food consumption (growth), wall collision, self-collision, and the tail-following edge case described.
    💡 Hint — think before readingThink through the data structures first. What classes do you need? What are their relationships? Write class signatures before any method bodies.

    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement the core Snake game tick() method. On each tick: move the snake one step in the current direction, check all collision types, handle food consumption, and return the game status.
    Hint — think before readingtick() computes newHead from head + direction offset. Checks: wall collision (out of bounds), self-collision (in body set), food collision (equals food position). Updates Deque and Set accordingly. Returns GAME_OVER, FOOD_EATEN, or MOVED.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — Snake game core
    enum Direction { UP(-1,0), DOWN(1,0), LEFT(0,-1), RIGHT(0,1); final int dr, dc; Direction(int r, int c){dr=r;dc=c;} } record Position(int row, int col) {} class SnakeGame { private final int rows, cols; private final Deque<Position> body = new ArrayDeque<>(); private final Set<Position> bodySet = new HashSet<>(); // O(1) collision private Position food; private Direction dir = Direction.RIGHT; private int score = 0; enum Status { MOVED, FOOD_EATEN, GAME_OVER } public Status tick() { Position head = body.peekFirst(); Position newHead = new Position(head.row()+dir.dr, head.col()+dir.dc); // Wall collision if (newHead.row() < 0 || newHead.row() >= rows || newHead.col() < 0 || newHead.col() >= cols) return Status.GAME_OVER; // Self collision — check BEFORE adding new head if (bodySet.contains(newHead)) return Status.GAME_OVER; body.addFirst(newHead); bodySet.add(newHead); if (newHead.equals(food)) { // food eaten — grow score++; food = randomFoodPosition(); return Status.FOOD_EATEN; } Position tail = body.removeLast(); bodySet.remove(tail); // move (no growth) return Status.MOVED; } }

    Design a URL Shortening Service

    encoding strategy, redirect performance, and scale considerations
    🧠 Intuition
    The core challenge isn't generating short codes — it's doing so without collisions at scale, fastA naive random-string approach needs collision checking on every write (does this code already exist?), adding latency and complexity at high write volume. A counter-based approach (base62-encode an auto-incrementing ID) guarantees uniqueness by construction, with zero collision checking needed.
    📐 Base62 Encoding Diagram
    💻 Core Service Logic
    Java
    class UrlShortenerService { private static final String ALPHABET = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789"; private final DistributedCounter idGenerator; // e.g., backed by Redis INCR, or pre-allocated ID ranges per node String shorten(String longUrl) { long id = idGenerator.next(); // globally unique, monotonically increasing String shortCode = base62Encode(id); db.save(shortCode, longUrl); // store the mapping return "https://short.ly/" + shortCode; } String resolve(String shortCode) { String cached = redisCache.get(shortCode); // cache-aside, since reads vastly outnumber writes if (cached != null) return cached; String longUrl = db.findByShortCode(shortCode); redisCache.set(shortCode, longUrl, Duration.ofHours(24)); return longUrl; } private String base62Encode(long id) { StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); while (id > 0) { sb.append(ALPHABET.charAt((int)(id % 62))); id /= 62; } return sb.reverse().toString(); } }
    💡 Scale-Specific Design Decisions
    Why not just hash the URL (e.g., MD5)?

    Hashing has a collision risk (two different URLs producing the same short code) requiring a collision-resolution strategy on every write. A counter-based approach avoids this category of bug entirely by construction.

    Distributed ID generation without a single bottleneck

    A single global counter becomes a write bottleneck and single point of failure at scale. Solution: pre-allocate ID ranges to each application server (e.g., server A gets IDs 1-1000, server B gets 1001-2000) — each server then generates locally without any cross-server coordination needed per request.

    Read-heavy optimization

    URL resolution (redirect) traffic vastly outnumbers shortening (write) traffic in virtually every real system. Heavy caching (Redis, even a CDN edge cache for very popular links) is the single highest-leverage optimization — read-path latency is what most affects user experience.

    Custom aliases and expiration

    Allow users to optionally request a custom short code (check availability instead of generating); support optional TTL on links for time-limited campaigns — both are common feature extensions worth mentioning proactively.

    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "What if two app servers are assigned overlapping ID ranges by mistake?"

    A: Use an atomic operation (Redis INCRBY, or a dedicated ID-generation service like Twitter's Snowflake) for range allocation itself, so the allocation step is race-condition-free even though the actual ID generation per server is local and fast afterward.

    Q: "How do you handle analytics (click counts) without slowing down the redirect?"

    A: Don't synchronously update a click counter on the critical redirect path. Instead, fire-and-forget an event to a queue (Kafka) and let an asynchronous consumer aggregate click counts — the redirect itself stays fast, unaffected by analytics processing.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    Design a URL shortening service like bit.ly. 100M URLs created/day, 10B redirects/day. Redirects must complete in under 50ms. Walk through encoding, storage, and the hot-path serving architecture.
    Read-to-write ratio is 100:1. Optimise the redirect path — it runs 100 times more often than creation. Creation can tolerate a few hundred ms. The redirect must be near-instant.
    Encoding: Redis atomic counter (INCR url:counter) gives a unique long ID. Encode to Base62 (a-z, A-Z, 0-9) — 7 characters covers 62^7 = 3.5 trillion URLs. Distributed counter: pre-allocate ranges per instance (instance A gets 1M-2M, B gets 2M-3M) — no Redis call per creation. Storage: PostgreSQL for durability — {code, long_url, user_id, created_at, expires_at}. Unique index on code. Redis for hot cache: GET url:{code} returns long_url, 24h TTL. Redirect hot path: CDN (Cloudflare) at the edge caches 301 redirect for popular codes — 90% of traffic never reaches origin. 9% hits Redis (sub-ms). 1% cold miss goes to Postgres, then warms cache.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: The same long URL is shortened by 1000 different users. Do you deduplicate?
    💭 Think First
    Deduplication saves storage but shares the short code among all users. Think about the ownership and analytics implications.
    → Complete Answer
    No deduplication by default: each creation gets a unique code. Each user owns their link, sees their own click analytics, controls expiry. Storage is manageable: 100M/day x 500 bytes/row = 50GB/day, easily archived. If you deduplicate: hash the long URL, look up existing code, return it. Problem: user A deletes the link — it disappears for users B through Z. Also breaks per-user analytics. Compromise: deduplicate only within the same user — if the same user shortens the same URL twice, return the existing code.
    Q: How do you track analytics — clicks, referrer, country, device — without slowing down the redirect?
    💭 Think First
    Click tracking must not add latency to the redirect. Any synchronous analytics work in the redirect path would hurt the 50ms target.
    → Complete Answer
    Async analytics: after sending the 302/301 response, publish ClickEvent{code, timestamp, ip, userAgent, referer} to Kafka. The redirect thread is never blocked by analytics work. Kafka consumer: MaxMind GeoIP maps IP to country in memory (no network call). User-agent parser extracts device and browser. Flink aggregates: clicks per code per hour. Store in click_analytics table. Dashboard query: SELECT date, COUNT(*) FROM click_analytics WHERE short_code=? GROUP BY date. Custom alias analytics page: show chart, top referrers, country breakdown, device pie chart.
    🎯 Practice
    Implement the UrlShortenerService above with an in-memory counter and HashMap-backed storage. Add the cache-aside resolve() logic and measure the difference in lookup time with a simulated cache hit vs miss.
    💡 Hint — think before readingThink through the data structures first. What classes do you need? What are their relationships? Write class signatures before any method bodies.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — approach
    // Step 1: Define interface / abstract class // Step 2: Choose the right collection (List/Map/Set/Queue) // Step 3: Implement operations one by one // Step 4: Add concurrency if needed (AtomicX / synchronized) // Step 5: Test each operation independently
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement the redirect endpoint. Check Redis first, fall back to Postgres on cache miss, warm the cache, and publish a click event to Kafka asynchronously — all within the same HTTP request handling.
    Hint — think before readingCheck Redis with O(1) GET. On miss: load from DB, write to Redis (fire-and-forget). Publish click event to Kafka without blocking the response. Return 302 redirect or 404.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — URL redirect endpoint
    @GetMapping("/{code}") public ResponseEntity<Void> redirect(@PathVariable String code, HttpServletRequest req) { // 1. Check Redis cache (hot path — sub-ms) String longUrl = redis.opsForValue().get("url:" + code); // 2. Cache miss — load from Postgres and warm cache if (longUrl == null) { longUrl = urlRepo.findByCode(code) .orElseThrow(() -> new NotFoundException(code)) .getLongUrl(); redis.opsForValue().set("url:" + code, longUrl, Duration.ofHours(24)); } // 3. Async analytics — never blocks the redirect final String url = longUrl; CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> kafka.send("click-events", new ClickEvent(code, req.getRemoteAddr(), req.getHeader("Referer", req.getHeader("User-Agent"))))); return ResponseEntity.status(302) .header("Location", url).build(); }

    Design a Scalable Chat Application

    WebSocket connections, presence, message delivery and ordering at scale
    🧠 Intuition
    The hard part isn't sending one message — it's maintaining millions of persistent connections and routing messages between them efficientlyUnlike REST APIs (stateless, any server can handle any request), chat requires a persistent WebSocket connection per online user. The system must track WHICH server holds WHICH user's connection, since messages need to be routed to the exact server instance maintaining the recipient's socket.
    📐 Connection Routing Architecture
    💡 Core Design Decisions
    Connection registry

    A shared, fast-lookup store (Redis) maps user_id → which WebSocket server instance currently holds their connection. When Server 1 needs to deliver a message to a user connected to Server 2, it publishes to a Redis Pub/Sub channel that Server 2 subscribes to.

    Message ordering and delivery guarantee

    Each message gets a monotonically increasing sequence number per conversation. Clients can detect gaps (missing sequence numbers) and request a resync — critical for handling brief disconnections without losing or duplicating messages.

    Offline message delivery

    If the recipient is offline, the message is persisted to a database/queue and delivered on their next connection (or via push notification). The connection registry returning "not found" for a user is the signal to fall back to persistent storage instead of live routing.

    Presence (online/offline/typing indicators)

    A separate, ephemeral, frequently-updated channel (also via Redis, often with short TTLs that auto-expire if a heartbeat isn't received) — kept distinct from durable message data since presence is inherently transient and doesn't need persistence.

    Horizontal scaling of WebSocket servers

    Each server handles a subset of total connections (limited by file descriptors/memory per server, typically tens of thousands per instance). A load balancer with sticky sessions (or a connection-aware router) ensures a client's reconnect attempts land predictably.

    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "How do you handle a WebSocket server crashing with thousands of active connections?"

    A: Clients detect the dropped connection (heartbeat/ping-pong timeout) and reconnect, getting routed (via load balancer) to a healthy server instance. The reconnecting client requests any missed messages since its last known sequence number — this is exactly why message ordering/sequence tracking matters.

    Q: "How would you support group chats with thousands of members efficiently?"

    A: Fan-out-on-write for small/medium groups (publish to each member's individual channel directly) vs fan-out-on-read for very large groups/channels (store once, members pull on connect/poll) — a classic trade-off mirroring how Twitter handles celebrity accounts with millions of followers differently from regular users.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    Design a scalable chat application. 500M users, 100M DAU, 50B messages/day. A message from Alice to Bob must be delivered within 500ms. If Bob is offline it must be delivered when he reconnects.
    Chat is a fan-out and delivery guarantee problem. Alice sends one message — it must reach all of Bob's devices. Each device may be connected to a different gateway server. Routing across servers is the hard part.
    Architecture: Client connects via WebSocket to a Gateway server. Gateway is stateful — maintains open connections. Message flow: Alice app → WebSocket → Message Service → store in Cassandra (durable first) → publish to Kafka → Fan-out Service → look up Bob's gateway servers from Redis {userId -> [gatewayId, ...]} → push to each gateway via Redis pub/sub → gateway pushes to Bob's WebSocket. Offline delivery: if Bob has no gateway entries (offline), message stays in Cassandra. On reconnect: gateway queries Cassandra for messages since lastSeenAt. Delivers in order. ACK updates lastSeenAt. Delivery receipt: when the server receives the message from Alice it sends a delivery ACK back (single tick). When Bob's device receives it, Bob's app sends a delivery confirmation to the server which forwards to Alice (double tick). Message routing: the server looks up which gateway server holds Bob's WebSocket connection (via Redis: GET ws-gateway:{bobId}) and forwards there. Read receipt: Bob's app sends ReadReceipt on message display → Message Service stores → Alice gets real-time update via WebSocket (blue tick).
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: Group chat with 1000 members. How do you fan out one message to 1000 users efficiently?
    💭 Think First
    Naive fan-out: for each of 1000 members, look up their gateways and push. That is 1000 DB lookups and 1000 gateway pushes per message.
    → Complete Answer
    Hybrid fan-out by group size: Small groups (under 100 members) — push model. Fan out immediately: bulk-fetch member gateways with Redis pipeline MGET, push to each. Large groups (1000+ members) — pull model. Store message in the group Cassandra partition. Online members receive a lightweight notification (push notification via FCM/APNs) prompting their app to fetch. The app pulls new messages on next foreground. Compute online intersection: Redis Set of online userIds. SINTER group:{groupId}:members and online:users gives only online members to push to — avoid pushing to offline members entirely.
    Q: How do you implement end-to-end encryption so the server cannot read messages?
    💭 Think First
    E2E encryption means only sender and recipient devices hold the keys. The server stores and forwards ciphertext without any ability to decrypt.
    → Complete Answer
    Signal Protocol (used by WhatsApp and Signal): each device generates an identity key pair and uploads the public key to the server. When Alice first messages Bob: fetch Bob's public key bundle, run X3DH (Extended Triple Diffie-Hellman) to derive a shared secret. Encrypt message with AES-256-GCM using that shared secret. Server stores and forwards the ciphertext blob. Bob's device runs the same X3DH with Alice's public key to derive the identical shared secret, then decrypts. Double Ratchet algorithm generates a new key for every message — compromising one message's key cannot decrypt any other message (forward secrecy and break-in recovery).
    🎯 Practice
    Sketch the connection registry data model and the exact sequence of Redis Pub/Sub operations for routing a message from a user on Server 1 to a recipient on Server 2. Then design the offline-delivery fallback path.
    💡 Hint — think before readingThink through the data structures first. What classes do you need? What are their relationships? Write class signatures before any method bodies.
