    🎯 Practice Task
    Design the Cassandra schema for storing chat messages. Support: fetch all messages in a conversation ordered by time, cursor pagination, and high write throughput without hotspots.
    Hint — think before readingPartition key is conversation_id — all messages for one conversation on one node. Clustering key is (created_at DESC, message_id) for time-ordered retrieval with unambiguous cursor pagination.
    → Worked Solution
    Cassandra CQL — messages table
    CREATE TABLE messages ( conversation_id UUID, created_at TIMESTAMP, message_id UUID, sender_id UUID, content_type TEXT, -- TEXT, IMAGE, VIDEO, FILE content TEXT, -- AES-256-GCM encrypted ciphertext status TEXT, -- SENT, DELIVERED, READ PRIMARY KEY ((conversation_id), created_at, message_id) ) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (created_at DESC, message_id DESC) AND compaction = {'class': 'TimeWindowCompactionStrategy', 'compaction_window_unit': 'DAYS', 'compaction_window_size': 1}; -- Latest 50 messages: SELECT * FROM messages WHERE conversation_id = :convId LIMIT 50; -- Cursor pagination (next page): SELECT * FROM messages WHERE conversation_id = :convId AND (created_at, message_id) < (:lastTime, :lastId) LIMIT 50;

    Design a Job Scheduler (System Scale)

    distributed scheduling across many worker nodes — beyond the single-process LLD version
    🧠 Intuition — How This Differs From the LLD Version
    The LLD Task Scheduler (Week 7) handles ONE process's PriorityQueue. This is the distributed version.At system scale, jobs must survive a single machine crashing, run exactly-once even with multiple scheduler instances racing to pick up the same job, and scale to millions of scheduled jobs (cron-style recurring jobs, one-off delayed jobs) across a fleet of workers — fundamentally a distributed coordination problem, not just a data structure problem.
    📐 Distributed Scheduler Architecture
    💻 Exactly-Once Claim — The Core Mechanism
    SQL — distributed lock via SKIP LOCKED
    -- Each scheduler instance runs this on a poll interval (e.g., every 5 seconds) -- FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED: if another instance has already locked a row, skip it -- instead of waiting — this is THE mechanism that prevents duplicate job execution BEGIN; SELECT id, job_type, payload FROM jobs WHERE run_at <= NOW() AND status = 'PENDING' ORDER BY run_at LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; -- claims rows atomically; other instances skip these rows entirely -- Mark claimed jobs as IN_PROGRESS with this instance's ID and a lock expiry UPDATE jobs SET status = 'IN_PROGRESS', lock_owner = :instanceId, lock_expiry = NOW() + INTERVAL '5 minutes' WHERE id IN (:claimedIds); COMMIT; -- After actual job execution completes (outside this transaction): -- UPDATE jobs SET status = 'COMPLETED' WHERE id = :jobId -- If a scheduler crashes mid-execution, lock_expiry eventually passes, and another -- instance's poll query picks the job back up (status reset to PENDING by a cleanup job)
    💡 Key Design Decisions
    Why poll the database instead of an in-memory PriorityQueue (like the LLD version)?

    An in-memory queue dies with the process. The database is the durable source of truth — jobs survive any single scheduler instance crashing, and any instance can pick up the work, which is the entire point of going from single-process to distributed.

    Recurring (cron-style) jobs

    Stored as a job definition with a cron expression rather than a single row; after each successful execution, the next run_at is computed and a new row (or updated row) is scheduled — keeps the claim mechanism identical for one-off and recurring jobs.

    Lock expiry as a crash-recovery mechanism

    If a scheduler instance crashes after claiming a job but before completing it, the lock_expiry timestamp eventually passes. A periodic cleanup process resets expired IN_PROGRESS jobs back to PENDING, letting another instance retry — critical for fault tolerance.

    Sharding for very high job volume

    At extreme scale, even SKIP LOCKED polling on one table becomes a bottleneck — shard jobs across multiple tables/databases (e.g., by job type or a hash of job_id), with each scheduler shard-group polling only its assigned shard.

    💬 Interview Follow-ups
    Q: "What if the job execution itself takes longer than the lock_expiry window?"

    A: The executing instance should periodically "heartbeat" — extending lock_expiry while still actively working — so the cleanup process doesn't prematurely release a job that's genuinely still in progress, distinguishing "still working" from "crashed."

    Q: "How is this different from just using a message queue (Kafka/SQS) for job execution?"

    A: A queue is great for the "execute once now" part, but doesn't naturally support arbitrary future scheduling (run this in 3 days) or complex recurrence (every weekday at 9am) — many real systems actually combine both: a scheduler polls the DB for due jobs and PUBLISHES them to a queue, letting a separate worker pool consume and execute, decoupling scheduling logic from execution capacity.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    Design a distributed job scheduler at system scale. 10M jobs/day, cron expressions, priorities, job dependencies (B runs after A), retry on failure. Execute within 1 second of the scheduled time.
    The naive approach — poll every job every second — is O(jobs) per second, completely unscalable. The key insight: pre-compute next execution times and store them in a sorted data structure keyed by trigger time.
    Architecture: JobDefinition in PostgreSQL. Next execution times in Redis sorted set ZADD job:ready {epochMs} {jobId}. Leader scheduler (one instance, elected via Redis SETNX lock) polls every second: ZRANGEBYSCORE job:ready 0 now → fetch due jobs → publish each to Kafka → update sorted set with next trigger time. Execution: Kafka consumer pool runs jobs in isolated threads. JobExecution row created per run. On failure: exponential backoff re-enqueue (1s, 2s, 4s, max 3 retries) → dead-letter queue → alert. Leader election: Redis lock with 10s TTL, refreshed every 5s by the leader. If leader dies, TTL expires and another instance wins within 10 seconds.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: How do you implement job dependencies — job B must run only after job A completes successfully?
    💭 Think First
    Dependencies form a DAG. When job A completes, you need to check which downstream jobs are now unblocked efficiently.
    → Complete Answer
    JobDependency table: {job_id, depends_on_job_id}. Redis counter per job: dep_count:{jobId} = number of incomplete dependencies. On job creation: set dep_count to the number of dependencies. On job completion: for each direct dependent, DECR dep_count:{dependentId}. If the result is 0: all dependencies satisfied — enqueue the dependent job immediately by adding it to the Redis sorted set with score = now(). This avoids scanning the full dependency table on every completion — O(direct_dependents) instead of O(all_jobs).
    Q: A job scheduled every minute is taking 90 seconds. Two overlapping instances could corrupt data. How do you handle this?
    💭 Think First
    Job duration exceeds the schedule interval. Two execution strategies exist — choose based on the job's semantics.
    → Complete Answer
    Strategy 1 — Skip on overlap (for idempotent jobs): before executing, acquire a Redis lock {jobId}:running with TTL = max expected duration. If the lock already exists: skip this trigger and log the skip. Good for: report generation, cache warming — latest run is sufficient. Strategy 2 — Queue on overlap (for accumulative jobs): always enqueue, run sequentially — one consumer per job ID ensures sequential processing. Good for: processing pending orders where every trigger must run. Alert on consistent overrun: if a job regularly exceeds its interval, it needs either optimisation or a longer schedule. Track p99 job duration in the JobExecution table.
    🎯 Practice
    Set up a Postgres table matching the schema implied above, and implement two competing "scheduler instances" (separate processes/threads) polling with SKIP LOCKED. Confirm no job is ever claimed by both simultaneously under concurrent polling.
    💡 Hint — think before readingThink through the data structures first. What classes do you need? What are their relationships? Write class signatures before any method bodies.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — approach
    // Step 1: Define interface / abstract class // Step 2: Choose the right collection (List/Map/Set/Queue) // Step 3: Implement operations one by one // Step 4: Add concurrency if needed (AtomicX / synchronized) // Step 5: Test each operation independently
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement the leader scheduler loop. Every second: acquire the Redis leader lock, fetch all due jobs from the sorted set, publish them to Kafka for execution, and update their next run time for recurring jobs.
    Hint — think before readingSpring @Scheduled(fixedDelay=1000) method. Try to acquire SETNX leader lock. On success: ZRANGEBYSCORE, for each job: Kafka send + ZREM + ZADD with next cron trigger time. On lock fail: skip (another instance is leader).
    → Worked Solution
    Java — leader scheduler with Redis sorted set
    @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 1000) public void tick() { // Only the leader triggers jobs — prevents double-execution if (!acquireLeaderLock()) return; long now = System.currentTimeMillis(); Set<String> due = redis.opsForZSet().rangeByScore("job:ready", 0, now); if (due == null || due.isEmpty()) return; due.forEach(jobId -> { redis.opsForZSet().remove("job:ready", jobId); kafka.send("job-executions", jobId); jobRepo.findById(jobId).ifPresent(job -> { if (job.getCronExpression() != null) { long next = CronExpression .parse(job.getCronExpression()) .next(ZonedDateTime.now()) .toInstant().toEpochMilli(); redis.opsForZSet().add("job:ready", jobId, next); } }); }); } private boolean acquireLeaderLock() { Boolean ok = redis.opsForValue() .setIfAbsent("scheduler:leader", instanceId, Duration.ofSeconds(10)); if (Boolean.TRUE.equals(ok)) return true; // Refresh TTL if we are already the leader if (instanceId.equals(redis.opsForValue().get("scheduler:leader"))) { redis.expire("scheduler:leader", Duration.ofSeconds(10)); return true; } return false; }

    OOP design · pattern: resource allocation with type matching
    🧠 Mental Model — Clarify Before You Code
    A Parking Lot is a classic OOP + resource allocation problem. The interviewer is testing: class hierarchy design, encapsulation, strategy pattern for spot selection, and thread safety.
    Always clarify: How many floors? Multiple vehicle types (bike/car/truck)? Pricing (flat/hourly)? Entry/exit tickets? Multiple entry/exit gates? Reservations? Start simple, offer to extend.
    📐 Class Design
    💻 Complete Implementation
    Java — Parking Lot full OOP design
    enum VehicleType { BIKE, CAR, TRUCK } abstract class Vehicle { protected final String licensePlate; protected final VehicleType type; Vehicle(String plate, VehicleType type) { this.licensePlate = plate; this.type = type; } } class Car extends Vehicle { Car(String p) { super(p, VehicleType.CAR); } } class Bike extends Vehicle { Bike(String p) { super(p, VehicleType.BIKE); } } class Truck extends Vehicle { Truck(String p){ super(p, VehicleType.TRUCK); } } class ParkingSpot { private final String id; private final VehicleType allowedType; private boolean occupied = false; private Vehicle parkedVehicle; ParkingSpot(String id, VehicleType type) { this.id = id; this.allowedType = type; } public boolean isAvailable() { return !occupied; } public boolean canFit(VehicleType t) { return !occupied && allowedType == t; } public synchronized void park(Vehicle v) { if (occupied) throw new IllegalStateException("Spot already occupied"); parkedVehicle = v; occupied = true; } public synchronized void free() { parkedVehicle = null; occupied = false; } public String getId() { return id; } } class Ticket { private static final AtomicInteger SEQ = new AtomicInteger(); final String id; final ParkingSpot spot; final Vehicle vehicle; final Instant entryTime = Instant.now(); Ticket(ParkingSpot s, Vehicle v) { this.id = "TKT-" + SEQ.incrementAndGet(); this.spot = s; this.vehicle = v; } } class ParkingFloor { private final int floorNum; private final List<ParkingSpot> spots; ParkingFloor(int floor, int bikes, int cars, int trucks) { this.floorNum = floor; spots = new ArrayList<>(); for(int i=0;i<bikes;i++) spots.add(new ParkingSpot(floor+"B"+i, VehicleType.BIKE)); for(int i=0;i<cars;i++) spots.add(new ParkingSpot(floor+"C"+i, VehicleType.CAR)); for(int i=0;i<trucks;i++) spots.add(new ParkingSpot(floor+"T"+i, VehicleType.TRUCK)); } public Optional<ParkingSpot> findAvailable(VehicleType type) { return spots.stream().filter(s -> s.canFit(type)).findFirst(); } public Map<VehicleType,Long> availability() { return spots.stream().filter(ParkingSpot::isAvailable) .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(s -> s.allowedType, Collectors.counting())); } } class ParkingLot { private static ParkingLot instance; private final List<ParkingFloor> floors; private final Map<String, Ticket> activeTickets = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); private final FeeStrategy feeStrategy; private ParkingLot(List<ParkingFloor> floors, FeeStrategy fee) { this.floors = floors; this.feeStrategy = fee; } public static synchronized ParkingLot getInstance() { /* Singleton */ if(instance == null) instance = new ParkingLot(buildFloors(), new HourlyFeeStrategy()); return instance; } public Ticket park(Vehicle v) { ParkingSpot spot = floors.stream() .flatMap(f -> f.findAvailable(v.type).stream()) .findFirst() .orElseThrow(() -> new RuntimeException("Lot full for " + v.type)); spot.park(v); Ticket t = new Ticket(spot, v); activeTickets.put(t.id, t); return t; } public double exit(String ticketId) { Ticket t = activeTickets.remove(ticketId); if(t == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid ticket"); t.spot.free(); return feeStrategy.calculate(t.entryTime, Instant.now(), t.vehicle.type); } } // Strategy Pattern for pricing interface FeeStrategy { double calculate(Instant entry, Instant exit, VehicleType type); } class HourlyFeeStrategy implements FeeStrategy { private static final Map<VehicleType,Double> RATES = Map.of( VehicleType.BIKE, 10.0, VehicleType.CAR, 20.0, VehicleType.TRUCK, 40.0); public double calculate(Instant entry, Instant exit, VehicleType type) { long hours = Duration.between(entry, exit).toHours() + 1; // ceil return hours * RATES.get(type); } }
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: "How do you handle concurrent parking — two threads finding the same last spot?"
    💭 Think First
    Two threads both call findAvailable() → both find spot "C1" → both call spot.park() → double booking. The race window is between find and park.
    → Solution
    Make ParkingSpot.park() synchronized + add an availability re-check inside: if already occupied when you get the lock, throw. The caller retries. Alternatively, use an AtomicBoolean for the occupied flag and CAS: occupied.compareAndSet(false, true) — only one thread can succeed. At the lot level, use a per-spot ReentrantLock or the Java synchronized keyword on the spot object.
    Q: "How would you add a reservation feature — reserve a spot in advance?"
    💭 Think First
    A reserved spot needs a time window. It must be blocked for that window and auto-released if the vehicle doesn't arrive.
    → Design extension
    Add SpotState enum: AVAILABLE, RESERVED, OCCUPIED. Add Reservation entity: spotId, vehicleType, startTime, endTime, reservationId. ParkingSpot.reserve(Reservation) transitions AVAILABLE → RESERVED. A scheduled cleanup task (ScheduledExecutorService) runs every minute and calls spot.cancelReservation() for expired reservations. Park with a reservation ticket validates the reservation hasn't expired before parking.
    Q: "How do you find the nearest available spot to the entrance?"
    💭 Think First
    Current design uses findFirst() which may return a spot far from entrance. Need ordering by proximity.
    → Solution
    Assign each spot a distance/priority (e.g., floor 1 closer than floor 2, spot number 1 closer than 20). Use a TreeMap<Integer, ParkingSpot> keyed by distance-from-entrance. Or maintain per-VehicleType PriorityQueues of available spots ordered by distance. When a spot is freed, add it back to the queue. O(log n) park and free operations.
    🏭 Multi-Threaded Parking Lot Extension
    "Make the parking lot thread-safe for 1000 concurrent vehicle arrivals. No double-booking. No missed available spots."
    The bottleneck is spot allocation. Two approaches: coarse-grained (lock the entire lot — simple but slow) vs fine-grained (lock per-spot — complex but scalable).
    Production approach: Fine-grained spot locking + CAS
    Java — thread-safe spot allocation
    class ParkingSpot { private final AtomicBoolean occupied = new AtomicBoolean(false); public boolean tryPark(Vehicle v) { if (!canFit(v.type)) return false; if (occupied.compareAndSet(false, true)) { // atomic — only ONE thread succeeds parkedVehicle = v; return true; } return false; // another thread grabbed it first — caller tries next spot } public void free() { parkedVehicle = null; occupied.set(false); } } // ParkingLot.park() loops through spots calling tryPark() — no global lock needed // Maintains per-type Semaphore counts for quick "lot full" check before scanning spots
    🎯 Practice
    Add a display board that shows real-time availability count per floor per vehicle type. Update it every time a vehicle parks or exits. How do you design this without polling?
    HintObserver pattern: ParkingSpot is the Subject. DisplayBoard is the Observer. When spot.park() or spot.free() is called, it fires an event. The DisplayBoard updates its count atomically.
    → Solution walkthrough
    Java — Observer for display board
    interface SpotObserver { void onSpotChanged(int floor, VehicleType type, boolean nowOccupied); } class DisplayBoard implements SpotObserver { private final Map<String, AtomicInteger> counts = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); public void onSpotChanged(int floor, VehicleType type, boolean nowOccupied) { String key = floor + ":" + type; counts.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new AtomicInteger(0)) .addAndGet(nowOccupied ? -1 : 1); // parked → -1, freed → +1 display(); } public void display() { counts.forEach((k,v) -> System.out.println(k + ": " + v.get())); } } // ParkingSpot holds List<SpotObserver>; calls observers in park() and free()

    Design an Elevator System

    single lift · multiple lifts · request feasibility · SCAN algorithm
    🧠 Mental Model — Clarify Scope First
    Elevator is an algorithmic + OOP design problem. Key decisions: (1) Request dispatching algorithm — which elevator serves which request? (2) Floor ordering within one elevator (SCAN/LOOK). (3) Thread safety for concurrent floor requests.
    Single elevator: easier — SCAN algorithm. Multiple elevators: assignment algorithm — nearest car, zoning, or load balancing.
    💻 Single Elevator — SCAN Algorithm
    Java — Single Elevator with SCAN (disk scheduling analogy)
    enum Direction { UP, DOWN, IDLE } enum DoorState { OPEN, CLOSED } class Elevator { private int currentFloor = 1; private Direction direction = Direction.IDLE; private DoorState doorState = DoorState.CLOSED; private final TreeSet<Integer> upQueue = new TreeSet<>(); // sorted ascending private final TreeSet<Integer> downQueue = new TreeSet<>(Collections.reverseOrder()); // External request: someone on floor F presses UP or DOWN button public synchronized void requestFloor(int floor, Direction dir) { if(dir == Direction.UP) upQueue.add(floor); else downQueue.add(floor); if(direction == Direction.IDLE) notifyAll(); } // Internal request: passenger inside presses destination floor button public synchronized void pressFloor(int floor) { if(floor > currentFloor) upQueue.add(floor); else downQueue.add(floor); } public void run() { while(true) { synchronized(this) { while(upQueue.isEmpty() && downQueue.isEmpty()) { direction = Direction.IDLE; try { wait(); } catch(InterruptedException e) { return; } } } processRequests(); } } private void processRequests() { // SCAN: exhaust UP queue going up, then DOWN queue going down while(!upQueue.isEmpty()) { direction = Direction.UP; int target = upQueue.pollFirst(); // smallest floor above or ahead moveTo(target); } while(!downQueue.isEmpty()) { direction = Direction.DOWN; int target = downQueue.pollFirst(); // largest floor (going down) moveTo(target); } } private void moveTo(int floor) { System.out.printf("Moving %s: floor %d → %d%n", direction, currentFloor, floor); currentFloor = floor; openDoor(); wait3Seconds(); closeDoor(); } private void openDoor() { doorState = DoorState.OPEN; System.out.println("Door OPEN at floor " + currentFloor); } private void closeDoor() { doorState = DoorState.CLOSED; System.out.println("Door CLOSED"); } }
    📐 Multiple Elevators — Dispatcher
    Java — Multi-elevator nearest-car dispatch
    class ElevatorDispatcher { private final List<Elevator> elevators; // Nearest Car algorithm: assign to elevator with minimum cost public void dispatch(int requestedFloor, Direction dir) { Elevator best = elevators.stream() .min(Comparator.comparingInt(e -> cost(e, requestedFloor, dir))) .orElseThrow(); best.requestFloor(requestedFloor, dir); } private int cost(Elevator e, int floor, Direction dir) { int dist = Math.abs(e.getCurrentFloor() - floor); if(e.getDirection() == Direction.IDLE) return dist; // idle: just distance if(e.getDirection() == dir) { // Moving same direction AND hasn't passed the floor yet → great candidate if((dir == Direction.UP && e.getCurrentFloor() <= floor) || (dir == Direction.DOWN && e.getCurrentFloor() >= floor)) return dist; // on the way } return dist + 1000; // wrong direction or already passed — high penalty } } // Real buildings use more sophisticated algorithms: // LOOK: like SCAN but reverses before hitting top/bottom floor // DESTINATION DISPATCH: passengers enter destination before boarding // → groups passengers going to same floor into same elevator → fewer stops
    🏭 Production Scenario
    You are designing the Elevator system for a 50-floor building with 6 elevators. During morning rush hour, 200 people arrive at the ground floor simultaneously. Your naive algorithm sends all 6 elevators to floor 1. How does a real SCAN algorithm handle this better?
    SCAN (also called the disk scheduling algorithm) moves in one direction, services all requests in that direction, then reverses. This prevents starvation and minimises travel distance. How do you assign requests to the best elevator?
    SCAN algorithm: Each elevator has a direction (UP/DOWN) and two queues: upQueue (TreeSet ascending) and downQueue (TreeSet descending). Moving UP: service all floors in upQueue in ascending order. At the top, switch to DOWN and service downQueue. This is O(n) travel for n requests — optimal. Request assignment: For a new request at floor F in direction D: score each elevator = distance to reach F + penalty if elevator is moving away. Assign to the lowest-score elevator. Morning rush optimisation: All 6 elevators detect heavy ground-floor demand. 3 elevators stay at ground, 3 service upper floors. This is a traffic pattern analysis extension — real Otis/Schindler elevators use ML models for this. Edge cases: Emergency stop button → immediately OPEN doors, disable SCAN, await maintenance. Overweight sensor → doors stay open, alert dispatched. Power failure → all elevators descend to ground (gravity + emergency battery).
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: "How do you check request feasibility — can this elevator reach floor F before its next committed stop?"
    💭 Think First
    The elevator has a committed queue. Feasibility = can the new request be served without violating time constraints on existing commitments.
    → Solution
    Calculate the arrival time to the requested floor by summing travel times for each committed stop in order. If the elevator is going UP and the new floor is above the current floor and below the next UP stop — it's on the way, insert it into the sorted queue and it's naturally feasible. If it's in the wrong direction, calculate total time with a detour. Accept if total time < SLA threshold.
    Q: "How do you handle emergency stops — fire alarm pulls all elevators to ground floor immediately?"
    💭 Think First
    This is a state transition. Elevators need an EMERGENCY state that overrides normal dispatch.
    → Design
    Observer pattern: FireAlarmSystem publishes EmergencyEvent. Each Elevator is an observer. On receiving the event: clear all queues, set state=EMERGENCY, add floor 0 to queue as the only destination. The door opens on ground and stays open until emergency is cleared. ElevatorDispatcher stops accepting new requests when any elevator is in EMERGENCY state.
    🎯 Practice
    Design the state machine for a single elevator door: OPEN, CLOSING, CLOSED, OPENING. Handle: door-open button (while CLOSING → re-opens), obstacle detected while CLOSING → back to OPEN.
    HintState pattern: each state has handle(Event) that transitions to next state. Events: OPEN_BUTTON, CLOSE_BUTTON, OBSTACLE, TIMER_EXPIRED. CLOSING state handles OBSTACLE → transition to OPENING.
    → Solution
    Java — Door state machine
    enum DoorEvent { OPEN_BTN, CLOSE_BTN, OBSTACLE, TIMER_EXPIRED } enum DoorState { OPEN, CLOSING, CLOSED, OPENING } class ElevatorDoor { private DoorState state = DoorState.CLOSED; public DoorState handle(DoorEvent event) { state = switch(state) { case CLOSED -> event == DoorEvent.OPEN_BTN ? DoorState.OPENING : state; case OPENING -> event == DoorEvent.TIMER_EXPIRED ? DoorState.OPEN : state; case OPEN -> event == DoorEvent.CLOSE_BTN ? DoorState.CLOSING : state; case CLOSING -> switch(event) { case OBSTACLE, OPEN_BTN -> DoorState.OPENING; // safety re-open case TIMER_EXPIRED -> DoorState.CLOSED; default -> state; }; }; System.out.println("Door → " + state); return state; } }

    Meeting Room Reservation System

    time slot booking · no double booking · recurrent meetings · capacity matching
    🧠 Mental Model
    Meeting room booking is an interval scheduling problem. Core challenge: detect overlaps efficiently. For recurrent meetings, generate the series of intervals and check each.
    Key entities: Room (capacity, amenities), Meeting (start, end, organizer, attendees), Booking (room + meeting). The system must atomically check-and-book to avoid double booking.
    💻 Complete Implementation
    Java — Meeting Room Reservation
    record TimeSlot(LocalDateTime start, LocalDateTime end) { boolean overlaps(TimeSlot other) { return !this.end.isAfter(other.end) ? !this.end.isBefore(other.start) : !this.start.isAfter(other.end); // Simpler: start < other.end AND end > other.start } } class Room { final String id, name; final int capacity; final Set<String> amenities; // PROJECTOR, WHITEBOARD, VIDEO_CONF private final List<Booking> bookings = new ArrayList<>(); public synchronized boolean isAvailable(TimeSlot slot) { return bookings.stream().noneMatch(b -> b.slot().overlaps(slot)); } public synchronized Booking book(TimeSlot slot, String organizer, List<String> attendees) { if(!isAvailable(slot)) throw new RoomNotAvailableException(id, slot); Booking b = new Booking(UUID.randomUUID().toString(), this, slot, organizer, attendees); bookings.add(b); return b; } public synchronized List<Booking> getBookings(LocalDate date) { return bookings.stream() .filter(b -> b.slot().start().toLocalDate().equals(date)) .sorted(Comparator.comparing(b -> b.slot().start())) .toList(); } } record Booking(String id, Room room, TimeSlot slot, String organizer, List<String> attendees) {} class MeetingRoomService { private final List<Room> rooms; // Find all rooms that fit the requirements public List<Room> findAvailable(TimeSlot slot, int attendeeCount, Set<String> required) { return rooms.stream() .filter(r -> r.capacity >= attendeeCount) .filter(r -> r.amenities.containsAll(required)) .filter(r -> r.isAvailable(slot)) .sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(r -> r.capacity)) // smallest fitting room first .toList(); } // Auto-book: find best room and book it public Booking autoBook(TimeSlot slot, int count, Set<String> needs, String org, List<String> att) { return findAvailable(slot, count, needs).stream().findFirst() .map(r -> r.book(slot, org, att)) .orElseThrow(() -> new NoRoomAvailableException()); } }
    ⚠️ Recurrent Meeting Scheduler
    Java — recurrent meetings with RRULE-style pattern
    enum RecurrenceType { DAILY, WEEKLY, MONTHLY } class RecurrentBookingRequest { LocalDateTime seriesStart, seriesEnd; // series end date Duration meetingDuration; RecurrenceType recurrence; Set<DayOfWeek> daysOfWeek; // for WEEKLY: which days (Mon, Wed, Fri) } class MeetingRoomService { public List<Booking> bookRecurrent(RecurrentBookingRequest req, Room room, String org) { List<TimeSlot> slots = generateSlots(req); // Check ALL slots are available before booking ANY — atomically synchronized(room) { boolean allFree = slots.stream().allMatch(room::isAvailable); if(!allFree) throw new PartialConflictException("Some slots already booked"); return slots.stream().map(s -> room.book(s, org, List.of())).toList(); } } private List<TimeSlot> generateSlots(RecurrentBookingRequest req) { List<TimeSlot> slots = new ArrayList<>(); LocalDateTime current = req.seriesStart; while(!current.isAfter(req.seriesEnd.toLocalDate().atEndOfDay())) { if(req.recurrence == RecurrenceType.WEEKLY && !req.daysOfWeek.contains(current.getDayOfWeek())) { current = current.plusDays(1); continue; } slots.add(new TimeSlot(current, current.plus(req.meetingDuration))); current = switch(req.recurrence) { case DAILY -> current.plusDays(1); case WEEKLY -> current.plusDays(1); // check each day, skip non-matching above case MONTHLY -> current.plusMonths(1); }; } return slots; } }
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Your company has 50 meeting rooms across 3 floors. 8 am every Monday, 200 calendar invites are sent simultaneously — all trying to book rooms for the same slots. Within 2 seconds, every room is double-booked. How do you fix the booking system?
    Double booking = check-then-book is not atomic. Two requests both see a room as free, both book it. This is a race condition. How do you make check + book atomic at the database level?
    Root cause: SELECT available rooms, then INSERT booking — two operations, not atomic. Another request can INSERT between your SELECT and INSERT. Fix 1 — DB constraint: Add a UNIQUE constraint on (room_id, date, start_time, end_time). Two simultaneous bookings for the same slot: one INSERT succeeds, the other throws a UNIQUE constraint violation. Catch it and return 409 Conflict. Fix 2 — Overlap detection query: Before inserting, run: SELECT 1 FROM bookings WHERE room_id=? AND date=? AND start_time < ? AND end_time > ? FOR UPDATE. The FOR UPDATE locks the rows so no concurrent booking can proceed. Fix 3 — Redis distributed lock: Before booking, SET booking:{room_id}:{slot} NX EX 5. Only one request acquires the lock. After DB insert, release the lock. Interview answer: Prefer the DB unique constraint approach — it is the simplest, most reliable, and requires no additional infrastructure. Redis lock adds complexity and a potential failure point.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: "With thousands of rooms and millions of bookings, how do you check availability efficiently?"
    💭 Think First
    Linear scan of all bookings per room is O(n) per query. At scale this won't work. What data structure supports interval overlap detection in O(log n)?
    → Interval tree / sorted list + binary search
    Keep bookings sorted by start time (TreeMap<LocalDateTime, Booking>). For overlap check: find the last booking starting before the requested slot's end. Check if it ends after the requested slot starts. O(log n) using TreeMap.floorEntry(). For even better performance: use an Interval Tree that supports O(log n + k) overlap queries where k = number of overlapping intervals found.
    Q: "How do you cancel a single occurrence of a recurring meeting without cancelling the whole series?"
    💭 Think First
    The series is a concept. Individual occurrences are the bookings. Cancelling one occurrence should only remove that booking, not the series rule.
    → Design
    Store RecurringSeriesId on each Booking. To cancel one occurrence: delete just that Booking. To cancel the series: delete all Bookings with that SeriesId. To modify "this and future" occurrences: end the old series at the modification date, create a new series from that date with the new parameters. This is how Google Calendar handles it.
    🎯 Practice
    List all bookings for a given date across all rooms, sorted by start time, and show which rooms are free during a given time window on that date.
    HintFor "list bookings": iterate all rooms, collect bookings for the date, merge into one list, sort by start. For "free rooms": find rooms where no booking overlaps the given window.
    → Solution
    Java
    public List<Booking> allBookingsForDate(LocalDate date) { return rooms.stream() .flatMap(r -> r.getBookings(date).stream()) .sorted(Comparator.comparing(b -> b.slot().start())) .toList(); } public List<Room> freeRoomsDuring(TimeSlot window) { return rooms.stream() .filter(r -> r.isAvailable(window)) .toList(); }

    Movie Ticket Booking System (BookMyShow)

    seat selection · concurrent booking · pricing tiers · payment integration
    🧠 Mental Model
    BookMyShow is a resource allocation system with seat state management. Key challenge: seat selection must be atomic — no two users can book the same seat. The system has a clear hierarchy: Movie → Show → Theater → Screen → Seat.
    Critical: At peak times (blockbuster release), millions of users hit the same show simultaneously. Must handle: concurrent seat locking, payment timeouts, seat release on payment failure.
    💻 Class Hierarchy + Seat Booking
    Java — BookMyShow LLD
    enum SeatStatus { AVAILABLE, LOCKED, BOOKED } enum SeatCategory { SILVER, GOLD, PLATINUM } class Seat { final String id; // "A1", "B12" final SeatCategory category; private SeatStatus status = SeatStatus.AVAILABLE; private String lockedBy; // userId who locked it private Instant lockExpiry; // auto-release after 10 min if payment not done public synchronized boolean lock(String userId) { if(status == SeatStatus.BOOKED) return false; if(status == SeatStatus.LOCKED && lockExpiry.isAfter(Instant.now())) return false; // still locked status = SeatStatus.LOCKED; lockedBy = userId; lockExpiry = Instant.now().plus(10, ChronoUnit.MINUTES); return true; } public synchronized boolean book(String userId) { if(status != SeatStatus.LOCKED || !lockedBy.equals(userId)) return false; if(lockExpiry.isBefore(Instant.now())) { status = SeatStatus.AVAILABLE; return false; } status = SeatStatus.BOOKED; return true; } public synchronized void release() { status = SeatStatus.AVAILABLE; lockedBy = null; } } class Show { final Movie movie; final Screen screen; final LocalDateTime showTime; private final List<Seat> seats; private final Map<SeatCategory, Double> pricing; public List<Seat> getAvailableSeats() { return seats.stream().filter(s -> s.status == SeatStatus.AVAILABLE).toList(); } public BookingResult lockSeats(List<String> seatIds, String userId) { List<Seat> toBook = seats.stream().filter(s -> seatIds.contains(s.id)).toList(); List<Seat> locked = new ArrayList<>(); for(Seat s : toBook) { if(!s.lock(userId)) { locked.forEach(Seat::release); // rollback — release already locked seats return BookingResult.failure("Seat " + s.id + " unavailable"); } locked.add(s); } double total = locked.stream().mapToDouble(s -> pricing.get(s.category)).sum(); return BookingResult.success(locked, total); } }
    📐 Booking Flow + Payment Integration
    Java — complete booking flow
    class BookingService { public Booking bookTickets(String showId, List<String> seatIds, String userId, PaymentInfo payment) { Show show = showRepo.findById(showId).orElseThrow(); // Step 1: Lock seats atomically (10-minute window for payment) BookingResult lock = show.lockSeats(seatIds, userId); if(!lock.success()) throw new SeatsUnavailableException(lock.message()); try { // Step 2: Process payment PaymentResult pay = paymentGateway.charge(userId, lock.totalAmount(), payment); if(!pay.success()) { lock.seats().forEach(Seat::release); // payment failed → release seats throw new PaymentFailedException(pay.reason()); } // Step 3: Confirm booking lock.seats().forEach(s -> s.book(userId)); Booking booking = new Booking(show, lock.seats(), userId, pay.transactionId()); bookingRepo.save(booking); notificationService.sendConfirmation(userId, booking); // async return booking; } catch(Exception e) { lock.seats().forEach(Seat::release); // any failure → always release throw e; } } }
    🏭 Production Scenario
    BookMyShow releases tickets for a sold-out concert. 500,000 users hit 'Book Now' simultaneously for 5,000 seats. Without protection: 5,000 seats sell to 50,000 people (10x oversell). Walk through how you prevent this.
    The core problem is concurrent decrement of a shared counter (available seats). You need exactly 5,000 atomic decrements to succeed — all others must fail. What mechanism guarantees this?
    Seat reservation with atomic operations: (1) Redis DECR available_seats — atomic decrement. If result >= 0: seat reserved for 10 minutes (lock window). If result < 0: INCR back (compensate), return sold-out. (2) User has 10 minutes to complete payment. (3) On payment success: mark seat SOLD in DB. On timeout or failure: INCR available_seats back (release lock). Why Redis not DB? DB row-level locks serialise all 500K requests through one bottleneck — 499,999 requests wait. Redis DECR is a single-threaded atomic operation on in-memory data — microsecond latency, millions of ops/second. Seat selection (specific seat): CAS on seat status: UPDATE seats SET status='HELD', held_by=?, held_until=? WHERE id=? AND status='AVAILABLE'. Only one UPDATE succeeds per seat. Zero rows affected = seat already taken. Queue-based approach for extreme scale: Put all booking requests in a Kafka queue. A single-threaded consumer processes them in order — simpler to reason about, but adds latency.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: "10,000 users all try to book the same show at 12:00 AM. How does your system handle this at scale?"
    💭 Think First
    Pure in-memory synchronized won't work across multiple servers. Need distributed coordination.
    → Distributed solution
    Distributed seat lock with Redis: SET seat:{showId}:{seatId}:lock {userId} NX EX 600 — NX means only set if not exists, EX 600 = expire in 10 minutes. Only one user gets the lock. Others get immediate "unavailable" feedback. At booking confirmation: persist to DB and delete the Redis lock. If payment times out: Redis auto-expires the lock, seat becomes available again.

    Queue-based fairness: For high-demand shows, use a virtual waiting room. Users enter a queue. System processes in order: issue booking tokens every second. Eliminates thundering herd against the seat locking layer.
    Q: A user holds 3 seats for 10 minutes but the payment gateway times out at minute 8. How do you release the seats and handle the partial state?
    💡 Think First
    The seats are HELD (locked) but payment never completed. The hold has a TTL. When it expires, what cleans up the state and what happens if the user tries to pay after expiry?
    ➔ Complete Answer
    Seat hold lifecycle: AVAILABLE → HELD (with 10-min TTL) → BOOKED (on payment success) or AVAILABLE (on TTL expiry or explicit release). Implementation: (1) Redis TTL: SET seat:{seatId}:hold {userId} EX 600. Expiry automatically releases the hold. (2) DB: UPDATE seats SET status='HELD', hold_expires_at=NOW()+10min WHERE status='AVAILABLE'. A background job (every minute): UPDATE seats SET status='AVAILABLE' WHERE status='HELD' AND hold_expires_at < NOW(). (3) Payment gateway timeout at minute 8: the payment is in UNKNOWN state — it may have succeeded or failed. Idempotent retry: retry with the same idempotency key — if it succeeded, get the success response. If it failed, the hold expires at minute 10 and seats are released. (4) User tries to pay after minute 10: check seat status first — if AVAILABLE, start a new booking flow. If BOOKED by someone else: return 409 Conflict with a clear message. Never charge the user for seats they no longer hold.
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement the seat reservation system: SeatReservationService.hold(userId, seatId) atomically holds a seat for 10 minutes (Redis TTL). SeatReservationService.confirm(userId, seatId) promotes HELD to BOOKED only if the hold is still valid. SeatReservationService.release(userId, seatId) explicitly releases a hold. Write a test verifying two concurrent hold() calls on the same seat only succeed for one.
    💡 Hinthold(): SET seat:{seatId}:held {userId} NX EX 600 — NX means "only set if Not eXists". Returns OK (success) or nil (already held). confirm(): check Redis key matches userId, then UPDATE DB seat status to BOOKED, delete Redis key. Test: two threads call hold() simultaneously — only one gets OK from Redis SETNX.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — atomic seat hold with Redis NX
    @Service class SeatReservationService { @Autowired StringRedisTemplate redis; @Autowired SeatRepository seatRepo; public boolean hold(String userId, String seatId) { String key = "seat:"+seatId+":held"; // SET key userId NX EX 600 — atomic: only sets if key doesn't exist Boolean ok = redis.opsForValue() .setIfAbsent(key, userId, Duration.ofSeconds(600)); return Boolean.TRUE.equals(ok); // true = this user got the hold } @Transactional public boolean confirm(String userId, String seatId) { String holder = redis.opsForValue().get("seat:"+seatId+":held"); if(!userId.equals(holder)) return false; // hold expired or belongs to another seatRepo.updateStatus(seatId, "BOOKED"); redis.delete("seat:"+seatId+":held"); return true; } public void release(String userId, String seatId) { // Only delete if this user owns the hold (Lua script for atomicity) redis.execute((RedisCallback<Object>) conn -> conn.eval( "if redis.call('get',KEYS[1])==ARGV[1] then return redis.call('del',KEYS[1]) else return 0 end" .getBytes(), ReturnType.INTEGER, 1, ("seat:"+seatId+":held").getBytes(), userId.getBytes())); } }
    🎯 Practice
    Design the seat layout for a screen: rows A-J, seats 1-20 per row. Category: A-C = PLATINUM, D-F = GOLD, G-J = SILVER. Generate all seats programmatically.
    HintUse char arithmetic: 'A' + rowIndex to get the row letter. SeatCategory determined by row letter comparison (≤ 'C' → PLATINUM etc). Two nested loops: rows × seats.
    → Solution
    Java
    static List<Seat> generateSeats(int rows, int seatsPerRow) { List<Seat> seats = new ArrayList<>(); for(int r = 0; r < rows; r++) { char rowLetter = (char)('A' + r); SeatCategory cat = rowLetter <= 'C' ? SeatCategory.PLATINUM : rowLetter <= 'F' ? SeatCategory.GOLD : SeatCategory.SILVER; for(int s = 1; s <= seatsPerRow; s++) seats.add(new Seat(rowLetter + String.valueOf(s), cat)); } return seats; }

    Design Expense Sharing App (Splitwise)

    expense types · balance calculation · debt simplification · settlement
    🧠 Mental Model
    Splitwise is a graph problem disguised as an expense tracker. Each user is a node; each debt is a directed weighted edge. "Simplify debts" = reduce the graph to minimum edges while preserving net balances for every node.
    Key insight: net balance per user = total owed to them − total they owe. Settlement: those with positive balance receive money from those with negative balance. Minimum transactions = greedy two-pointer on sorted net balances.
    💻 Core Implementation
    Java — Splitwise with debt simplification
    enum SplitType { EQUAL, EXACT, PERCENTAGE, SHARES } class Expense { final String id, description; final double totalAmount; final User paidBy; final Map<User, Double> owes; // who owes how much of this expense } class Split { abstract double calculateShare(User user, List<User> participants, double total); } class EqualSplit extends Split { public double calculateShare(User u, List<User> all, double total) { return total / all.size(); // ₹1000 / 4 people = ₹250 each } } class ExactSplit extends Split { private final Map<User, Double> exactAmounts; public double calculateShare(User u, List<User> all, double total) { return exactAmounts.get(u); // Alice: ₹400, Bob: ₹600 (pre-specified) } } class PercentageSplit extends Split { private final Map<User, Double> percentages; // must sum to 100 public double calculateShare(User u, List<User> all, double total) { return total * percentages.get(u) / 100.0; } } class ExpenseBook { // balance[A][B] = how much A owes B (positive) or B owes A (negative) private final Map<String, Map<String, Double>> balances = new HashMap<>(); public void addExpense(User paidBy, double total, List<User> participants, Split split) { for(User p : participants) { if(p.equals(paidBy)) continue; double owes = split.calculateShare(p, participants, total); // p owes paidBy += owes balances.computeIfAbsent(p.id, k -> new HashMap<>()).merge(paidBy.id, owes, Double::sum); // paidBy is owed by p += owes balances.computeIfAbsent(paidBy.id, k -> new HashMap<>()).merge(p.id, -owes, Double::sum); } } public List<String> getBalanceSummary(User user) { var userBal = balances.getOrDefault(user.id, Map.of()); return userBal.entrySet().stream() .filter(e -> Math.abs(e.getValue()) > 0.001) .map(e -> e.getValue() > 0 ? user.name + " owes " + e.getKey() + ": ₹" + e.getValue() : e.getKey() + " owes " + user.name + ": ₹" + Math.abs(e.getValue())) .toList(); } } // DEBT SIMPLIFICATION — minimum transactions algorithm class DebtSimplifier { public List<String> simplify(Map<String, Double> netBalances) { // net = totalReceived - totalPaid per person List<String> transactions = new ArrayList<>(); List<Map.Entry<String,Double>> sorted = new ArrayList<>(netBalances.entrySet()); sorted.sort(Map.Entry.comparingByValue()); int lo = 0, hi = sorted.size() - 1; while(lo < hi) { double give = -sorted.get(lo).getValue(); // most negative (owes most) double recv = sorted.get(hi).getValue(); // most positive (owed most) double amt = Math.min(give, recv); transactions.add(sorted.get(lo).getKey() + " pays " + sorted.get(hi).getKey() + ": ₹" + amt); sorted.get(lo).setValue(sorted.get(lo).getValue() + amt); sorted.get(hi).setValue(sorted.get(hi).getValue() - amt); if(Math.abs(sorted.get(lo).getValue()) < 0.001) lo++; if(Math.abs(sorted.get(hi).getValue()) < 0.001) hi--; } return transactions; } }
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Your Splitwise group has 8 friends after a 2-week trip with 47 expenses. Naively, 8 people need to settle in 7 transactions each = 56 transactions. Your settle() method should minimise this to at most 7 transactions total. How?
    Compute the net balance for each person first (positive = owed money, negative = owes money). Then greedily match the largest creditor with the largest debtor. This is the 'minimum cash flow' problem.
    Algorithm: (1) Compute net balance per person: for each expense, payer gets +amount, each participant gets -(amount/n). (2) Separate into creditors (positive net) and debtors (negative net). Use max-heaps for both. (3) Greedily: pop largest creditor and largest debtor. Transfer min(creditor, |debtor|). Push the remainder back if non-zero. Repeat. Result: n-1 transactions maximum for n people, regardless of number of expenses. For 8 people: at most 7 transactions. Implementation: PriorityQueue<double[]> creditors (max-heap), PriorityQueue<double[]> debtors (max-heap by absolute value). Each element: [personIndex, amount]. Precision: Use BigDecimal for money, not double. Rounding errors in double accumulate across 47 expenses and cause 1-paisa discrepancies in settlement.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: "Why is the two-pointer greedy approach optimal for debt simplification?"
    💭 Think First
    After calculating net balances, the total "owed" equals total "to receive" (zero-sum). We need to settle using minimum transactions.
    → Proof of optimality
    Each iteration of the two-pointer eliminates at least one person from the debt graph (either the biggest debtor or biggest creditor reaches zero). N people can settle in at most N-1 transactions. The greedy two-pointer achieves this bound because: it always makes progress toward eliminating someone, and no transaction is wasted (each payment moves two people closer to zero). Any fewer transactions would require someone to owe multiple people in one payment — not how money works.
    Q: "How do you handle multi-currency expenses?"
    💭 Think First
    If Alice paid in USD and Bob owes in INR, you need a single reference currency for balance calculation.
    → Solution
    Store all amounts in a base currency (USD). At expense creation time, convert the paid amount to USD using the exchange rate at that moment (snapshot, not real-time). Store both the original amount+currency and the converted USD amount. Balances are calculated in USD. Display converts back to the user's preferred currency. Store the exchange rate used at expense creation — never recalculate historical expenses with new rates.
    🎯 Practice
    4 people go on a trip. Alice pays ₹1200 (dinner, all 4 equal). Bob pays ₹800 (taxi, 3 people: Bob, Carol, Dave equal). Carol pays ₹600 (hotel, all 4 equal). Calculate net balances and minimum transactions to settle.
    HintCalculate what each person paid vs what they owed: Alice paid ₹1200 owes ₹1200/4=₹300+₹600/4=₹150=₹450 net. Work out all 4 net balances, then apply the two-pointer algorithm.
    → Full worked solution
    Worked example
    // What each person owes (owed): // Dinner ₹1200 / 4: Alice=300, Bob=300, Carol=300, Dave=300 (Alice paid → Alice owed=0 net from this) // Taxi ₹800 / 3: Bob=267, Carol=267, Dave=266 (Bob paid → Bob owed=0 net from this) // Hotel ₹600 / 4: Alice=150, Bob=150, Carol=150, Dave=150 (Carol paid → Carol owed=0 net from this) // Net balance = paid - owed: // Alice: paid 1200, owed (300+0+150) = 450 → NET = +750 (others owe Alice) // Bob: paid 800, owed (0+267+150) = 417 → NET = +383 (others owe Bob) // Carol: paid 600, owed (300+267+150)= 717 → NET = -117 (Carol owes others) // Dave: paid 0, owed (300+266+150)= 716 → NET = -716 (Dave owes others) // Verification: 750 + 383 - 117 - 716 = 300... adjust for rounding // Two-pointer simplification: // Sorted: Dave(-716), Carol(-117), Bob(+383), Alice(+750) // Dave(716) → Alice(750): Dave pays Alice ₹716. Dave done. Alice: +34 // Carol(117) → Alice(34): Carol pays Alice ₹34. Alice done. Carol: -83 // Carol(83) → Bob(383): Carol pays Bob ₹83. Carol done. // Result: 3 transactions (optimal for 4 people)

    Design a Stock Trading Platform (Zerodha/Groww)

    order matching engine · portfolio · real-time feed · order types
    🧠 Mental Model
    A stock trading platform's core is the Order Matching Engine — a priority queue of buy orders (highest price first) and sell orders (lowest price first). When the best buy price ≥ best sell price, a trade executes.
    Key components: OrderBook (bids + asks), MatchingEngine, Portfolio, MarketDataFeed. The hardest part is the matching engine: thread safety + correct price-time priority.
    💻 Order Book + Matching Engine
    Java — Order Book with price-time priority matching
    enum OrderType { MARKET, LIMIT, STOP_LOSS } enum OrderSide { BUY, SELL } enum OrderStatus { PENDING, PARTIAL, FILLED, CANCELLED } class Order { final String id, symbol, userId; final OrderSide side; final OrderType type; final double price; // limit price; 0 for MARKET int quantity; // remaining unfilled quantity final Instant createdAt = Instant.now(); OrderStatus status = OrderStatus.PENDING; } class OrderBook { private final String symbol; // BUY orders: highest price first (max-heap). Same price → earliest time first. private final TreeMap<Double, Queue<Order>> bids = new TreeMap<>(Collections.reverseOrder()); // descending price // SELL orders: lowest price first (min-heap). Same price → earliest time first. private final TreeMap<Double, Queue<Order>> asks = new TreeMap<>(); // ascending price public synchronized List<Trade> addOrder(Order order) { List<Trade> trades = new ArrayList<>(); if(order.side == OrderSide.BUY) trades = matchBuy(order); else trades = matchSell(order); if(order.quantity > 0) addToBook(order); // unfilled remainder goes to book return trades; } private List<Trade> matchBuy(Order buy) { List<Trade> trades = new ArrayList<>(); while(buy.quantity > 0 && !asks.isEmpty()) { double bestAsk = asks.firstKey(); // LIMIT order: only match if buy price >= best ask price if(buy.type == OrderType.LIMIT && buy.price < bestAsk) break; Queue<Order> sellQueue = asks.get(bestAsk); Order sell = sellQueue.peek(); int filled = Math.min(buy.quantity, sell.quantity); trades.add(new Trade(buy, sell, bestAsk, filled)); buy.quantity -= filled; sell.quantity -= filled; if(sell.quantity == 0) { sellQueue.poll(); if(sellQueue.isEmpty()) asks.remove(bestAsk); } } return trades; } private void addToBook(Order o) { (o.side == OrderSide.BUY ? bids : asks) .computeIfAbsent(o.price, p -> new LinkedList<>()).add(o); } public double getBestBid() { return bids.isEmpty() ? 0 : bids.firstKey(); } public double getBestAsk() { return asks.isEmpty() ? 0 : asks.firstKey(); } public double getSpread() { return getBestAsk() - getBestBid(); } } record Trade(Order buyer, Order seller, double price, int quantity) {} class Portfolio { private final Map<String, Position> positions = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); public void onTrade(Trade trade, boolean isBuyer) { int qty = isBuyer ? trade.quantity() : -trade.quantity(); positions.compute(trade.buyer().symbol, (sym, pos) -> { if(pos == null) pos = new Position(sym, 0, 0); return pos.update(qty, trade.price()); }); } }
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Zerodha processes 10 million stock orders during the 9:15 AM market open. All orders arrive in the same second. Your Order Book must match buy orders (bids) with sell orders (asks) in microseconds. How do you design it to handle this?
    An Order Book is a price-time priority queue on both sides. Best bid = highest price buyer. Best ask = lowest price seller. Matching = when best_bid >= best_ask. What data structure gives you O(log n) insert and O(1) best-price access?
    Order Book structure: Two sides: BID (buy orders, max-heap by price then time) and ASK (sell orders, min-heap by price then time). TreeMap<Price, Queue<Order>> — price levels as keys, FIFO queue at each level. Matching engine: On new buy order at price P: while ASK.bestPrice() <= P and order not filled: take from ASK.bestLevel(), fill, emit Trade event. Remaining quantity becomes a resting order in BID. Order types: Market order: fill immediately at best available price, no resting. Limit order: fill up to limit price, rest the remainder. Stop order: activate when market touches trigger price, then becomes market/limit. Performance: TreeMap operations O(log n). At 10M orders/second: use a lock-free array-backed order book (pre-allocated price levels array, no GC pressure). Real exchanges (NSE, NASDAQ) use custom C++ with hardware timestamps.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: "How do you make the matching engine thread-safe without making it a bottleneck?"
    💭 Think First
    A single lock on the entire OrderBook serializes all orders for a symbol. That's correct but slow. Real exchanges process millions of orders/second.
    → Production approach
    One thread per symbol (single-threaded per OrderBook). The matching engine for INFY runs on thread T1, RELIANCE on T2. No shared state between them — no locking needed within a symbol. Incoming orders are routed to the correct symbol's queue. The queue is thread-safe (ConcurrentLinkedQueue). The matching engine thread consumes from the queue single-threaded. This is how real exchanges work: complete serialization per instrument, no inter-instrument lock contention.
    Q: "What is a circuit breaker in stock trading and how would you implement it?"
    💭 Think First
    Circuit breaker = automatic trading halt when price moves too fast (prevents flash crashes).
    → Implementation
    After each trade, check: if currentPrice moved more than X% from the last circuit-check price within N minutes → halt trading for this symbol. Set symbol status to HALTED. Reject all new orders with HaltedException. After the halt period (e.g. 15 minutes), resume trading with a call auction (collect all orders, match at single clearing price). Implement at the OrderBook level: check after every trade execution and before accepting new orders.
    🎯 Practice
    Given order book: Bids: [₹102×100, ₹101×200], Asks: [₹103×150, ₹104×100]. A market BUY order for 200 shares arrives. Walk through the matching step by step and show the final order book state.
    HintMarket BUY matches against lowest asks first. Best ask = ₹103×150. Buy 150 at ₹103 (ask exhausted). Still need 50 shares. Next ask = ₹104×100. Buy 50 at ₹104. Order filled. Ask book: ₹104×50 remaining.
    → Step-by-step solution
    Order matching trace
    // Initial state: // Bids: 102×100, 101×200 // Asks: 103×150, 104×100 // Incoming: MARKET BUY 200 // Round 1: Best ask = 103×150. min(200, 150) = 150. Trade: 150@₹103 // Buy remaining = 200-150 = 50. Ask 103 exhausted → removed. // Asks: 104×100 // Round 2: Best ask = 104×100. min(50, 100) = 50. Trade: 50@₹104 // Buy remaining = 50-50 = 0. Buy order fully filled. // Ask 104: 100-50 = 50 remaining. // Final state: // Bids: 102×100, 101×200 (unchanged — no sell orders) // Asks: 104×50 (partially consumed) // Trades executed: [150@₹103, 50@₹104] // Average fill price: (150×103 + 50×104) / 200 = ₹103.25

    Design a Shopping Cart

    cart management · pricing rules · inventory check · checkout flow
    🧠 Mental Model
    A shopping cart is a temporary state container. It needs: add/remove/update items, real-time price calculation with discounts, inventory validation at checkout, and atomicity (can't checkout if stock becomes unavailable between add and buy).
    Cart storage decision: per-user session (Redis, TTL-based) vs DB-persisted (survive browser close). For logged-in users: DB. For guests: Redis/localStorage.
    💻 Cart + Pricing Engine
    Java — Shopping Cart with discount engine
    class CartItem { final String productId; final String name; final double unitPrice; int quantity; double subtotal() { return unitPrice * quantity; } } class Cart { private final String userId; private final Map<String, CartItem> items = new LinkedHashMap<>(); // insertion order private String couponCode; public void addItem(Product product, int qty) { items.compute(product.id, (id, existing) -> { if(existing == null) return new CartItem(product.id, product.name, product.price, qty); existing.quantity += qty; return existing; // merge quantities }); } public void removeItem(String productId) { items.remove(productId); } public void updateQty(String productId, int qty) { if(qty <= 0) removeItem(productId); else items.computeIfPresent(productId, (id, item) -> { item.quantity = qty; return item; }); } public CartSummary getSummary(PricingEngine engine) { double subtotal = items.values().stream().mapToDouble(CartItem::subtotal).sum(); double discount = engine.calculateDiscount(this); double tax = engine.calculateTax(subtotal - discount); return new CartSummary(subtotal, discount, tax, subtotal - discount + tax); } } // Strategy pattern for discount rules interface DiscountRule { double apply(Cart cart); boolean isApplicable(Cart cart); } class MinOrderDiscount implements DiscountRule { private final double minAmount, discountPct; public boolean isApplicable(Cart c) { return c.getSubtotal() >= minAmount; } public double apply(Cart c) { return c.getSubtotal() * discountPct / 100; } } class PricingEngine { private final List<DiscountRule> rules; public double calculateDiscount(Cart cart) { return rules.stream() .filter(r -> r.isApplicable(cart)) .mapToDouble(r -> r.apply(cart)) .max().orElse(0); // apply best discount, not stacked } } // Checkout with inventory validation class CheckoutService { @Transactional public Order checkout(Cart cart, PaymentInfo payment) { // 1. Validate inventory for ALL items first (fail fast) cart.getItems().forEach((pid, item) -> { if(!inventoryService.hasStock(pid, item.quantity)) throw new InsufficientStockException(item.name); }); // 2. Reserve inventory (SELECT FOR UPDATE per product) cart.getItems().forEach((pid, item) -> inventoryService.reserve(pid, item.quantity)); // 3. Process payment var summary = cart.getSummary(pricingEngine); paymentGateway.charge(cart.getUserId(), summary.totalAmount(), payment); // 4. Create order, clear cart Order order = orderService.create(cart); cartRepo.delete(cart.getUserId()); return order; } }
    🏭 Production Scenario
    You are designing a Shopping Cart for an e-commerce app. The interviewer asks: "How do you apply the best discount when a user has 3 competing promo codes — 10% off, flat ₹200 off, or buy-2-get-1-free?" Show your class design.
    This is Strategy Pattern for discount calculation. Each promo is a strategy. The cart evaluates all applicable strategies and picks the best one for the customer.
    DiscountStrategy interface: calculate(Cart cart) → BigDecimal discount. Implementations: PercentageDiscount(10%), FlatDiscount(₹200), BuyNGetMDiscount(2,1). CartService.applyBestDiscount(cart, List<DiscountStrategy>): runs each strategy, picks the maximum discount. Key design decisions: strategies are stateless (the discount percentage is a constructor arg, not mutable state) — can be shared/cached. Cart is immutable during discount calculation — strategies read but do not modify it. The BuyNGetMDiscount needs CartItem quantities and prices to compute which items are free — it receives the full Cart, not just the total.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: How do you handle discount stacking — can a user apply two promos simultaneously?
    💭 Think First
    Stacking discounts requires a clear policy: can multiple strategies combine, or is it always best-of-one?
    → Complete Answer
    Business policy first: most e-commerce platforms allow stacking of different types (one percentage + one flat) but not two of the same type. Model this with DiscountType enum (PERCENTAGE, FLAT, BOGO). CartService.applyDiscounts: group strategies by type, take the best within each type, sum the allowed combination. Use a DiscountPolicy class to encode the rules — this separates business logic from the Cart domain. Alternative: CompositeDiscountStrategy wraps a list and applies all of them sequentially — flexible but can result in over-discounting if not bounded.
    Q: A user adds an item to the cart but it is out of stock. How do you handle this at checkout?
    💭 Think First
    Cart state can diverge from inventory state between add-to-cart and checkout. Optimistic locking prevents overselling.
    → Complete Answer
    Reservation pattern: when checkout starts, attempt to reserve (decrement) inventory for each cart item using optimistic locking (UPDATE inventory SET qty=qty-1, version=version+1 WHERE id=? AND qty>=1 AND version=?). If any item fails (version mismatch or qty=0): roll back all reservations, return a clear error listing which items are out of stock. Hold the reservation for 15 minutes (TTL in Redis or DB). If payment fails: release reservations. If payment succeeds: confirm and mark as shipped. This prevents double-selling without long-held locks.
    🎯 Practice
    Cart has: Laptop ₹50,000 × 1, Mouse ₹1,000 × 2, Keyboard ₹2,000 × 1. Rules: 10% off orders over ₹10,000. Coupon SAVE500 = flat ₹500 off. 18% GST on discounted amount. Calculate final payable.
    HintSubtotal = 50000+2000+2000 = ₹54,000. Rule 1: 10% = ₹5,400. Coupon: ₹500. Apply best (or both if stackable — clarify with interviewer). Most systems: apply coupon AFTER percentage discount.
    → Solution
    Calculation
    // Subtotal = 50,000 + (1,000×2) + 2,000 = ₹54,000 // 10% discount (order > ₹10,000) = ₹5,400 → after: ₹48,600 // Coupon SAVE500 = ₹500 → after: ₹48,100 // 18% GST on ₹48,100 = ₹8,658 // Final payable = ₹48,100 + ₹8,658 = ₹56,758 // Non-stackable alternative: best discount only = max(5400, 500) = 5400 // After discount: 54000 - 5400 = 48600. GST 18% = 8748. Total = 57348
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement the applyBestDiscount method. Given a Cart and a list of DiscountStrategy, return the strategy that gives the highest discount along with the discount amount.
    Hint — think before readingStream the strategies, compute each discount, find the max by discount amount, return both the winning strategy and the amount. Use a record BestDiscount{strategy, amount} as the return type.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — best discount selector
    record BestDiscount(DiscountStrategy strategy, BigDecimal amount) {} class CartService { public BestDiscount applyBestDiscount(Cart cart, List<DiscountStrategy> strategies) { return strategies.stream() .map(s -> new BestDiscount(s, s.calculate(cart))) .filter(bd -> bd.amount().compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) > 0) .max(Comparator.comparing(BestDiscount::amount)) .orElse(new BestDiscount(null, BigDecimal.ZERO)); } }
