    Design a Text Editor with Undo/Redo

    Command Pattern · operation history · cursor management · real editor internals
    🧠 Mental Model
    A text editor with undo/redo is the canonical Command Pattern example. Every user action (insert, delete, replace) is encapsulated as a Command object with execute() and undo() methods. Undo = pop from undo stack and call undo(). Redo = pop from redo stack and re-execute.
    Key insight: redo stack is cleared whenever a new command is executed — you can't redo after a new edit, just like real editors.
    💻 Command Pattern Text Editor
    Java — Text Editor with Undo/Redo
    // Document: uses StringBuilder for O(1) amortized insert/delete near end, O(n) elsewhere // Production editors use Piece Table or Rope for O(log n) everywhere class Document { private StringBuilder content = new StringBuilder(); private int cursorPos = 0; public void insert(int pos, String text) { content.insert(pos, text); cursorPos = pos + text.length(); } public String delete(int pos, int len) { String deleted = content.substring(pos, pos + len); content.delete(pos, pos + len); cursorPos = pos; return deleted; } public String getContent() { return content.toString(); } } // Command interface — every action implements this interface Command { void execute(); void undo(); String describe(); } class InsertCommand implements Command { private final Document doc; private final int pos; private final String text; InsertCommand(Document doc, int pos, String text) { this.doc = doc; this.pos = pos; this.text = text; } public void execute() { doc.insert(pos, text); } public void undo() { doc.delete(pos, text.length()); } public String describe() { return "Insert '" + text + "' at " + pos; } } class DeleteCommand implements Command { private final Document doc; private final int pos, len; private String deleted; // saved during execute() for undo() DeleteCommand(Document doc, int pos, int len) { this.doc = doc; this.pos = pos; this.len = len; } public void execute() { deleted = doc.delete(pos, len); } public void undo() { doc.insert(pos, deleted); } public String describe() { return "Delete " + len + " chars at " + pos; } } class ReplaceCommand implements Command { private final Document doc; private final int pos, len; private final String newText; private String oldText; public void execute() { oldText = doc.delete(pos, len); doc.insert(pos, newText); } public void undo() { doc.delete(pos, newText.length()); doc.insert(pos, oldText); } public String describe() { return "Replace at " + pos; } } class TextEditor { private final Document document = new Document(); private final Deque<Command> undoStack = new ArrayDeque<>(); private final Deque<Command> redoStack = new ArrayDeque<>(); public void execute(Command cmd) { cmd.execute(); undoStack.push(cmd); redoStack.clear(); // new action invalidates redo history } public boolean undo() { if(undoStack.isEmpty()) return false; Command cmd = undoStack.pop(); cmd.undo(); redoStack.push(cmd); return true; } public boolean redo() { if(redoStack.isEmpty()) return false; Command cmd = redoStack.pop(); cmd.execute(); undoStack.push(cmd); return true; } public List<String> getHistory() { return undoStack.stream().map(Command::describe).toList(); } }
    🏭 Production Scenario
    A user types 1,000 characters in your text editor, then hits Ctrl+Z (undo) 1,000 times to get back to blank. Then hits Ctrl+Shift+Z (redo) 500 times. Each undo/redo must complete in under 1ms. How do you implement this?
    Undo/Redo = two stacks. Execute pushes to undo stack. Undo pops from undo stack and pushes to redo stack. Redo pops from redo stack and pushes to undo stack. The Command pattern makes each operation an object you can reverse.
    Command pattern: Command interface with execute() and undo(). Each operation (InsertCommand, DeleteCommand, ReplaceCommand) implements both. InsertCommand.undo() = delete the inserted text at the same position. DeleteCommand.undo() = re-insert the deleted text at the same position. Two stacks: Deque<Command> undoStack, redoStack. On execute(cmd): cmd.execute(); undoStack.push(cmd); redoStack.clear() (new action invalidates redo history). On undo: cmd = undoStack.pop(); cmd.undo(); redoStack.push(cmd). On redo: cmd = redoStack.pop(); cmd.execute(); undoStack.push(cmd). Performance: O(1) per undo/redo. 1ms budget is trivially met — stack push/pop + string operation. Macro commands: CompositeCommand wraps a list of Commands — undo reverses all in reverse order. Used for 'paste 500 characters' as one undoable action. Memory limit: Cap undoStack at 1,000 items. When full, drop the oldest (bottom of stack) — oldest actions become permanent.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: "StringBuilder is O(n) for insert in the middle. How do real editors like VS Code handle large files?"
    💭 Think First
    A 10MB file, and you insert one character in the middle — shifting 5MB of content is O(n). Real editors need O(log n).
    → Piece Table data structure
    Piece Table: Two immutable buffers — original file content + an append-only add buffer. A list of "pieces" (pointer, start, length) describes the current document. Insertion = add new text to the add buffer, split the affected piece into three pieces. Deletion = split the piece, remove the middle piece. All operations are O(log n) with a balanced BST of pieces. VS Code, Microsoft Word historically, and many other editors use Piece Table.

    Rope: A binary tree of string chunks. Concatenation, split, and indexing are O(log n). Used by text editors needing efficient arbitrary insertions/deletions.
    Q: "How do you implement cursor movement: Home, End, Ctrl+Left (word jump)?"
    💭 Think First
    Cursor position is an index into the document. Movement = recalculate that index based on the movement type.
    → Implementation
    Java
    class Cursor { private int pos; private final Document doc; void moveHome() { String c = doc.getContent(); int lineStart = c.lastIndexOf('\n', pos - 1); pos = lineStart == -1 ? 0 : lineStart + 1; } void moveEnd() { String c = doc.getContent(); int lineEnd = c.indexOf('\n', pos); pos = lineEnd == -1 ? c.length() : lineEnd; } void wordJumpLeft() { // Ctrl+Left: skip to start of previous word String c = doc.getContent(); int p = pos - 1; while(p > 0 && !Character.isLetterOrDigit(c.charAt(p))) p--; // skip whitespace while(p > 0 && Character.isLetterOrDigit(c.charAt(p-1))) p--; // skip word pos = p; } }
    🎯 Practice
    Add a macro recording feature: user presses "Record", performs N actions, presses "Stop", then "Play" to replay those actions. How does the Command Pattern make this trivial?
    HintMacroCommand is itself a Command that holds a List<Command>. execute() calls each command's execute() in order. undo() calls each command's undo() in reverse order. Recording = capture Commands into a list instead of executing them. Play = execute the MacroCommand.
    → Solution
    Java — Macro as Composite Command
    class MacroCommand implements Command { private final List<Command> commands; MacroCommand(List<Command> commands) { this.commands = new ArrayList<>(commands); } public void execute() { commands.forEach(Command::execute); } public void undo() { ListIterator<Command> it = commands.listIterator(commands.size()); while(it.hasPrevious()) it.previous().undo(); // undo in reverse order } public String describe() { return "Macro(" + commands.size() + " steps)"; } } // Composite Pattern: MacroCommand IS-A Command → undo stack treats it as one action // Pressing Ctrl+Z once undoes the entire macro. Elegant.

    Design a Spreadsheet (Excel)

    cell model · formula evaluation · dependency graph · cycle detection
    🧠 Mental Model
    A spreadsheet is a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) of cell dependencies. When cell A1 changes, all cells that depend on A1 must recalculate. The evaluation order must respect dependencies (topological sort). Circular references = cycles in the DAG = error.
    Key design: each cell either holds a raw value or a formula. A formula references other cells. Changing a cell triggers re-evaluation of all dependents in topological order.
    💻 Spreadsheet with Formula Evaluation
    Java — Spreadsheet with dependency tracking
    class Cell { final String id; // "A1", "B3" private String formula; // null if raw value private double cachedValue; private final Set<String> dependencies = new HashSet<>(); // cells this cell reads } class Spreadsheet { private final Map<String, Cell> cells = new HashMap<>(); private final Map<String, Set<String>> dependents = new HashMap<>(); // dependents[A1] = {B1, C3} means B1 and C3 have formulas referencing A1 public void setCell(String cellId, String value) { Cell cell = cells.computeIfAbsent(cellId, id -> new Cell(id)); // Remove old dependency edges cell.dependencies.forEach(dep -> dependents.getOrDefault(dep, Set.of()).remove(cellId)); cell.dependencies.clear(); if(value.startsWith("=")) { cell.formula = value; Set<String> refs = parseReferences(value); if(hasCycle(cellId, refs)) throw new CircularReferenceException(cellId); refs.forEach(ref -> { cell.dependencies.add(ref); dependents.computeIfAbsent(ref, k -> new HashSet<>()).add(cellId); }); } else { cell.formula = null; cell.cachedValue = Double.parseDouble(value); } // Re-evaluate this cell and all dependents in topological order for(String toEval : topologicalOrder(cellId)) { evaluate(cells.get(toEval)); } } private void evaluate(Cell cell) { if(cell.formula == null) return; // raw value, no eval needed cell.cachedValue = formulaParser.evaluate(cell.formula, this); } // BFS/DFS from cellId through dependents — collect in topological order private List<String> topologicalOrder(String start) { List<String> order = new ArrayList<>(); Queue<String> queue = new LinkedList<>(); Set<String> visited = new HashSet<>(); queue.add(start); while(!queue.isEmpty()) { String cur = queue.poll(); if(visited.add(cur)) { order.add(cur); dependents.getOrDefault(cur, Set.of()).forEach(queue::add); } } return order; } // Cycle detection: DFS from proposed new dependencies — would adding these create a cycle? private boolean hasCycle(String cellId, Set<String> refs) { Set<String> visited = new HashSet<>(); return refs.stream().anyMatch(ref -> dfs(ref, cellId, visited)); } private boolean dfs(String cur, String target, Set<String> visited) { if(cur.equals(target)) return true; // found cycle back to cellId if(!visited.add(cur)) return false; return dependents.getOrDefault(cur, Set.of()).stream() .anyMatch(dep -> dfs(dep, target, visited)); } public double getValue(String cellId) { return cells.containsKey(cellId) ? cells.get(cellId).cachedValue : 0; } } // SUM formula: =SUM(A1:A5) — evaluates sum of a range class SumFormula { public double evaluate(String range, Spreadsheet sheet) { // Parse "A1:A5" → expand to [A1, A2, A3, A4, A5] → sum values return expandRange(range).stream().mapToDouble(sheet::getValue).sum(); } private List<String> expandRange(String range) { String[] parts = range.split(":"); char col1 = parts[0].charAt(0), col2 = parts[1].charAt(0); int row1 = Integer.parseInt(parts[0].substring(1)); int row2 = Integer.parseInt(parts[1].substring(1)); List<String> cells = new ArrayList<>(); for(char c = col1; c <= col2; c++) for(int r = row1; r <= row2; r++) cells.add(String.valueOf(c) + r); return cells; } }
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Your spreadsheet has a formula in C1: =A1+B1. A1 has =D1*2. D1 has =C1+1. When the user updates D1, which cells need to recalculate and in what order? What happens if you don't detect the circular dependency?
    This is a directed graph problem. Cells are nodes. A formula dependency is a directed edge. Recalculation order = topological sort of the dependency graph. Circular dependency = cycle in the graph — infinite loop if not detected.
    Dependency graph: When a formula is entered in cell X, parse its dependencies. For each dependency Y: add directed edge Y → X (Y is depended on by X). When Y changes: find all cells that depend on Y (BFS/DFS from Y in the dependency graph) and recalculate in topological order. Cycle detection: Before adding edges for a new formula, run DFS from the formula's cell. If you can reach the cell being edited (the formula's cell appears as its own ancestor), reject the formula with 'Circular Reference' error. Topological sort for recalculation: Kahn's algorithm (BFS with in-degree tracking). Process cells with in-degree 0 first, decrement neighbors' in-degrees. This gives the correct recalculation order — a cell is only computed after all its dependencies are up to date. Incremental update: Don't recalculate the whole sheet. Only recalculate the subgraph reachable from the changed cell. For large sheets (1M cells), this reduces recalculation from O(n) to O(affected cells).
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: "How does topological sort ensure cells evaluate in the right order?"
    💭 Think First
    If B1 = A1 * 2 and C1 = B1 + 1, changing A1 must recalculate B1 first, then C1. Wrong order = C1 uses stale B1 value.
    → Kahn's algorithm for spreadsheet
    When A1 changes, BFS through the dependents graph: A1 → B1, C1 → D1. This BFS order is automatically topological (a node is visited only after all its dependencies have been processed). Kahn's algorithm: compute in-degree for each cell in the re-eval set. Process zero-in-degree cells first. Remove them, decrement their dependents' in-degree. Repeat. Guarantees correct evaluation order.
    Q: A spreadsheet has 1 million rows and a formula in column C that depends on all of column A. When one cell in column A changes, how do you avoid recalculating all 1 million C cells?
    💡 Think First
    Recalculating all 1M cells on every change is O(n) — too slow. The dependency graph tells you WHICH cells actually need to change. Can you narrow it down?
    ➔ Complete Answer
    Dirty marking + lazy evaluation: when A5 changes, mark all cells that depend on A5 as DIRTY (traverse the dependency graph from A5, mark reachable nodes). Do NOT recalculate yet. When the user reads cell C5 (which depends on A-column): check if C5 is dirty. If dirty: recalculate just C5 (recursively ensuring its dependencies are clean first). If not dirty: return cached value. This is lazy evaluation — only recalculate what is actually READ after a change. For the SUM(A:A) formula: SUM depends on all of column A. When A5 changes: SUM is marked dirty. On next read of SUM: recalculate. Optimisation: if SUM(A:A) was 10,000 and A5 changed from 100 to 150: new SUM = old SUM - 100 + 150 = 10,050. Incremental update in O(1) instead of O(n). This is how Excel and Google Sheets handle large SUM/AVERAGE formulas efficiently.
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement dirty-mark + lazy evaluation for a spreadsheet. CellGraph.markDirty(cellId) traverses the dependency graph and marks all dependent cells as dirty. CellGraph.getValue(cellId) returns the cached value if clean, or triggers recalculation if dirty. Handle the incremental SUM optimisation: when one cell in a summed range changes, update SUM in O(1) instead of O(n).
    💡 HintmarkDirty: BFS/DFS from the changed cell through the dependency graph. Set dirty=true on every reachable cell. getValue: if dirty, recursively get values of all dependencies (they trigger their own recalculation if dirty), compute this cell's formula, cache the result, set dirty=false. SUM optimisation: store the last SUM value. On cell change in range: newSUM = oldSUM - oldCellValue + newCellValue.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — dirty-mark lazy evaluation
    class CellGraph { private final Map<String, Cell> cells = new HashMap<>(); // dependents[A] = set of cells that DEPEND ON A (must be dirtied when A changes) private final Map<String, Set<String>> dependents = new HashMap<>(); public void markDirty(String cellId) { if(!cells.containsKey(cellId)) return; cells.get(cellId).setDirty(true); // BFS: propagate dirtiness to all dependents Queue<String> queue = new LinkedList<>(dependents.getOrDefault(cellId, Set.of())); while(!queue.isEmpty()) { String dep = queue.poll(); cells.get(dep).setDirty(true); queue.addAll(dependents.getOrDefault(dep, Set.of())); } } public double getValue(String cellId) { Cell cell = cells.get(cellId); if(!cell.isDirty()) return cell.getCachedValue(); // cache hit // Recalculate: evaluate formula using dependency values double result = cell.evaluate(this); // recursively calls getValue on dependencies cell.setCachedValue(result); cell.setDirty(false); return result; } }
    🎯 Practice
    Set A1=5, B1=10, C1=A1+B1 (=15), D1=C1*2 (=30). Now set A1=8. Trace exactly which cells recalculate and in what order. What if D1 also referenced B1 directly?
    Hintdependents[A1]={C1}. dependents[C1]={D1}. Topological order from A1: A1 → C1 → D1. Set A1=8 → C1=8+10=18 → D1=18*2=36. With D1 also referencing B1: dependents[B1]={C1, D1}. Order still: C1 before D1 (C1 is D1's dependency).
    → Trace
    Evaluation trace
    // Before: A1=5, B1=10, C1=15, D1=30 // setCell("A1", "8") // topologicalOrder("A1") = [A1, C1, D1] (BFS through dependents) // Evaluate A1: raw value=8 (no formula, cached directly) // Evaluate C1: formula "=A1+B1" → getValue("A1")=8 + getValue("B1")=10 = 18 // Evaluate D1: formula "=C1*2" → getValue("C1")=18 * 2 = 36 // Final: A1=8, B1=10, C1=18, D1=36 ✓ // If D1 = "=C1*2 + B1": // D1 depends on C1 AND B1 // dependents[B1] = {C1, D1}; dependents[C1] = {D1} // Topological sort ensures C1 evaluated before D1 (D1 has in-degree 2: waits for both) // Order: A1 → C1 → D1 (C1 processes first, then D1 sees updated C1)
    LLD: Files & Search
    File Systems, Search & Dictionaries
    Unix find · In-Memory FS · Trie Autocomplete · Phone Directory · Dictionary App
    📁
    File System + find
    Composite Pattern · predicates · cd navigation · log storage
    🔍
    Autocomplete + Trie
    top-K suggestions · phone directory · dictionary app

    Design a File System + Unix find Command

    Composite Pattern · directory traversal · boolean predicates · in-memory FS
    🧠 Mental Model
    A file system is the canonical Composite Pattern example. File and Directory both implement the same interface (FileSystemNode). Directory contains a List of FileSystemNodes — so the tree is recursive. find command = DFS traversal with predicate filtering.
    Composite Pattern insight: client code treats files and directories uniformly. Operations like size(), search(), list() work polymorphically — Directory.size() recursively sums children, File.size() returns its own size.
    💻 Composite File System + find Command
    Java — File System with Composite Pattern
    // Composite Pattern: File and Directory share the same interface abstract class FileSystemNode { protected String name; protected Directory parent; protected LocalDateTime createdAt = LocalDateTime.now(); protected LocalDateTime modifiedAt = LocalDateTime.now(); abstract long size(); abstract boolean isDirectory(); public String getName() { return name; } public String getPath() { return parent == null ? "/" + name : parent.getPath() + "/" + name; } public String extension() { int dot = name.lastIndexOf('.'); return dot == -1 ? "" : name.substring(dot + 1); } } class File extends FileSystemNode { private final long fileSize; private String content; File(String name, long size) { this.name = name; this.fileSize = size; } public long size() { return fileSize; } public boolean isDirectory() { return false; } } class Directory extends FileSystemNode { private final List<FileSystemNode> children = new ArrayList<>(); Directory(String name) { this.name = name; } public void add(FileSystemNode node) { node.parent = this; children.add(node); } public boolean isDirectory() { return true; } public long size() { // recursive — delegates to children return children.stream().mapToLong(FileSystemNode::size).sum(); } public List<FileSystemNode> list() { return Collections.unmodifiableList(children); } public Optional<FileSystemNode> findChild(String name) { return children.stream().filter(c -> c.name.equals(name)).findFirst(); } } // Unix find command — Strategy Pattern for predicates interface FindPredicate { boolean test(FileSystemNode node); default FindPredicate and(FindPredicate other) { return n -> test(n) && other.test(n); } default FindPredicate or(FindPredicate other) { return n -> test(n) || other.test(n); } default FindPredicate not() { return n -> !test(n); } } // Built-in predicates (Specification Pattern) class NamePredicate implements FindPredicate { private final String pattern; // glob: "*.java" public boolean test(FileSystemNode n) { return n.getName().matches(pattern.replace(".","\\.").replace("*",".*")); } } class SizePredicate implements FindPredicate { private final long minBytes, maxBytes; public boolean test(FileSystemNode n) { return n.size() >= minBytes && n.size() <= maxBytes; } } class ExtensionPredicate implements FindPredicate { private final String ext; public boolean test(FileSystemNode n) { return !n.isDirectory() && n.extension().equals(ext); } } class TypePredicate implements FindPredicate { private final boolean wantDir; public boolean test(FileSystemNode n) { return n.isDirectory() == wantDir; } } class ModifiedAfterPredicate implements FindPredicate { private final LocalDateTime threshold; public boolean test(FileSystemNode n) { return n.modifiedAt.isAfter(threshold); } } class FindCommand { public List<FileSystemNode> find(Directory root, FindPredicate predicate) { List<FileSystemNode> results = new ArrayList<>(); dfs(root, predicate, results); return results; } private void dfs(FileSystemNode node, FindPredicate pred, List<FileSystemNode> results) { if(pred.test(node)) results.add(node); if(node.isDirectory()) { ((Directory) node).list().forEach(child -> dfs(child, pred, results)); } } } // Usage: find all .java files larger than 1KB, not in test directories FindCommand finder = new FindCommand(); FindPredicate p = new ExtensionPredicate("java") .and(new SizePredicate(1024, Long.MAX_VALUE)) .and(new NamePredicate("*Test*").not()); List<FileSystemNode> results = finder.find(root, p);
    ⚠️ cd with dash — In-Memory File System Navigation
    Java — File system navigation with cd -
    class FileSystemShell { private Directory currentDir; private Directory previousDir; // for "cd -" private final Directory root; public void cd(String path) { if(path.equals("-")) { // cd - : go to previous dir if(previousDir == null) throw new RuntimeException("No previous dir"); Directory tmp = currentDir; currentDir = previousDir; previousDir = tmp; return; } Directory prev = currentDir; if(path.equals("/")) { currentDir = root; previousDir = prev; return; } if(path.equals("..")) { currentDir = currentDir.parent != null ? currentDir.parent : root; previousDir = prev; return; } Directory start = path.startsWith("/") ? root : currentDir; String[] parts = path.replaceAll("^/","").split("/"); Directory target = start; for(String part : parts) { if(part.equals(".")) continue; if(part.equals("..")) { target = target.parent != null ? target.parent : root; continue; } target = (Directory) target.findChild(part) .filter(FileSystemNode::isDirectory) .orElseThrow(() -> new RuntimeException("No such directory: " + part)); } previousDir = currentDir; currentDir = target; } public String pwd() { return currentDir.getPath(); } public List<String> ls() { return currentDir.list().stream().map(FileSystemNode::getName).sorted().toList(); } }
    🏭 Production Scenario
    An interviewer asks you to design a Unix-like file system with a find command. find /home -name "*.java" -size +100KB. How do you represent the tree and compose the predicates?
    File system = Composite Pattern (File and Directory share the same interface). find = DFS traversal with a composed predicate. The predicate composition (AND, OR, NOT) is the interesting design challenge.
    Composite: FileSystemNode (interface: getName, getSize, isDirectory, getChildren). File and Directory implement it. Directory.getSize() recursively sums children. FindPredicate interface: test(FileSystemNode) → boolean. Implementations: NamePredicate (glob match), SizePredicate (>, <, = comparison), ExtensionPredicate. Composition: AndPredicate(p1, p2), OrPredicate(p1, p2), NotPredicate(p). find command builds the predicate tree from CLI args and runs a DFS, collecting nodes where predicate.test(node) returns true. This is exactly the Specification Pattern.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: How does your find implementation handle symbolic links to prevent infinite loops?
    💭 Think First
    A symlink can point to a parent directory, creating a cycle. DFS without cycle detection would loop forever.
    → Complete Answer
    Track visited inodes (or absolute paths) in a Set<String>. Before DFS-ing into a directory, check if its canonical path is already in the visited set. If yes, skip it (symlink cycle detected). Add the path to visited before recursing into children. This is the same approach used by the real find command's -follow flag. Without -follow, find does not follow symlinks at all (it reports the symlink itself, not its target) — simpler and cycle-safe by default.
    Q: The find command needs to support -mtime (modified in last N days). How do you add this without changing existing predicates?
    💭 Think First
    This is an Open/Closed Principle question. Adding a new predicate type should not modify existing code.
    → Complete Answer
    Create MTimePredicate implements FindPredicate. It accepts a Duration (lastNDays) and tests node.getLastModified().isAfter(Instant.now().minus(lastNDays, DAYS)). Register it in the predicate parser — the switch that converts CLI args to predicates. No existing predicate classes change. The DFS traversal does not change. The predicate composition (And/Or/Not) does not change. This is exactly what OCP means: the find system is open for extension (new predicate type) closed for modification (existing classes unchanged).
    🎯 Practice
    Design a Log Storage System: append logs with a timestamp, and efficiently query all logs between two timestamps. Logs arrive in order. Handle queries for "last N minutes" of logs.
    HintSince logs arrive in order (monotonically increasing timestamps), store them in an ArrayList. Binary search (Collections.binarySearch or TreeMap) finds the start/end indices for a time range in O(log n). For "last N minutes": compute startTime = now - N minutes, binary search for that position.
    → Solution
    Java — Log Storage with binary search range queries
    class LogStorage { record LogEntry(Instant timestamp, String level, String message) {} private final List<LogEntry> logs = new ArrayList<>(); // always sorted by timestamp public void append(String level, String message) { logs.add(new LogEntry(Instant.now(), level, message)); } public List<LogEntry> query(Instant from, Instant to) { int lo = lowerBound(from), hi = upperBound(to); return lo > hi ? List.of() : logs.subList(lo, hi + 1); } public List<LogEntry> lastMinutes(int minutes) { return query(Instant.now().minus(minutes, ChronoUnit.MINUTES), Instant.now()); } private int lowerBound(Instant t) { // first index with timestamp >= t int lo = 0, hi = logs.size(); while(lo < hi) { int mid = (lo + hi) / 2; if(logs.get(mid).timestamp().isBefore(t)) lo = mid + 1; else hi = mid; } return lo; } private int upperBound(Instant t) { // last index with timestamp <= t int lo = -1, hi = logs.size() - 1; while(lo < hi) { int mid = (lo + hi + 1) / 2; if(logs.get(mid).timestamp().isAfter(t)) hi = mid - 1; else lo = mid; } return lo; } }
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement the DFS find method. Given a root FileSystemNode and a FindPredicate, return all matching nodes in the tree. Handle both files and directories correctly.
    Hint — think before readingDFS: add the current node to results if predicate matches. If the node is a directory, recurse into each child. Return the accumulated results list.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — find with DFS + predicate
    class FileSystem { public List<FileSystemNode> find(FileSystemNode root, FindPredicate pred) { List<FileSystemNode> results = new ArrayList<>(); dfs(root, pred, results, new HashSet<>()); return results; } private void dfs(FileSystemNode node, FindPredicate pred, List<FileSystemNode> res, Set<String> visited) { if(!visited.add(node.getCanonicalPath())) return; // cycle guard if(pred.test(node)) res.add(node); if(node.isDirectory()) node.getChildren().forEach(child -> dfs(child, pred, res, visited)); } }

    Search, Autocomplete & Phone Directory

    Trie data structure · prefix search · top-K suggestions · phone directory
    🧠 Mental Model
    Trie (prefix tree) is the go-to data structure for prefix-based search. Each node represents one character. A path from root to a marked node spells a complete word. All words sharing a prefix share the same initial path — prefix search is O(prefix length), not O(total words).
    For Google Search Autocomplete: Trie + frequency scoring. Each Trie node stores the top-K results for any query with that prefix — updated on insert, returned directly on query. O(prefix length) lookup regardless of total number of words.
    💻 Trie + Top-K Autocomplete
    Java — Trie with top-K frequency-based suggestions
    class TrieNode { final Map<Character, TrieNode> children = new HashMap<>(); boolean isEnd = false; int frequency = 0; // how many times this word was searched // Cache top-K suggestions for fast O(1) prefix lookup final PriorityQueue<WordFreq> topK = new PriorityQueue<>(3, Comparator.comparingInt(w -> w.freq)); // min-heap of size K } record WordFreq(String word, int freq) {} class AutocompleteSystem { private final TrieNode root = new TrieNode(); private static final int K = 3; // Insert a word with its search frequency public void insert(String word, int freq) { TrieNode node = root; for(char c : word.toCharArray()) { node.children.putIfAbsent(c, new TrieNode()); node = node.children.get(c); updateTopK(node, word, freq); // update cached top-K at every prefix node } node.isEnd = true; node.frequency = freq; } private void updateTopK(TrieNode node, String word, int freq) { WordFreq wf = new WordFreq(word, freq); node.topK.offer(wf); if(node.topK.size() > K) node.topK.poll(); // evict lowest frequency } // O(prefix.length) — no traversal needed, just follow the path public List<String> getSuggestions(String prefix) { TrieNode node = root; for(char c : prefix.toCharArray()) { node = node.children.get(c); if(node == null) return List.of(); // prefix not found } return node.topK.stream() .sorted((a,b) -> b.freq() - a.freq()) // highest frequency first .map(WordFreq::word).toList(); } // When user searches a word: increment its frequency and re-insert public void recordSearch(String word) { // Find existing node, increment frequency, update topK at all prefix nodes TrieNode node = root; int newFreq = 1; for(char c : word.toCharArray()) { node = node.children.get(c); if(node == null) break; if(node.isEnd) { newFreq = node.frequency + 1; break; } } insert(word, newFreq); // re-insert with updated frequency } } // PHONE DIRECTORY — Trie for phone number prefix search // Key difference: leaf stores the contact, intermediate nodes may also be contacts class PhoneDirectory { private final TrieNode root = new TrieNode(); public void addContact(String phone, String name) { TrieNode node = root; for(char c : phone.toCharArray()) { node.children.putIfAbsent(c, new TrieNode()); node = node.children.get(c); } node.isEnd = true; // node.contactName = name; (store name at end node) } public List<String> searchByPrefix(String prefix) { TrieNode node = root; for(char c : prefix.toCharArray()) { node = node.children.get(c); if(node == null) return List.of(); } List<String> results = new ArrayList<>(); collectAll(node, new StringBuilder(prefix), results); return results; } private void collectAll(TrieNode node, StringBuilder current, List<String> results) { if(node.isEnd) results.add(current.toString()); node.children.forEach((c, child) -> { current.append(c); collectAll(child, current, results); current.deleteCharAt(current.length() - 1); // backtrack }); } }
    🏭 Production Scenario
    You are building autocomplete for a search box. The user types 'ja' in 50ms and expects suggestions within 100ms total. You have 10 million indexed terms. A naive scan of all 10M terms takes 2 seconds. How do you make it 100x faster?
    Linear scan of 10M terms is O(n) — too slow. A Trie gives O(prefix_length) lookup + returns all words with that prefix. But returning ALL words with prefix 'ja' might be 100K results. You need top-K by frequency.
    Trie with top-K at each node: Each TrieNode stores: Map<Character, TrieNode> children, boolean isEnd, List<String> topK (top 10 most frequent words with this prefix, pre-computed at insert time). On insert: traverse/create nodes for each character. At each node, update topK if the new word has higher frequency than the 10th-ranked word. On search('ja'): traverse to the 'a' node in O(2) steps, return node.topK directly — O(1) after traversal. Memory optimisation: Store only the top-10 words at each node, not all completions. 10M words × average 6 characters × 10 suggestions × 20 bytes = ~12GB naive. With Radix Trie (compressed): 10x smaller. With Bloom filter pre-check: skip rare prefixes entirely. Ranking signals: topK sorted by: search frequency × recency score × personalisation boost. Update topK asynchronously from a Kafka stream of search events — don't update Trie on every search request.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: "At Google scale, there are billions of queries. How does the real autocomplete system work?"
    💭 Think First
    A single in-memory Trie can't hold billions of queries. It needs to be distributed, and frequency needs to be updated in real-time from query logs.
    → Distributed approach
    Offline pipeline: MapReduce/Spark aggregates the last 7 days of search logs → computes top-K queries per prefix. Results stored in a distributed key-value store (Bigtable, Redis Cluster) keyed by prefix string.
    Online serving: Client request → API server → lookup prefix in Redis → return top-K. No Trie in production request path — precomputed results make it O(1).
    Personalization layer: User's own search history is merged with global results. User's recent "python" searches boost "python" above "python tutorial" for them specifically.
    Update frequency: Batch jobs run hourly/daily. Breaking news (sudden spike in "earthquake") handled by a real-time streaming layer (Kafka → Flink) that updates top-K for trending queries.
    Q: "How do you implement spell-check suggestions (Levenshtein distance based search in Trie)?"
    💭 Think First
    Prefix search is exact — only matches the exact prefix. Spell check needs fuzzy matching: words within edit distance 1 or 2.
    → BFS/DFS with edit distance pruning
    Maintain a row of the Levenshtein DP matrix as you DFS through the Trie. At each node, compute the new row using the standard DP formula. If the minimum value in the current row exceeds the max allowed edit distance, prune that branch. At leaf nodes (isEnd=true), if the last row value ≤ max distance, it's a valid suggestion. This elegantly combines Trie traversal with DP computation, running O(26 × word_length × dictionary_size) in worst case but with heavy pruning in practice.
    🎯 Practice
    Design a Dictionary App: store words with meanings, support: addWord(word, meaning), getMeaning(word), searchByPrefix(prefix) returning all words starting with prefix, and deleteWord(word).
    HintTrie for the word structure. Each leaf (isEnd=true) node stores the meaning. addWord → insert into Trie, store meaning at end node. getMeaning → traverse to end, return meaning. searchByPrefix → traverse to prefix node, DFS collect all end nodes. deleteWord → mark isEnd=false (lazy delete) or fully remove leaf nodes walking back up.
    → Solution
    Java — Dictionary with Trie
    class DictionaryApp { static class Node { Map<Character, Node> ch = new HashMap<>(); boolean isEnd; String meaning; } private final Node root = new Node(); public void addWord(String word, String meaning) { Node n = root; for(char c : word.toCharArray()) n = n.ch.computeIfAbsent(c, k -> new Node()); n.isEnd = true; n.meaning = meaning; } public Optional<String> getMeaning(String word) { Node n = root; for(char c : word.toCharArray()) { n = n.ch.get(c); if(n == null) return Optional.empty(); } return n.isEnd ? Optional.of(n.meaning) : Optional.empty(); } public List<String> searchByPrefix(String prefix) { Node n = root; for(char c : prefix.toCharArray()) { n = n.ch.get(c); if(n == null) return List.of(); } List<String> res = new ArrayList<>(); dfs(n, new StringBuilder(prefix), res); return res; } private void dfs(Node n, StringBuilder sb, List<String> res) { if(n.isEnd) res.add(sb.toString()); n.ch.forEach((c, child) -> { sb.append(c); dfs(child, sb, res); sb.deleteCharAt(sb.length()-1); }); } public boolean deleteWord(String word) { return delete(root, word, 0); } private boolean delete(Node n, String w, int i) { if(i == w.length()) { if(!n.isEnd) return false; n.isEnd = false; n.meaning = null; return n.ch.isEmpty(); } char c = w.charAt(i); Node child = n.ch.get(c); if(child == null) return false; boolean shouldDelete = delete(child, w, i+1); if(shouldDelete) n.ch.remove(c); return shouldDelete && !n.isEnd && n.ch.isEmpty(); } }
