    Java Data Types & Memory Model

    primitives vs objects · stack vs heap · boxing/unboxing traps
    🧠 Mental Model
    Stack = scratch paper per thread. Heap = shared whiteboard.Every thread gets its own stack — local variables and method frames live here, disappear when the method returns. Objects created with new go on the heap, shared across all threads, managed by GC. Primitives (int, boolean, double) live directly on the stack — no object header, no GC overhead, no null. Their wrapper types (Integer, Boolean) are heap objects.
    📐 Primitive vs Wrapper
    PrimitiveWrapperDefault ValueCan be null?Used in Collections?
    intInteger0NoNo (use Integer)
    booleanBooleanfalseNoNo
    doubleDouble0.0NoNo
    longLong0LNoNo
    charCharacter'\u0000'NoNo
    💻 The Boxing/Unboxing Traps
    Java — traps every interviewer tests
    // TRAP 1: Integer cache (-128 to 127) — == works by accident Integer a = 127, b = 127; System.out.println(a == b); // TRUE — cached objects, same reference Integer c = 128, d = 128; System.out.println(c == d); // FALSE — different heap objects, use .equals()! // TRAP 2: NullPointerException from unboxing Integer count = null; int total = count + 1; // NPE! Unboxing null Integer throws NullPointerException // TRAP 3: Performance in tight loops Long sum = 0L; // ← Long (object) for (long i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) sum += i; // 1M Long objects created! Use long sum=0L // RULE: use primitives everywhere possible. Use wrappers only when: // - Storing in collections (List<Integer>, Map<String, Double>) // - Need null to mean "unknown/not set" // - Using generic types (Optional<Integer>, CompletableFuture<Boolean>)
    🏭 Production Scenario
    A senior engineer reviews your code and says: 'You have an Integer cache bug'. The code is: Integer a = 127; Integer b = 127; System.out.println(a == b); // prints true. Integer c = 128; Integer d = 128; System.out.println(c == d); // prints false. Why?
    Integer is a wrapper class. == compares object references, not values. But 127 prints true. Java must be doing something special for small integers. What is the Integer cache range?
    Integer cache: Java caches Integer objects for values -128 to 127 (inclusive) in a static cache at class loading time. Integer.valueOf(127) always returns the same cached object. So a == b compares the same object reference → true. Integer.valueOf(128) creates a NEW object each time → c == d compares two different object references → false. Fix: Always use .equals() to compare Integer values: c.equals(d) → true. Never use == for object comparison (except for null checks and intentional reference equality). Other boxing traps: Long has the same -128 to 127 cache. Double and Float have NO cache — every Double.valueOf() creates a new object. Boolean: only two instances (TRUE and FALSE), always use == safely. Auto-unboxing NPE: Integer x = null; int y = x; → NullPointerException at the unboxing step. Always null-check before auto-unboxing. Performance: Boxing creates garbage. In hot loops, use int not Integer. For collections of primitives: use int[] or libraries like Eclipse Collections/Trove.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: "What is the difference between == and .equals() for Strings?"
    💭 Think
    == compares references (addresses). .equals() compares content. String pool complicates ==.
    → Complete answer
    Java
    String s1 = "hello"; // string pool String s2 = "hello"; // same pool object String s3 = new String("hello"); // new heap object s1 == s2; // TRUE — both point to pool s1 == s3; // FALSE — s3 is different heap object s1.equals(s3); // TRUE — same characters // RULE: ALWAYS use .equals() for String comparison. == is luck.
    Q: "What is deep copy vs shallow copy?"
    💭 Think
    Shallow: copies the reference. Deep: copies the entire object graph recursively.
    → Answer with code
    Java
    class Order { List<Item> items; // mutable field } // SHALLOW COPY — same items list reference Order copy = new Order(); copy.items = original.items; // modifying copy.items ALSO changes original.items! // DEEP COPY — independent copy of entire graph Order deepCopy = new Order(); deepCopy.items = new ArrayList<>(original.items); // new list, same Item references // For truly deep: copy each Item too, recursively // Production approach: serialise/deserialise, or use libraries (ModelMapper, MapStruct)
    🎯 Practice
    Write a method deepCopy(List<int[]> original) that returns a completely independent copy — modifying the returned list or its arrays must not affect the original.
    Hintnew ArrayList<>(original) copies the list but the int[] arrays inside are still shared references. You need to copy each array too with Arrays.copyOf().
    → Solution
    Java
    public static List<int[]> deepCopy(List<int[]> original) { return original.stream() .map(arr -> Arrays.copyOf(arr, arr.length)) .collect(Collectors.toList()); }

    equals() vs == · hashCode() Contract

    the most common Java bug source — know it cold
    🧠 The Golden Rule
    If a.equals(b) → a.hashCode() MUST == b.hashCode(). The reverse is NOT required.Violate this and HashMap/HashSet silently breaks. Two "equal" objects can land in different buckets and never find each other on lookup. This is one of the most common bugs in production Java code.
    💻 Correct Implementation
    Java — always override both together
    class Employee { private final String empId; private final String department; @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { if (this == o) return true; // same reference if (!(o instanceof Employee e)) return false; // null-safe + type check return Objects.equals(empId, e.empId) && Objects.equals(department, e.department); } @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(empId, department); // MUST use same fields as equals() } } // WHAT BREAKS if you only override equals(): // Set<Employee> set = new HashSet<>(); // set.add(new Employee("E1", "Eng")); // set.contains(new Employee("E1", "Eng")); // returns FALSE! // Because: hashCode() returns different values → different bucket → not found
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: "What are the contracts equals() must satisfy?"
    💭 Think
    Java defines 5 mathematical properties all equals() implementations must maintain.
    → The 5 contracts
    Reflexive: a.equals(a) is always true
    Symmetric: a.equals(b) ↔ b.equals(a)
    Transitive: a=b and b=c → a=c
    Consistent: same result for repeated calls (unless fields change)
    Null-safe: a.equals(null) always returns false (never throws NPE)
    Q: "Why should you use immutable fields for HashMap keys?"
    💭 Think
    What happens to the hashCode if you mutate a key after inserting it?
    → The mutable key bug
    The hashCode changes, but the entry stays in the OLD bucket. Future get() calls compute the NEW hash, look in the new bucket — find nothing. The entry is stranded forever: not accessible, not GC'd. This is a silent memory leak. Rule: use immutable objects (String, Integer, enums, record types) as map keys.
    🏭 Production Scenario
    "Our user deduplication Map is supposed to contain unique users by email, but we're seeing duplicates. Code review shows equals() is overridden but nothing else. What's wrong?"
    HashSet uses hashCode() to find the bucket first, then equals() within the bucket. If hashCode() isn't overridden, two equal-by-email users land in different buckets — equals() never runs.
    Root cause: hashCode() not overridden → default Object.hashCode() returns memory address → two User objects with same email have different hashCodes → land in different buckets → Set thinks they're distinct.
    Fix: Override hashCode() using the same email field as equals(). Verify with a unit test: set.add(u1); set.add(new User(same email)); assert set.size() == 1.
    🎯 Practice
    Write a Point class (x, y). Then demonstrate the bug: put Point(1,1) in a HashMap with value "A", then call map.get(new Point(1,1)) — show it returns null without hashCode, and "A" with hashCode.
    HintWithout hashCode(), two new Point(1,1) instances have different identity hashes → different buckets → get() can't find it. With Objects.hash(x,y) they produce the same hash → same bucket → equals() finds it.
    → Solution
    Java
    record Point(int x, int y) {} // Java 16+ record: auto-generates equals+hashCode+toString Map<Point, String> map = new HashMap<>(); map.put(new Point(1,1), "A"); System.out.println(map.get(new Point(1,1))); // "A" ✓ — record gives correct hashCode // Classic class without hashCode: would print null

    Checked vs Unchecked Exceptions

    exception hierarchy · try-catch-finally execution order · custom exceptions
    🧠 Mental Model
    Checked = compiler forces you to handle it. Unchecked = programming error you're trusted to avoid.Checked exceptions (extends Exception) model RECOVERABLE external failures: file not found, network timeout, DB connection lost. Unchecked (extends RuntimeException) model PROGRAMMING BUGS: null pointer, index out of bounds, illegal argument. The compiler enforces checked exceptions because the caller MUST decide: handle or propagate.
    📐 Exception Hierarchy
    💻 try-catch-finally Execution Order + Custom Exceptions
    Java
    // EXECUTION ORDER: try → (catch if exception) → finally ALWAYS public int demo() { try { return 1; // "1" is SAVED, finally runs first } finally { System.out.println("finally"); // ALWAYS runs, even with return // return 2; ← if uncommented, OVERRIDES the return 1! } } // returns 1 (finally ran but didn't override) // CUSTOM EXCEPTIONS — interview pattern class InsufficientFundsException extends Exception { // CHECKED — caller must handle private final double shortfall; public InsufficientFundsException(double shortfall) { super("Insufficient funds, shortfall: " + shortfall); this.shortfall = shortfall; } public double getShortfall() { return shortfall; } } class InvalidOrderStateException extends RuntimeException { // UNCHECKED — programming error public InvalidOrderStateException(String msg) { super(msg); } } // try-with-resources — automatically closes AutoCloseable resources try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection(); PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql)) { // conn and ps are closed automatically even if exception thrown } catch (SQLException e) { throw new DataAccessException(e); }
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Your code calls a third-party library method that throws a checked IOException. A teammate says 'just wrap it in RuntimeException and move on'. Your tech lead says 'that is an anti-pattern'. Who is right and why?
    Checked exception means the compiler forces callers to handle it. Wrapping in RuntimeException makes it unchecked — callers are no longer forced to handle it. When is this appropriate and when is it harmful?
    When wrapping IS appropriate: The caller genuinely cannot recover from the exception (e.g., a config file not found at startup — no point propagating IOException through 10 layers, wrap it in an IllegalStateException with a clear message). The exception represents a programming error that should never happen in correct code. Spring does this: JdbcTemplate wraps all SQLExceptions in DataAccessException (unchecked) — because callers usually cannot meaningfully handle DB-level errors. When wrapping is an anti-pattern: The caller CAN and SHOULD handle the exception (file not found → prompt user for a different file, network timeout → retry logic). Wrapping makes it easy for callers to accidentally swallow the exception. Rules: (1) If the caller can recover: keep it checked. (2) If it's a system-level failure the caller cannot handle: wrap in a descriptive RuntimeException. (3) ALWAYS preserve the original exception as the cause: new RuntimeException('Failed to load config', originalException) — never lose the stack trace. (4) Log at the wrapping site: log.error('Failed to process', e) before re-throwing.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: "When would you choose checked vs unchecked for your own custom exception?"
    💭 Think
    Is the caller expected to recover from this? Or is it a programming mistake?
    → Decision rule
    Use checked when the caller CAN and SHOULD recover: "file not found" → try another path; "network timeout" → retry. Use unchecked when it's a programming bug that should never happen in correct code: "null argument" → fix the code; "invalid state transition" → fix the state machine. Modern practice: many frameworks (Spring) default to unchecked for all exceptions — checked exceptions create verbose signatures and don't compose well with lambdas.
    Q: "What happens when both catch and finally throw exceptions?"
    💭 Think
    There can only be one exception propagating. Which one wins?
    → The suppressed exception trap
    If finally throws, it REPLACES the original exception. The original is lost — silently swallowed. This is why finally blocks should never throw. In try-with-resources, Java handles this better: if both the body and close() throw, the close() exception is added as a suppressed exception (accessible via getSuppressed()), and the body exception propagates. Use Throwable.getSuppressed() to see them.
    🎯 Practice
    Implement a method readConfig(String path) that reads a JSON config file. It should: throw a checked ConfigNotFoundException if the file doesn't exist, throw an unchecked ConfigParseException if the JSON is malformed, and always close the reader.
    HintUse try-with-resources for the reader (auto-close). Catch FileNotFoundException and wrap in ConfigNotFoundException (checked). Catch JSONParseException and wrap in ConfigParseException (unchecked — caller can't fix bad JSON at runtime).
    → Solution
    Java
    class ConfigNotFoundException extends Exception { ConfigNotFoundException(String path) { super("Config not found: " + path); } } class ConfigParseException extends RuntimeException { ConfigParseException(String path, Throwable cause) { super("Invalid JSON in: " + path, cause); } } public Config readConfig(String path) throws ConfigNotFoundException { try (BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(path))) { return objectMapper.readValue(reader, Config.class); } catch (FileNotFoundException e) { throw new ConfigNotFoundException(path); // checked — caller decides what to do } catch (IOException e) { throw new ConfigParseException(path, e); // unchecked — can't recover from bad JSON } }

    Collections Framework

    List · Set · Map · Queue — choosing the right one and why
    🧠 Decision Tree
    Ask three questions: do you need duplicates? does order matter? do you need key-value pairs?Need duplicates + order → List. No duplicates → Set. Key-value lookups → Map. FIFO/LIFO processing → Queue/Deque. The specific implementation choice (ArrayList vs LinkedList, HashMap vs TreeMap) depends on access patterns — always justify your choice in an interview.
    ⚠️ The Complete Comparison Matrix
    InterfaceImplementationOrderDuplicatesNullget(i)Best For
    ListArrayListInsertionYesYesO(1)Random access, iteration
    ListLinkedListInsertionYesYesO(n)Deque operations only
    SetHashSetNoneNo1 nullN/AFast contains(), dedup
    SetLinkedHashSetInsertionNo1 nullN/ADedup + insertion order
    SetTreeSetSortedNoNoN/ASorted unique elements
    MapHashMapNoneKeys: No1 null keyO(1)General key-value lookup
    MapLinkedHashMapInsertionKeys: No1 null keyO(1)LRU cache, ordered map
    MapTreeMapSorted keyKeys: NoNoO(log n)Range queries, sorted keys
    QueueArrayDequeFIFO/LIFOYesNoN/AStack, queue, sliding window
    QueuePriorityQueueHeap orderYesNoN/ATop-K, scheduling
    💻 Interview-Critical Patterns
    Java — patterns every SDE-2 must know
    // 1. Top-K elements with PriorityQueue (min-heap of size K) int[] topK(int[] nums, int k) { PriorityQueue<Integer> minHeap = new PriorityQueue<>(); for (int n : nums) { minHeap.offer(n); if (minHeap.size() > k) minHeap.poll(); // evict smallest } return minHeap.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).toArray(); } // 2. LRU cache via LinkedHashMap (accessOrder=true) var lru = new LinkedHashMap<Integer, Integer>(16, 0.75f, true) { protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<Integer,Integer> e) { return size() > 100; } }; // 3. Frequency map pattern Map<String, Long> freq = words.stream() .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(w -> w, Collectors.counting())); // 4. Safely iterate and remove (use removeIf) list.removeIf(s -> s.startsWith("temp-")); // 5. Collections utility — unmodifiable view (not a copy!) List<String> immutable = Collections.unmodifiableList(mutableList); // List.of() (Java 9+) creates truly immutable, throws on add/set List<String> fixed = List.of("a", "b", "c");
    🏭 Production Scenario
    You have a List of 1 million User objects and you need to: filter active users, sort by last login date, take the top 1000, and extract their email addresses. A colleague writes 4 separate for-loops. You rewrite it as a Stream chain. What is the performance difference?
    Four for-loops create 3 intermediate collections (1M active users list, sorted list, top-1000 list). Stream operations are lazy — filter + sorted + limit + map are fused into one pass where possible. What does 'lazy' mean for limit?
    Stream laziness: filter() and map() are lazy — they don't execute until a terminal operation (collect, findFirst) is called. limit(1000) is a short-circuit operation — once 1000 elements are collected, processing stops. sorted() is a stateful intermediate operation — it must see ALL elements before it can sort (not lazy). Performance comparison: 4 for-loops: 1M filter → 800K intermediate list → sort 800K → take 1000 → map 1000 → 3 intermediate collections, ~3M object allocations. Stream: filter → sort all matching → limit to 1000 → map — 1 intermediate sort, no intermediate lists. Parallel stream: users.parallelStream() splits the list across CPU cores. For CPU-bound operations (complex filtering, heavy mapping): parallel can be 4-8x faster. For I/O-bound or very fast operations: parallel is slower (thread coordination overhead). fail-fast vs fail-safe: ArrayList iterator: fail-fast — throws ConcurrentModificationException if list is modified during iteration. CopyOnWriteArrayList iterator: fail-safe — iterates over a snapshot, never throws, but may not see recent writes.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: "What is fail-fast vs fail-safe iterator?"
    💭 Think
    What happens when the collection is modified during iteration?
    → Answer
    Fail-fast: HashMap, ArrayList iterators check a modCount. If collection is modified during iteration (not via iterator.remove()), throws ConcurrentModificationException immediately. Fail-safe: CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentHashMap iterate a snapshot/view — never throw CME but may not see concurrent updates. Use fail-safe when iterating under concurrent modification; use fail-fast (and iterator.remove()) for single-threaded safe removal during iteration.
    Q: "TreeMap vs HashMap — when do you choose TreeMap?"
    💭 Think
    TreeMap has O(log n) vs HashMap's O(1). When is the sort order worth that cost?
    → Answer
    Choose TreeMap when: (1) You need keys in sorted order (alphabetical, numeric). (2) You need range queries: subMap(from, to), headMap(to), tailMap(from) — "give me all entries with keys between 'A' and 'M'". (3) You need first/last key: firstKey(), floorKey(). Use case: a leaderboard where you need "all players with score between 1000 and 2000" — TreeMap makes this trivially efficient.
    🎯 Practice
    Given a string, find the first non-repeating character. Input: "aabbcde" → output: 'c'. Write it using only one pass through the string.
    HintLinkedHashMap preserves insertion order. Map each char to its count. Second pass (over entry set in insertion order) finds first entry with count==1. Actually you can do it in one string pass if you track first-seen index too.
    → Solution
    Java
    public char firstNonRepeating(String s) { Map<Character, Integer> count = new LinkedHashMap<>(); // preserves insertion order for (char c : s.toCharArray()) count.merge(c, 1, Integer::sum); return count.entrySet().stream() .filter(e -> e.getValue() == 1) .map(Map.Entry::getKey) .findFirst().orElse('\0'); }

    ThreadLocal — Per-Thread State

    the right tool for request-scoped context · and the memory-leak trap
    🧠 Mental Model
    ThreadLocal is like giving each thread its own private locker.Every thread that reads/writes a ThreadLocal variable gets its own completely independent copy. Thread A setting userId="U1" doesn't affect Thread B's userId — even though they share the same ThreadLocal object reference. This is perfect for request-scoped context in web applications: each HTTP request runs on its own thread, so each has its own private copy of request context, user details, transaction state.
    💻 Production Use Case: Request Context
    Java — Spring-style request context via ThreadLocal
    public class RequestContext { private static final ThreadLocal<RequestContext> CTX = new ThreadLocal<>(); private String userId, traceId, tenantId; public static void set(RequestContext ctx) { CTX.set(ctx); } public static RequestContext get() { return CTX.get(); } public static void clear() { CTX.remove(); } // CRITICAL — see memory leak below } // Filter: runs per-request, sets and clears context @Component public class RequestContextFilter implements Filter { public void doFilter(ServletRequest req, ServletResponse res, FilterChain chain) throws IOException, ServletException { try { HttpServletRequest http = (HttpServletRequest) req; RequestContext ctx = new RequestContext(); ctx.setUserId(http.getHeader("X-User-Id")); ctx.setTraceId(http.getHeader("X-Trace-Id")); RequestContext.set(ctx); chain.doFilter(req, res); // whole request runs with this context available } finally { RequestContext.clear(); // MUST CLEAR — thread returns to pool, not cleaned up by GC } } } // Anywhere in the call stack (Service, Repository, etc.) — no parameter passing needed: String userId = RequestContext.get().getUserId(); // thread-safe, no synchronization needed
    ⚠️ The Memory Leak Trap
    Thread pools reuse threads — ThreadLocals persist!

    In a web server (Tomcat, Netty), threads are pooled — they don't die after each request. If you set a ThreadLocal but don't call remove(), the value stays on that thread for its entire lifetime. The next request served by the same thread sees the PREVIOUS request's context. This is a privacy violation AND a memory leak. Always call ThreadLocal.remove() in a finally block after each request.

    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: "How does ThreadLocal work internally?"
    💭 Think
    Each Thread object has a map. The ThreadLocal is the key.
    → Internals
    Each Thread object has a field: Thread.threadLocals of type ThreadLocalMap. When you call threadLocal.set(value), Java looks up the current Thread, gets its ThreadLocalMap, and puts an entry: {this ThreadLocal → value}. When you call threadLocal.get(), it retrieves the current Thread's map and looks up this ThreadLocal as the key. So the data lives on the Thread, not the ThreadLocal object — which is why threads have independent copies.
    Q: "When should you use InheritableThreadLocal?"
    💭 Think
    What if you spawn child threads from a request thread — do they need the same context?
    → Answer
    InheritableThreadLocal copies the parent thread's value to child threads at creation time. Use when spawning new threads that need the request context (e.g., trace ID for distributed tracing in async sub-tasks). Warning: if you use thread pools, the parent's context is copied at pool-thread creation time (once), not at task submission time — so the inherited value may be stale. Libraries like TransmittableThreadLocal (Alibaba) solve this for thread-pool scenarios.
    🏭 Payment Gateway Scenario — Thread-Safe Balance Updates
    "Design a payment gateway where multiple transactions process concurrently and account balance updates must be thread-safe, consistent, and auditable."
    Multiple threads updating the same balance → race condition. Need: atomicity for the update, isolation between unrelated accounts, audit trail of each transaction, rollback on failure.
    Solution 1: Database-level locking (Preferred for production)
    Java — optimistic locking via JPA @Version
    @Entity class Account { @Id String id; BigDecimal balance; @Version long version; // JPA auto-increments on every update } @Transactional public void debit(String accountId, BigDecimal amount) { Account acc = accountRepo.findById(accountId).orElseThrow(); if (acc.getBalance().compareTo(amount) < 0) throw new InsufficientFundsException(amount.subtract(acc.getBalance()).doubleValue()); acc.setBalance(acc.getBalance().subtract(amount)); accountRepo.save(acc); // If another thread updated account between our read and save: // JPA throws OptimisticLockException → transaction rolls back → caller retries // No data corruption possible — version mismatch caught at save time } // ThreadLocal used here for: audit logging the current userId without parameter passing // RequestContext.get().getUserId() → saved with each transaction audit record
    Solution 2: In-memory atomic operations (for rate limiting, counters) Use ConcurrentHashMap + compute() for per-account in-memory state, backed by periodic DB sync. Suitable for non-critical metrics, not financial balances.
    🎯 Practice
    Implement a multi-tenant request logger that logs each request with the current tenant ID, without passing the tenant ID as a parameter through 5 service layers.
    HintThreadLocal holds the tenant ID for the duration of the request. A Filter sets it at the start, removes it in finally. Every service layer reads it from the ThreadLocal — no parameter passing needed.
    → Solution
    Java
    public class TenantContext { private static final ThreadLocal<String> TENANT = new ThreadLocal<>(); public static void set(String id) { TENANT.set(id); } public static String get() { return TENANT.get(); } public static void clear() { TENANT.remove(); } } // Filter: TenantContext.set(request.getHeader("X-Tenant-Id")) in try, clear() in finally // AOP logging aspect: log.info("[{}] {}", TenantContext.get(), message) — no params needed

    wait() vs sleep() vs join()

    the three thread-pause mechanisms — completely different purposes
    🧠 Mental Model
    sleep() = set an alarm and rest. wait() = wait for someone to wake you. join() = wait for another thread to finish its work.These are the three ways a thread gives up CPU time, but they differ fundamentally in: what class they belong to, whether they release locks, and what wakes them up.
    ⚠️ Key Differences Table
    MethodDefined onReleases lock?Woken up byMust be in synchronized?
    sleep(ms)Thread (static)NO — holds lockTimer expiry / interruptNo
    wait()ObjectYES — releases monitornotify() / notifyAll() / interruptYES — must own monitor
    join()ThreadN/A (not lock-based)Target thread terminatesNo
    💻 wait/notify — Producer-Consumer Pattern
    Java — wait/notify correctly
    class BoundedBuffer<T> { private final Queue<T> queue = new LinkedList<>(); private final int capacity; public synchronized void put(T item) throws InterruptedException { while (queue.size() == capacity) { // WHILE, not if — guard against spurious wakeups wait(); // releases lock + suspends; woken by take()'s notifyAll() } queue.add(item); notifyAll(); // wake any waiting consumers } public synchronized T take() throws InterruptedException { while (queue.isEmpty()) { wait(); // wait for producer } T item = queue.poll(); notifyAll(); // wake any waiting producers return item; } } // CRITICAL: Always use WHILE loop around wait(), never IF. // "Spurious wakeups" — JVM can wake a thread without notify() being called. // The while re-checks the condition and re-waits if still not satisfied.
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Your background thread is stuck. A colleague suggests 'call thread.stop()'. You say that is dangerous. Another suggests Thread.sleep(). The real fix is wait()/notify(). When should you use each and why is stop() dangerous?
    thread.stop() is deprecated and dangerous. sleep() wastes CPU in a busy-wait pattern. wait()/notify() is the proper inter-thread coordination mechanism. What is the difference between them at the JVM level?
    Thread.stop() — never use: Deprecated since Java 1.1. stop() throws a ThreadDeath error at an arbitrary point in the thread's execution, potentially while holding a lock — leaves shared objects in an inconsistent state. The lock is released but the object's invariants are broken. Thread.sleep(ms): Current thread pauses for ms milliseconds. Thread keeps all locks it holds. Useful for: delay/backoff, rate limiting within a single thread. Not useful for: waiting for a condition (you don't know when the condition becomes true). Object.wait(): Must be called inside synchronized(obj). Releases the obj's lock and suspends the thread. Another thread calls obj.notify() → the waiting thread re-acquires the lock and continues. Use for: producer-consumer, waiting for a condition. Always in a while loop (spurious wakeups): while(!condition) { obj.wait(); } LockSupport.park(): Modern alternative to wait(). Used by java.util.concurrent internals. More precise: LockSupport.parkNanos(nanos) for nanosecond precision. join(): Current thread waits until the target thread finishes. Used to wait for a spawned thread to complete before proceeding.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: "Why does wait() release the lock but sleep() doesn't? What's the implication?"
    💭 Think
    wait() is designed for inter-thread communication — the waiting thread must let others in to make progress and call notify().
    → Answer
    wait() is designed for condition-based waiting: "I'm waiting for something to be true — let others in to make it true, then wake me." If wait() held the lock, nobody could enter the synchronized block to call notify() — deadlock guaranteed. sleep() is just a time delay with no inter-thread communication intent — it doesn't need to release the lock. Implication: NEVER call sleep() inside a synchronized block if other threads need that lock during the sleep period — they'll be blocked unnecessarily.
    Q: "What is a spurious wakeup and how do you protect against it?"
    💭 Think
    The JVM and OS can wake a waiting thread without notify() being called. Why and how do you defend?
    → Answer
    POSIX threads (which the JVM sits on) allow spurious wakeups as a side effect of how condition variables work at the OS level — it's a performance trade-off in the OS implementation. Defense: ALWAYS use a while loop instead of if: while (!condition) { wait(); }. After every wakeup (spurious or real), re-check the condition. If still not satisfied, call wait() again. This is the idiomatic Java pattern for wait/notify.
    🎯 Practice
    Implement a Semaphore-like class using only wait/notifyAll that allows at most N threads to access a resource concurrently.
    HintTrack a counter of "permits available". acquire() waits while permits==0. release() increments permits and notifies. Use synchronized + while loop + wait().
    → Solution
    Java
    class MySemaphore { private int permits; MySemaphore(int n) { this.permits = n; } public synchronized void acquire() throws InterruptedException { while (permits == 0) wait(); // while: guard against spurious wakeups permits--; } public synchronized void release() { permits++; notifyAll(); // wake all waiting threads; they'll re-check permits } } // Production: use java.util.concurrent.Semaphore instead — but knowing the // wait/notify implementation demonstrates deep understanding.

    Class Loading Mechanism

    Bootstrap · Platform · Application · Delegation model · practical impact
    🧠 Mental Model
    Class loading is hierarchical: always ask your parent first.When a class is needed, the JVM follows the Parent Delegation Model: the Application ClassLoader delegates to Platform ClassLoader, which delegates to Bootstrap ClassLoader. The Bootstrap ClassLoader tries to load from its classes (java.lang, java.util). Only if it fails does the child try. This prevents malicious code from replacing java.lang.String with a fake version — Bootstrap always wins for core classes.
    📐 Delegation Hierarchy
    💻 Custom ClassLoader & Class Loading in Practice
    Java — class loading lifecycle + custom loader
    // Class Loading has 3 phases: // 1. LOADING — read .class file bytes (via ClassLoader) // 2. LINKING: Verify (bytecode valid?) → Prepare (allocate static fields) → Resolve (symbolic refs) // 3. INITIALIZATION — run static initializer blocks and assign static field values // Classes loaded only ONCE per ClassLoader — subsequent loads return cached Class object Class<?> clazz = Class.forName("com.example.Service"); // loads (if not already loaded) Object instance = clazz.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance(); // reflection instantiation // Custom ClassLoader — load plugins, hot-reload, bytecode transformation class PluginClassLoader extends ClassLoader { private final Path pluginDir; @Override protected Class<?> findClass(String name) throws ClassNotFoundException { try { byte[] bytes = Files.readAllBytes(pluginDir.resolve(name.replace(".","/") + ".class")); return defineClass(name, bytes, 0, bytes.length); // registers with JVM } catch (IOException e) { throw new ClassNotFoundException(name, e); } } } // Hot reload: create a NEW PluginClassLoader, load the class — old instance is GC'd when no refs
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Your app uses two versions of the same library — v1.0 in your code and v2.0 pulled in transitively. At runtime, the wrong version's class is loaded and methods are missing. How does Java's class loading work and how do you diagnose this?
    Java class loading uses a parent delegation model. Three built-in loaders: Bootstrap, Platform, Application. A class is loaded by the first loader in the hierarchy that can find it. In Maven: closest-wins dependency resolution determines which JAR is on the classpath.
    Parent delegation: When ClassLoader is asked to load Foo, it first asks its parent. Bootstrap (rt.jar/java.*) → Platform (javax.*, ext) → Application (classpath). This prevents you from shadowing java.lang.String with your own version. Class loading phases: Loading (find .class, create Class object) → Linking (verify bytecode, prepare static fields, resolve symbolic refs) → Initialisation (run static blocks). Diagnosing version conflicts: Add -verbose:class JVM flag → prints every class load with its source JAR. Or: getClass().getProtectionDomain().getCodeSource().getLocation() prints the JAR that loaded a class. Fix: In Maven: mvn dependency:tree shows the conflict. Use <exclusions> to exclude the transitive version, declare your required version explicitly. In multi-module apps: parent POM <dependencyManagement> pins versions for all child modules. OSGi / custom ClassLoaders: If you need true classloader isolation (different versions in the same JVM), use OSGi or a custom ClassLoader per module — used by application servers (Tomcat, JBoss).
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: "What is ClassNotFoundException vs NoClassDefFoundError?"
    💭 Think
    One happens at runtime via reflection. The other happens when a class was there at compile time but missing at runtime.
    → Answer
    ClassNotFoundException: Thrown by Class.forName() or ClassLoader.loadClass() when the class file isn't found. It's a checked exception — expected when loading optional plugins. NoClassDefFoundError: Thrown when the JVM finds a class reference in bytecode (it was there at compile time) but can't find the class file at runtime. This is an Error — it means the classpath is broken (jar missing, version mismatch). ClassNotFoundException = programmatic loading failed. NoClassDefFoundError = classpath/deployment problem.
    Q: How does Spring Boot handle class loading for dynamically loaded plugins at runtime without restarting the JVM?
    💡 Think First
    If you load a new JAR at runtime, its classes need a ClassLoader that can find them. The default Application ClassLoader only knows the classpath at startup. How do you make new JARs visible?
    ➔ Complete Answer
    Create a URLClassLoader with the JAR's URL: new URLClassLoader(new URL[]{jar.toURI().toURL()}, Thread.currentThread().getContextClassLoader()). Load the plugin class: classLoader.loadClass("com.plugin.MyPlugin"). Cast to a known interface (PluginInterface) and invoke. Each plugin gets its own ClassLoader — different plugins can use different versions of the same library (ClassLoader isolation). Spring Boot DevTools uses this pattern: a restart ClassLoader is swapped on file change, reloading only application classes while keeping JVM-level classes (Spring framework, dependencies) in the parent ClassLoader. This makes restarts fast (typically under 1 second). For full hot-swap without restart: JRebel uses Java Instrumentation API (java.lang.instrument) to redefine classes in-place without a new ClassLoader.
    🎯 Practice Task
    A multi-tenant SaaS loads each customer's plugin as a separate JAR at runtime. Each plugin may use a different version of a shared library (e.g., Jackson 2.14 vs 2.15). The app itself uses Jackson 2.16. Implement isolated ClassLoading so plugins cannot interfere with each other or with the host application.
    💡 HintEach plugin gets its own URLClassLoader with the plugin JAR as its classpath. Set the HOST application ClassLoader as the parent — but override loadClass() to check the plugin JAR FIRST (child-first delegation), breaking the default parent-first delegation. This means the plugin's Jackson 2.14 is loaded from the plugin JAR, not the host's Jackson 2.16.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — isolated plugin ClassLoader
    class PluginClassLoader extends URLClassLoader { private static final Set<String> HOST_PACKAGES = Set.of("java.", "javax.", "com.myapp.api."); // always from host PluginClassLoader(URL[] pluginJarUrls, ClassLoader hostLoader) { super(pluginJarUrls, hostLoader); } @Override protected Class<?> loadClass(String name, boolean resolve) throws ClassNotFoundException { // Host packages: always delegate to parent (consistency) if(HOST_PACKAGES.stream().anyMatch(name::startsWith)) return super.loadClass(name, resolve); // Plugin classes: try plugin JAR first (child-first) try { return findClass(name); } // look in plugin JAR catch (ClassNotFoundException e) { return super.loadClass(name, resolve); // fall back to host } } } // Usage: var loader = new PluginClassLoader( new URL[]{pluginJar.toURI().toURL()}, Thread.currentThread().getContextClassLoader()); Class<?> pluginClass = loader.loadClass("com.customer.Plugin"); PluginInterface plugin = (PluginInterface) pluginClass.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance();
    🎯 Practice
    Explain when you'd use a custom ClassLoader in a real project. What problem does it solve that the standard classpath doesn't?
    HintThink about: loading plugins/extensions at runtime without restarting, loading the same class from different JARs simultaneously (multi-version), bytecode manipulation for AOP/profiling, sandboxing untrusted code.
    → Answer
    Real use cases
    // 1. IDE Plugin systems (IntelliJ, Eclipse) — each plugin has its own ClassLoader // → plugins can use different library versions without conflicts // → plugin can be unloaded by dereferencing its ClassLoader // 2. Application servers (Tomcat, JBoss) — each WAR gets its own ClassLoader // → two WARs can use different versions of the same library // 3. Hot code reload (JRebel, Spring DevTools) // → replace ClassLoader with new one pointing to recompiled classes // 4. Bytecode instrumentation (Java agents, AOP, profilers like YourKit) // → override loadClass() to transform bytecode before defineClass() // → add logging/timing/null checks to every method without source changes // 5. Secure sandboxing — restrict what loaded code can access // → override loadClass() to block certain package loads // → used in online judge systems to prevent sandbox escapes

    Scenario: Payment Gateway Thread Safety

    the complete answer — multiple approaches, trade-offs, production thinking
    🧠 The Question
    "You are developing a payment gateway where multiple transactions are processed concurrently. How would you ensure thread-safe account balance updates?"This tests: your understanding of race conditions, your knowledge of Java concurrency primitives AND database-level locking, your ability to weigh trade-offs, and whether you think about production concerns (audit, rollback, performance).
    ⚠️ The Wrong Answer
    Java — naive and broken
    // ✗ BROKEN — check-then-act is not atomic class Account { private double balance; public void debit(double amount) { if (balance >= amount) { // Thread A reads 1000, Thread B reads 1000 balance -= amount; // BOTH subtract 900 → balance goes negative! } } } // Also wrong: synchronized on the method alone doesn't help if accounts // in a real system are fetched from DB — the in-memory object isn't shared!
    💻 The Complete Answer — 3 Layers
    Java + Spring — production-grade solution
    // LAYER 1: Entity with optimistic locking (handles 99% of cases) @Entity public class Account { @Id private String id; private BigDecimal balance; @Version private long version; // incremented on every save } @Service public class PaymentService { @Transactional // LAYER 2: DB transaction wraps everything public Payment processPayment(PaymentRequest req) { // LAYER 3: Pessimistic lock for critical paths (overdraft prevention) Account acc = accountRepo.findByIdWithLock(req.getAccountId()); // SELECT FOR UPDATE if (acc.getBalance().compareTo(req.getAmount()) < 0) throw new InsufficientFundsException(req.getAmount().subtract(acc.getBalance()).doubleValue()); acc.setBalance(acc.getBalance().subtract(req.getAmount())); accountRepo.save(acc); Payment payment = new Payment(req, PaymentStatus.SUCCESS); paymentRepo.save(payment); // audit record — immutable history eventPublisher.publishEvent(new PaymentProcessedEvent(payment)); // async: email, analytics return payment; } } // Repository with pessimistic lock query interface AccountRepository extends JpaRepository<Account, String> { @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) // SELECT ... FOR UPDATE @Query("SELECT a FROM Account a WHERE a.id = :id") Optional<Account> findByIdWithLock(String id); }
    💡 Trade-off Discussion (What Interviewers Want to Hear)
    Optimistic vs Pessimistic Locking

    Optimistic (JPA @Version): low contention, high throughput, fails with OptimisticLockException on conflict — retry needed. Good for read-heavy, occasionally-conflicting scenarios.
    Pessimistic (SELECT FOR UPDATE): blocks other transactions — lower throughput but zero retry logic. Good for financial operations where conflicts are common and double-spending is catastrophic.

    Why NOT use synchronized in Java for this?

    synchronized is JVM-local. In a multi-instance deployment (2+ pods), Thread-A on Pod-1 and Thread-B on Pod-2 can both read the same account from DB simultaneously — Java synchronization doesn't help. You NEED database-level locking to coordinate across instances.

    Idempotency

    Payment retries must be safe. Each payment request gets a client-generated idempotency key. Server stores the result keyed by idempotency key. Duplicate requests return the cached result — no double-charge.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    A payment service processes 500 concurrent transactions. Each transaction reads account balance, checks it is sufficient, deducts the amount. Under load, accounts go negative. Diagnose and fix.
    Read-check-act on shared mutable state without synchronization = race condition. Two threads both read balance=1000, both check 1000>=800, both deduct 800. Balance becomes 200 instead of the correct -600 rejection.
    Root cause: check-then-act is not atomic. Three solutions: (1) synchronized method: entire deduct() synchronized — correct but serializes all transactions for one account. (2) Optimistic locking in DB: UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-? WHERE id=? AND balance>=? — let the DB handle atomicity. Zero rows updated = insufficient funds. Best for distributed systems. (3) Account-level lock: ConcurrentHashMap<accountId, ReentrantLock> — lock per account, not globally. Transactions on different accounts run in parallel. Same-account transactions serialize. Production answer: always use DB-level atomic update for financial transactions — never rely on application-level locking across multiple servers.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: Two transactions simultaneously transfer money between Account A and Account B. How do you prevent deadlock?
    💭 Think First
    Transaction 1: lock A, then lock B. Transaction 2: lock B, then lock A. Classic deadlock. What is the prevention strategy?
    → Complete Answer
    Lock ordering: always acquire locks in a consistent global order (e.g., by account ID, lowest first). Transaction 1 and Transaction 2 both try to lock min(A,B) first, then max(A,B). No circular wait is possible. Implementation: if(account1.id < account2.id) { lock(account1); lock(account2); } else { lock(account2); lock(account1); }. This is the standard deadlock prevention technique for multi-resource locking. Alternative: use a single DB transaction with SELECT FOR UPDATE on both rows in a consistent order — the DB handles the deadlock detection and retries.
    Q: How do you write a unit test that reliably catches this race condition?
    💭 Think First
    Race conditions are non-deterministic — they may not appear on every run. How do you make the test deterministic?
    → Complete Answer
    Use CountDownLatch to synchronize thread starts: both threads are set up and waiting at a latch. The test releases them simultaneously. Use a tight loop (10000 iterations) to increase the probability of interleaving. Assert the final balance — if it ever goes negative, the test fails. Better: use a testing framework like jcstress (Java Concurrency Stress Tests) which uses ByteBuddy to instrument memory access and explore all possible thread interleavings systematically. For production code: rely on TDD with DB-level atomic operations (easier to reason about) rather than trying to test all concurrency scenarios at the unit level.
    🎯 Practice
    An account has balance ₹1000. Two concurrent requests both try to debit ₹900. Design the system so exactly one succeeds and one gets "insufficient funds" — no negative balance possible.
    HintWithout a lock, both read ₹1000, both see ₹1000 >= ₹900, both subtract → -₹800. With SELECT FOR UPDATE, the second transaction blocks until the first commits — then reads ₹100, which is less than ₹900, and fails correctly.
    → Answer
    SQL + Java — the correct flow
    -- Transaction A: -- BEGIN; -- SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id='ACC1' FOR UPDATE; → locks row, gets 1000 -- (balance=1000 >= 900: ok) -- UPDATE accounts SET balance=100 WHERE id='ACC1'; -- COMMIT; → releases lock -- Transaction B (was blocked on SELECT FOR UPDATE): -- Now gets the lock, reads balance=100 -- (100 < 900: InsufficientFunds) → ROLLBACK -- Result: A succeeds (balance=100), B fails gracefully. No negative balance possible. -- This is why SELECT FOR UPDATE is the correct tool for financial debit operations.
    🎯 Practice Task
    Fix the PaymentService.deduct(accountId, amount) method using DB-level optimistic locking. The method should return true if the deduction succeeded and false if the balance was insufficient — never allowing a negative balance.
    Hint — think before readingUse a single atomic UPDATE with a WHERE balance >= amount condition. Check the number of rows affected — 0 means the condition failed (insufficient funds), 1 means success. No application-level locking needed.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — atomic DB deduction
    @Service class PaymentService { @Autowired JdbcTemplate jdbc; @Transactional public boolean deduct(String accountId, BigDecimal amount) { // Atomic: check + deduct in ONE SQL statement int rows = jdbc.update( "UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id = ? AND balance >= ?", amount, accountId, amount ); return rows == 1; // 0 = insufficient funds, 1 = success // No application lock needed — DB guarantees atomicity within the transaction } }

    Java 8+ Features

    Lambda · Functional Interfaces · Optional · Method References · the patterns interviews test
    🧠 Mental Model
    Java 8 brought functional programming to Java — functions as first-class citizens.Before Java 8, you passed behavior via anonymous inner classes (verbose). Lambda expressions are syntactic sugar for single-method interface implementations. A functional interface is any interface with exactly one abstract method — the target for a lambda. Four built-in functional interfaces cover 95% of use cases.
    📐 Four Core Functional Interfaces
    InterfaceSignatureUseExample
    Function<T,R>R apply(T t)Transform: T → Rs -> s.toUpperCase()
    Predicate<T>boolean test(T t)Filter: T → booleann -> n > 0
    Consumer<T>void accept(T t)Side effect: consume TSystem.out::println
    Supplier<T>T get()Factory: produce TArrayList::new
    💻 Interview-Critical Java 8 Patterns
    Java 8 — patterns you will be asked to write
    // METHOD REFERENCES — 4 types users.forEach(System.out::println); // instance method of specific object users.stream().map(User::getName); // instance method of arbitrary instance users.stream().filter(Objects::nonNull); // static method users.stream().map(User::new); // constructor reference // OPTIONAL — chain without null checks Optional<String> name = userRepo.findById(id) .map(User::getProfile) // skipped if empty .map(Profile::getDisplayName) // skipped if empty .filter(n -> !n.isBlank()); String display = name .orElseGet(() -> "Anonymous"); // lazy default — only evaluated if needed // COMPOSE FUNCTIONS Function<String, String> trim = String::strip; Function<String, String> upper = String::toUpperCase; Function<String, String> sanitize = trim.andThen(upper); // trim THEN upper // PREDICATE CHAINING Predicate<User> active = u -> u.isActive(); Predicate<User> premium = u -> u.isPremium(); users.stream().filter(active.and(premium)).collect(Collectors.toList()); // CUSTOM FUNCTIONAL INTERFACE @FunctionalInterface interface ThrowingFunction<T, R> { R apply(T t) throws Exception; // lets lambdas throw checked exceptions }
    🏭 Production Scenario
    You are code-reviewing a junior's PR. They wrote a loop to collect active user emails: List emails = new ArrayList<>(); for (User u : users) { if (u.isActive()) emails.add(u.getEmail()); }. Rewrite this using Java 8 streams, Optional, and method references. Then explain what happens if getEmail() can return null.
    Stream: filter(isActive) → map(getEmail) → collect(toList()). But if getEmail() can return null, you get a list with nulls. Use filter(Objects::nonNull) after map, or change getEmail() to return Optional.
    Stream rewrite: users.stream().filter(User::isActive).map(User::getEmail).collect(Collectors.toList()). Method references (User::isActive, User::getEmail) are more readable than lambdas when the lambda body is a single method call. Handling null emails: Option 1: .filter(Objects::nonNull) after map. Option 2: Change signature to Optional<String> getEmail() and use .flatMap(User::getEmail). Optional best practices: Optional.isPresent() then .get() is the old pattern — prefer: optional.ifPresent(email -> send(email)), optional.map(String::toUpperCase).orElse('N/A'), optional.orElseThrow(() -> new RuntimeException('email required')). Never: optional.get() without checking (throws NoSuchElementException). Java 8 vs Java 17 streams: Java 16: Collectors.toList() replaced by .toList() (returns immutable list). Java 17+: record classes, sealed classes, pattern matching instanceof. Java 21: virtual threads (Project Loom) — instead of CompletableFuture for async, use virtual threads with blocking I/O directly.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: "What is the difference between map() and flatMap() in Optional?"
    💭 Think
    map() wraps the result in Optional. flatMap() is used when the function already returns Optional.
    → Answer with code
    Java
    // findById returns Optional<User> // getAddress returns Optional<Address> (might not have address) // map() → would give Optional<Optional<Address>> (nested, bad) Optional<Optional<Address>> bad = userRepo.findById(id).map(User::getAddress); // flatMap() → flattens to Optional<Address> (correct) Optional<Address> addr = userRepo.findById(id).flatMap(User::getAddress);
    Q: "Can lambda expressions access local variables? Why must they be effectively final?"
    💭 Think
    Lambdas can outlive the method they're defined in. Local variables are on the stack — which disappears.
    → Answer
    Yes, but only effectively final (not modified after assignment) local variables. Why: lambdas can be executed in different threads or after the enclosing method returns — the local variable's stack frame is long gone. Java solves this by CAPTURING a copy of the variable's value into the lambda at definition time. If the variable were mutable, which copy would be authoritative? Java sidesteps the problem entirely: if you modify it, the compiler rejects the capture. Instance variables and static variables are fine (they're on heap, live independently).
    🎯 Practice
    Write a pipeline that: takes a list of orders, removes cancelled ones, groups remaining by customerId, computes total value per customer, returns top 5 customers by value as a List<String> of "customerId:totalValue".
    Hintfilter → groupingBy with summingDouble → entrySet stream → sorted reversed → limit 5 → map to formatted string.
    → Solution
    Java
    List<String> top5 = orders.stream() .filter(o -> o.getStatus() != Status.CANCELLED) .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::getCustomerId, Collectors.summingDouble(Order::getValue))) .entrySet().stream() .sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Double>comparingByValue().reversed()) .limit(5) .map(e -> e.getKey() + ":" + e.getValue()) .collect(Collectors.toList());

    Object Creation Internals · Immutable Classes · CompletableFuture

    new keyword JVM steps · TLAB · heap allocation · immutable checklist · thenCompose vs thenApply · async pipelines
    🧠 What Happens When You Write new MyObject()
    JVM — object creation internals (Q7)
    // Step 1: CLASS LOADING (if not already loaded) // JVM finds MyObject.class via ClassLoader (parent delegation) // Verifies bytecode -> prepares static fields -> runs static {} blocks // Step 2: MEMORY ALLOCATION in heap // Each thread has a TLAB (Thread-Local Allocation Buffer) — a private chunk of Eden // Allocation = bump-pointer: just advance pointer by sizeof(MyObject). No locking. // TLAB full? Request a new TLAB from Eden via CAS (lock-free). Eden full? Minor GC. // Step 3: ZERO INITIALIZATION // All fields set to defaults: int=0, boolean=false, Object=null, double=0.0 // Step 4: CONSTRUCTOR RUNS (bytecode: invokespecial <init>) // Stack frame created. super() called first (Object.<init> at top of every chain) // Instance initializer blocks run. Constructor body runs. Fields set to real values. // Step 5: REFERENCE RETURNED // Pointer to heap object assigned to the variable. // SAFE PUBLICATION: final fields are guaranteed visible to all threads after construction // Non-final fields without volatile/synchronized = unsafe publication risk // JIT OPTIMISATION: Escape Analysis + Stack Allocation // If object never escapes the method, JIT may allocate on the STACK instead of heap // Stack objects are freed when method returns — zero GC pressure // Scalar replacement: fields may be promoted to CPU registers directly
    Making a Class Immutable — the Complete Checklist (Q12)
    Java — immutable class (all 6 rules)
    public final class Money { // Rule 1: final class (no subclassing) private final BigDecimal amount; // Rule 2: private final fields private final String currency; private final List<String> tags; public Money(BigDecimal amount, String currency, List<String> tags) { this.amount = amount; // BigDecimal is immutable this.currency = currency; // String is immutable this.tags = List.copyOf(tags); // Rule 3: defensive copy of mutable input } // Rule 4: NO setters public BigDecimal getAmount() { return amount; } public String getCurrency() { return currency; } public List<String> getTags() { return List.copyOf(tags); } // Rule 5: defensive copy on get public Money add(Money other) { // Rule 6: return new instance for mutations if(!currency.equals(other.currency)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Currency mismatch"); return new Money(amount.add(other.amount), currency, tags); } } // Java 16+ shortcut: record Point(double x, double y) {} — auto-immutable value type // Benefits: thread-safe by default, safe HashMap key, hashCode can be cached, // no defensive copies needed when sharing across threads
    CompletableFuture — thenApply vs thenCompose vs allOf (Q10)
    Java — CompletableFuture composition operators
    // thenApply: transform result — like Stream.map (T -> U, wraps in CF automatically) CompletableFuture<String> name = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchUser(id)) .thenApply(User::getName); // CF<User> -> CF<String> // thenCompose: flatMap — when the transform ITSELF returns a CompletableFuture // Without thenCompose: .thenApply(u -> fetchOrderAsync(u.id)) = CF<CF<Order>> (wrong!) // With thenCompose: flattened CF<Order> (correct) CompletableFuture<Order> order = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchUser(id)) .thenCompose(user -> fetchOrderAsync(user.getId())); // fetchOrderAsync returns CF<Order> // thenCombine: merge two INDEPENDENT futures when both complete var report = userFuture.thenCombine(orderFuture, (user, order) -> buildReport(user, order)); // allOf: wait for ALL of N futures (N can be any number) var productF = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> productSvc.fetch(id), ioPool); var inventoryF = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> inventorySvc.fetch(id), ioPool); var priceF = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> pricingSvc.fetch(id), ioPool); CompletableFuture.allOf(productF, inventoryF, priceF) .orTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // Java 9+: throws TimeoutException after 2s .join(); return new PageDto(productF.join(), inventoryF.join(), priceF.join()); // all done, safe to join // exceptionally: fallback on failure (like catch block in async) productF.exceptionally(ex -> Product.UNKNOWN) // if productF fails, use UNKNOWN // CompletableFuture vs Future: // Future.get() BLOCKS the calling thread. No composition, no callbacks. // CompletableFuture: non-blocking callbacks (thenApply, thenCompose), composable chains, // exception handling (exceptionally, handle), timeout (orTimeout), cancellable
    🏭 Production Scenario
    A product detail page calls ProductService, InventoryService, and PricingService sequentially. Total latency = 900ms (3 x 300ms each). The page load SLA is 500ms. You cannot reduce each service's response time. How do you redesign the page loading using CompletableFuture?
    Three independent calls — none depends on the result of another. Run them in parallel. Total time becomes max(300, 300, 300) = 300ms. What CompletableFuture method waits for ALL of N independent futures?
    Solution — parallel allOf: Launch all three supplyAsync() calls simultaneously using a dedicated I/O thread pool (not ForkJoinPool.commonPool() which is shared). allOf() returns a CF that completes when ALL three complete. orTimeout(2, SECONDS) adds a hard deadline. If any individual call fails: exceptionally() returns a safe fallback — the page renders with partial data rather than a 500. Total latency: max(300, 300, 300) = 300ms, well within the 500ms SLA. Why NOT commonPool: commonPool has parallelism = CPU cores (e.g., 8). If 20 concurrent page loads each make 3 calls = 60 concurrent I/O operations — all 8 threads blocked waiting for network. New requests starve. Fix: Executors.newFixedThreadPool(50) for I/O-bound tasks.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: What is the difference between thenApply and thenApplyAsync? When does thenApply cause thread starvation?
    💡 Think First
    thenApply runs the callback in the thread that completed the previous stage. If that thread is a ForkJoinPool worker and the callback blocks, the worker is stuck. How many workers does the common pool have?
    ➔ Complete Answer
    thenApply: runs the callback in the completing thread. If the completing thread is a ForkJoinPool worker and the callback does blocking I/O (e.g., another HTTP call), that worker thread is blocked for the duration. With commonPool (8 threads) and 10 concurrent requests each blocking for 300ms, all 8 threads are consumed — new completions queue. thenApplyAsync(fn, executor): submits fn to the given executor, freeing the completing thread immediately. Rule of thumb: use plain thenApply for fast, non-blocking transforms (field mapping, string formatting, arithmetic). Use thenApplyAsync for anything that blocks (I/O, sleep, external calls) — pass a dedicated executor for I/O work.
    Q: Can an immutable class still cause thread-safety issues? Explain unsafe publication.
    💡 Think First
    Immutable objects cannot be modified — so there is nothing to synchronise after construction. But what if another thread reads the object reference before the constructor finishes? Due to instruction reordering, is this possible?
    ➔ Complete Answer
    Yes — unsafe publication. The JMM allows the JIT and CPU to reorder instructions. The three steps of new MyObject(): (1) allocate memory, (2) write default values, (3) run constructor — can be reordered so that the reference is stored before the constructor completes. Another thread reads the reference and sees a partially-constructed object with null fields. Safe publication guarantees: (1) final fields: JMM guarantees all final fields are visible to any thread that obtains the reference after construction. (2) volatile reference: volatile write happens-before volatile read — the full object is visible. (3) Static initialiser: class loading is synchronised by the JVM. (4) Synchronised put to a ConcurrentHashMap. Java records and immutable classes with all-final fields are safely published. Non-final fields even in an "immutable by convention" class are not guaranteed to be safely published.
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement an immutable ImmutableOrder class: orderId (String), items (List of OrderItem), totalAmount (BigDecimal), createdAt (Instant). Then use CompletableFuture to build an OrderSummaryService that in parallel: (1) enriches each order item with its current price from PricingService, (2) validates each item is still in stock via InventoryService. Both calls are async. If either fails for an item, mark the item as UNAVAILABLE — never fail the whole response.
    💡 HintImmutableOrder: final class, all-final fields, defensive copy of List in constructor, copyOf in getter, withItems() returns new ImmutableOrder. For the async enrichment: for each item, create a CompletableFuture that combines price and inventory (thenCombine), with exceptionally fallback. Collect all per-item futures into a list, CompletableFuture.allOf(array), join all.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — immutable class + CompletableFuture enrichment
    public final class ImmutableOrder { private final String orderId; private final List<OrderItem> items; private final BigDecimal totalAmount; private final Instant createdAt; public ImmutableOrder(String id, List<OrderItem> items, BigDecimal total, Instant at) { this.orderId = id; this.items = List.copyOf(items); this.totalAmount = total; this.createdAt = at; } public List<OrderItem> getItems() { return List.copyOf(items); } public ImmutableOrder withItems(List<OrderItem> newItems) { return new ImmutableOrder(orderId, newItems, totalAmount, createdAt); } } // Async enrichment public CompletableFuture<ImmutableOrder> enrich(ImmutableOrder order) { List<CompletableFuture<OrderItem>> futures = order.getItems().stream() .map(item -> { var priceFuture = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> pricingSvc.getPrice(item.sku()), ioPool); var stockFuture = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> inventorySvc.inStock(item.sku()), ioPool); return priceFuture.thenCombine(stockFuture, (price, inStock) -> item.withPrice(price).withAvailable(inStock)) .exceptionally(ex -> item.asUnavailable()); // per-item fallback }).collect(toList()); return CompletableFuture.allOf(futures.toArray(new CompletableFuture[0])) .thenApply(v -> order.withItems(futures.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).collect(toList()))); }
