    ConcurrentHashMap & volatile vs synchronized

    thread safety internals · when each mechanism is right
    🧠 ConcurrentHashMap Internal Design
    ConcurrentHashMap is NOT just a synchronized HashMap. It uses segment-level locking (Java 7) then CAS + bin-level locking (Java 8+) to allow concurrent reads AND concurrent writes to different buckets simultaneously.A synchronized HashMap blocks ALL threads for every read and write. ConcurrentHashMap allows N threads to read simultaneously and M threads to write to different buckets simultaneously — massive throughput difference at scale.
    💻 ConcurrentHashMap — Thread-Safe Patterns
    Java — the right way to use ConcurrentHashMap
    ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer> wordCount = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); // ✗ WRONG — check-then-act: NOT atomic, race condition if (!wordCount.containsKey(word)) wordCount.put(word, 1); else wordCount.put(word, wordCount.get(word) + 1); // Thread A and B both read 5, both write 6! // ✓ CORRECT — atomic compound operations wordCount.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum); // atomic: if absent put 1, else apply sum wordCount.compute(word, (k, v) -> v == null ? 1 : v + 1); // atomic compute wordCount.computeIfAbsent(word, k -> 0); // atomic: only if absent // ✓ For atomic long counters: ConcurrentHashMap.LongAdder (better than AtomicLong under high contention) ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> freq = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); freq.computeIfAbsent(word, k -> new LongAdder()).increment(); // fully concurrent, no lock // HOW IT WORKS INTERNALLY (Java 8+): // - Reads: completely lock-free using volatile reads from the node array // - Writes: CAS (Compare-And-Swap) for empty bins; synchronized on individual bin head for collisions // - Resizing: multiple threads help with the resize concurrently (transfer protocol) // - size(): LongAdder cells, no lock needed // - vs Hashtable/Collections.synchronizedMap: those lock the ENTIRE map for every operation
    ⚠️ volatile vs synchronized — Exact Guarantees
    Featurevolatilesynchronized
    VisibilityYes — flushes to main memoryYes — acquires/releases memory barrier
    AtomicityNo — read-modify-write NOT atomicYes — entire block is atomic
    Mutual exclusionNo — multiple threads can execute simultaneouslyYes — only one thread at a time
    PerformanceFaster — no lock acquisitionSlower — monitor acquire/release
    Use caseFlag variables, status signalsCompound actions, invariants
    Java — volatile vs synchronized
    // volatile: correct for stop-flag (read by main, written by thread) volatile boolean running = true; new Thread(() -> { while (running) { doWork(); } }).start(); running = false; // visible to the thread immediately due to volatile // volatile: WRONG for counter (read-modify-write is 3 ops, not atomic) volatile int count = 0; count++; // NOT atomic! Two threads: both read 5, both increment, both write 6 → lost update // synchronized: correct for compound actions private int count = 0; public synchronized void increment() { count++; } // atomic: only one thread at a time // Better: AtomicInteger (CAS-based, no lock, better performance than synchronized) AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger(0); count.incrementAndGet(); // atomic, lock-free count.compareAndSet(5, 6); // CAS: set to 6 only if current value is 5
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Your microservice caches user sessions in a HashMap inside a singleton. Under load (50 concurrent users), sessions are randomly disappearing or getting corrupted. No exceptions are thrown. How do you diagnose and fix this?
    HashMap is not thread-safe. Concurrent reads and writes can cause: lost updates (two threads put different keys and one is lost), infinite loops during resize in Java 7 (or corrupted tree structure in Java 8+), or returning null for a key that was just put. No exception is thrown — silent data corruption.
    Root cause: HashMap.put() is not atomic. During a resize (rehash), one thread is moving entries to the new array while another thread reads — it sees half-migrated state. Result: lost entries, null returns for present keys, or in Java 7: infinite loop in the linked list chain. Fix options: (1) ConcurrentHashMap — thread-safe, O(1) get/put, lock-free reads, fine-grained CAS writes. Use for most cases. (2) Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap()) — coarse-grained lock on every operation, slower, iteration still needs external synchronisation. (3) If read-heavy: CopyOnWriteArrayList pattern is not applicable for maps, but you can use a volatile reference to an immutable map + replace-on-write. ConcurrentHashMap internals (Java 8+): 16 buckets initially, each bucket is an independent node. Writes to different buckets proceed in parallel (no global lock). CAS for empty bucket insertion (no lock at all). Synchronized on the bin head only for collision handling. Converts to red-black tree when bin size exceeds 8 (TREEIFY_THRESHOLD).
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: "What is the Java Memory Model and why does it matter for multithreading?"
    💭 Think
    CPUs and compilers reorder instructions and cache values in registers. Without rules, threads see inconsistent views of memory.
    → Answer
    The JMM defines happens-before relationships: if action A happens-before action B, A's results are visible to B. Key happens-before rules: (1) Monitor unlock → lock by another thread. (2) volatile write → subsequent volatile read of same variable. (3) Thread start → first action of the started thread. (4) All actions in a thread → join() by another thread. Without these relationships, the JVM and CPU can reorder writes, and threads may see stale values from cache.
    Q: "What is a race condition vs a deadlock vs a livelock?"
    💭 Think
    Three different concurrency failure modes, each with distinct symptoms and fixes.
    → Definitions + examples
    Race condition: Non-deterministic result due to unsynchronized concurrent access. Two threads both increment a counter → result depends on scheduling. Fix: synchronize.
    Deadlock: Thread A holds lock L1, waits for L2. Thread B holds L2, waits for L1. Both blocked forever. Fix: always acquire locks in consistent order; use tryLock with timeout.
    Livelock: Threads keep responding to each other but make no progress. Like two people in a hallway both stepping aside simultaneously — forever. Fix: add randomized backoff.
    🎯 Practice
    Implement a thread-safe singleton that is: lazily initialized, uses double-checked locking correctly, and works in a multi-instance JVM environment.
    Hintvolatile on the instance field is mandatory for DCL to work correctly. Without it, partially constructed objects can be visible to other threads due to JVM instruction reordering. Alternative: use the static holder pattern (no volatile needed).
    → Solution
    Java — two correct singleton patterns
    // Pattern 1: Double-Checked Locking (volatile REQUIRED) class ConfigManager { private static volatile ConfigManager instance; // volatile prevents reordering private ConfigManager() {} public static ConfigManager getInstance() { if (instance == null) { // first check — no lock (fast path) synchronized (ConfigManager.class) { if (instance == null) // second check — under lock instance = new ConfigManager(); } } return instance; } } // Pattern 2: Static Holder (preferred — simpler, correct without volatile) class ConfigManager { private static class Holder { static final ConfigManager INSTANCE = new ConfigManager(); // class loaded lazily } public static ConfigManager getInstance() { return Holder.INSTANCE; } } // JVM guarantees class initialization is thread-safe — Holder class loaded only once, // lazily (when getInstance() is first called), by the JVM's class loading lock.

    JVM Architecture & Garbage Collection

    memory areas · GC algorithms · tuning · what interviewers actually ask
    🧠 JVM Memory Areas
    The JVM divides memory into areas with different lifetimes and purposes. Understanding this lets you diagnose OutOfMemoryErrors, tune GC, and explain memory leaks.
    📐 JVM Memory Layout
    💻 GC Algorithms — Know the Trade-offs
    CollectorAlgorithmPauseThroughputUse when
    Serial GCStop-the-world, single threadLongLowSingle-core, batch jobs
    Parallel GCStop-the-world, multi-threadMediumHighThroughput-first batch apps
    G1 GC (default Java 9+)Region-based, concurrent markingPredictable <200msGoodGeneral purpose, heap 4-32GB
    ZGC (Java 15+)Fully concurrent<1msGoodUltra-low latency, huge heaps
    ShenandoahConcurrent compaction<10msGoodLow-latency on any heap size
    GC tuning flags — what to know for interviews
    # Basic heap sizing java -Xms512m -Xmx4g -XX:+UseG1GC MyApp # -Xms: initial heap (set equal to -Xmx to avoid resizing overhead) # -Xmx: max heap # -XX:+UseG1GC: explicit G1 (default Java 9+) # GC logging (diagnose production issues) java -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags MyApp # Shows: GC type, duration, heap before/after, promotion rates # Common OOM causes: # java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space → too many live objects, increase -Xmx, fix leak # java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace → too many classes loaded (class loader leak), increase -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize # java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: GC overhead limit exceeded → GC spending > 98% of time, tiny heap
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Production alert: your service is throwing java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: GC overhead limit exceeded at 3am every Sunday. Heap is 8GB. The error occurs after exactly 6 hours of uptime. How do you diagnose and resolve this?
    GC overhead limit exceeded means the JVM is spending more than 98% of time in GC and recovering less than 2% of heap. This means the heap is almost completely full of live objects. This is almost always a memory leak. The 6-hour pattern suggests a slow leak accumulating over time.
    Immediate diagnosis: Add -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/tmp/ to JVM flags. On next OOM, a heap.hprof file is generated. Open in Eclipse MAT or IntelliJ Profiler. Look for: Retained Heap — what single object tree is consuming the most memory? Dominator tree — what object is preventing GC of the most memory? Common Sunday-3am leak patterns: (1) Scheduled job that accumulates results in a static collection without clearing. (2) Caffeine/Guava cache with no eviction policy (unbounded). (3) ThreadLocal variables not cleaned up — thread pool threads live forever, their ThreadLocals accumulate. (4) Event listener registered but never de-registered. JVM memory areas: Heap (Young: Eden+Survivor, Old Gen) — where your objects live. Metaspace (non-heap) — class metadata; OOM here means too many class definitions (dynamic proxy/CGLIB in Spring). Stack — per-thread; StackOverflowError means infinite recursion. G1GC tuning: -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200 -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=16m — G1 is the default from Java 9+, best for large heaps with pause time requirements.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: "How does the Young Generation garbage collection work? What is the Eden/Survivor space model?"
    💭 Think
    Most objects die young. GC should optimize for collecting the short-lived objects cheaply.
    → Minor GC walkthrough
    1. New objects allocated in Eden (fast bump-pointer allocation)
    2. When Eden fills → Minor GC triggered (Stop-The-World, fast ~5-50ms)
    3. Live objects in Eden copied to Survivor S0. Dead objects collected.
    4. Next Minor GC: live from Eden + S0 copied to S1. S0 cleared.
    5. Objects surviving N GC cycles (default: 15) → promoted to Old Gen
    6. Old Gen fills → Major GC (much slower — must scan all live objects)

    Why copying? Compacts live objects automatically — no fragmentation. Much faster than mark-sweep for short-lived objects.
    Q: "How do you diagnose a memory leak in a Java production application?"
    💭 Think
    Symptoms: heap grows over time, eventually OOM. Need to find what's holding references.
    → Diagnosis steps
    1. Enable GC logging → confirm Old Gen growing without leveling off
    2. Capture heap dump: jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof or jmap -dump:format=b,file=heap.hprof <pid>
    3. Analyze with Eclipse MAT or VisualVM: "Leak Suspects" report shows objects with most retained heap
    4. Common causes: static collections that grow unbounded, ThreadLocal not cleared, unclosed streams/connections, event listeners not deregistered, HashMap with mutable keys
    🎯 Practice
    Explain what happens to memory when: (1) a local variable goes out of scope, (2) a static field holds a collection that grows, (3) an inner class holds a reference to its outer class.
    HintLocal variable → stack frame popped → reference gone → heap object eligible for GC (if no other refs). Static field → lives for app lifetime → objects in it never collected. Inner class → non-static inner class holds implicit reference to outer → if inner class escapes (e.g., passed to another thread), outer can't be GC'd.
    → Answer
    Java — memory reference analysis
    // 1. Local variable out of scope → GC eligible void process() { List<String> temp = new ArrayList<>(); // heap object } // temp goes out of scope → no reference → GC eligible at next collection // 2. Static collection leak class Cache { static final Map<String, Object> CACHE = new HashMap<>(); // lives FOREVER // Fix: use WeakHashMap (GC-able entries) or set a max size with eviction } // 3. Inner class capturing outer class reference class Activity { // Android-style example, applies to any long-lived async task class DataLoader extends AsyncTask { // non-static: holds Activity reference // If this task runs for 60s, Activity can't be GC'd for 60s → memory leak // Fix: make DataLoader static + WeakReference to Activity, or cancel on destroy } }

    Design Patterns — Singleton · Factory · Builder · Observer

    intent · implementation · real-world usage · interview pitfalls
    🧠 Mental Model — Why Patterns Exist
    Design patterns are named solutions to recurring design problems. Interviewers want to know: WHEN to use each, not just HOW to implement it.The GOF (Gang of Four) patterns are grouped: Creational (how objects are created), Structural (how objects are composed), Behavioral (how objects communicate).
    💻 Builder Pattern — Most Requested
    Java — Builder (correct implementation)
    // Problem: Object with 10 optional fields → telescoping constructors or null-heavy setters // Solution: Builder separates construction from representation class HttpRequest { private final String url, method, body; private final Map<String, String> headers; private final int timeoutMs; private HttpRequest(Builder b) { // private constructor — only Builder can create this.url = Objects.requireNonNull(b.url, "url required"); this.method = b.method; this.body = b.body; this.headers = Map.copyOf(b.headers); this.timeoutMs = b.timeoutMs; } public static class Builder { private String url, method = "GET", body; private final Map<String, String> headers = new HashMap<>(); private int timeoutMs = 5000; public Builder url(String url) { this.url = url; return this; } public Builder method(String m) { this.method = m; return this; } public Builder header(String k, String v) { headers.put(k,v); return this; } public Builder timeoutMs(int t) { this.timeoutMs = t; return this; } public HttpRequest build() { return new HttpRequest(this); } } } // Usage: fluent, self-documenting HttpRequest req = new HttpRequest.Builder() .url("https://api.example.com/orders") .method("POST") .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + token) .timeoutMs(3000) .build();
    📐 Factory Pattern
    Java — Factory Method
    // Problem: Caller shouldn't know or care which concrete class to instantiate // Solution: Factory method returns the right implementation based on context interface PaymentProcessor { void process(Payment payment); } class PaymentProcessorFactory { public static PaymentProcessor create(PaymentMethod method) { return switch (method) { case CARD -> new StripeProcessor(); case UPI -> new RazorpayProcessor(); case WALLET -> new PaytmProcessor(); default -> throw new UnsupportedOperationException(method.name()); }; } } // Spring version: @Qualifier or Map injection (paymentProcessors Map autowired by bean name) // Factory decouples the caller from concrete implementations — add new payment methods // by adding a new class, not by modifying the caller (Open/Closed Principle)
    ⚠️ Observer Pattern
    Java — Observer (also: EventBus, Spring ApplicationEvent)
    // Problem: One event (order placed) → multiple independent reactions (email, SMS, analytics) // Solution: Observer — subject notifies all registered observers interface OrderObserver { void onOrderPlaced(Order order); } class OrderService { private final List<OrderObserver> observers = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); public void placeOrder(Order order) { orderRepo.save(order); observers.forEach(o -> o.onOrderPlaced(order)); // notify all } } // Spring equivalent: ApplicationEventPublisher (decoupled, async, transactional) // Modern Java: Reactive Streams (Project Reactor, RxJava) for async observer patterns
    🏭 Production Scenario
    An interviewer shows you a class with a private static volatile instance field, a private constructor, and a static getInstance() method with double-checked locking. They ask: "What pattern is this, why volatile, and when would you replace it?"
    This is the Singleton with DCL. The volatile is required to prevent instruction reordering during object construction. Know all three reasons and all three alternative implementations.
    Pattern: Singleton — guarantees one instance per JVM. Why volatile: Without volatile, the JIT can reorder the three steps of new Singleton(): (1) allocate memory, (2) write default values, (3) run constructor. A thread can see a non-null but partially-constructed instance after step 1. Volatile adds a memory barrier preventing this reorder. Alternatives: Static holder (preferred): private static class Holder { static final Singleton I = new Singleton(); } — JVM class loading is thread-safe, zero explicit synchronization. Enum singleton: enum Singleton { INSTANCE; } — serialization-safe, reflection-safe. When to replace: With Spring @Bean @Scope("singleton") — the container manages lifecycle, constructor injection makes it testable.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: Explain the Factory Method vs Abstract Factory pattern with a concrete Spring example.
    💭 Think First
    Factory Method: one product, subclasses decide. Abstract Factory: families of related products, one factory creates the whole family. The difference is the number of products.
    → Complete Answer
    Factory Method: NotificationServiceFactory with abstract createChannel() — EmailFactory returns EmailChannel, SMSFactory returns SmsChannel. One product type per factory subclass. Abstract Factory: UIComponentFactory with createButton(), createTextField(), createDialog() — all three belong to the same UI family. WindowsFactory creates all Windows variants, MacFactory creates all Mac variants. In Spring: the ApplicationContext IS an Abstract Factory — it creates entire families of related beans (the full application context). @Configuration classes with multiple @Bean methods are Abstract Factories: one class creates a family of related beans (DataSource, JdbcTemplate, TransactionManager) that must be consistent with each other.
    Q: The Builder pattern vs telescoping constructors vs @Builder. When does each fail?
    💭 Think First
    All three create objects. Each has a failure mode. Know the specific scenario where each breaks down.
    → Complete Answer
    Telescoping constructors: Pizza(String size) { this(size, "thin"); } Pizza(String size, String crust) {...} — scales to 8 parameters and you have 2^8 combinations. Impossible to maintain. Builder: mandatory fields in constructor, optional via methods, validation in build(). Fails when: you need compile-time enforcement of step ORDER (use Step Builder instead). @Builder (Lombok): generates boilerplate. Fails when: (1) mandatory field enforcement — @Builder.Default can set defaults but nothing prevents calling build() without a mandatory field (add @NonNull). (2) cross-field validation (size==LARGE required if crust==STUFFED) — must add a custom build() method. (3) immutability — Lombok @Builder builds a mutable object by default; add @Value for immutable.
    🎯 Practice
    Implement a Strategy pattern for sorting: SortService.sort(List, SortStrategy) where strategy can be BubbleSort, QuickSort, or MergeSort. The caller picks the algorithm without if-else chains.
    HintStrategy = interface with one method. Each algorithm implements it. SortService holds a reference to the strategy. Caller injects the strategy — Strategy Pattern is essentially dependency injection of behavior.
    → Solution
    Java
    @FunctionalInterface interface SortStrategy<T extends Comparable<T>> { void sort(List<T> list); } class SortService<T extends Comparable<T>> { private SortStrategy<T> strategy; void setStrategy(SortStrategy<T> s) { this.strategy = s; } void sort(List<T> list) { strategy.sort(list); } } // Lambda as strategy (since SortStrategy is @FunctionalInterface): service.setStrategy(list -> Collections.sort(list)); // built-in sort service.setStrategy(list -> list.sort(Comparator.reverseOrder())); // reverse // Runtime switching: change strategy based on list size (small→bubble, large→merge)
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement the Observer pattern for a stock price alert system. StockTicker publishes price changes. Multiple AlertHandler implementations (EmailAlert, SMSAlert, DashboardAlert) subscribe. An alert fires only when price moves more than 5%.
    Hint — think before readingStockObserver interface with onPriceChange(String ticker, double oldPrice, double newPrice). StockTicker holds a list of observers. notify() checks if abs(change) > 5% before firing. Handlers implement the interface independently.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — Observer for stock alerts
    @FunctionalInterface interface StockObserver { void onPriceChange(String ticker, double old, double now); } class StockTicker { private final List<StockObserver> observers = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); private double lastPrice; private final String ticker; public void subscribe(StockObserver o) { observers.add(o); } public void unsubscribe(StockObserver o) { observers.remove(o); } public void updatePrice(double newPrice) { double changePct = Math.abs((newPrice - lastPrice) / lastPrice * 100); if(changePct > 5.0) { // only notify on significant moves double old = lastPrice; observers.forEach(o -> o.onPriceChange(ticker, old, newPrice)); } lastPrice = newPrice; } }

    @Bean vs @Component · IoC & DI Deep Dive

    when to use each · ApplicationContext vs BeanFactory · bean lifecycle
    🧠 Mental Model
    @Component = "Spring, manage this class for me." @Bean = "Spring, I'll create this object myself — just manage what I return."@Component is class-level: Spring scans, finds, instantiates, wires. @Bean is method-level inside a @Configuration class: YOU write the instantiation code, Spring manages the result. Use @Bean when you don't own the source (third-party libraries), need conditional creation, or need fine-grained constructor control.
    💻 @Bean vs @Component — When to Use Each
    Java — Spring Boot
    // ✓ @Component (+ @Service, @Repository, @Controller) — for YOUR classes @Service // specialized @Component — semantic hint, also triggers exception translation public class OrderService { private final OrderRepository repo; public OrderService(OrderRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; } } // ✓ @Bean — for third-party objects or when you need constructor control @Configuration public class InfraConfig { @Bean // you can't annotate ObjectMapper class — it's Jackson's class public ObjectMapper objectMapper() { return new ObjectMapper() .registerModule(new JavaTimeModule()) .disable(DeserializationFeature.FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES); } @Bean // conditional — only if redis.enabled=true @ConditionalOnProperty("redis.enabled") public RedisTemplate<String,Object> redisTemplate(RedisConnectionFactory cf) { var t = new RedisTemplate<String,Object>(); t.setConnectionFactory(cf); return t; } } // Stereotype differences (all are @Component): // @Service — business logic layer // @Repository — data access layer (also enables @PersistenceExceptionTranslation) // @Controller — Spring MVC request handler // @RestController — @Controller + @ResponseBody on every method
    📐 ApplicationContext vs BeanFactory
    FeatureBeanFactoryApplicationContext
    Bean instantiationLazy (on first getBean())Eager by default (at startup)
    AOP supportNoYes
    Event publishingNoYes (ApplicationEvent)
    I18n / MessageSourceNoYes
    Environment/PropertiesNoYes
    Use in productionNever (legacy)Always
    BeanFactory is the base interface. ApplicationContext extends it with enterprise features. In any Spring Boot app you always use ApplicationContext — BeanFactory is a theoretical distinction for interviews.
    ⚠️ Bean Lifecycle — What Interviewers Ask About
    Java — bean lifecycle hooks
    // Lifecycle: Instantiate → Inject deps → @PostConstruct → (use) → @PreDestroy @Service public class CacheService { private Map<String, Object> cache; @PostConstruct // runs AFTER dependency injection, before service is used public void init() { cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); loadWarmData(); // can't do this in constructor — deps not injected yet } @PreDestroy // runs on graceful shutdown — clean up resources public void shutdown() { cache.clear(); log.info("Cache service shut down cleanly"); } } // Why not in constructor? @Autowired fields are injected AFTER the constructor runs. // If you access them in the constructor, they're null. @PostConstruct is the safe hook.
    🏭 Production Scenario
    A junior developer puts @Autowired on a field in a @Component class. It works in tests and production. A senior engineer says 'use constructor injection instead'. The junior asks why — the result is the same. What is the real difference?
    Both inject the dependency. The difference is when the injection happens (construction time vs after construction), what happens if the dependency is null, and whether you can create the object without Spring in a unit test.
    Field injection problem 1 — testability: With field injection: new OrderService() — the userRepo field is null (Spring didn't inject it). You need Spring context or Mockito's @InjectMocks. With constructor injection: new OrderService(mockRepo) — you inject the mock directly, no Spring needed. Much simpler unit tests. Field injection problem 2 — immutability: Field-injected dependencies can be replaced after construction (someone calls reflection to set the field). Constructor-injected dependencies are final — truly immutable. Field injection problem 3 — hidden dependencies: Too many @Autowired fields is a warning sign (class has too many responsibilities). Constructor injection makes this visible — a constructor with 8 parameters is obviously too large. Field injection hides the mess. @Bean vs @Component: @Component (and @Service, @Repository, @Controller): Spring auto-detects via @ComponentScan. Use for YOUR classes. @Bean: manual registration in a @Configuration class. Use for: third-party classes you cannot annotate, classes requiring complex construction logic, or creating multiple instances of the same type with different configurations. Bean lifecycle: Constructor → @Autowired injection → @PostConstruct → (application runs) → @PreDestroy → destroy.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: "How does Spring resolve circular dependencies?"
    💭 Think
    A depends on B, B depends on A. How can either be fully created first?
    → Complete answer
    Spring uses a three-level cache for singleton beans to handle circular deps via field/setter injection:
    1. Instantiates A (calls constructor) → A is partially constructed, put in "early exposure" cache
    2. Starts injecting A's dependencies → needs B
    3. Instantiates B → B needs A → finds A's partial instance in early cache → injects it
    4. B is fully constructed → injected into A → A fully constructed

    BUT: This does NOT work for constructor injection. Spring can't create A without B (needed in constructor), can't create B without A — deadlock. Spring throws BeanCurrentlyInCreationException.

    The real fix: A circular dependency usually signals a design problem (SRP violation). Refactor to extract a shared dependency C that both A and B use.
    Java — break the cycle with @Lazy
    // Workaround (not recommended — fix the design instead): @Service class ServiceA { private final ServiceB b; ServiceA(@Lazy ServiceB b) { this.b = b; } // inject a proxy, resolve lazily } // @Lazy creates a proxy for B — the real B is only instantiated on first method call
    Q: "Explain Spring Boot Auto-Configuration. How does it work internally?"
    💭 Think
    You add spring-boot-starter-web and suddenly Tomcat, Jackson, DispatcherServlet all work. How?
    → Internals
    1. @SpringBootApplication includes @EnableAutoConfiguration
    2. Spring Boot reads META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports (previously spring.factories) — a list of ~140 AutoConfiguration classes
    3. Each AutoConfiguration class uses @ConditionalOn* annotations to decide whether to activate:
      @ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class) — only if DataSource is on classpath
      @ConditionalOnMissingBean(DataSource.class) — only if YOU haven't defined one yourself
      @ConditionalOnProperty("spring.datasource.url") — only if property is set
    4. If conditions match, the AutoConfiguration creates the beans with sensible defaults
    5. YOUR beans always take precedence (ConditionalOnMissingBean) — you can override any default
    Java — how DataSourceAutoConfiguration works (simplified)
    @Configuration @ConditionalOnClass({ DataSource.class, EmbeddedDatabaseType.class }) @ConditionalOnMissingBean({ DataSource.class, XADataSource.class }) class DataSourceAutoConfiguration { @Bean @ConditionalOnProperty(prefix="spring.datasource", name="url") public DataSource dataSource(DataSourceProperties props) { return props.initializeDataSourceBuilder().build(); } } // Run with --debug to see Auto-Configuration Report: which configs activated and why
    Q: "How does Spring manage externalized configuration? application.properties vs .yml?"
    💭 Think
    Where does Spring look for config? What's the priority order? What's the structural difference between .properties and .yml?
    → Complete answer
    Priority order (highest wins):
    1. Command line args: --server.port=9090
    2. OS environment variables: SERVER_PORT=9090
    3. application-{profile}.properties (e.g., application-prod.yml)
    4. application.properties / application.yml
    5. Default values in @Value / @ConfigurationProperties

    .properties vs .yml: Functionally identical — .yml is YAML format (hierarchical, less repetition), .properties is flat key=value. Spring Boot supports both. Use .yml for complex nested config (less repetitive), .properties for simple flat values.

    @ConfigurationProperties (preferred over @Value for groups):
    Java
    @ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "payment") @Validated // enables @NotNull, @Min etc on fields public record PaymentConfig( @NotBlank String gatewayUrl, @Min(1) @Max(30) int timeoutSeconds, boolean sandboxMode ) {} // application.yml: // payment: // gateway-url: https://api.payment.com // timeout-seconds: 10 // sandbox-mode: false
    🎯 Practice
    You have a third-party HttpClient library. Create a Spring @Bean for it that reads its base URL and timeout from application properties, and make it a singleton that's shared across the application.
    HintCan't use @Component (don't own HttpClient source). Use @Bean in @Configuration. Inject the config via @Value or @ConfigurationProperties. Singleton is the default scope.
    → Solution
    Java
    @Configuration public class HttpClientConfig { @Value("${http.client.base-url}") private String baseUrl; @Value("${http.client.timeout-ms:5000}") private int timeoutMs; // default 5000 @Bean // singleton by default — Spring creates once, reuses everywhere public HttpClient httpClient() { return HttpClient.newBuilder() .baseUri(URI.create(baseUrl)) .connectTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(timeoutMs)) .build(); } }

    Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP)

    cross-cutting concerns · @Before/@After/@Around · real use cases · the order management scenario
    🧠 Mental Model
    AOP = inject behavior at method boundaries without touching the method.Logging, security checks, transaction management, performance monitoring — these concerns cut across all layers. Without AOP you'd repeat the same code in hundreds of methods. With AOP, you define it once in an Aspect and declare which methods it applies to via a Pointcut expression. Spring creates a proxy around your bean — method calls go through the proxy, which runs the aspect before/after.
    📐 AOP Terminology + How Spring Does It
    💻 Complete AOP Example — Logging + Performance + Security
    Java — Spring AOP
    @Aspect @Component public class AuditAspect { // Pointcut: all public methods in any class annotated @Service @Pointcut("within(@org.springframework.stereotype.Service *)") public void serviceLayer() {} // @Around: most powerful — controls execution, can modify args/return value @Around("serviceLayer()") public Object measurePerformance(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp) throws Throwable { long start = System.currentTimeMillis(); try { Object result = pjp.proceed(); // actually call the method long elapsed = System.currentTimeMillis() - start; log.info("[{}] {}ms", pjp.getSignature().getName(), elapsed); return result; } catch (Throwable t) { log.error("[{}] FAILED: {}", pjp.getSignature().getName(), t.getMessage()); throw t; // re-throw so caller still sees the exception } } // Custom annotation: @Auditable marks specific methods to audit @After("@annotation(com.example.Auditable)") public void auditAction(JoinPoint jp) { auditLog.record(RequestContext.get().getUserId(), jp.getSignature().getName(), jp.getArgs()); } // @AfterThrowing: only runs if exception propagates @AfterThrowing(pointcut = "serviceLayer()", throwing = "ex") public void logException(JoinPoint jp, Exception ex) { alertService.notify("Exception in " + jp.getSignature() + ": " + ex.getMessage()); } }
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: "How would you implement JWT security using AOP instead of a filter?"
    💭 Think
    A custom annotation @Secured on controller methods. An AOP aspect intercepts and validates the JWT from the RequestContext before the method runs.
    → Solution
    Java
    @Target(ElementType.METHOD) @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) @interface RequiresRole { String[] value(); } @Aspect @Component class SecurityAspect { @Before("@annotation(requiresRole)") public void checkRole(JoinPoint jp, RequiresRole requiresRole) { User user = RequestContext.get().getCurrentUser(); if (user == null) throw new UnauthorizedException("Not authenticated"); for (String role : requiresRole.value()) { if (!user.hasRole(role)) throw new ForbiddenException("Requires: " + role); } } } // Usage: @RequiresRole({"ADMIN", "MANAGER"}) on any service method
    Q: "What is the self-invocation AOP limitation and how do you fix it?"
    💭 Think
    AOP works through a proxy. When you call this.method(), you bypass the proxy.
    → Answer with solutions
    Java
    class OrderService { public void placeOrder() { processPayment(); // ✗ calls this.processPayment() — bypasses proxy, @Transactional ignored! } @Transactional public void processPayment() { ... } } // Fix 1: Inject self (the proxy) via @Autowired @Autowired private OrderService self; // Spring injects the proxy, not "this" public void placeOrder() { self.processPayment(); } // goes through proxy ✓ // Fix 2: Extract to a separate Spring bean — the real fix // PaymentService.processPayment() → always called through proxy from external bean
    🏭 Order Management Scenario
    "Design an order management system where inventory updates, payment processing, and invoice generation are independent services. Use Spring Events or AOP."
    The order placement is the primary action. Inventory/payment/invoice are side effects. They shouldn't block the order confirmation, and they shouldn't be tangled in the OrderService. How do you decouple?
    Architecture: Spring Events for async side effects + AOP for cross-cutting concerns
    Java — Spring Events + AOP order system
    // 1. Order domain event record OrderPlacedEvent(Order order) {} // 2. OrderService — only owns order creation @Service class OrderService { @Autowired ApplicationEventPublisher events; @Transactional public Order placeOrder(OrderRequest req) { Order order = orderRepo.save(new Order(req)); events.publishEvent(new OrderPlacedEvent(order)); // fire and... let listeners decide return order; // returns immediately — payment/inventory are async } } // 3. Independent listeners — each team owns their own @Component class InventoryListener { @Async // non-blocking — doesn't delay order confirmation @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT) // only fires if order transaction committed public void onOrderPlaced(OrderPlacedEvent e) { inventoryService.reserve(e.order().getItems()); } } @Component class InvoiceListener { @Async @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT) public void onOrderPlaced(OrderPlacedEvent e) { invoiceService.generate(e.order()); } } // 4. AOP handles cross-cutting: all service methods get timing, logging, audit // without any service knowing about it — exactly as shown in the aspect above
    Why @TransactionalEventListener: Without it, the event fires even if the order transaction later rolls back — you'd reserve inventory for an order that doesn't exist. AFTER_COMMIT ensures the event fires only when the order is durably committed.
    🎯 Practice
    Implement a @RateLimit(requestsPerMinute=60) annotation. Create an AOP aspect that enforces it on annotated methods — reject with RateLimitExceededException if the caller exceeds the rate.
    HintStore per-caller request counts in a ConcurrentHashMap (key: caller IP from RequestContext). Use a scheduled task or TTL mechanism to reset counts per minute. In the @Before aspect, check and increment the counter atomically.
    → Solution
    Java
    @Target(METHOD) @Retention(RUNTIME) @interface RateLimit { int requestsPerMinute() default 60; } @Aspect @Component class RateLimitAspect { private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, AtomicInteger> counts = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); @Scheduled(fixedRate = 60_000) // reset every minute public void reset() { counts.clear(); } @Before("@annotation(rateLimit)") public void check(JoinPoint jp, RateLimit rateLimit) { String key = RequestContext.get().getClientIp() + ":" + jp.getSignature().getName(); int count = counts.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new AtomicInteger()).incrementAndGet(); if (count > rateLimit.requestsPerMinute()) throw new RateLimitExceededException("Limit: " + rateLimit.requestsPerMinute() + "/min"); } }

    Securing REST APIs — JWT & OAuth2

    complete Spring Security setup · token flow · refresh tokens · the questions interviewers ask
    🧠 Mental Model
    JWT = a signed ID card. OAuth2 = the ID card issuance system. Spring Security = the bouncer.JWT (JSON Web Token) is a self-contained token: header.payload.signature. The payload carries claims (userId, roles, expiry). Any service with the public key can verify it — no DB call needed. OAuth2 is the protocol for token issuance, delegation, and refresh. Spring Security is the framework that intercepts requests, validates tokens, and populates the SecurityContext.
    📐 JWT Structure + OAuth2 Flow
    💻 Complete Spring Security + JWT Implementation
    Spring Boot 3 — JWT security
    // 1. JWT generation (on login) @Service class JwtService { private final SecretKey key = Keys.secretKeyFor(SignatureAlgorithm.HS256); private static final long ACCESS_TTL = 15 * 60 * 1000; // 15 minutes public String generateToken(UserDetails user) { return Jwts.builder() .setSubject(user.getUsername()) .claim("roles", user.getAuthorities().stream().map(a -> a.getAuthority()).toList()) .setIssuedAt(new Date()) .setExpiration(new Date(System.currentTimeMillis() + ACCESS_TTL)) .signWith(key) .compact(); } public Claims validateAndParse(String token) { return Jwts.parserBuilder().setSigningKey(key).build() .parseClaimsJws(token).getBody(); // throws if expired or tampered } } // 2. Security filter — runs on every request @Component class JwtAuthFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter { @Override protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, FilterChain chain) throws ServletException, IOException { String header = req.getHeader("Authorization"); if (header != null && header.startsWith("Bearer ")) { try { Claims claims = jwtService.validateAndParse(header.substring(7)); List<GrantedAuthority> roles = ((List<?>) claims.get("roles")).stream() .map(r -> (GrantedAuthority) () -> r.toString()).toList(); SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication( new UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(claims.getSubject(), null, roles)); } catch (JwtException e) { res.setStatus(HttpServletResponse.SC_UNAUTHORIZED); return; } } chain.doFilter(req, res); } } // 3. Security config @Configuration @EnableWebSecurity class SecurityConfig { @Bean public SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http, JwtAuthFilter jwtFilter) throws Exception { return http .csrf(AbstractHttpConfigurer::disable) // stateless API — no CSRF needed .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(STATELESS)) .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a .requestMatchers("/auth/**").permitAll() .requestMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN") .anyRequest().authenticated()) .addFilterBefore(jwtFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class) .build(); } }
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Your mobile app sends a JWT in every API request. A user reports: 'I logged out but my account was still accessible from another device for 15 minutes.' How does this happen and how do you fix JWT logout?
    JWT is stateless — the server validates the signature and expiry, but has no record of which tokens are 'logged out'. Logout on the client just deletes the token locally — the token itself is still valid until it expires. How do you invalidate a token server-side without making the system stateful?
    Root cause: JWT is stateless. The server does not store issued tokens. When the user logs out, the client deletes the token — but if the same token is used from another device (or intercepted), it is still valid until its exp claim. A 15-minute access token TTL means up to 15 minutes of continued access after logout. Solution 1 — short TTL + refresh token: Access token TTL = 5 minutes (not 15). Refresh token stored server-side (DB or Redis). On logout: invalidate the refresh token. The access token expires naturally in 5 minutes — attacker has a 5-minute window at most. Solution 2 — token blocklist: Store invalidated JWTs in Redis SET with TTL = remaining token lifetime. On each request: check Redis before validating. Con: makes JWT stateful again, adds 1 Redis lookup per request. Solution 3 — token version in DB: User record has token_version integer. JWT payload includes token_version. On logout: increment user's token_version. On each request: validate JWT AND check JWT's token_version == DB's token_version. Old tokens fail the version check. Production choice: Short-lived access tokens (5min) + refresh token revocation is the most common approach — minimal added statefulness, good security trade-off.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: "How do you revoke a JWT before it expires?"
    💭 Think
    JWTs are self-contained and stateless. You can't "delete" them server-side. What are your options?
    → Three strategies
    1. Short TTL + refresh tokens: Access tokens expire in 15min. Even if stolen, attacker has a small window. Refresh tokens are stored server-side and revocable immediately.
    2. Token blocklist: Maintain a Redis set of revoked token IDs (jti claim). On each request, check if the token's jti is in the blocklist. Re-introduces statefulness but enables instant revocation.
    3. Version counter per user: Store a tokenVersion in DB. Include it in JWT. On validation, compare JWT version to DB version. Increment DB version to invalidate all existing tokens for that user.

    Production recommendation: Short access token TTL (15min) + revocable refresh tokens covers most cases without a blocklist overhead.
    Q: "JWT vs Session-based authentication — when do you choose each?"
    💭 Think
    Sessions require server-side state storage. JWT is stateless. What does each trade off?
    → Trade-off answer
    Session-based: Session ID stored in cookie, session data on server (memory/Redis). Instant revocation. Works for traditional web apps. Problem: requires sticky sessions or shared session store in multi-instance deployments.
    JWT: Token contains all claims — no server state. Horizontally scalable (any instance validates). Harder to revoke. Larger than session cookie. Better for APIs, microservices, mobile clients.
    Rule: Stateful monolithic web app → sessions. Stateless APIs / microservices / mobile → JWT.
    🎯 Practice
    Implement a refresh token flow: when the access token expires, the client sends the refresh token to /auth/refresh and gets a new access token. The refresh token must be: stored in DB, single-use (rotated on each use), and revokable per user.
    HintRefreshToken entity: token (UUID), userId, expiresAt, used (boolean). On /auth/refresh: validate not expired + not used → mark used → generate new access token + new refresh token → save new refresh token.
    → Solution
    Java
    @Entity @Table(name = "refresh_tokens") class RefreshToken { @Id UUID id; String userId; Instant expiresAt; boolean used; } @PostMapping("/auth/refresh") public TokenResponse refresh(@RequestBody RefreshRequest req) { RefreshToken rt = refreshRepo.findByIdAndUsedFalse(UUID.fromString(req.token())) .orElseThrow(() -> new UnauthorizedException("Invalid refresh token")); if (rt.getExpiresAt().isBefore(Instant.now())) throw new UnauthorizedException("Refresh token expired"); rt.setUsed(true); refreshRepo.save(rt); // mark old token as used (single-use) String newAccess = jwtService.generateToken(userService.load(rt.getUserId())); RefreshToken newRefresh = refreshRepo.save(new RefreshToken(rt.getUserId(), now().plus(7, DAYS))); return new TokenResponse(newAccess, newRefresh.getId().toString()); }

    OAuth2 vs JWT — Complete Comparison

    token format vs authorization protocol · flows · SSO · Spring Security setup · interview-depth
    🧠 Mental Model
    JWT is a token FORMAT. OAuth2 is an AUTHORIZATION PROTOCOL. They work together, not against each other. OAuth2 defines HOW to get a token (flows, actors, endpoints). JWT defines WHAT the token looks like (header.payload.signature). Most confusion: people say "we use JWT" when they mean "we issue our own JWT tokens" without using the full OAuth2 protocol. Both can coexist — an OAuth2 server typically issues JWT-formatted tokens.
    DimensionJWT (token format)OAuth2 (protocol)
    What it isSelf-contained signed token (RFC 7519)Authorization framework (RFC 6749)
    Stateless?Yes — server validates signature, no DB lookupDepends: opaque tokens=stateful, JWT=stateless
    ContainsClaims: sub, exp, roles, custom fieldsFlows: auth code, client credentials, implicit
    RevocationHard — wait for exp or use blocklistOpaque tokens: delete from DB instantly
    Use caseInternal API auth, stateless user sessionsThird-party login (Google/GitHub), delegated access, SSO
    ActorsIssuer + Verifier (2 actors)Resource Owner, Client, Auth Server, Resource Server
    Spring supportspring-security + JJWT libraryspring-security-oauth2-resource-server + Keycloak/Auth0
    OAuth2 Authorization Code Flow (most secure, most common)
  • User clicks "Login with Google" — your app redirects to Google with: client_id, redirect_uri, scope, state (CSRF token)GET https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/auth?client_id=...&scope=openid+email&state=xyz
  • User authenticates + consents at Google — Google redirects to your redirect_uri with a short-lived codeGET https://yourapp.com/callback?code=abc123&state=xyz
  • Your SERVER exchanges code for tokens — server-to-server call (never exposed to browser): code + client_secret -> access_token + refresh_tokenPOST /token {code, client_id, client_secret, redirect_uri}
  • Access token used for API calls — typically a JWT, validated by Resource Server using the Auth Server's public key (JWKS endpoint)Authorization: Bearer eyJ...
    • 🏭 Production Scenario
    Your team says "we use JWT for auth". A senior asks: "Is that OAuth2?" Another teammate says "OAuth2 is more secure than JWT." Both statements need clarification. How do you explain?
    JWT is a format. OAuth2 is a protocol. You can use JWT without OAuth2 (simple internal auth). OAuth2 can use opaque tokens (not JWT). The security comparison is apples vs oranges.
    Clarification 1 — "We use JWT" is not the same as "we use OAuth2": If you issue your own tokens without the OAuth2 flows (no auth server, no grant types, no consent), you have a custom JWT auth system — not OAuth2. That is fine for internal apps. Clarification 2 — OAuth2 is not "more secure than JWT": OAuth2 is a protocol. JWT is a format. The security depends on implementation. An OAuth2 system using opaque tokens can be more easily revocable than one using JWT. A JWT system with short TTL + rotation is secure for most use cases. When you need full OAuth2: Third-party login (let users log in with Google). Delegated authorization (a partner app accesses user data). Enterprise SSO (Keycloak, Okta, Auth0). When simple JWT is enough: Your own app, internal microservices, M2M auth — no third parties, no consent flows needed.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: Explain Authorization Code flow vs Client Credentials flow. When do you use each?
    💡 Think First
    Authorization Code involves a user (Resource Owner). Client Credentials has no user — just machine-to-machine. When is there a user present vs not?
    ➔ Complete Answer
    Authorization Code: A user is present. User delegates access to your app (e.g., your app reads user's Google Calendar). The user authenticates at the Auth Server and gives consent. Your app gets tokens scoped to that user. Client Credentials: No user. Machine-to-machine (M2M). Service A calls Service B with a service-level token. Service A authenticates with its own client_id + client_secret and gets a token valid for "all calls from service A". Used for: scheduled jobs, background workers, microservice-to-microservice auth. In Spring: spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.my-service.authorization-grant-type=client_credentials.
    Q: How do you implement SSO across 5 microservices using OAuth2 and Spring Boot?
    💡 Think First
    SSO = one login grants access to all services. Central Auth Server. Each service validates tokens independently. What Spring configuration does each service need?
    ➔ Complete Answer
    Architecture: Central Identity Provider (Keycloak or Auth0). Each of the 5 microservices is a Spring Resource Server. User flow: User logs in once to Keycloak, gets JWT access token. Presents token to any microservice. Each microservice validates JWT locally using Keycloak's public key from the JWKS endpoint — no call to Keycloak per request. Spring config per service:
    Spring — Resource Server JWT config
    spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.jwk-set-uri=\ https://keycloak/realms/myrealm/protocol/openid-connect/certs @Configuration class SecurityConfig { @Bean public SecurityFilterChain chain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception { return http .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a .requestMatchers("/actuator/health").permitAll() .anyRequest().authenticated()) .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults())) .build(); } }
    Service-to-service: use Client Credentials grant — each service has its own client credentials.
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement JWT-based auth in Spring Boot: (1) POST /auth/login returns accessToken (15min) and refreshToken (7d). (2) Protected endpoints validate the Bearer token. (3) POST /auth/refresh issues a new accessToken from a valid refreshToken. (4) POST /auth/logout invalidates the refreshToken.
    💡 HintJwtService: generate tokens with JJWT, validate signature + expiry. JwtAuthFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter. RefreshToken entity stored in DB with userId, tokenHash, expiresAt, used flag. Logout: mark used=true or delete the refresh token.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Spring Boot — complete JWT auth flow
    @PostMapping("/auth/login") public AuthResponse login(@RequestBody LoginRequest req) { Authentication auth = authManager.authenticate( new UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(req.email(), req.password())); UserDetails user = (UserDetails) auth.getPrincipal(); return new AuthResponse( jwtService.generateAccessToken(user), // 15 min expiry refreshTokenService.create(user) // 7 days, stored in DB ); } // JwtAuthFilter — validates Bearer token on every request @Override protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, FilterChain chain) throws IOException, ServletException { String token = extractBearer(req); if(token != null && jwtService.isValid(token)) { UserDetails user = userService.loadUserByUsername(jwtService.extractUsername(token)); SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication( new UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(user, null, user.getAuthorities())); } chain.doFilter(req, res); } // Refresh token endpoint @PostMapping("/auth/refresh") public AccessTokenResponse refresh(@RequestBody RefreshRequest req) { return refreshTokenService.validate(req.refreshToken()) // checks DB + expiry + not-used .map(rt -> new AccessTokenResponse(jwtService.generateAccessToken(rt.user()))) .orElseThrow(() -> new InvalidTokenException("Refresh token invalid or expired")); } // Logout: invalidate refresh token @PostMapping("/auth/logout") @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT) public void logout(@RequestBody RefreshRequest req) { refreshTokenService.invalidate(req.refreshToken()); // mark used=true or delete }

    Global Exception Handling + REST API Best Practices

    @ControllerAdvice · ProblemDetail RFC 7807 · validation errors · API versioning · URI vs header · error response design
    🧠 Mental Model
    Without global exception handling: every controller has its own try-catch, error formats are inconsistent (some return String, some JSON, some HTML), and a new developer adds a new exception type and forgets to handle it in 12 controllers. With @ControllerAdvice: one class handles ALL exceptions for ALL controllers. Consistent format, single place to add new handlers, nothing escapes.
    Spring Boot — complete @ControllerAdvice with RFC 7807 ProblemDetail
    @RestControllerAdvice // = @ControllerAdvice + @ResponseBody class GlobalExceptionHandler extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler { // 1. Business rule violation (your custom exception) @ExceptionHandler(InsufficientFundsException.class) public ProblemDetail handleInsufficientFunds(InsufficientFundsException ex) { ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY, ex.getMessage()); pd.setTitle("Insufficient Funds"); pd.setType(URI.create("https://api.myapp.com/errors/insufficient-funds")); pd.setProperty("accountId", ex.getAccountId()); pd.setProperty("shortfall", ex.getShortfall()); return pd; // RFC 7807 format: {type, title, status, detail, ...extensions} } // 2. Resource not found @ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class) @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND) public ProblemDetail handleNotFound(ResourceNotFoundException ex) { return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, ex.getResourceType() + " not found: " + ex.getId()); } // 3. Validation errors (@Valid on @RequestBody) @Override protected ResponseEntity<Object> handleMethodArgumentNotValid( MethodArgumentNotValidException ex, ...) { ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatus(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST); pd.setTitle("Validation Failed"); Map<String,String> errors = ex.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().stream() .collect(toMap(FieldError::getField, FieldError::getDefaultMessage)); pd.setProperty("violations", errors); return ResponseEntity.badRequest().body(pd); } // 4. Catch-all for unexpected exceptions (never expose stack traces) @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR) public ProblemDetail handleUnexpected(Exception ex, WebRequest req) { log.error("Unexpected error for request {}", req.getDescription(false), ex); return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, "An internal error occurred. Reference: " + correlationId()); // Never include ex.getMessage() here — could expose internals } }
    REST API Versioning — all 4 strategies
    REST — API versioning strategies
    // Strategy 1: URI versioning (most visible, most common) @GetMapping("/api/v1/users/{id}") // v1 @GetMapping("/api/v2/users/{id}") // v2 — breaking change in response schema // Pros: clear, cacheable, easy to test in browser. Cons: pollutes URL design. // Strategy 2: Header versioning @GetMapping(value = "/api/users/{id}", headers = "X-API-Version=2") // Request: GET /api/users/1 + Header: X-API-Version: 2 // Pros: clean URLs. Cons: not cacheable by CDN (header is not part of cache key by default). // Strategy 3: Accept header (content negotiation) @GetMapping(value = "/api/users/{id}", produces = "application/vnd.myapp.v2+json") // Request: GET /api/users/1 + Accept: application/vnd.myapp.v2+json // RESTful purists prefer this. GitHub uses this. Hard for clients to use. // Strategy 4: Query parameter @GetMapping("/api/users/{id}") public User getUser(@PathVariable String id, @RequestParam(defaultValue="1") int version) {} // Request: GET /api/users/1?version=2 // Pros: simple. Cons: version leaks into query string, not RESTful. // Production recommendation: URI versioning (/api/v1, /api/v2) // Run v1 and v2 simultaneously. Deprecate v1 with Sunset header. // Response: Deprecation: true, Sunset: Sat, 01 Jan 2026 00:00:00 GMT
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Your payment API returns a 500 Internal Server Error with the raw Java stack trace in the response body. A security researcher reports it exposes your framework version, internal class names, and database schema structure. You also have no consistent error format — some endpoints return {"error": "not found"}, others return plain strings, others return HTML. Fix both issues without changing every controller.
    Two problems: (1) exposing internals in error responses = security vulnerability. (2) inconsistent formats = bad DX. @ControllerAdvice centralises both. ProblemDetail (RFC 7807) standardises the format. One class fixes everything.
    Step 1 — Add @RestControllerAdvice: Create GlobalExceptionHandler extending ResponseEntityExceptionHandler. This intercepts ALL exceptions thrown by ANY controller before the response is sent. Step 2 — Adopt RFC 7807 ProblemDetail: Spring Boot 3.x includes ProblemDetail built-in. Response format: {"type": "https://api.myapp.com/errors/insufficient-funds", "title": "Insufficient Funds", "status": 422, "detail": "Balance $50 short", "accountId": "acc-123"}. Type is a URI that links to documentation — clients can programmatically identify error types. Step 3 — Never expose internals: The catch-all @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) logs the full exception server-side (with correlation ID for tracing) but returns ONLY a generic message to the client. The security researcher will now see {"status": 500, "detail": "An internal error occurred. Reference: abc-123"}. Step 4 — Validation errors: @Valid on @RequestBody triggers MethodArgumentNotValidException — override handleMethodArgumentNotValid() to return a structured list of field violations instead of a 400 with no body.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: What is the difference between @ControllerAdvice and @RestControllerAdvice? When does your exception handler NOT catch an exception?
    💡 Think First
    @ControllerAdvice + @ResponseBody = @RestControllerAdvice. But there are cases where @ControllerAdvice cannot intercept — exceptions thrown in filters, for example. The DispatcherServlet is bypassed for filter exceptions.
    ➔ Complete Answer
    @ControllerAdvice catches exceptions thrown inside @Controller and @RestController methods and their @Service / @Component calls within the same thread. It does NOT catch: (1) Exceptions in Filters — filters run before DispatcherServlet, so @ControllerAdvice never sees them. Fix: implement ErrorController or use a filter's try-catch to forward to /error. (2) @Async methods in a separate thread — the exception is stored in the Future/CompletableFuture, not propagated to the MVC layer. Fix: set a custom AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler. (3) Exceptions in @Scheduled methods — same thread isolation issue. Fix: wrap in try-catch or set a TaskScheduler error handler. For filter exceptions: implement BasicErrorController or register a custom Filter that catches exceptions and writes the ProblemDetail response directly.
    Q: How do you add request validation for a complex @RequestBody object? What annotations are available and what happens when validation fails?
    💡 Think First
    Spring Boot uses JSR-380 (Bean Validation). Add @Valid to the @RequestBody parameter. Validation runs automatically before the controller method body executes. What happens if validation fails?
    ➔ Complete Answer
    Add @Valid (or @Validated) to the @RequestBody parameter. On the DTO: @NotNull, @NotBlank, @Size(min=1, max=255), @Email, @Min(0), @Pattern(regexp="..."), @Future (date must be in future), @Valid on nested objects. On validation failure: Spring throws MethodArgumentNotValidException BEFORE your controller method runs. Your @ControllerAdvice catches it. getBindingResult().getFieldErrors() gives you a list of all field violations — field name + message. Custom validator: implement ConstraintValidator<MyAnnotation, String>. Override isValid(). Use @Constraint(validatedBy=MyValidator.class) on your custom annotation. Cross-field validation: implement Validator interface and override validate(). Use @Validated at class level to validate method parameters (not just request bodies) — useful for @PathVariable and @RequestParam validation.
    🎯 Practice Task
    Build a complete error handling setup: (1) Custom ResourceNotFoundException and InsufficientFundsException with relevant fields. (2) @RestControllerAdvice that handles both with appropriate HTTP status codes (404, 422). (3) Validation on a CreateOrderRequest DTO (@NotNull orderId, @Positive amount, @NotEmpty items list). (4) Catch-all that logs with correlation ID but returns a generic message. Test all 4 error paths.
    💡 HintResourceNotFoundException: 404, includes resourceType + id. InsufficientFundsException: 422, includes accountId + shortfall. Validation: override handleMethodArgumentNotValid to collect all field errors into a map. Catch-all: log.error with MDC.get("correlationId") for tracing, return generic ProblemDetail. Test: MockMvc + @WebMvcTest, verify response status + body fields.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Spring Boot — complete error handling + validation
    // Custom exceptions class ResourceNotFoundException extends RuntimeException { private final String resourceType, id; ResourceNotFoundException(String type, String id) { super(type + " not found: " + id); this.resourceType=type; this.id=id; } } // Request DTO with validation record CreateOrderRequest( @NotBlank String customerId, @Positive BigDecimal amount, @NotEmpty List<@NotNull String> itemIds ) {} // Controller @PostMapping("/api/v1/orders") public Order create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateOrderRequest req) { return orderService.create(req); // throws ResourceNotFoundException or InsufficientFundsException } // GlobalExceptionHandler (see full version above) // Test @Test void invalidRequest_returns400WithViolations() throws Exception { mockMvc.perform(post("/api/v1/orders") .content("{\"amount\":-10,\"itemIds\":[]}") .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)) .andExpect(status().isBadRequest()) .andExpect(jsonPath("$.violations.amount").exists()) .andExpect(jsonPath("$.violations.customerId").exists()); }
    JPA/Hibernate
    JPA / Hibernate
    caching · locking · N+1 — interview-depth
    🗄️
    Hibernate Complete
    get/load · caching · dirty checking · locking · N+1

    JPA/Hibernate Deep Dive

    get() vs load() · caching levels · dirty checking · entity lifecycle · locking
    🧠 Mental Model — Session as Unit of Work
    A Hibernate Session is a short-lived "unit of work" — it tracks every entity you load and automatically detects and persists changes.This is dirty checking: Hibernate takes a snapshot of each entity when it's loaded, compares it to the current state at flush time, and generates UPDATE statements only for what changed. You don't call save() — just modify the entity and Hibernate handles the rest (within a transaction).
    ⚠️ get() vs load() — A Classic Interview Question
    MethodDB hit?ReturnsIf not foundUse when
    entityManager.find() / session.get()ImmediatelyReal entity or nullReturns nullYou need the data NOW or might not exist
    session.load() / getReference()Deferred (lazy)Proxy objectObjectNotFoundException when proxy accessedYou only need the ID for a FK relationship
    Java — practical difference
    // get() — hits DB immediately, returns null if not found User user = session.get(User.class, 42L); // SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=42 if (user == null) { /* handle */ } // getReference() — returns proxy, NO DB hit until you access a field User userRef = em.getReference(User.class, 42L); // NO DB hit yet order.setUser(userRef); // Just sets the FK — still NO DB hit em.persist(order); // Inserts order with user_id=42, never loads the User! // Perfect when you only need the ID for a FK reference, not the actual data
    📐 Hibernate Caching — Two Levels
    CacheScopeDefault?Shared?Purpose
    First-Level Cache (L1)Session / EntityManagerAlways onPer-session onlyWithin one transaction: same entity loaded twice → 1 DB hit
    Second-Level Cache (L2)SessionFactory (app-wide)Off by defaultAll sessions share itAcross transactions: reduces DB hits for frequently-read entities
    Query CacheSessionFactoryOff by defaultAll sessions shareCaches JPQL query results (not entities) — invalidated on any change to entity type
    Java — L2 cache setup
    @Entity @Cache(usage = CacheConcurrencyStrategy.READ_WRITE) // enable L2 for this entity public class Country { // good candidate: rarely changes, read millions of times @Id private String code; private String name; } // application.yml: // spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.cache.use_second_level_cache: true // spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.cache.region.factory_class: EhCacheRegionFactory // L2 cache strategies: // READ_ONLY: immutable entities (safest, fastest) // NONSTRICT_READ_WRITE: occasional updates, small window of stale data ok // READ_WRITE: transactional reads/writes (most correct, most overhead) // TRANSACTIONAL: fully transactional cache (JTA required)
    💻 Dirty Checking + Entity Lifecycle
    Java — entity states
    // 4 Entity States: // TRANSIENT: new object, not associated with any Session, not in DB User user = new User("John"); // Transient // PERSISTENT: associated with an open Session, tracked for changes em.persist(user); // or session.get() returns Persistent entity user.setEmail("john@example.com"); // dirty — Hibernate WILL UPDATE this at flush // DETACHED: Session is closed, entity still in memory but NOT tracked em.close(); user.setEmail("new@email.com"); // change NOT tracked — no automatic UPDATE em.merge(user); // re-attach to new session — Hibernate generates UPDATE // REMOVED: scheduled for deletion from DB em.remove(user); // DELETE issued at flush // DIRTY CHECKING mechanism: // On session flush (before commit), Hibernate compares each persistent entity // to its snapshot taken when it was loaded. // If any field differs → generates UPDATE SQL for only the changed fields. // You NEVER need to call save() on a managed entity — just modify it!
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: "How do Optimistic and Pessimistic locking differ? When do you use each?"
    💭 Think
    Optimistic assumes conflicts are rare and checks at save time. Pessimistic prevents conflicts by blocking at read time.
    → Full comparison
    Java — both locking types
    // OPTIMISTIC LOCKING — @Version, detects conflict at save time @Entity class Product { @Id long id; int stock; @Version int version; // auto-incremented by Hibernate on every UPDATE } // Transaction A reads product (version=5), Transaction B reads same (version=5) // A updates stock=9, Hibernate: UPDATE product SET stock=9, version=6 WHERE id=1 AND version=5 ✓ // B tries to update stock=9, Hibernate: UPDATE ... WHERE id=1 AND version=5 → 0 rows updated // → throws OptimisticLockException → B retries from fresh read // Good for: low-to-medium contention, high read-to-write ratio // PESSIMISTIC LOCKING — SELECT FOR UPDATE, blocks at read time @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) @Query("SELECT p FROM Product p WHERE p.id = :id") Optional<Product> findByIdForUpdate(long id); // Transaction A locks row → Transaction B BLOCKS at the SELECT // When A commits and releases, B reads the UPDATED value // Good for: high contention, critical writes (financial), must-not-fail scenarios
    Q: "What is the N+1 problem and how do you prevent it in JPA?"
    💭 Think
    Loading a list of entities and accessing a lazy collection on each one triggers N additional queries.
    → Three solutions
    Java — N+1 prevention
    // ✗ N+1: 1 query for orders + N queries for each order's items List<Order> orders = orderRepo.findAll(); // SELECT * FROM orders orders.forEach(o -> o.getItems().size()); // SELECT * FROM items WHERE order_id=? × N times! // ✓ Fix 1: JOIN FETCH in JPQL (eager load in single query) @Query("SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.items") List<Order> findAllWithItems(); // ✓ Fix 2: @EntityGraph (same as JOIN FETCH but declarative) @EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"items", "items.product"}) List<Order> findAll(); // ✓ Fix 3: @BatchSize (reduces N queries to N/batchSize) @Entity class Order { @BatchSize(size = 50) // loads 50 order's items at once @OneToMany List<Item> items; } // Choose JOIN FETCH for small result sets, @BatchSize for pagination // (JOIN FETCH + LIMIT causes Hibernate's "firstResult/maxResults specified // with collection fetch" warning — it fetches ALL then paginates in memory!)
    🏭 Stock Quantity Scenario
    "In a product catalog service, multiple users update stock quantities simultaneously. How do you implement JPA locking to maintain data consistency and prevent overselling?"
    Overselling = stock goes negative because two threads both read stock=1, both see stock > 0, both decrement. Need to prevent concurrent reads from both seeing the "last item".
    Complete solution: Pessimistic locking for purchase flow
    Java — anti-overselling implementation
    @Entity class Product { @Id long id; @Column(nullable = false) int stockQuantity; @Version int version; // backup: optimistic lock in case pessimistic is bypassed } interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long> { @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) // SELECT ... FOR UPDATE — blocks concurrent reads @Query("SELECT p FROM Product p WHERE p.id = :id") Optional<Product> findByIdWithLock(long id); } @Service class PurchaseService { @Transactional public void purchase(long productId, int qty) { Product p = productRepo.findByIdWithLock(productId) .orElseThrow(() -> new ProductNotFoundException(productId)); if (p.getStockQuantity() < qty) throw new OutOfStockException(productId, qty, p.getStockQuantity()); p.setStockQuantity(p.getStockQuantity() - qty); // dirty checking handles UPDATE // No save() needed — @Transactional flushes automatically on commit // Lock released on transaction commit — next waiter reads updated stock } } // Alternative for high-throughput: atomic SQL update without loading entity @Modifying @Query("UPDATE Product p SET p.stockQuantity = p.stockQuantity - :qty " + "WHERE p.id = :id AND p.stockQuantity >= :qty") int decrementStock(long id, int qty); // returns 0 if stock insufficient — check it!
    🎯 Practice
    Explain what happens when you detach an entity, modify it, then call merge(). How does Hibernate decide what to update in the DB?
    Hintmerge() re-attaches a detached entity to a new Session by loading the current DB state, copying the detached entity's fields over it, then marking it dirty. Think: what fields get copied? What if the DB changed while the entity was detached?
    → Answer
    Java — merge internals
    // Step 1: session.get(User.class, detachedUser.getId()) — loads fresh from DB // Step 2: copies ALL fields from detachedUser onto the freshly loaded entity // Step 3: the freshly loaded entity is now dirty → UPDATE generated at flush // IMPORTANT: merge() returns a NEW managed instance (the loaded+updated one) // The original detached object is still detached — don't use it further! User managed = em.merge(detachedUser); // use "managed", not "detachedUser" // If DB was modified while detached (and using @Version): // merge() will trigger OptimisticLockException — version mismatch // → caller must refresh and retry, or handle the conflict

    HLD Interview Approach + Back-of-Envelope Estimation

    40-minute script · clarify → estimate → design · QPS · storage · bandwidth · the numbers every interviewer expects
    🧠 The HLD Interview Script (40 minutes)
  • Minutes 0–5: Clarify requirements — Never start designing immediately. Ask exactly 3 questions: (1) Who are the users and what is the core use case? (2) What is the scale — DAU, QPS, data size? (3) Any specific constraints — latency SLA, consistency requirements, geography? Write the answers on the whiteboard. This sets the scope and shows senior thinking."Before I design, let me clarify scope. Are we building read-heavy or write-heavy? Do we need global distribution? What's the expected QPS at peak?"
  • Minutes 5–10: Back-of-envelope estimation — Calculate QPS, storage, bandwidth. Use these numbers to justify your design choices later. Round aggressively — interviewers want order-of-magnitude reasoning, not precise math.1M DAU × 10 actions/day = 10M actions/day ÷ 86,400s ≈ 116 QPS avg. Peak = 5× = 580 QPS. Storage: 10M × 1KB/action = 10GB/day = 3.6TB/year.
  • Minutes 10–15: High-level design — Draw the major components: client → API Gateway → services → DB/cache. Explain request flow for the most important endpoint. Do not go deep yet — cover breadth first."Client → CDN → Load Balancer → App servers (stateless, horizontally scalable) → Redis cache → PostgreSQL primary → Read replicas"
  • Minutes 15–35: Deep dive — Interviewer picks 1-2 components to go deep on. Database schema, sharding strategy, caching layer, real-time delivery, consistency model. This is where you differentiate SDE-2 from SDE-1.
  • Minutes 35–40: Scale + edge cases — How does the design handle 10× traffic? What fails first? Hotspot keys, thundering herd, single points of failure. Show you can think about failure modes.
    • Back-of-Envelope Estimation — the Numbers
    Estimation reference sheet — memorise these
    // TIME 1 day = 86,400 seconds ≈ 100K seconds (use 10^5) 1 month = 2.5M seconds ≈ 3M seconds 1 year = 31.5M seconds ≈ 30M seconds // QPS ESTIMATION (the most common interview calculation) // Given: DAU (Daily Active Users), actions per user per day QPS_avg = DAU × actions_per_day / 86,400 QPS_peak = QPS_avg × 5 // rule of thumb: peak = 5× average // Example: Twitter-scale 300M DAU × 20 tweets+reads/day = 6B actions/day QPS_avg = 6B / 100K = 60,000 QPS QPS_peak = 60,000 × 5 = 300,000 QPS // need distributed system // STORAGE ESTIMATION // Key sizes to memorise: char/byte = 1 byte | int = 4 bytes long/double = 8 bytes | UUID = 16 bytes URL = ~100 bytes | tweet = ~280 bytes = 300B image thumb = ~10KB | HD image = ~300KB 1min video = ~50MB (compressed 720p) // Example: URL Shortener storage 100M new URLs/day × 500 bytes/URL = 50GB/day = 18TB/year Redis cache for hot URLs: 20% of URLs = 20M × 500B = 10GB // fits in one Redis node // BANDWIDTH ESTIMATION // Inbound (writes): QPS_write × payload_size // Outbound (reads): QPS_read × payload_size × read_write_ratio // Example: Instagram // Write: 10M photo uploads/day × 300KB = 3TB/day inbound = 34MB/s // Read: 300M users × 50 photos/day viewed × 10KB thumb = 150TB/day = 1.7GB/s outbound // → Need CDN to serve images at edge (origin cannot handle 1.7GB/s) // MEMORY/CACHE ESTIMATION // Rule: cache 20% of daily requests (80/20 rule — 20% of data = 80% of reads) cache_size = QPS_read × 86,400 × 0.2 × avg_object_size // SERVERS NEEDED // Assume 1 server handles 1000 QPS (simple REST, 1 CPU core) servers_needed = QPS_peak / 1000 // then add 2× for redundancy
    Common Estimation Examples (practice these 5)
    BOE — 5 classic interview estimates
    // 1. WhatsApp (1B users, 50 messages/day/user) QPS_write = 1B × 50 / 100K = 500K msg/s Storage/day = 1B × 50 × 100B = 5TB/day → 1.8PB/year Bandwidth = 500K msg/s × 100B = 50MB/s inbound // 2. YouTube (2B users, 1B watch hours/day, 500 hours uploaded/min) QPS_view = 1B hours × 3600 / 86,400 = ~41M concurrent streams Upload storage = 500hr/min × 60min × 1hr × 3GB/hr = 90TB/day raw After encoding (5 resolutions × 1/10 compression): 450TB/day CDN outbound = 41M streams × 4Mbps = 164Tbps → need massive CDN // 3. Twitter (300M DAU, 600M tweets/day reads, 100K writes/day per user) QPS_read = 600M / 100K = 6,000 QPS avg | peak = 30K QPS QPS_write = 100M tweets/day / 100K = 1,000 write QPS Storage = 100M tweets/day × 300B = 30GB/day = 11TB/year Read:Write ratio = 1000:1 → heavy read optimisation needed // 4. Uber (10M rides/day, driver location updates every 5s) Active drivers at peak = 1M drivers × 30% active = 300K Location update QPS = 300K drivers / 5s = 60K writes/s Storage = 60K/s × 50B × 86,400 = 260GB/day location data // 5. Rate Limiter Service (100M users, 100 requests/user/day) QPS = 100M × 100 / 100K = 100K rate-check QPS Redis: each check = INCR + EXPIRE = 2 ops = 200K Redis ops/s 1 Redis node = 100K ops/s → need 2-3 Redis nodes
    🏭 Production Scenario
    You are asked to design a notification system. Before drawing any components, the interviewer says: "How many notifications are we talking about?" Walk through your estimation: 100M users, each gets 10 push notifications + 2 emails + 1 SMS per day. What are the QPS, storage, and infrastructure implications?
    Estimate each channel separately — push, email, SMS have very different latency requirements and costs. Then derive the infrastructure needed. Do not just say "we need Kafka" — derive WHY from the numbers.
    Push notifications: 100M × 10/day = 1B/day = 11,600/s avg | peak = 58K/s. Each push = ~500B payload → 29MB/s outbound to FCM/APNs. Email: 100M × 2/day = 200M/day = 2,300/s. Each email = ~5KB → 11.5MB/s to SES/SendGrid. SMS: 100M × 1/day = 100M/day = 1,150/s. Most expensive per message — use Twilio/SNS, batch where possible. Infrastructure implications from numbers: 58K push/s → cannot do synchronous HTTP to FCM for each — need Kafka queue (58K msg/s is within Kafka's range) with N workers consuming and calling FCM in batches.
