Email at 2,300/s → single SES account has 14 emails/s default limit — need rate limiting + multiple accounts or SendGrid enterprise. Storage: 100M users × 30 days history × 11 notifications × 500B = 16.5TB → use Cassandra (write-heavy, time-series access pattern). This is SDE-2 thinking: the numbers DRIVE the architecture choices, not the other way around.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: The interviewer asks "how many servers do you need?" for a service handling 100K QPS. Walk through the calculation.
    💡 Think First
    Server capacity depends on: what the server does (CPU-bound vs I/O-bound), connection pool size, and whether you have caching. A typical REST API server handles 1K-10K QPS. What assumptions do you make explicit?
    ➔ Complete Answer
    State your assumptions explicitly: "Assuming a typical Spring Boot service with DB calls, no heavy computation — each server handles ~1000 QPS." 100K QPS / 1K per server = 100 servers. Add 2× buffer for redundancy and rolling deployments = 200 servers. Add 50% for auto-scaling headroom = 300 servers at peak. In Kubernetes: 300 pods, each with 1 CPU and 1GB RAM = 300 vCPUs and 300GB RAM. At $0.05/vCPU-hour on AWS = $10,800/month compute. This is a realistic answer. Interviewers want to see you reason about numbers, not just say "horizontally scale with Kubernetes." The number gives you credibility.
    Q: What are the top 3 bottlenecks in almost every system design, and how do you identify which one you hit first?
    💡 Think First
    Every system has a weakest link. Usually it is the DB, not the app servers. The app servers are stateless and horizontally scalable. The DB is stateful and harder to scale. After the DB, what else?
    ➔ Complete Answer
    The three universal bottlenecks: (1) Database write throughput: a single PostgreSQL primary handles ~5K-10K writes/second. Beyond that: connection pool exhaustion, lock contention, WAL write bottleneck. Fix: sharding, read replicas for reads, command query responsibility segregation (CQRS). (2) Network bandwidth: servers have 1-10Gbps NICs. At 1Gbps = 125MB/s. If you are serving 300KB images at 60K QPS: 300KB × 60K = 18GB/s — far exceeds NIC capacity. Fix: CDN — serve from edge, not origin. (3) Memory/cache misses: cache miss = DB call = 10-100ms. At 100K cache misses/s = DB overloaded. Fix: increase cache size, improve cache key design, use consistent hashing to avoid thundering herd. How to identify first bottleneck: calculate utilisation for each layer. The layer closest to 100% utilisation breaks first.
    🎯 Practice Task
    Do the full back-of-envelope estimation for a URL Shortener service: 100M URLs created per day, 10B redirects per day (100:1 read:write ratio). Calculate: (1) write QPS and read QPS, (2) storage for 5 years, (3) Redis cache size for 20% of daily reads, (4) bandwidth for redirect responses, (5) number of app servers needed. Then state what this means for your architecture choices.
    💡 HintWrite QPS = 100M / 86,400 ≈ 1,200/s. Read QPS = 10B / 86,400 ≈ 115,000/s. Storage: each URL record ≈ 500B. Cache: 20% of 10B daily reads × average object size. Bandwidth: each redirect = 301 response ≈ 500B. Servers: at 1K QPS each (I/O bound with DB calls, but Redis cache reduces DB load significantly).
    ➡ Worked Solution
    BOE — URL Shortener complete estimation
    // 1. QPS Write QPS = 100M / 86,400 = 1,157/s ≈ 1,200 writes/s Read QPS = 10B / 86,400 = 115,740/s ≈ 116K reads/s (peak: 580K/s) // 2. Storage for 5 years // Each URL record: short_code(7B) + long_url(200B) + created_at(8B) + ttl(8B) ≈ 500B Daily = 100M × 500B = 50GB/day 5 years = 50GB × 365 × 5 = 91TB // manageable in PostgreSQL with sharding // 3. Redis cache size // Cache 20% of URLs (80/20 rule: 20% URLs = 80% traffic) Hot URLs = 100M × 0.20 = 20M URLs Cache size = 20M × 500B = 10GB // fits in single Redis node (r6g.large = 13GB) // With caching: 80% of 116K reads/s = 92.8K served from Redis (sub-ms) // Only 23.2K reads/s reach PostgreSQL — very manageable // 4. Bandwidth // Each redirect response: HTTP 301 + Location header ≈ 500B Outbound = 116K/s × 500B = 58MB/s = 0.46Gbps // within single server NIC // 5. App servers // With Redis cache: each server handles ~10K QPS (mostly in-memory ops) Read servers = 116K / 10K = 12 servers → round to 20 with redundancy Write servers = 1,200 / 1K = 2 servers → round to 4 with redundancy // Architecture implications from numbers: // - Read:Write = 100:1 → separate read and write paths (CQRS) // - Redis cache fits in memory → cache-aside with 24h TTL // - 91TB over 5 years → single PostgreSQL shard works, add range sharding by created_at if needed // - No CDN needed (redirect responses are tiny) — CDN for destination content, not our service

    Design an E-Commerce Order Tracking System

    requirements · architecture · DB schema · real-time updates · scale
    🧠 Framework: Always Start With Requirements
    Never start drawing boxes. Start with: Functional requirements, Non-functional requirements, Scale estimates, then Architecture.Interviewers evaluate your thinking process as much as your final design. A candidate who clarifies requirements before designing is an SDE-2. One who jumps straight to microservices is a junior.
    📐 Requirements → Architecture
    System Design Framework
    // FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS (clarify these first): // - Users can track order status in real-time // - Status transitions: PLACED → CONFIRMED → PACKED → SHIPPED → DELIVERED // - Users get push notifications on status change // - Sellers can update order status // - Order history searchable by date/status // NON-FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS: // - 10M orders/day, peak: 500K concurrent users checking status // - Status update → visible to user in < 2 seconds // - 99.9% availability // - Order history queryable for up to 2 years // SCALE ESTIMATES: // Orders/day: 10M → ~115 orders/sec avg, ~1000/sec peak // Status updates/day: ~30M (3 updates per order avg) // Read:Write ratio: ~20:1 (users check status more than sellers update it)
    💻 Architecture + Key Design Decisions
    💡 Key Design Decisions to Discuss
    Why Redis for current status?

    99% of reads want "what's the current status?" — not full history. Redis stores the latest status per orderId with O(1) lookup. Postgres stores the full audit trail (every transition). This read-path separation handles the 20:1 read:write ratio efficiently.

    Real-time updates via WebSocket

    When seller updates status: Order Service writes to Postgres + Redis, publishes OrderStatusChanged event to Kafka. Notification Service consumes → sends push notification. WebSocket Gateway consumes → pushes to any connected clients viewing that order. Users not connected at update time see fresh status from Redis on next page load.

    Database schema

    orders: id, customer_id, created_at, current_status. order_status_history: id, order_id, status, timestamp, updated_by — append-only, never updated. Index on order_id + timestamp for history queries. Partition by created_at for 2-year retention.

    State machine validation

    Prevent invalid transitions (DELIVERED → PLACED). Implement as a Java enum with allowed next-states. The Order Service rejects any transition not in the allowed set. This is the State Pattern applied at the system design level.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    You are designing the order tracking system for a food delivery app. A customer places an order and wants to see real-time status: Placed → Confirmed → Being Prepared → Out for Delivery → Delivered. The status update on the customer's phone should appear within 2 seconds of the actual status change. How do you architect this?
    Real-time push from server to client. HTTP is pull (client requests) — but you need server push. Options: polling (wasteful), long polling (better but still HTTP overhead), Server-Sent Events (SSE, one-way push), WebSockets (bi-directional). What does the data flow look like from restaurant to customer?
    Architecture: Restaurant app → POST /order/{id}/status → OrderService → publishes StatusChangedEvent to Kafka → NotificationService consumes → pushes to customer via WebSocket (or SSE). WebSocket for customer: Customer app opens WS connection on order placed. WS session stored in memory: Map<orderId, WsSession>. When Kafka consumer receives StatusChangedEvent: look up WsSession by orderId → session.sendMessage(statusUpdate). Multiple servers problem: If you have 10 app servers, the WS connection is on server 3, but the Kafka consumer might run on server 7. Fix: each server subscribes to a Redis Pub/Sub channel (order:{orderId}). Server 7 publishes to Redis channel. Server 3 (which holds the WS) is subscribed and receives it → forwards to the WS session. Fallback for web: If WS not supported: SSE (one-way stream, simpler, reconnects automatically). If SSE not supported: polling every 5 seconds (least efficient but universally compatible). Offline customers: If customer is not connected when status changes: send FCM/APNs push notification. Customer reconnects → fetches current status via REST.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: "How do you handle 500K concurrent users polling for status updates?"
    💭 Think
    Polling 500K users × every 30s = ~17K requests/sec just for status checks. How do you serve this without DB hits?
    → Answer
    L1: CDN caching for non-personalized status pages (public tracking pages). L2: Redis for current status — all 500K users hitting Redis, not Postgres. Redis can handle 100K+ reads/sec on a single instance. L3: Switch to WebSocket — instead of polling, push updates only when status actually changes. Reduces 17K requests/sec to near-zero baseline with occasional pushes.
    Q: "How do you handle the case where Kafka consumer is down and status updates are missed?"
    💭 Think
    Kafka retains messages. Consumer group offset is committed only after successful processing.
    → Answer
    Kafka retains messages for a configurable period (default 7 days). Consumer group tracks its offset. When the consumer restarts, it picks up from where it left off — no messages lost. For the WebSocket push path: connected clients that missed the update will see the correct status from Redis on their next interaction or on reconnect (which triggers a fresh status fetch).
    🎯 Practice
    Design the state machine for order status transitions. Which transitions are valid? How do you enforce this in Java and at the DB level?
    HintUse Java enum with a Set of valid next states. Enforce in the service layer (throw InvalidTransitionException) AND at DB level with a CHECK constraint or trigger to prevent invalid direct SQL updates.
    → Solution
    Java — order status state machine
    enum OrderStatus { PLACED (Set.of(CONFIRMED, CANCELLED)), CONFIRMED (Set.of(PACKED, CANCELLED)), PACKED (Set.of(SHIPPED)), SHIPPED (Set.of(DELIVERED, RETURNED)), DELIVERED (Set.of(RETURNED)), CANCELLED (Set.of()), RETURNED (Set.of()); private final Set<OrderStatus> allowed; OrderStatus(Set<OrderStatus> allowed) { this.allowed = allowed; } public void validateTransition(OrderStatus next) { if (!allowed.contains(next)) throw new InvalidTransitionException(this + " → " + next + " not allowed"); } }

    Design a Rate Limiter

    algorithms · distributed enforcement · production patterns
    🧠 Mental Model
    A rate limiter answers: "Has this client used up their quota for the current time window?"The challenge is doing this accurately, efficiently, and across multiple server instances — a purely in-memory counter only works on a single server. Production rate limiters use Redis as a shared counter store, ensuring all instances agree on the current usage.
    ⚠️ Four Algorithms — Know All, Explain Trade-offs
    AlgorithmHow it worksProsCons
    Fixed Window CounterCount requests per fixed 1-min window. Reset at :00 each minute.Simple, O(1)Burst at window edge: 2× traffic in 2 seconds (end of old + start of new window)
    Sliding Window LogStore timestamp of every request. Count how many in last 60s.Most accurate, no edge burstO(n) memory per user — impractical at scale
    Sliding Window CounterBlend current and previous window counts by time elapsed in current window.Accurate, O(1) spaceApproximate (within ~1% error)
    Token BucketBucket refills at constant rate. Each request consumes a token. Allow burst up to bucket capacity.Allows controlled bursting, O(1)Slightly more complex to implement
    💻 Token Bucket in Redis (Production Implementation)
    Java + Redis — distributed token bucket
    // Redis Lua script for atomic token bucket check + decrement // Lua runs atomically on Redis — no race conditions private static final String LUA_SCRIPT = """ local key = KEYS[1] local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[1]) local refill_rate = tonumber(ARGV[2]) -- tokens per second local now = tonumber(ARGV[3]) -- current timestamp in ms local requested = tonumber(ARGV[4]) -- tokens requested (usually 1) local bucket = redis.call('HMGET', key, 'tokens', 'last_refill') local tokens = tonumber(bucket[1]) or capacity local last_refill = tonumber(bucket[2]) or now -- Refill based on time elapsed local elapsed = (now - last_refill) / 1000 tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + elapsed * refill_rate) if tokens >= requested then tokens = tokens - requested redis.call('HMSET', key, 'tokens', tokens, 'last_refill', now) redis.call('EXPIRE', key, 3600) -- cleanup after 1h of inactivity return 1 -- allowed else return 0 -- denied end """; @Service class RateLimiter { public boolean allowRequest(String clientId, int capacity, int refillPerSec) { String key = "ratelimit:" + clientId; Long result = redisTemplate.execute( new DefaultRedisScript<>(LUA_SCRIPT, Long.class), List.of(key), capacity, refillPerSec, System.currentTimeMillis(), 1 ); return result != null && result == 1L; } } // Spring Filter wiring: // @Order(1) filter checks rate limit before any controller runs // Returns 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After header if denied // Lua atomicity ensures correctness across 100 app server instances
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Your API Gateway serves 500 microservices. A single buggy client sends 50,000 requests/second and brings down three downstream services. You need to add rate limiting without deploying new servers. The limit must be enforced consistently across 12 API Gateway instances. How do you design it?
    In-memory counter per instance will not work — 12 instances each allow 100 req/s = 1200 total instead of 100. You need a shared atomic counter. What data store gives you atomic increment with TTL in under 1ms?
    Redis as shared counter (Token Bucket via Lua script): Every API Gateway instance calls Redis on each request. A Lua script atomically: (1) GETs current token count for client_id, (2) refills tokens based on elapsed time, (3) consumes one token if available, (4) returns allow/deny. The Lua script runs atomically on Redis — no race condition across 12 instances. Key design decisions: (1) Rate limit key = client_id + window (e.g. user:123:2024-01-15:10:30). (2) Redis TTL = window size — keys auto-expire. (3) Fallback if Redis is down: fail-open (allow all) or fail-closed (deny all) — business decision. (4) Sliding window log (most accurate) vs Fixed window (simplest) vs Token bucket (best for burst control). Headers to return: X-RateLimit-Limit: 100, X-RateLimit-Remaining: 47, X-RateLimit-Reset: 1705312260, Retry-After: 30 (on 429).
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: "How do you handle rate limiting for APIs with different tiers (free: 100/hr, premium: 10K/hr)?"
    💭 Think
    The algorithm is the same — just parameterize capacity and refill rate per user tier.
    → Answer
    Fetch the user's tier from JWT claims or a Redis-cached user-config lookup. Pass tier-specific capacity and refill_rate to the rate limiter. Redis key includes the user ID (not just IP) so tier boundaries are per-user: ratelimit:user:U123. For API key-based access: rate limit on the API key, not the IP.
    Q: "What headers should a rate-limited API return?"
    💭 Think
    Clients need to know their limit, remaining quota, and when to retry.
    → Standard headers
    On every response: X-RateLimit-Limit: 100, X-RateLimit-Remaining: 43, X-RateLimit-Reset: 1720000000 (Unix timestamp of window reset). On 429: Retry-After: 30 (seconds until next token available). These allow clients to implement smart backoff without guessing.
    🎯 Practice
    Implement a Fixed Window Counter rate limiter using only Redis INCR and EXPIRE commands. Allow 100 requests per minute per client IP.
    HintKey = "ratelimit:{ip}:{current_minute}". INCR the key. If the returned value is 1 (first request), set EXPIRE to 60. If value > 100, deny. Atomic because INCR is atomic in Redis.
    → Solution
    Java — fixed window with Redis
    public boolean isAllowed(String clientIp, int limit) { String minute = String.valueOf(System.currentTimeMillis() / 60_000); String key = "rl:" + clientIp + ":" + minute; Long count = redisTemplate.opsForValue().increment(key); // atomic INCR if (count == 1) redisTemplate.expire(key, 65, SECONDS); // first req: set expiry (65s buffer) return count <= limit; } // Edge case: at minute boundary, up to 2× limit possible in 2 seconds. // Sliding Window Counter solves this — blend previous window's count proportionally.

    Design a URL Shortener

    encoding strategy · redirect performance · analytics · scale
    🧠 Requirements First
    Clarify before designing:Write 100M URLs/day? Read (redirect) 10B/day? Custom aliases? Analytics? Expiry? The read:write ratio (100:1) determines where to invest: optimize the redirect path, not the write path.
    💻 Core Design: Base62 Encoding + Distributed Counter
    Java — complete URL shortener
    // WHY counter over random? Counter = guaranteed unique. Random = collision check needed. // WHY Base62? 62 chars (a-z, A-Z, 0-9) × 7 chars = 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion unique codes. class UrlShortener { private static final String ALPHABET = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789"; private String encode(long id) { StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); while (id > 0) { sb.append(ALPHABET.charAt((int)(id % 62))); id /= 62; } return sb.reverse().toString(); } public String shorten(String longUrl) { // ID generation: Redis INCR (single instance) OR pre-allocated ranges per server long id = redis.incr("url:counter"); String code = encode(id); db.save(new UrlMapping(code, longUrl, Instant.now())); redis.setex("url:" + code, 86400, longUrl); // cache for 24h return "https://srt.ly/" + code; } public String resolve(String code) { // Redis cache-aside — 99% of popular URLs served from cache String cached = redis.get("url:" + code); if (cached != null) { recordClickAsync(code); return cached; } return db.findByCode(code) .map(m -> { redis.setex("url:" + code, 86400, m.getLongUrl()); return m.getLongUrl(); }) .orElseThrow(() -> new NotFoundException(code)); } private void recordClickAsync(String code) { kafka.publish("url-clicks", new ClickEvent(code, Instant.now())); // Analytics consumer aggregates: clicks per URL per day/hour // Don't block the redirect path for analytics! } }
    💡 Scale Discussion
    Redirect latency optimization

    The redirect path MUST be fast — users are waiting. CDN at the edge: cache popular short codes at CDN level (Cache-Control: max-age=3600). For 80% of popular URLs, the CDN handles the redirect without hitting your servers at all.

    Counter scaling with pre-allocation

    A single Redis INCR handles ~100K ops/sec — sufficient for most cases. For higher scale: each app server pre-allocates a range (Server A: 1M-2M, Server B: 2M-3M) from a Zookeeper/DB counter. Servers generate IDs locally within their range — no Redis contention.

    DB choice and schema

    Write path: Cassandra or DynamoDB for high write throughput. Key: shortCode, Value: { longUrl, createdAt, userId, clickCount, expiresAt }. Read path: Redis cache in front. Read replicas if using SQL.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    Design a URL shortening service. The interviewer asks: "Walk me through what happens when a user hits https://srt.ly/abc123 and why each step is necessary."
    This tests whether you can trace a request end-to-end through the stack. Each step has a reason — CDN for latency, Redis for speed, DB for durability. Explain the WHY.
    Request path: (1) DNS resolves srt.ly to Cloudflare CDN IP. (2) CDN checks its cache for abc123 — if found, returns 301 redirect directly (no origin hit, <10ms). (3) Cache miss: CDN forwards to origin. (4) Origin load balancer selects an app server. (5) App server: GET url:abc123 from Redis — if found (<1ms), return 302 redirect. (6) Redis miss: query PostgreSQL by code index lookup (B-tree, O(log n)). (7) Write to Redis with 24h TTL (warm the cache). (8) Return 302. Async after response: publish ClickEvent to Kafka for analytics. 301 vs 302: 301 (permanent) — browser caches forever, no repeat origin calls, but you lose click analytics. 302 (temporary) — browser asks origin every time, you capture every click. Use 301 for unimportant links, 302 for tracked links.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: How do you generate the short code? Compare MD5 hash vs Base62 counter vs random UUID.
    💭 Think First
    Three common approaches with different trade-off profiles. Know which fails at scale and which requires coordination.
    → Complete Answer
    MD5 hash of long URL: deterministic (same URL always same code), but 32-char hex needs truncation to 7 chars, causing collisions — must check DB and regenerate on collision, adding latency. Random UUID: no coordination, but 36-char UUID shortened to 7 chars has ~0.1% collision rate at 1B URLs. Base62 counter: auto-increment ID (Redis INCR or DB sequence) → encode to Base62. 7 chars = 62^7 = 3.5 trillion unique codes. Zero collisions, deterministic length, sortable. Downside: requires a shared counter (coordination). Distribute via pre-allocated ranges (instance A gets 1M-2M, B gets 2M-3M). Production: Base62 counter with pre-allocated ranges is the best choice.
    Q: Custom aliases (e.g. srt.ly/mypromo) need to be unique. How do you enforce this efficiently?
    💭 Think First
    Custom aliases are user-provided and must not conflict with each other or with auto-generated codes.
    → Complete Answer
    Database UNIQUE constraint on the code column — the DB enforces uniqueness at the storage layer. Application layer: catch DataIntegrityViolationException (Spring) or SQLIntegrityConstraintViolationException — return 409 Conflict with a clear message. For high-volume alias creation: check Redis first (SET NX with short TTL as a soft reservation) before the DB write, to avoid hammering the DB with conflicting writes. Namespace separation: auto-generated codes use a numeric Base62 prefix range (1-9 first char), custom aliases allow alphanumeric freely — they can never collide by design. Rate limit custom alias creation per user to prevent squatting.
    🎯 Practice
    How would you add custom aliases (e.g., srt.ly/my-promo) while maintaining the counter-based system for auto-generated codes? Handle conflicts.
    HintCustom aliases don't go through the counter. They're validated for uniqueness with a DB check. Race condition: two users both check "my-promo" is available simultaneously → both try to insert. Solve with unique constraint on shortCode column + catch constraint violation.
    → Solution
    Java
    public String shortenWithAlias(String longUrl, String alias) { try { db.save(new UrlMapping(alias, longUrl, Instant.now())); // alias is shortCode return "https://srt.ly/" + alias; } catch (DataIntegrityViolationException e) { // unique constraint violated throw new AliasConflictException("Alias '" + alias + "' is already taken"); } } // DB schema: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON url_mappings(short_code); // The DB unique constraint handles the race condition atomically. // No need for application-level distributed locking.
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement the Base62 encoder and decoder. encode(1000000) should return a short string. decode("4c92") should return 1000000. Use the alphabet 0-9a-zA-Z.
    Hint — think before readingBase62: repeatedly take modulo 62 to get digits (least significant first), map each to the alphabet, reverse. Decode: iterate chars, multiply accumulator by 62, add the char's index in the alphabet.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — Base62 encode/decode
    class Base62 { private static final String ALPHA = "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"; public static String encode(long n) { if(n == 0) return "0"; StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); while(n > 0) { sb.append(ALPHA.charAt((int)(n % 62))); n /= 62; } return sb.reverse().toString(); } public static long decode(String s) { long n = 0; for(char c : s.toCharArray()) n = n * 62 + ALPHA.indexOf(c); return n; } }

    Design a Pastebin / Code Sharing App

    TTL · content-addressed storage · short link generation · scaling reads vs writes · CDN
    🧠 Mental Model
    Pastebin = write-once read-many content store with expiry. Users write a blob of text or code once. Millions of readers hit the short link over the next hours or days. Then it expires. This access pattern screams: cache aggressively, scale reads independently of writes, never update (only create + expire). The technical challenges are: short link generation (no collisions), TTL enforcement, and handling viral pastes at 100x normal read rate.
    Core Design Decisions
  • Short link generation — Base62-encoded auto-increment counter (e.g. ID=10000 → "2Bi"). 7 characters = 62^7 = 3.5 trillion unique codes. No collision by design. Alternative: MD5 hash of content, but collisions require retry logic.paste.ly/2Bi → looks up 2Bi in Redis/DB → returns content
  • Content storage strategy — Text in DB (PostgreSQL) for <1MB pastes. Large files/code in S3 with the DB storing only the S3 key. DB stores: id, short_code, s3_key, content_type, created_at, expires_at, view_count.SELECT content FROM pastes WHERE short_code='2Bi' AND (expires_at IS NULL OR expires_at > NOW())
  • TTL enforcement — expires_at column + scheduled job (pg_cron or a Spring @Scheduled task) deletes expired rows nightly. For S3: use S3 Object Expiration lifecycle policy. Redis cache entries get their own TTL = (expires_at - now).Redis: SET paste:2Bi {content} EXAT 1705312260 (Unix expiry timestamp)
  • Read scaling — reads are 100x more frequent than writes. Cache popular pastes in Redis. CDN (CloudFront) caches public pastes at edge nodes globally — viral paste served from 50ms CDN cache not from origin.Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600 on GET /paste/2Bi response
  • Write path — POST /paste → validate size (<10MB) → generate short code → store in DB → async replicate to S3 if large → cache in Redis with TTL → return short URL. Idempotency: not needed (each paste is a new creation).
    • ComponentTech ChoiceWhy
    Short code generationRedis INCR + Base62 encodeAtomic, distributed, no collision, fast
    Content storage (<1MB)PostgreSQL text columnACID, simple, queryable metadata
    Content storage (>1MB)AWS S3Cheap, durable, unlimited scale
    Read cacheRedis with TTL = expires_atSub-ms reads, automatic expiry
    Global distributionCloudFront CDNServe viral pastes from edge, reduce origin load
    Expiry enforcementS3 lifecycle + pg_cronAutomatic, no application code needed
    Syntax highlightingClient-side (Prism.js)Zero server cost, instant, rich language support
    🏭 Production Scenario
    A paste containing a viral code snippet gets shared on Hacker News. It receives 500,000 reads in 10 minutes — 830 reads/second. Your origin has 5 app servers each handling 200 req/s = 1000 req/s capacity. Normally fine, but 800 req/s for ONE paste would saturate your DB. How does your architecture handle this?
    The paste was written once. All 500K reads are for the exact same content. This is a perfect cache hit scenario. Where should the cache be to intercept 800 req/s before they reach the DB?
    CDN absorbs the spike: On the first read after the paste is created, the app server returns the paste with Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600. CloudFront caches this at its edge nodes. Subsequent 499,999 reads hit the CDN — zero requests reach your origin. DB sees exactly 1 read for that paste. Redis as fallback cache: For pastes that are not CDN-cached yet, Redis serves them in <1ms. The DB only gets hit on a Redis miss (cold cache), which means only the very first read after creation. Cache invalidation on early delete: User deletes the paste early. (1) Delete from DB. (2) DELETE paste:{code} from Redis. (3) CDN: issue a CloudFront invalidation (takes ~1-5 minutes to propagate globally). During propagation, CDN may still serve the deleted paste — acceptable for most use cases. If not acceptable: use short max-age (60s) instead of long (3600s).
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: How do you prevent abuse — someone uploading 10,000 pastes per minute or uploading 1GB files?
    💡 Think First
    Two distinct abuse vectors: rate abuse (too many pastes) and size abuse (too large pastes). Each needs a different control. Think API Gateway for rate, and at the application layer for size.
    ➔ Complete Answer
    Rate limiting: API Gateway enforces max 10 paste creations/minute per IP (unauthenticated) or per user_id (authenticated). Token bucket in Redis — same pattern as the Rate Limiter design. Return 429 with Retry-After header. Size limiting: Max paste size = 10MB (text) enforced at the API layer before writing to DB. For S3 uploads: use pre-signed URLs with a content-length-range condition — S3 itself rejects oversized uploads, preventing bypass. Content moderation: Async scan via AWS Rekognition (images) or regex patterns for known malicious signatures. If detected: mark paste as removed, serve 404 on the short link. Storage quota per user: Track total_bytes per user_id in a separate quota table. Enforce in the write path before accepting the paste.
    Q: How do you implement private (password-protected) pastes? How does this affect your caching strategy?
    💡 Think First
    Public paste: CDN caches freely. Private paste: CDN must not cache it — the response depends on whether the viewer knows the password. How do you signal this to CDN?
    ➔ Complete Answer
    Storage: Add is_private=true + password_hash=bcrypt(password) to the pastes table. Read path: GET /paste/2Bi → check is_private → if true: require password in request header or redirect to password form. Validate bcrypt(provided) == stored hash. Caching: Private pastes must NOT be cached by CDN. Set Cache-Control: private, no-store on the response — CDN will not cache, every request hits origin. Redis: only cache after password validation, keyed by paste_id + session (not globally accessible). Alternative for high traffic private pastes: Generate a signed token after password validation (HMAC of paste_id + expiry). Redirect to a signed URL. CDN caches the response for that signed URL for its short TTL (5 minutes). This balances privacy with CDN performance.
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement the core Pastebin backend in Spring Boot. Requirements: (1) POST /paste accepts text content and optional TTL in hours — returns a short URL. (2) GET /paste/{code} returns the content or 404 if expired/not found. (3) Short codes are generated from a Redis counter using Base62. (4) Redis caches pastes with a TTL matching the expiry. (5) A scheduled job cleans up expired DB rows daily.
    💡 HintRedis INCR gives you a unique auto-incrementing ID — Base62 encode it for the short code. On GET: check Redis first (cache hit = no DB call). On miss: query DB, check expires_at, update Redis with remaining TTL. @Scheduled(cron="0 2 * * *") for the cleanup job (runs at 2am daily).
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Spring Boot — Pastebin core implementation
    @RestController class PasteController { @Autowired PasteService svc; @PostMapping("/paste") public PasteResponse create(@RequestBody PasteRequest req) { return svc.create(req.content(), req.ttlHours()); // returns {shortUrl, expiresAt} } @GetMapping("/paste/{code}") public ResponseEntity<String> get(@PathVariable String code) { return svc.get(code) .map(ResponseEntity::ok) .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build()); // 404 if expired or missing } } @Service class PasteService { @Autowired StringRedisTemplate redis; @Autowired PasteRepository repo; public PasteResponse create(String content, int ttlHours) { // 1. Generate unique short code via Redis atomic counter long id = redis.opsForValue().increment("paste:counter"); String code = Base62.encode(id); // e.g. 10000 -> "2Bi" Instant expiresAt = ttlHours > 0 ? Instant.now().plusSeconds(ttlHours * 3600L) : null; // null = never expires // 2. Store in DB (source of truth) repo.save(new Paste(code, content, expiresAt)); // 3. Cache in Redis with TTL if(expiresAt != null) { redis.opsForValue().set("paste:"+code, content, Duration.between(Instant.now(), expiresAt)); // auto-expires } else { redis.opsForValue().set("paste:"+code, content); // no TTL } return new PasteResponse("https://paste.ly/"+code, expiresAt); } public Optional<String> get(String code) { // 1. Redis cache hit (sub-ms) String cached = redis.opsForValue().get("paste:"+code); if(cached != null) return Optional.of(cached); // 2. Cache miss: query DB, check expiry return repo.findByCode(code) .filter(p -> p.getExpiresAt() == null || p.getExpiresAt().isAfter(Instant.now())) // not expired .map(p -> { // Warm cache for future reads long ttlSecs = p.getExpiresAt() == null ? 86400 : Duration.between(Instant.now(), p.getExpiresAt()).getSeconds(); redis.opsForValue().set("paste:"+code, p.getContent(), Duration.ofSeconds(ttlSecs)); return p.getContent(); }); } // Nightly cleanup: delete expired rows from DB @Scheduled(cron = "0 0 2 * * *") // 2am every day public void cleanExpired() { int deleted = repo.deleteExpiredBefore(Instant.now()); log.info("Cleaned {} expired pastes", deleted); } }

    Design Instagram / Twitter News Feed

    fanout on write vs fanout on read · social graph · feed ranking · celebrity problem · eventual consistency
    🧠 Mental Model
    A news feed is a personalised, ranked stream of posts from people you follow. The hard problem: when Alice posts, her 10 million followers all need to see it in their feed within seconds. Naive approach — query all posts from all people you follow on every page load — kills the database at scale. Two fundamental approaches: Push (fanout on write) or Pull (fanout on read). Real systems use a hybrid.
    ApproachHow it worksProCon
    Fanout on Write (Push)When Alice posts, immediately write the post ID into each follower's feed cacheRead is instant: just fetch pre-built feed from RedisCelebrity problem: Cristiano Ronaldo posts → 500M writes in one second
    Fanout on Read (Pull)When Bob opens his feed, query posts from all people he follows, merge, rankWrite is instant; works for celebritiesRead is slow: must query N followees' posts and merge
    Hybrid (production)Push for regular users (under 10K followers). Pull for celebrities. Merge at read time.Fast reads AND handles celebritiesMore complex logic; must detect and handle high-follower accounts differently
    Feed Generation Architecture
  • Post creation: Alice posts → write to Posts table (post_id, user_id, content, created_at) → publish PostCreated event to Kafka.Topic: user-posts | Key: alice_id | Value: {post_id, content, media_url, timestamp}
  • FanoutService consumes PostCreated. For normal users (followers < 10K): fetch Alice's follower list from FollowerGraph service → for each follower, push post_id into their feed list in Redis (LPUSH feed:{follower_id} {post_id}, LTRIM to 1000).Redis: LPUSH feed:bob_id post_abc | LTRIM feed:bob_id 0 999 (keep latest 1000)
  • Feed read: Bob opens app → GET /feed → FeedService reads post_ids from Redis (LRANGE feed:bob_id 0 49) → batch-fetches post details from Posts service → fetches engagement counts from Redis (likes:post_id, comments:post_id) → ranks by score (recency + engagement) → returns paginated feed.
  • Celebrity handling: Accounts with >10K followers flagged as celebrities. On Bob's feed load: FeedService fetches Bob's pre-built feed PLUS latest posts from each celebrity Bob follows (pull, limit 5 per celebrity) → merge and re-rank → return.
  • Feed ranking signals: Recency (time decay), engagement (likes/comments/shares), relationship strength (you interact with Alice often → her posts rank higher), content type preference (Bob prefers videos → boost video posts).
    • 🏭 Production Scenario
    Cristiano Ronaldo (500M followers) posts a photo. Within 1 second, 50 million followers open Instagram. Under pure fanout-on-write, you need 500 million Redis writes in that second. Your Redis cluster cannot handle this. Under pure fanout-on-read, 50 million users each query all the people they follow — your Posts DB gets 50M × 500 people followed = 25 billion DB reads per second. Neither approach works alone. Design the hybrid.
    The celebrity problem: fanout-on-write works for normal users (1K followers = 1K writes per post, manageable). It breaks for celebrities. Fanout-on-read works for celebrities (they post infrequently, their posts are fetched from one place). It breaks for normal users at high read volume.
    Hybrid architecture: Classify users at post-creation time. If poster has <10K followers: fanout-on-write — push post_id to all follower feed caches immediately (asynchronously via Kafka workers). If poster has >10K followers (celebrity): do NOT fanout — store the post in a celebrity-posts table only. At read time: FeedService fetches Bob's pre-built feed (from Redis, built by fanout-on-write from normal users). Then for each celebrity Bob follows: fetch their latest 5 posts from the celebrity-posts table (indexed by user_id, created_at DESC). Merge both lists. Re-rank by score. Return top 50. Why this works: Normal users: O(followers) writes per post, fast reads. Celebrities: O(1) write per post, O(celebrities_followed) reads per feed load — Bob follows 20 celebrities, so 20 reads per page load — acceptable. Eventual consistency: The pre-built feed may be slightly stale (a few seconds behind). This is acceptable for social media. Financial systems need strong consistency; social feeds do not.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: How do you implement the "unfollow" operation correctly so unfollowed users' posts disappear from the feed immediately?
    💡 Think First
    If feeds are pre-built caches, unfollowing does not automatically remove posts from the cached feed. The cache has post IDs but not "who posted this". How do you handle this at read time?
    ➔ Complete Answer
    Two approaches: (1) Lazy filtering at read time: When Bob unfollows Alice, mark the relationship as unfollowed in the FollowerGraph (immediate). When Bob next fetches his feed, FeedService filters out any post_ids authored by Alice before returning. The cache still has Alice's posts but they are filtered out. Over time the cache naturally expires or gets replaced by new posts. Simplest approach. (2) Active cache cleanup: On unfollow, publish UnfollowEvent → FeedCleanupService fetches Alice's recent post_ids → removes them from Bob's feed cache (Redis LREM). More complex, more immediate. Production choice: Lazy filtering is simpler and sufficient for social media — the feed is eventually consistent anyway. The user expects to see the change on next load, not in real-time.
    Q: How do you handle the "seen posts" problem — a user scrolls through 50 posts, then comes back later and should not see the same posts again?
    💡 Think First
    The pre-built feed is a list of post_ids. Pagination by offset would re-show posts if new posts are inserted at the top. Cursor-based pagination solves this. What is the cursor?
    ➔ Complete Answer
    Cursor = the last-seen post_id + timestamp. Client stores the cursor after each feed load. On next request: send cursor → FeedService fetches posts newer than the cursor for unseen content, or picks up from cursor position for "scroll down" pagination. Redis sorted set (ZSET) is ideal: ZADD feed:bob_id {score=timestamp} {post_id}. ZRANGEBYSCORE feed:bob_id {cursor_timestamp} +inf LIMIT 50 returns unseen posts ordered by time. ZREVRANGEBYSCORE for newest-first ordering. The client's cursor is the timestamp of the last post it received. This ensures: (1) No duplicate posts on scroll down. (2) New posts appear at top on refresh. (3) Works even if posts are deleted from the feed (deleted post_id simply not returned from Posts service lookup).
    🎯 Practice Task
    Design the data model and API for a Twitter-like news feed. Include: (1) Database schema for users, posts, and follows. (2) Redis data structure for pre-built feeds. (3) POST /post endpoint that creates a post and triggers async fanout. (4) GET /feed endpoint with cursor-based pagination. (5) How you distinguish celebrity vs normal users.
    💡 HintPosts table: post_id (UUID), user_id, content, media_url, created_at. Follows table: follower_id, followee_id, created_at. Redis: ZSET feed:{user_id} with score=epoch_ms and member=post_id. Fanout via Kafka: PostCreated event consumed by FanoutWorkers. Celebrity threshold: store follower_count in user profile, check at fanout time.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java/SQL — News Feed core implementation
    -- Schema CREATE TABLE posts(post_id UUID PK, user_id UUID, content TEXT, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ); CREATE TABLE follows(follower_id UUID, followee_id UUID, PRIMARY KEY(follower_id, followee_id)); CREATE INDEX idx_posts_user_time ON posts(user_id, created_at DESC); CREATE INDEX idx_follows_followee ON follows(followee_id); -- "who follows Alice?" // POST /post → create post → fanout @PostMapping("/post") public Post createPost(@RequestBody PostRequest req, @AuthenticationPrincipal User user) { Post post = postRepo.save(new Post(user.id(), req.content())); kafka.send("post-created", new PostCreatedEvent(post.id(), user.id(), user.followerCount())); return post; } // FanoutConsumer: runs async, fans out to followers' feed caches @KafkaListener(topics = "post-created") public void fanout(PostCreatedEvent event) { if(event.followerCount() > 10_000) return; // celebrity: skip fanout, pull at read time followRepo.findFollowers(event.userId()).forEach(followerId -> { redis.opsForZSet().add("feed:"+followerId, event.postId(), event.timestamp().toEpochMilli()); redis.opsForZSet().removeRange("feed:"+followerId, 0, -1001); // keep latest 1000 }); } // GET /feed?cursor=1705312260000&limit=20 @GetMapping("/feed") public FeedResponse getFeed(@RequestParam long cursor, @AuthenticationPrincipal User user) { // 1. Fetch pre-built feed (normal users' posts) Set<String> postIds = redis.opsForZSet() .reverseRangeByScore("feed:"+user.id(), cursor, Double.MAX_VALUE, 0, 21); // +1 for hasMore // 2. Merge celebrity posts (pull model for high-follower accounts) List<String> celebPostIds = getCelebPosts(user.id(), cursor); postIds.addAll(celebPostIds); // 3. Batch fetch post details, rank, return List<Post> posts = postRepo.findAllById(postIds).stream() .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Post::createdAt).reversed()) .limit(20).collect(toList()); boolean hasMore = postIds.size() > 20; long nextCursor = posts.isEmpty() ? cursor : posts.get(posts.size()-1).createdAt().toEpochMilli(); return new FeedResponse(posts, nextCursor, hasMore); }

    Design a Unique ID Generator Service

    Snowflake algorithm · timestamp + machine ID + sequence · clock skew · 64-bit IDs · distributed coordination
    🧠 Mental Model
    A unique ID generator must produce IDs that are: globally unique (no two machines ever produce the same ID), roughly time-ordered (IDs generated later are larger — enables range queries), and fast (generate millions per second without coordination). The naive solution — a database auto-increment — is a single point of failure and a write bottleneck. The Snowflake algorithm (Twitter, 2010) solves this with a 64-bit integer composed of three parts: timestamp + machine ID + sequence.
    Snowflake ID Structure (64 bits total)
    Snowflake bit layout
    | 1 bit | 41 bits | 10 bits | 12 bits | | unused | timestamp (ms) | machine ID | sequence number | | 0 | ms since custom epoch| 0-1023 | 0-4095 | Timestamp: milliseconds since custom epoch (e.g. 2020-01-01) 41 bits = 2^41 ms = ~69 years before overflow Machine ID: 10 bits = 1024 unique machines Can split: 5 bits datacenter ID + 5 bits machine ID within datacenter Sequence: 12 bits = 4096 IDs per millisecond per machine Reset to 0 every millisecond Max throughput: 1024 machines × 4096 IDs/ms = ~4 million IDs/ms = 4 billion IDs/second Example ID generated at time T, machine 5, sequence 100: = (T - epoch) << 22 | (5 << 12) | 100
    ApproachProsConsUse when
    DB Auto-incrementSimple, guaranteed uniqueSingle point of failure, write bottleneckLow-scale, single DB
    UUID v4 (random)No coordination, easyNot sortable, 128 bits, poor index localityWhen order does not matter
    UUID v7 (time-ordered)Sortable, 128-bit, no coordination128 bits (larger than int64)Modern systems that accept 128-bit IDs
    Snowflake (Twitter)Sortable, 64-bit, fast, distributedRequires machine ID coordination, clock skew riskHigh-scale, need sortable int64
    Redis INCRSimple, atomicRedis is a dependency, single node bottleneckModerate scale, already using Redis
    🏭 Production Scenario
    You are designing the ID generation for a payment system processing 100K transactions/second across 50 data centres. Requirements: IDs must be globally unique, sortable by creation time (for efficient range queries like "get all transactions from today"), fit in a 64-bit integer (for efficient DB storage), and require no central coordination per ID generation. The current UUID v4 approach is failing because random UUIDs cause B-tree index fragmentation — inserts are O(log n) with random page access instead of append-mostly.
    UUID v4 is random — inserts go to random pages in the B-tree index, causing page splits and random I/O. A time-ordered ID (Snowflake) would insert at the end of the index (monotonically increasing) — sequential writes, much faster. How do you coordinate machine IDs across 50 data centres?
    Choose Snowflake: 64-bit, time-ordered, no per-ID coordination, 4B IDs/second capacity. Machine ID coordination: Each Snowflake node needs a unique machine ID (0-1023). On startup: node requests a machine ID from ZooKeeper (or a central lease service). ZooKeeper assigns the lowest available ID and maintains a lease. If the node crashes, the lease expires and the ID is reassigned. Alternatively: use the last 10 bits of the pod's IP address (works if IPs are unique within the cluster — they are in Kubernetes). Clock skew problem: If a machine's clock goes backwards (NTP adjustment), the next ID could have a smaller timestamp than the previous — violating time-ordering and potentially duplicating IDs in the same millisecond. Fix: if current_time < last_timestamp, wait until current_time catches up before generating a new ID. If the skew is large (>1 second): refuse to generate IDs and alert ops — better to be unavailable than to produce duplicate IDs in a payment system. DB index improvement: Snowflake IDs are monotonically increasing within a millisecond → B-tree inserts are always at the rightmost leaf page → no page splits → sequential I/O → 10x faster insert performance vs UUID v4.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: What happens if two Snowflake nodes are assigned the same machine ID? How do you detect and prevent this?
    💡 Think First
    Two nodes with the same machine ID can produce identical IDs if they generate at the same millisecond with the same sequence number. This is a catastrophic collision in a payment system. How does your machine ID assignment prevent this?
    ➔ Complete Answer
    Prevention: ZooKeeper ephemeral node per machine ID. A node creates /snowflake/machine-ids/42 as an ephemeral ZooKeeper node on startup. If the node crashes, ZooKeeper deletes the ephemeral node automatically (session timeout ~30s). Another node trying to create /snowflake/machine-ids/42 gets a NodeExists exception — it tries the next available ID. No two live nodes can hold the same machine ID because only one can own the ephemeral ZooKeeper node. Detection: each Snowflake node logs its machine ID on startup. A monitoring system (Prometheus) can alert if two nodes report the same machine ID in their metrics. Also: add the machine ID to a Redis SET on startup (SADD active-machine-ids 42) and check for duplicates.
    Q: Compare Snowflake with ULID (Universally Unique Lexicographically Sortable Identifier). When would you choose ULID over Snowflake?
    💡 Think First
    ULID = 128-bit ID: 48-bit millisecond timestamp + 80-bit random. No machine ID needed — randomness handles uniqueness. What does this trade off vs Snowflake?
    ➔ Complete Answer
    ULID: 128 bits (16 bytes) vs Snowflake's 64 bits (8 bytes) — 2x storage. No coordination needed (no machine ID assignment, no ZooKeeper). Encoded as 26-character Base32 string (URL-safe, case-insensitive). Monotonically increasing within the same millisecond (random portion is also incremented). Choose ULID when: you want no coordination infrastructure (startup simplicity), you accept 128-bit IDs, you want a human-readable string form. Choose Snowflake when: storage efficiency matters (int64 is the cheapest DB column type), you need proven high-throughput (4B/sec), you already have coordination infrastructure. Production trend: UUID v7 (standardised in RFC 9562, 2024) is replacing both — it is time-ordered (first 48 bits = millisecond timestamp), uses random bits for uniqueness within a millisecond, and is a standard UUID (works in existing UUID columns). New systems should consider UUID v7 first.
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement a Snowflake ID generator in Java. Requirements: (1) 64-bit long ID. (2) Bits: 1 unused | 41 timestamp | 10 machine ID | 12 sequence. (3) Thread-safe — multiple threads can call nextId() concurrently. (4) Handles clock skew — if current time goes backwards, wait until it catches up. (5) Sequence wraps around per millisecond.
    💡 HintKeep lastTimestamp and sequence as instance fields. Synchronize nextId(). If currentMs == lastTimestamp: increment sequence, check if it overflows 4096 (if so, wait for next ms). If currentMs > lastTimestamp: reset sequence to 0. If currentMs < lastTimestamp: clock went backwards — wait or throw. Compose the ID with bit shifts: (timestamp << 22) | (machineId << 12) | sequence.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — Snowflake ID generator
    class SnowflakeIdGenerator { private static final long EPOCH = 1577836800000L; // 2020-01-01 private static final long MAX_SEQ = (1L << 12) - 1; // 4095 private static final long MACHINE_BITS = 10; private static final long SEQ_BITS = 12; private final long machineId; private long lastTimestamp = -1L; private long sequence = 0L; SnowflakeIdGenerator(long machineId) { if(machineId < 0 || machineId > (1L<<MACHINE_BITS)-1) throw new IllegalArgumentException("machineId must be 0-1023"); this.machineId = machineId; } public synchronized long nextId() { long now = System.currentTimeMillis() - EPOCH; if(now < lastTimestamp) { // Clock went backwards — wait until it catches up long wait = lastTimestamp - now; if(wait > 5) throw new IllegalStateException("Clock skew too large: "+wait+"ms"); while(System.currentTimeMillis() - EPOCH < lastTimestamp) { /* spin */ } now = System.currentTimeMillis() - EPOCH; } if(now == lastTimestamp) { sequence = (sequence + 1) & MAX_SEQ; if(sequence == 0) { // sequence exhausted this millisecond → wait for next ms while((now = System.currentTimeMillis() - EPOCH) <= lastTimestamp) { /* spin */ } } } else { sequence = 0; // new millisecond → reset sequence } lastTimestamp = now; return (now << (MACHINE_BITS + SEQ_BITS)) | (machineId << SEQ_BITS) | sequence; } // Decode for debugging public static Map<String,long> decode(long id) { return Map.of( "timestamp", (id >> 22) + EPOCH, "machineId", (id >> 12) & 0x3FFL, "sequence", id & 0xFFFL ); } }

    Design Google Maps / Navigation System

    Dijkstra · A* · map tiles · geo-search · routing at scale · live traffic · ETA
    🧠 Mental Model
    Google Maps has two completely different problems: (1) Map rendering — serve 256×256 pixel tiles for every zoom level and location. (2) Routing — find the fastest path between two points in a road network with billions of edges. Each problem requires a different architecture. The road network is a directed weighted graph: intersections = nodes, roads = edges, weight = travel time (not distance). Routing = shortest path in this graph.
  • Map tiles: The world is divided into a grid at each zoom level (zoom 0 = 1 tile for whole world, zoom 20 = 1M+ tiles). Each tile is a 256×256 PNG pre-rendered from OpenStreetMap or proprietary data. On pan/zoom: client requests 9 tiles around the viewport. CDN serves tiles — cache hit rate is ~99% for popular areas. Tile URL: /tiles/{zoom}/{x}/{y}.png.Tile storage at zoom 18 (city block level): ~4 trillion tiles × 50KB avg = 200PB. Only render and store tiles for populated areas (~1% of Earth's surface).
  • Graph representation: Road network stored as adjacency list: Map<NodeId, List<Edge(toNode, weight)>>. Weight = estimated travel time (distance ÷ speed limit). For a city: ~1M nodes, ~3M edges. For a country: ~100M nodes, ~300M edges. Stored in memory on routing servers — OSM road data for the US is ~8GB compressed.
  • Routing algorithms: Dijkstra: O((V+E) log V) with a priority queue. Correct but slow for continental routing (too many nodes). A* with heuristic (straight-line distance to destination): same complexity but explores fewer nodes (guided search). Bidirectional Dijkstra: run from source AND destination simultaneously, meet in the middle — 2× faster. Contraction Hierarchies (used by Google): pre-process the graph to add "shortcuts" between important nodes (highways). Routing then only explores high-level nodes first — 1000× faster than Dijkstra for long routes.
  • Live traffic: GPS traces from all navigation users → aggregate anonymously into speed readings per road segment → update edge weights in the routing graph every 5 minutes. ETA = sum of (distance_i / speed_i) along the route.
  • Geo-search (find nearby restaurants): Geohash divides the world into a grid of variable-precision string codes. Nearby query: find all POIs with geohash prefix matching current location + 8 neighbours. Indexed in Redis (GEOADD, GEORADIUS) or Elasticsearch geo_point. QuadTree: recursive spatial subdivision — query = traverse from root to leaf covering the query bounding box.
    • 🏭 Production Scenario
    A user in Mumbai requests a route to Pune (150km, ~3hr drive). Naive Dijkstra on the full India road graph (100M nodes, 300M edges) would take 30 seconds. Google Maps returns a route in 200ms. What algorithmic and infrastructure techniques make this possible?
    Dijkstra on 300M edges is O(E log V) = ~3 billion operations. That is seconds, not milliseconds. The key insight: you do not need to explore all nodes. Road networks have a natural hierarchy — interstate highways connect distant cities faster than local streets. An algorithm that exploits this hierarchy can skip most nodes.
    Contraction Hierarchies (CH): Pre-process the graph offline (takes hours but only done once). Assign each node an importance level (more important = more shortcuts through it — major intersections, highway ramps). Add "shortcut" edges: if the fastest path from A to C goes through B and B has lower importance than both A and C, add edge A→C with weight(A→B)+weight(B→C). This collapses the unimportant nodes. At query time: only explore nodes of increasing importance from source, and decreasing importance toward destination. Mumbai to Pune: explores only ~10,000 high-importance nodes (highways, major intersections) instead of 100M. Query time: 50ms. Graph partitioning: Divide India into regions. Store each region's graph on a dedicated server. Routing request: identify source and destination regions → route within each region + find the best inter-region path. For long routes: only load the relevant region graphs. Result caching: Cache popular routes (Mumbai→Pune is requested millions of times/day) with a 5-minute TTL for traffic freshness. Cache key: origin_geohash + destination_geohash + time_of_day. Redis with 64GB RAM caches ~100M routes.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: How does Google Maps calculate ETA that accounts for current traffic, historical patterns, and predictive traffic?
    💡 Think First
    ETA = time to travel each road segment summed up. The weight of each edge is the travel time. But travel time changes by time of day, day of week, and current conditions. How do you model all three?
    ➔ Complete Answer
    Edge weights have three components: (1) Historical baseline: average speed on this road at this time of day + day of week, from years of GPS trace data. Tuesday 8am on NH48 near Mumbai = 20km/h (heavy traffic). Same road Sunday 2am = 80km/h. (2) Real-time adjustment: current GPS traces from active navigation users on that road → compute live speed → blend with historical: weight = 0.7 × historical + 0.3 × live. (3) Predictive: if your route will reach a segment in 45 minutes, use the predicted traffic for 45 minutes from now (based on historical patterns for that day/time). ML model trained on years of data. The routing algorithm uses these time-dependent edge weights: not just Dijkstra but time-dependent shortest path — the optimal route changes based on when you traverse each segment.
    Q: How would you design the "find all restaurants within 2km" feature? Compare Geohash vs QuadTree vs PostGIS vs Elasticsearch.
    💡 Think First
    This is a geospatial range query. You need to find all points within a radius of a given location. A simple lat/lon index does not work well for this — a 2D range query on two independent columns is O(n). What data structures handle 2D spatial queries efficiently?
    ➔ Complete Answer
    Geohash: Encode lat/lon as a string (longer = more precise). Nearby points share a prefix. Query: find all POIs where geohash starts with the prefix for the current cell + 8 neighbours. Works well for Redis: GEOADD key lon lat member, GEORADIUS key lon lat 2 km. O(log n). Best for: simple radius queries, already using Redis. QuadTree: Recursively divide space into quadrants. Each leaf node holds POIs in that area. Query: traverse tree to find all quadrants overlapping the 2km circle. Best for: uniform distribution, in-memory, low latency. R-Tree (PostGIS): Index spatial objects (points, polygons). Query: ST_DWithin(geom, ST_Point(lon, lat), 2000). Best for: complex spatial queries, already using PostgreSQL, need polygon/line queries not just points. Elasticsearch geo_point: Built-in geo queries. Best for: already using Elasticsearch for search, need to combine text search + geo filter ("Italian restaurant within 2km"). Production choice: Redis GEORADIUS for pure proximity queries (fastest, O(log n)), PostGIS for complex geo + relational queries, Elasticsearch if combining with full-text search.
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement Dijkstra's algorithm for a road network graph. Input: adjacency list Map<Integer, List<int[]{to, weight}>>, source node, destination node. Output: shortest travel time and the path. Then implement A* with straight-line distance as the heuristic — compare how many nodes each explores.
    💡 HintDijkstra: PriorityQueue ordered by distance from source. Poll minimum, relax neighbours, skip if already processed. Track previous[] array to reconstruct path. A*: PriorityQueue ordered by (g(n) + h(n)) where g=actual distance from source, h=heuristic (straight-line to destination). A* explores far fewer nodes for road networks because the heuristic guides it toward the destination.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Java — Dijkstra + A* for road network
    int[] dijkstra(Map<Integer, List<int[]>> graph, int src, int dst, int n) { int[] dist = new int[n]; Arrays.fill(dist, Integer.MAX_VALUE); int[] prev = new int[n]; Arrays.fill(prev, -1); dist[src] = 0; // PQ: {dist, node} PriorityQueue<int[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a,b) -> a[0]-b[0]); pq.offer(new int[]{0, src}); while(!pq.isEmpty()) { int[] cur = pq.poll(); int d=cur[0], u=cur[1]; if(d > dist[u]) continue; // stale entry if(u == dst) break; // found shortest path for(int[] edge : graph.getOrDefault(u, List.of())) { int v=edge[0], w=edge[1]; if(dist[u] + w < dist[v]) { dist[v] = dist[u] + w; prev[v] = u; pq.offer(new int[]{dist[v], v}); } } } return prev; // reconstruct path by following prev[] from dst to src } // A*: replace priority by (g + h) where h = heuristic distance to dst // pq.offer(new int[]{dist[v] + heuristic(v, dst), v}); // heuristic(u, dst) = Haversine distance(coords[u], coords[dst]) / max_speed // Result: A* explores ~10x fewer nodes than Dijkstra for road networks // Key: heuristic must be admissible (never overestimates) for A* to be correct

    Design a Distributed Key-Value Store (Redis-like)

    storage engine · consistent hashing · replication · CAP trade-offs
    🧠 What This Tests
    This question tests distributed systems fundamentals: how do you partition data across nodes, replicate for fault tolerance, and handle consistency vs availability trade-offs?You don't need to design the full Redis — focus on 3 key decisions: How do you distribute keys across nodes? How do you handle node failure? What consistency guarantee do you offer?
    📐 Architecture
    💻 Consistent Hashing — The Core Algorithm
    Java — consistent hashing ring
    class ConsistentHashRouter { private final TreeMap<Long, String> ring = new TreeMap<>(); private static final int VIRTUAL_NODES = 150; // per physical node for even distribution public void addNode(String nodeId) { for (int i = 0; i < VIRTUAL_NODES; i++) { long hash = hash(nodeId + "-VN" + i); ring.put(hash, nodeId); } } public String getNode(String key) { if (ring.isEmpty()) throw new RuntimeException("No nodes"); long hash = hash(key); // Find the first node at or after this hash on the ring Map.Entry<Long, String> entry = ring.ceilingEntry(hash); return (entry != null ? entry : ring.firstEntry()).getValue(); } public void removeNode(String nodeId) { ring.entrySet().removeIf(e -> e.getValue().equals(nodeId)); // Only keys previously owned by this node need remapping — not all keys // This is why consistent hashing is better than simple modulo hash for dynamic clusters } private long hash(String key) { return MurmurHash3.hash32(key.getBytes()) & 0xFFFFFFFFL; // 32-bit unsigned } } // WHY virtual nodes? Without them: 3 physical nodes → each owns exactly 1/3 of keyspace. // Adding 4th node: rebalances ~1/4 of ALL keys. With virtual nodes: // Adding a node adds 150 virtual positions → each taking a small slice from many nodes. // Result: near-uniform distribution and smooth rebalancing.
    🏭 Production Scenario
    You are building a Redis-like distributed key-value store. You have 6 nodes. You need to add a 7th node to handle growing traffic. How do you redistribute the data without downtime and without moving all the data?
    Naive approach: 7 nodes means new hash function modulo 7. Almost every key maps to a different node — you must move nearly all data. Consistent hashing solves this — adding a node only redistributes 1/n of the keys.
    Consistent hashing: Place nodes on a virtual ring (0 to 2^32). Each node maps to multiple positions on the ring (virtual nodes — e.g. 150 virtual nodes per physical node for better distribution). A key maps to the first node clockwise from hash(key). Adding Node 7: it takes positions on the ring. Only keys that now map to Node 7's range (previously served by its clockwise neighbour) need to move. ~1/7 of keys move, 6/7 stay put. Data migration: (1) Add Node 7 to the ring configuration (broadcast to all nodes via gossip protocol). (2) Node 7's clockwise neighbour begins streaming its keys that fall in Node 7's range. (3) During migration: write to BOTH nodes (old and new). Reads: try new node first, fall back to old. (4) After migration complete: stop dual writes. Replication: Each key is replicated to the next 2 nodes clockwise (replication factor 3). Write quorum: 2 of 3 must ACK. Read quorum: 2 of 3. This gives: survive 1 node failure with no data loss. Gossip protocol: Each node periodically exchanges state with 3 random peers. Node failures detected when a node fails to respond to heartbeats from multiple peers — consensus avoids false positives.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: "How do you handle read/write consistency when data is replicated?"
    💭 Think
    This is the CAP theorem in practice. You can tune consistency vs availability per-operation.
    → Quorum-based consistency
    With replication factor N=3: W=2 (write to 2 nodes before acknowledging) + R=2 (read from 2 nodes, take latest) = R+W > N → strong consistency guarantee.
    Tunable options: W=1, R=1 → highest availability, eventual consistency (Dynamo-style). W=3, R=1 → strong consistency on read, write needs all nodes. W=1, R=3 → write fast, read is authoritative.
    Production default: W=quorum, R=quorum (majority) — balances between availability and consistency for most use cases.
    Q: "What happens when a node fails? How does the system recover?"
    💭 Think
    Node failure = some keys are temporarily owned by a failed node. Who takes over?
    → Failure handling
    Detection: Heartbeat + gossip protocol. Nodes periodically ping neighbors. Coordinator marks node as failed after 3 missed heartbeats.
    Immediate: Requests for failed node's keys are routed to its replicas (degraded but available).
    Recovery: When node comes back, it runs anti-entropy (Merkle tree comparison) to sync missed writes from replicas. Hinted handoff: while node A is down, writes to A's keys are stored on adjacent node with a hint to forward to A when it recovers.
    🎯 Practice
    Design the internal data structure for a single KV store node that supports: get(key), set(key, value, ttl), delete(key), and automatic expiry of TTL-ed keys.
    HintHashMap for O(1) get/set/delete. A PriorityQueue (min-heap by expiry time) or TreeMap (sorted by expiry) for TTL eviction. A background thread checks the heap periodically and removes expired keys.
    → Solution
    Java
    class KVStore { private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, String> store = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long> expiry = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); public Optional<String> get(String key) { Long exp = expiry.get(key); if (exp != null && System.currentTimeMillis() > exp) { delete(key); return Optional.empty(); } return Optional.ofNullable(store.get(key)); } public void set(String key, String value, long ttlMs) { store.put(key, value); if (ttlMs > 0) expiry.put(key, System.currentTimeMillis() + ttlMs); } public void delete(String key) { store.remove(key); expiry.remove(key); } @Scheduled(fixedRate = 1000) // lazy eviction sweep every second public void evict() { long now = System.currentTimeMillis(); expiry.entrySet().stream() .filter(e -> e.getValue() < now) .map(Map.Entry::getKey) .forEach(this::delete); } }

    Design a User Authentication System

    registration · login · session management · password security · scale
    🧠 Requirements
    Authentication at scale = correctness + security + performance simultaneously.Users care about speed (login in <500ms). Security team cares about breach resistance (what happens if DB is leaked?). Platform team cares about scale (10M users, 100K concurrent logins).
    💻 The Complete Secure Implementation
    Java — password security + login flow
    // NEVER store plain text passwords or MD5/SHA1 hashes (rainbow-table vulnerable) // USE: bcrypt, Argon2, or PBKDF2 — deliberately slow, salted hash functions @Service class AuthService { private final PasswordEncoder encoder = new BCryptPasswordEncoder(12); // 12=work factor // REGISTRATION @Transactional public User register(RegisterRequest req) { if (userRepo.existsByEmail(req.email())) throw new EmailAlreadyExistsException(req.email()); User user = new User(); user.setEmail(req.email().toLowerCase().trim()); user.setPasswordHash(encoder.encode(req.password())); // bcrypt: unique salt per user user.setEmailVerified(false); user.setCreatedAt(Instant.now()); userRepo.save(user); sendVerificationEmail(user); // async — don't block registration return user; } // LOGIN — timing-safe comparison public TokenPair login(LoginRequest req) { User user = userRepo.findByEmail(req.email()) .orElseThrow(() -> new AuthException("Invalid credentials")); // don't say "email not found"! if (!encoder.matches(req.password(), user.getPasswordHash())) throw new AuthException("Invalid credentials"); // same message — no info leak if (!user.isEmailVerified()) throw new AuthException("Please verify your email first"); String accessToken = jwtService.generateAccess(user); // 15 min String refreshToken = tokenService.createRefresh(user); // 7 days, stored in DB auditLog.logLogin(user.getId(), req.ipAddress()); return new TokenPair(accessToken, refreshToken); } } // BRUTE-FORCE PROTECTION: // Redis counter: "login:fail:{email}" → INCR, EXPIRE 15min // After 5 failures: lock account for 15min OR require CAPTCHA // Rate limiting at gateway: max 10 login attempts/min per IP
    💡 Security Checklist
    Password storage: bcrypt with work factor 12

    bcrypt is intentionally slow (~250ms at factor 12). This means even if your DB is leaked, cracking one password takes 250ms per guess — brute force is impractical. Factor 12 is a good production default; raise to 13 or 14 as hardware improves.

    Timing attacks: always encode even for non-existent users

    If you return "user not found" instantly and "wrong password" after 250ms bcrypt check, an attacker can enumerate valid emails by timing the response. Fix: always run encoder.matches() even if user not found (against a dummy hash), ensuring uniform response time.

    HTTPS everywhere + secure cookie flags

    Refresh tokens in httpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict cookies — not in localStorage (XSS vulnerable). Access tokens in memory (JS variable) or Authorization header — short-lived enough that XSS exposure is limited.

    🏭 Production Scenario
    Design the password reset flow. A user clicks "Forgot Password", enters their email, gets a reset link, and sets a new password. What are the security requirements for the token?
    Reset tokens are a security boundary. A weak token = account takeover. Think about: token entropy, single-use, expiry, storage (hashed), and the email oracle problem.
    Token requirements: (1) Cryptographically random: SecureRandom.nextBytes(32) → Base64 URL-safe encoded. Not predictable, not guessable. (2) Single-use: mark as used in DB on first redemption. (3) Short-lived: 15-minute TTL stored in DB. (4) Hashed in DB: store SHA-256(token) — if DB is breached, tokens are not directly usable. The user gets the raw token in the email; you verify by hashing and comparing. (5) Email oracle prevention: always respond "If that email exists, we sent a reset link" — never confirm or deny email existence. (6) Rate-limit: max 3 reset requests per email per hour.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: How do you securely store passwords? What makes bcrypt better than SHA-256?
    💭 Think First
    Never store plaintext passwords. Never use MD5 or SHA-256 alone. Know why bcrypt is the right choice and what its parameters mean.
    → Complete Answer
    SHA-256 alone is fast — an attacker with a GPU can compute billions of hashes per second and brute-force common passwords. bcrypt is intentionally slow: the cost factor (rounds) controls the work factor. cost=12 means 2^12 iterations — ~300ms on a modern CPU. Attacker can only try ~3 passwords/second per GPU. bcrypt also embeds a random salt automatically — prevents rainbow table attacks. Spring Security: BCryptPasswordEncoder(strength=12). On login: passwordEncoder.matches(rawPassword, storedHash) — bcrypt handles the salt extraction internally. For new systems: consider Argon2 (winner of the Password Hashing Competition, memory-hard — even harder to GPU-crack).
    Q: How do you protect the login endpoint from brute-force attacks?
    💭 Think First
    An attacker can try millions of password combinations. What layers of protection do you add?
    → Complete Answer
    Layered defence: (1) Rate limit by IP: max 10 login attempts per minute per IP (Redis sliding window counter). Return 429 with Retry-After header. (2) Account lockout: max 5 failed attempts per account → lock for 15 minutes. Notify user by email. Prevents targeted account attacks even from distributed IPs. (3) CAPTCHA after 3 failures: show CAPTCHA to distinguish human vs bot. (4) Password pepper: a server-side secret added to the password before bcrypt — if DB is stolen without the pepper (stored separately in a secrets manager), hashes cannot be cracked. (5) Monitor and alert: Grafana alert on login failure rate spike → potential credential stuffing attack.
    🎯 Practice
    Design the "Forgot Password" flow. A user clicks "reset password" → what happens? Consider: security (valid for limited time), usability (clear UX), and abuse prevention (can't spam reset emails).
    HintGenerate a cryptographically random token (UUID or SecureRandom). Store hash of token in DB with userId and expiresAt. Email the raw token. On reset: hash the submitted token, find in DB, validate not expired, update password, invalidate token. Rate limit emails per email address per hour.
    → Solution
    Java — secure password reset
    public void initiateReset(String email) { userRepo.findByEmail(email).ifPresent(user -> { // don't reveal if email exists if (rateLimiter.isLimited("reset:" + email, 3, Duration.ofHours(1))) return; // silently rate-limit — don't tell attacker they're being limited String rawToken = UUID.randomUUID().toString().replace("-", ""); String tokenHash = sha256(rawToken); // store hash, send raw (like password hashing) resetTokenRepo.save(new PasswordReset(tokenHash, user.getId(), now().plus(1, HOURS))); emailService.sendReset(user.getEmail(), rawToken); // link: /reset?token=rawToken }); // Always return 200 regardless — don't reveal if email exists } public void confirmReset(String rawToken, String newPassword) { PasswordReset reset = resetTokenRepo.findByTokenHash(sha256(rawToken)) .filter(r -> r.getExpiresAt().isAfter(now()) && !r.isUsed()) .orElseThrow(() -> new InvalidTokenException()); reset.setUsed(true); resetTokenRepo.save(reset); User user = userRepo.findById(reset.getUserId()).orElseThrow(); user.setPasswordHash(encoder.encode(newPassword)); userRepo.save(user); // Invalidate all existing sessions/refresh tokens for security sessionService.invalidateAll(user.getId()); }
    🎯 Practice Task
    Implement the password reset token generation, storage, and verification in Spring Boot. Tokens must be single-use, expire after 15 minutes, and be stored as a hash.
    Hint — think before readingGenerate 32 random bytes, Base64URL-encode for the email link. Hash with SHA-256 for DB storage. On verification: hash the submitted token, look up in DB, check expiry, check not used, mark used.
    → Worked Solution
    Java — secure password reset
    @Service class PasswordResetService { @Autowired PasswordResetRepo repo; @Autowired EmailService email; public void initiateReset(String userEmail) { byte[] raw = new byte[32]; new SecureRandom().nextBytes(raw); String token = Base64.getUrlEncoder().encodeToString(raw); // sent in email String hashed = sha256Hex(token); // stored in DB Instant expiry = Instant.now().plusSeconds(900); // 15 min TTL repo.save(new ResetToken(userEmail, hashed, expiry)); email.send(userEmail, "https://app.com/reset?t=" + token); } @Transactional public void resetPassword(String token, String newPwd) { String hashed = sha256Hex(token); ResetToken rt = repo.findByHash(hashed) .filter(t -> !t.isUsed() && t.getExpiry().isAfter(Instant.now())) .orElseThrow(() -> new InvalidTokenException()); rt.setUsed(true); repo.save(rt); // single-use userRepo.updatePassword(rt.getEmail(), bcrypt(newPwd)); } }

    Payment System Design — 1M+ Transactions Daily

    idempotency · atomic transfer · Saga vs 2PC · Outbox pattern · distributed locking · NEFT/UPI internals
    🧠 Mental Model
    Payment systems exist to solve one hard problem: money must never disappear or double. Every other requirement — idempotency, Saga, distributed locking, Outbox — exists to serve this. NEFT processes in batches every 30 minutes. UPI is near-real-time (10 seconds). Both demand exactly-once processing.
    Core Pillars for 1M+ Transactions/Day
  • Idempotency — every request has a unique transaction ID. Server stores the result. Retries return the SAME result, never process twice.INSERT INTO transactions (id,...) ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING RETURNING *
  • Atomic debit + credit — both accounts change or neither does. Single DB transaction for same-DB scenario. Saga pattern for cross-service scenario.
  • Distributed locking — prevent concurrent updates to the same account. Redis SETNX or SELECT FOR UPDATE prevent double-spend.
  • Audit log — every state transition recorded immutably. Append-only journal table. Never UPDATE or DELETE payment records.
  • Reconciliation — nightly job compares your DB with the bank's settlement file. Flags discrepancies for manual review.
    • PatternHow it worksWhen to useTrade-off
    2PC (Two-Phase Commit)Coordinator asks all participants to prepare, then commit/rollbackAll services use same XA-compatible DBBlocking, slow, single point of failure
    Saga — ChoreographyServices emit events, each listens and compensates on failureHighly decoupled microservicesComplex, hard to trace, compensation logic scattered
    Saga — OrchestrationCentral orchestrator explicitly calls each service, handles rollbackPayment flows where you need one place to see stateOrchestrator is a bottleneck, must be fault-tolerant
    Outbox PatternWrite event to same DB transaction as the business recordGuarantee exactly-once event publishing after DB writeRequires CDC (Debezium) or polling, slight delay
    🏭 Production Scenario
    Design a payment processing system handling 1M transactions/day. Alice transfers Rs 10,000 to Bob. The system must be atomic (both update or neither), idempotent (retries don't double-charge), and auditable. Walk through the complete flow.
    Atomicity requires that debit and credit are a single unit. Idempotency requires that retrying the same payment produces the same result. Auditability means never modifying or deleting payment records.
    Flow: (1) Client sends transfer request with a client-generated idempotency key. (2) PaymentService checks idempotency table — if key exists, return stored result. (3) Create PaymentTransaction (PENDING) + insert into outbox table in one DB transaction. (4) Debit Alice using optimistic lock (@Version). (5) Outbox CDC publishes PaymentDebited event to Kafka. (6) CreditService consumes event, credits Bob. (7) Publishes PaymentCompleted. (8) PaymentTransaction updated to COMPLETED. Why Outbox? Without it: debit succeeds, then app crashes before publishing to Kafka. Debit happened but credit never runs. Money lost. With Outbox: the event is in the DB table — CDC will always pick it up and publish, even after a crash. 1M/day = ~12 transactions/second average. Peak is 10x = 120/sec.
