    GitHub Actions — CI/CD pipeline
    # .github/workflows/deploy.yml name: CI/CD on: push: branches: [main] jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-java@v4 with: { java-version: '17', distribution: 'temurin' } - run: ./gradlew test build-push: needs: test runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Login to ECR uses: aws-actions/amazon-ecr-login@v2 - run: | docker build -t $ECR_REGISTRY/myapp:$GITHUB_SHA . docker push $ECR_REGISTRY/myapp:$GITHUB_SHA deploy: needs: build-push runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Deploy to K8s run: | kubectl set image deployment/myapp \ myapp=$ECR_REGISTRY/myapp:$GITHUB_SHA kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp

    Circuit Breaker + Production Resilience

    Resilience4j · CLOSED/OPEN/HALF-OPEN states · Bulkhead · fallback · cascade failure prevention
    🧠 Mental Model
    Circuit Breaker = an automatic switch that opens when a downstream service is failing, preventing your threads from drowning in timeouts. Without it: InventoryService takes 8s to timeout. 100 threads pile up waiting. OrderService runs out of threads. New requests queue. Your service goes down — cascade failure. With circuit breaker: after 5 failures, circuit opens. Next 1000 requests return a fallback in 1ms. Threads stay free. Your service stays up.
  • CLOSED — normal operation. All requests pass through. Failure count tracked in a sliding window.If failure rate exceeds threshold (e.g. 50%) -> transition to OPEN
  • OPEN — all requests fail immediately with fallback. No call to the downstream service. Fast-fail preserves your threads.Duration: waitDurationInOpenState (default 60s), then -> HALF-OPEN
  • HALF-OPEN — let a limited number of probe requests through. If they succeed -> CLOSED (service recovered). If they fail -> OPEN again.permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState: 5
    • PatternWhat it preventsResilience4j annotation
    Circuit BreakerCascade failure from slow/failing downstream@CircuitBreaker(name, fallbackMethod)
    BulkheadOne service consuming all threads@Bulkhead(name, type=THREADPOOL)
    Rate LimiterOverloading a downstream service@RateLimiter(name)
    RetryTransient failures (network blip)@Retry(name)
    Time LimiterRequests hanging indefinitely@TimeLimiter(name)
    🏭 Production Scenario
    OrderService calls InventoryService synchronously. InventoryService becomes slow (p99=8s due to a DB issue). 100 threads in OrderService are blocked. New order requests fail with timeouts. How do you stop the cascade failure without deploying InventoryService?
    Timeouts alone are not enough — they let the thread fail after 8s but still block it. You need to stop calling InventoryService entirely once it is clearly failing, and return a safe fallback instantly.
    Immediate fix — Circuit Breaker + Fallback: Add Resilience4j @CircuitBreaker around the InventoryService call with a 2s TimeLimiter. After 5 failures in 10 calls (50% rate), circuit opens. Subsequent calls return a cached/fallback inventory value immediately — threads freed, OrderService recovers. Fallback strategy options: (1) Return last-known cached inventory (Redis GET last_inventory:{productId}). (2) Assume in-stock optimistically, verify asynchronously after order placed. (3) Return clear degraded response — let the user know inventory status is temporarily unavailable. Config: failure-rate-threshold=50, sliding-window-size=10, wait-duration-in-open-state=30s, permitted-calls-in-half-open-state=3.
    Interview Follow-up Chain
    Q: What is the Bulkhead pattern and how does it complement Circuit Breaker?
    💡 Think First
    Circuit Breaker stops calling a failing service. But what if the service is just slow and your ALL your threads get consumed waiting? How do you prevent one slow service from starving all others?
    ➔ Complete Answer
    Bulkhead isolates thread pools per downstream service. Without it: InventoryService slowness consumes all 200 threads in OrderService — even calls to PaymentService (which is healthy) start queuing. With Bulkhead: InventoryService gets its own thread pool (20 threads). If all 20 are blocked, InventoryService calls are rejected immediately with a BulkheadFullException — PaymentService calls use their own pool and are completely unaffected. Resilience4j: @Bulkhead(name="inventory", type=THREADPOOL) with maxConcurrentCalls=20 and maxWaitDuration=100ms. The metaphor: watertight compartments in a ship — one flooding compartment does not sink the ship.
    Q: How do you design the fallback for a circuit-broken service? What are the options and trade-offs?
    💡 Think First
    The fallback must run when the real service is unavailable. What data do you have available? What is the worst acceptable outcome for the user?
    ➔ Complete Answer
    Fallback options by quality: (1) Cached value (best): Redis GET last_known:{key} — stale but informed. Update the cache in the background when circuit closes. (2) Optimistic default: assume the happy path (assume in-stock, verify async). Risk: over-promising. Compensate with an async check and email if assumption was wrong. (3) Graceful degradation: return the page/response without the unavailable data. Show "inventory status temporarily unavailable" instead of blocking the entire page load. (4) Static default: return a hardcoded safe value. Worst quality but always available. Key principle: the fallback must be faster and more reliable than the real service — if the fallback also fails, you have not solved anything.
    🎯 Practice Task
    Configure Resilience4j Circuit Breaker in a Spring Boot app around an InventoryClient. Show: (1) the application.yml config with 50% failure threshold and 30s open duration, (2) the @CircuitBreaker annotation with a fallback method that returns cached inventory, (3) how to expose circuit breaker state via Spring Boot Actuator, (4) a unit test that verifies the circuit opens after failures.
    💡 HintAdd resilience4j-spring-boot3 and spring-boot-starter-aop dependencies. The fallback method must have the same return type as the main method plus an Exception parameter. Actuator: management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=circuitbreakers. Test: use CircuitBreakerRegistry to assert state transitions.
    ➡ Worked Solution
    Spring Boot — Resilience4j Circuit Breaker complete setup
    # application.yml resilience4j.circuitbreaker.instances.inventory: failure-rate-threshold: 50 sliding-window-size: 10 wait-duration-in-open-state: 30s permitted-calls-in-half-open-state: 3 automatic-transition-from-open-to-half-open-enabled: true management.health.circuitbreakers.enabled: true management.endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,circuitbreakers // InventoryClient with Circuit Breaker + Bulkhead @Service class InventoryClient { @Autowired RestTemplate rest; @Autowired InventoryCache cache; @CircuitBreaker(name = "inventory", fallbackMethod = "getFallback") @Bulkhead(name = "inventory", type = Bulkhead.Type.SEMAPHORE) @TimeLimiter(name = "inventory") public CompletableFuture<Inventory> getInventory(String productId) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> rest.getForObject("/inventory/" + productId, Inventory.class)); } // Fallback: same signature + Exception param public CompletableFuture<Inventory> getFallback(String id, Exception e) { log.warn("Circuit open for inventory {}: {}", id, e.getClass().getSimpleName()); return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(cache.getLastKnown(id)); } } // Unit test: verify circuit opens after failures @Test void circuitOpensAfterFailures() { CircuitBreaker cb = circuitBreakerRegistry.circuitBreaker("inventory"); assertEquals(CircuitBreaker.State.CLOSED, cb.getState()); // Simulate 5 failures (50% of 10-call window) for(int i=0; i<10; i++) { try { cb.executeSupplier(() -> { throw new RuntimeException("fail"); }); } catch(Exception ignored) {} } assertEquals(CircuitBreaker.State.OPEN, cb.getState()); // circuit opened // Verify fallback is returned immediately (no real call) }
